It descends to an orbifold metric on the moduli space ℳ_g = 𝒯_g / Mod_g. The WP metric is incomplete, has negative sectional curvature, and its geodesic flow is Anosov. A natural Morse function on ℳ_g is the length of the shortest closed geodesic (the systole) sys : ℳ_g → ℝ>0. This function is proper and Morse‑Bott; its critical points correspond to Riemann surfaces where the systolic geodesic is not unique or has multiplicities.

The Morse index of a critical surface equals the number of independent directions in which the systole can be decreased while staying in ℳ_g. Wolpert (1985) showed that the Hessian of sys at a critical point is related to the second variation of length of the systolic geodesic and to the WP curvature. The sublevel sets {sys ≤ L} are compact and their topology stabilizes as L grows. Mirzakhani (2007) computed the WP volumes of ℳ_g,n by integrating the symplectic form over the moduli space and used the McShane identity to derive recursive formulas. These volumes are polynomials in π² whose coefficients count intersection numbers of ψ‑classes on the Deligne–Mumford compactification.

Applying Morse theory to the function sys yields a cell decomposition of ℳ_g whose cells are indexed by the combinatorial types of systolic graphs. The resulting Morse complex computes the rational homology of ℳ_g. In particular, the Euler characteristic χ(ℳ_g) = (−1)g−1 (2g−2)! ζ(2g−1) / (2π²)2g−2 can be recovered from the alternating sum of critical points weighted by their indices. The Morse‑Bott spectral sequence degenerates at the E₁ page because the critical manifolds are products of lower‑dimensional moduli spaces, reflecting the boundary stratification of ℳ_g.

Morse Theory for the Chern–Simons Functional on 3‑Manifolds and the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev Invariant

For a compact simple Lie group G and an integer level k > 0, the Chern–Simons path integral

Z_k(Y) = ∫𝒜/𝒢 exp(2πi k CS(A)) 𝒟A

defines the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev (WRT) invariant of a closed 3‑manifold Y. In the semiclassical limit k → ∞, the stationary phase approximation localizes the integral to the critical points of CS, i.e. flat G‑connections. Each flat connection A contributes a factor exp(2πi k CS(A)) times the square root of the Reidemeister torsion τ(Y, A) and a Maslov index correction. The sum over all flat connections reproduces the asymptotic expansion of Z_k(Y).

Morse theory provides a rigorous finite‑dimensional approximation: one perturbs the Chern–Simons functional by a Morse function f on the finite‑dimensional space of flat connections modulo gauge (the character variety). The critical points of CS + ε f are non‑degenerate and correspond to the original flat connections. The Morse complex of this perturbed functional, with coefficients in the representation ring of the quantum group U_q(g) at q = exp(2πi/(k+h∨)), computes the WRT invariant. The differential counts gradient flow lines weighted by the quantum 6j‑symbols, which encode the representation theory of U_q(g).

Andersen and Hansen (2006) proved that the resulting topological quantum field theory is isomorphic to the Reshetikhin–Turaev TQFT constructed from modular tensor categories. The Morse‑theoretic viewpoint clarifies the role of the framing anomaly: a change of framing shifts the level k by the dual Coxeter number h∨, which corresponds to adding a multiple of the Chern–Simons invariant of the trivial connection. The Verlinde formula for the dimension of the space of conformal blocks on a surface Σ_g emerges as the Euler characteristic of the Morse complex on the moduli space of flat connections on Σ_g.

  • Confusing the Yamabe functional with the Einstein–Hilbert functional; the former varies only within a conformal class, the latter varies the full metric.
  • Assuming the Casson invariant is defined for all 3‑manifolds; it is originally defined only for homology spheres, and extensions to rational homology spheres require careful treatment of reducible connections.
  • Treating the Donaldson invariants as Morse homology of the Yang–Mills functional without accounting for the bubbling compactification and the μ‑map.
  • Believing the Weil–Petersson metric is complete; it is incomplete, and its completion is the Deligne–Mumford compactification, which affects properness of Morse functions.
  • Neglecting the framing dependence of the WRT invariant; a change of framing multiplies Z_k(Y) by a root of unity exp(2πi c/24) where c is the central charge.
  • Using the spectral flow index for the Chern–Simons functional without specifying a trivialisation of the determinant line bundle; the index is only well‑defined modulo 8 for SU(2).
  • Overlooking the Morse‑Bott nature of the systole function on ℳ_g; critical manifolds are not isolated, and one must use a Morse‑Bott complex or a small perturbation.

Morse Theory and the Topology of Configuration Spaces

Configuration spaces, denoted Ck(M), are fundamental objects in topology, robotics, and statistical mechanics. They represent the space of k distinct, unordered points in a manifold M. More formally, Ck(M) = (Mk - Δ) / Sk, where Mk is the k-fold Cartesian product of M, Δ is the "fat diagonal" (points where at least two coordinates coincide), and Sk is the symmetric group acting by permuting coordinates. Morse theory provides powerful tools to understand the homology and homotopy type of these intricate spaces.

To apply Morse theory, one constructs a suitable Morse function on Ck(M). A common choice involves distance functions or potential energy functions. For instance, consider a function f: Ck(M) → ℝ that measures the sum of squared distances between pairs of points, or the sum of distances from a fixed reference point in M. The critical points of such functions correspond to specific geometric arrangements of the k points. For example, if M is a sphere and k=2, a distance function might have critical points when the two points are antipodal, or when they coincide (which is excluded by definition, but indicates a boundary phenomenon). More generally, critical points often correspond to configurations where the points are "as far apart" or "as close together" as possible under certain constraints, or exhibit specific symmetries.

The Morse index of a critical point in Ck(M) provides information about the local topology around that configuration. For example, in the study of robot motion planning, Ck(M) represents the space of possible positions for k robots on a workspace M. A Morse function can be defined as the "cost" of a configuration, and its critical points correspond to bottlenecks or stable/unstable equilibria in the robot's movement. The Morse inequalities then relate the number of critical points of different indices to the Betti numbers of Ck(M), offering insights into the complexity of motion planning algorithms.

Another significant application is in the study of knot and link invariants. While not directly on Ck(M), related configuration spaces of arcs or loops can be equipped with energy functionals whose critical points correspond to specific geometric types of knots. For instance, the total curvature functional on the space of closed curves in ℝ³ can be studied via Morse theory, where critical points are often related to geodesics or minimal surfaces in higher-dimensional settings. The homology of configuration spaces is known to be related to various algebraic structures, including Lie algebras and operads, and Morse theory offers a geometric pathway to compute these homologies, especially for M = ℝ² or M = ℝ³ where the homology is often trivial for k points but becomes non-trivial for ordered configurations or specific boundary conditions.

The study of configuration spaces of points on surfaces (M = Σg) is particularly rich, with connections to mapping class groups and moduli spaces. For example, the space of k distinct points on a Riemann surface is closely related to the moduli space of curves with k marked points. Morse theory on these spaces, often using height functions or energy functionals derived from hyperbolic geometry, can reveal their intricate topological structure, including their Betti numbers and Euler characteristics. The critical points often correspond to configurations where points are aligned along geodesics or exhibit maximal symmetry, providing a combinatorial handle on their complex topology.

The Morse-Smale-Witten Complex and its Homological Significance

While the basic Morse complex uses the number of critical points to bound Betti numbers, the Morse-Smale-Witten complex (MSW complex) provides a direct method to compute the homology of a manifold M. This construction elevates Morse theory from an inequality to an exact computational tool. It requires a Morse function f: M → ℝ and a Riemannian metric on M, which together define a gradient vector field ∇f. The crucial additional ingredient is the concept of a Morse-Smale system.

A pair (f, g), where f is a Morse function and g is a Riemannian metric, forms a Morse-Smale system if the stable and unstable manifolds of all critical points intersect transversally. The stable manifold Ws(p) of a critical point p consists of all points x ∈ M such that the gradient flow φt(x) converges to p as t → ∞. Similarly, the unstable manifold Wu(p) consists of points x such that φt(x) converges to p as t → -∞. Transversality ensures that these intersections are "clean" and well-behaved, preventing pathologies that could complicate the counting of flow lines.

The MSW complex C*(f) is a chain complex where the chain groups Ck(f) are free abelian groups (or vector spaces over a field) generated by the critical points of index k. The differential ∂: Ck(f) → Ck-1(f) is defined by counting the gradient flow lines connecting critical points. Specifically, for critical points p of index k and q of index k-1, the coefficient of q in ∂p is the signed count of flow lines from p to q. A flow line from p to q is a trajectory of the gradient flow that starts at p (as t → -∞) and ends at q (as t → ∞). The "signed count" involves assigning a sign to each flow line based on the orientation of the unstable manifold of p and the stable manifold of q, ensuring that ∂² = 0, which is a fundamental property of any chain complex.

The remarkable theorem by Witten (1982), building on earlier work by Smale, asserts that the homology of the Morse-Smale-Witten complex H*(C*(f)) is isomorphic to the singular homology H*(M) of the manifold M. This provides a combinatorial and geometric method to compute topological invariants. Witten's contribution involved deforming the de Rham complex using the Morse function, leading to a complex whose cohomology is isomorphic to the de Rham cohomology (and thus singular cohomology by de Rham's theorem). This "Witten deformation" makes the connection between the geometric flow lines and algebraic cohomology explicit and rigorous, particularly by relating the differential to a perturbed de Rham operator.

The MSW complex is a powerful tool because it provides a concrete algorithm for computing homology. While the existence of a Morse-Smale system is generic (i.e., such systems exist for almost all choices of Morse functions and metrics), constructing one explicitly and counting flow lines can be computationally intensive. However, its theoretical significance is immense, offering a deep connection between the local geometry of a function (its critical points and gradient flow) and the global topology of the manifold. It underpins many modern developments in Floer homology and other infinite-dimensional Morse theories, where similar complexes are constructed to compute various homologies of infinite-dimensional spaces.

Understanding the Morse Index in a Simple Case
Consider the function f: ℝ² → ℝ given by f(x, y) = x³ - 3x + y². Identify its critical points and determine their Morse indices. Relate these to the local topology around each point.
First, find the critical points by setting the gradient to zero: ∂f/∂x = 3x² - 3 = 0 ⇒ x² = 1 ⇒ x = ±1 ∂f/∂y = 2y = 0 ⇒ y = 0 So, the critical points are P₁ = (1, 0) and P₂ = (-1, 0). Next, compute the Hessian matrix H(f) at each critical point: H(f) = [[∂²f/∂x², ∂²f/∂x∂y], [∂²f/∂y∂x, ∂²f/∂y²]] = [[6x, 0], [0, 2]] At P₁ = (1, 0): H(f)(1, 0) = [[6, 0], [0, 2]] The eigenvalues are 6 and 2. Both are positive. The Morse index is the number of negative eigenvalues, which is 0. This corresponds to a local minimum. The local topology is like a disk (a 0-handle). At P₂ = (-1, 0): H(f)(-1, 0) = [[-6, 0], [0, 2]] The eigenvalues are -6 and 2. One is negative, one is positive. The Morse index is 1. This corresponds to a saddle point. The local topology is like a product of an interval and a line (a 1-handle). In summary: - P₁ = (1, 0) is a local minimum (index 0). - P₂ = (-1, 0) is a saddle point (index 1). These indices reflect the local shape of the graph of f around these points.
Visualizing Gradient Flows for Morse Theory
When tackling problems involving Morse functions, especially those asking about critical points and indices, try to visualize the gradient flow. Imagine the manifold as a landscape and the function value as altitude. Gradient flow lines are paths of steepest descent. Critical points are peaks, valleys, or saddles. A local minimum (index 0) acts as a sink for all nearby flow lines. A saddle point (index 1 for a 2-manifold) has one direction of descent and one of ascent. A local maximum (index 2 for a 2-manifold) acts as a source. This intuition helps in understanding the attachment of handles and the overall topological changes as sublevel sets grow.

Morse Theory and Symplectic Homology: The Viterbo Conjecture

Symplectic homology (SH) is a powerful invariant in symplectic geometry, extending the ideas of Floer homology to a broader class of symplectic manifolds. While Hamiltonian Floer homology (HF) is defined for closed symplectic manifolds and counts intersection points of Lagrangian submanifolds, symplectic homology is typically defined for exact symplectic manifolds (M, ω) with contact type boundary ∂M. An exact symplectic manifold means its symplectic form ω is exact, i.e., ω = dλ for some 1-form λ, often called the Liouville form. A contact type boundary means that the Liouville vector field Xλ (defined by ιXλω = λ) points strictly outwards along ∂M.

The construction of symplectic homology relies on an infinite-dimensional Morse theory for the action functional on the loop space of M. Specifically, for a generic choice of a Hamiltonian H: M × S¹ → ℝ, one considers the action functional AH(γ) = ∫S¹ γ*λ - ∫S¹ H(γ(t), t) dt, defined on the space of contractible loops Ω(M) in M. The critical points of this functional are the periodic orbits of the Hamiltonian vector field XH associated with H. However, unlike Hamiltonian Floer homology which counts periodic orbits of a specific period, symplectic homology considers all periodic orbits and their iterates, often requiring a sequence of Hamiltonians that grow quadratically at infinity.

The Viterbo Conjecture, now a theorem due to various mathematicians including Viterbo, Salamon, and others, establishes a profound connection between symplectic homology and the loop space homology of the underlying manifold. It states that for an exact symplectic manifold (M, ω) with a contact type boundary, its symplectic homology SH*(M) is isomorphic to the loop space homology H*(Ω(M)) of M. This is a remarkable result because SH*(M) is constructed using symplectic geometry and dynamics (periodic orbits), while H*(Ω(M)) is a purely topological invariant. The isomorphism implies that the symplectic structure imposes strong constraints on the topology of the manifold's loop space.

The Viterbo Conjecture has significant implications for symplectic rigidity and the study of symplectic capacities. Symplectic capacities are numerical invariants of symplectic manifolds that measure their "size" in a symplectically invariant way. The existence of non-trivial symplectic homology groups implies the existence of certain periodic orbits, which in turn can be used to define or bound symplectic capacities. For example, the Ekeland-Hofer capacities are closely related to the critical values of the action functional used in symplectic homology. The technical challenges in defining symplectic homology and proving the Viterbo Conjecture include ensuring transversality for the infinite-dimensional functional, dealing with compactness issues for the moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves (which are used to define the differential in the Floer complex), and handling the contact type boundary conditions.

Symplectic homology has also found applications in the study of Lagrangian submanifolds and their intersections, providing a tool to detect the existence of such submanifolds and to understand their properties. It forms a cornerstone of modern symplectic topology, bridging the gap between dynamical systems, differential geometry, and algebraic topology, and offering a powerful framework for understanding the intricate structure of symplectic manifolds.

Morse Theory and the Geometry of Minimal Surfaces: Higher Index Theory

The study of minimal surfaces, surfaces that locally minimize area, is a classical subject in differential geometry. Morse theory provides a natural framework for understanding their existence, stability, and topological properties. The relevant functional is the area functional A(Σ) = ∫Σ dvol, defined on the space of surfaces (or submanifolds) embedded in a Riemannian manifold N. Critical points of this functional are precisely the minimal surfaces.

For a given minimal surface Σ embedded in N, its stability is determined by the second variation of the area functional. This leads to the Jacobi operator (or stability operator), a self-adjoint elliptic differential operator acting on normal vector fields along Σ. The Morse index of a minimal surface Σ, denoted Index(Σ), is defined as the number of negative eigenvalues of the Jacobi operator. A minimal surface is called stable if its index is 0, meaning it is a local minimum of the area functional. If the index is positive, the surface is unstable; there are directions in the space of surfaces along which the area can be decreased.

The Morse index provides crucial geometric and topological information. For example, for minimal surfaces in ℝ³, the index is related to the genus and the number of boundary components. A classical result by Fischer-Colbrie and Schoen (1980) states that a complete stable minimal surface in ℝ³ must be a plane. This highlights how the index constrains the global geometry. For embedded minimal surfaces, the index can also be related to the number of "ends" or the topology of the ambient manifold. For instance, in a compact manifold, the existence of a stable minimal surface often implies strong topological constraints on the manifold itself.

Higher index theory for minimal surfaces explores the properties of minimal surfaces with Index(Σ) > 0. These surfaces are not local minima but rather saddle points of the area functional. Their existence is often established using min-max methods, which are a form of infinite-dimensional Morse theory. In min-max theory, one constructs families of surfaces and finds a "bottleneck" surface that minimizes area within that family. This bottleneck surface is often a minimal surface, and its Morse index is related to the dimension of the family used in the min-max construction. For example, the existence of minimal spheres of arbitrary index in S³ has been shown, demonstrating the richness of the critical point structure of the area functional.

The study of the Morse index of minimal surfaces also connects to the topology of the space of minimal surfaces itself. By considering the area functional on a suitable space of surfaces, one can use Morse theory to understand the connected components and homology of this space. The critical points (minimal surfaces) act as building blocks, and the flow lines of the gradient of the area functional (mean curvature flow) describe how surfaces deform towards minimal configurations. Understanding the index of these critical points is essential for a comprehensive topological picture of the space of minimal submanifolds within a given ambient manifold.

Morse Theory in Geometric Group Theory: Growth Functions and Cayley Graphs

Geometric group theory studies infinite groups by examining their geometric properties, often by associating a metric space (like a Cayley graph) to the group. Morse theory, traditionally applied to smooth manifolds, finds surprising and powerful analogues and applications in this discrete, large-scale geometric context. While not directly applying smooth Morse functions, the underlying philosophy of understanding global structure through local critical behavior is highly relevant.

A key concept is the growth function of a finitely generated group G with respect to a generating set S. This function, denoted γS(n), counts the number of group elements whose word length (distance from the identity in the Cayley graph) is at most n. The asymptotic behavior of γS(n) (e.g., polynomial, exponential) is a fundamental invariant of the group. Morse theory provides a framework to understand the "shape" of the Cayley graph and thus its growth. For instance, a group is said to be hyperbolic if its Cayley graph satisfies a certain "thin triangle" condition, implying a strong sense of negative curvature. In such groups, the geometry is dominated by "geodesics" that behave much like gradient flow lines in classical Morse theory.

The concept of a "Morse function" in geometric group theory often takes the form of a Busemann function or a height function on the Cayley graph or a related geometric model of the group. For example, a Busemann function measures the "distance from infinity" in a hyperbolic group. Its "critical points" or regions correspond to specific geometric features, such as "bottlenecks" or "flares" in the group's structure. The "index" in this context might relate to the number of directions in which the function can decrease, analogous to the unstable manifold dimension.

Another application involves the study of Morse quasi-geodesics. A quasi-geodesic in a metric space is a path that is "almost" a geodesic. A quasi-geodesic is Morse if any quasi-geodesic that stays "close" to it must also be a quasi-geodesic that stays "close" to the original one. This property is analogous to the stability of gradient flow lines between critical points in smooth Morse theory. Morse quasi-geodesics play a crucial role in understanding the large-scale geometry of groups, particularly in the context of relatively hyperbolic groups and mapping class groups. They provide a way to identify "rigid" or "well-behaved" directions within the group's geometry, which can be thought of as "flow lines" connecting different "critical regions" of the group's structure.

Furthermore, Morse theory has been used to study the topology of spaces associated with groups, such as the Rips complex or the classifying space for proper actions. By defining appropriate functions on these (often high-dimensional and combinatorial) spaces, one can use discrete Morse theory or analogous techniques to compute their homology and understand their connectivity. This provides a powerful link between the algebraic properties of groups and the topological properties of spaces they act upon, revealing deep structural insights that are often inaccessible through purely algebraic methods.

Common Traps in Advanced Morse Theory

  • Confusing Symplectic Homology with Hamiltonian Floer Homology: While both are Floer-theoretic constructions, Symplectic Homology (SH) is typically defined for exact symplectic manifolds with contact type boundaries and relates to the loop space homology of the manifold, whereas Hamiltonian Floer Homology (HF) is for closed symplectic manifolds and counts fixed points of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms or Lagrangian intersections. Their underlying functionals and technical requirements differ significantly.
  • Assuming the Viterbo Conjecture Holds for All Symplectic Manifolds: The Viterbo Conjecture (SH*(M) ≅ H*(Ω(M))) is specific to exact symplectic manifolds with contact type boundaries. It does not generalize directly to arbitrary closed symplectic manifolds or those without a contact type boundary, where the relationship between SH and loop space homology is more complex or non-existent.
  • Overlooking the Morse-Smale Condition for the MSW Complex: The direct computation of homology via the Morse-Smale-Witten complex relies critically on the transversality of stable and unstable manifolds of critical points. Without this Morse-Smale condition, the differential ∂² = 0 might not hold, and the complex might not compute the correct homology. This condition is generic but not trivial to ensure in practice.
  • Misinterpreting the Morse Index of Minimal Surfaces: The Morse index of a minimal surface is the number of negative eigenvalues of the Jacobi operator, indicating directions of area decrease. It is not simply related to the genus or boundary components in a universal formula, but rather reflects the stability of the surface within its ambient space. A high index implies high instability, not necessarily high topological complexity in terms of genus.
  • Applying Smooth Morse Theory Directly to Discrete Structures: While geometric group theory draws inspiration from Morse theory, the application to Cayley graphs or group-related spaces often involves discrete Morse theory or analogous combinatorial techniques, not the direct application of differentiable functions and gradient flows on smooth manifolds. The "critical points" and "flow lines" are interpreted in a combinatorial or large-scale geometric sense.
  • Neglecting the Role of the Metric in Morse Theory: The Riemannian metric is crucial for defining the gradient vector field and thus the gradient flow lines, which are essential for constructing the Morse complex and understanding handle decompositions. Different metrics can lead to different gradient flows, though the resulting homology is invariant.
  • Assuming all Morse Functions are "Nice": While Morse functions are generic, constructing them explicitly with specific properties (e.g., only one critical point of highest index) can be challenging. Many theoretical results rely on the existence of such functions, but their practical construction often requires advanced techniques.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Scalar Curvature: Advanced Aspects

The space R+(M) of Riemannian metrics with positive scalar curvature on a closed manifold M carries a natural stratification by the Morse index of the Einstein–Hilbert functional restricted to this open subset. Critical points correspond to Einstein metrics with positive scalar curvature; their unstable manifolds are finite‑dimensional and can be identified with spaces of solutions to the linearised Einstein equations. The Morse–Bott picture emerges because the diffeomorphism group acts with non‑trivial stabilisers, producing critical manifolds rather than isolated points. By analysing the gradient flow of the Perelman F-functional on R+(M) one obtains a handle decomposition whose handles are indexed by the number of negative eigenvalues of the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on symmetric 2‑tensors. This decomposition yields constraints on the topology of R+(M); for instance, when M is a spin manifold of dimension ≥ 5 the A-genus vanishes, forcing R+(M) to be empty. In dimensions four the Seiberg–Witten invariants provide obstructions that can be read off from the Morse complex of the Chern–Simons–Dirac functional on the configuration space of connections and spinors. The resulting spectral sequence converges to the homology of R+(M) and has been used to distinguish exotic smooth structures on R4.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Ricci Curvature: Advanced Aspects

For the subspace Ric+(M)subsetR(M) of metrics with positive Ricci curvature, the relevant functional is the Ricci flow entropy introduced by Perelman. Its critical points are gradient Ricci solitons with positive Ricci curvature; the only compact examples are Einstein metrics. The linearisation of the Ricci flow at an Einstein metric gives a self‑adjoint operator on symmetric 2‑tensors whose negative spectrum determines the Morse index. Because the Ricci flow is not a gradient flow for a functional on the whole space of metrics, one works with the W-entropy, which is monotone along the flow and whose critical points are precisely the gradient shrinking solitons. The unstable manifolds of these critical points are modelled on the negative eigenspaces of the Lichnerowicz Laplacian twisted by the soliton potential. A handle decomposition of Ric+(M) can be constructed by flowing a generic metric downward in W-entropy; the attaching maps are governed by the dynamics of ancient solutions. This machinery underlies the proof that Ric+(M) is either empty or contractible for many manifolds, and it provides a framework for the classification of 3‑manifolds admitting positive Ricci curvature.

Worked Example: Morse Index of the Round Sphere in Ric+(Sn)
Compute the Morse index of the round metric g0 on Sn as a critical point of the W-entropy restricted to Ric+(Sn).
The round metric is an Einstein metric with operatorname{Ric}= (n-1)g0. The Lichnerowicz Laplacian on symmetric 2‑tensors decomposes under the SO(n+1) action into irreducible components: trace part, divergence‑free trace‑free part, and pure‑gauge part. The eigenvalues are known explicitly: the trace‑free divergence‑free tensors correspond to spherical harmonics of degree ℓ≥ 2 with eigenvalue λℓ= ℓ(ℓ+n-1)-2. The W-entropy second variation equals the negative of this operator shifted by the soliton potential. Negative eigenvalues occur exactly for ℓ=2, giving multiplicity ((n+2)(n-1))/(2). The pure‑gauge directions are neutral because they correspond to the diffeomorphism group action. Hence the Morse index of g0 in Ric+(Sn) is ((n+2)(n-1))/(2).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Morse index of a symmetric space inside a curvature‑positive stratum, identify the relevant functional (Einstein–Hilbert, F, W), write down the linearised operator, and use representation theory to count negative eigenvalues. Remember that gauge directions contribute zero modes, not negative ones.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Sectional Curvature: Advanced Aspects

The space Sec+(M) of metrics with strictly positive sectional curvature is a much smaller open subset of R(M). Its topology is approached via the energy functional on the space of geodesic loops, whose critical points are closed geodesics. The Morse index of a closed geodesic equals the number of conjugate points along it, counted with multiplicity. By the Morse–Bott theory of the energy functional on the free loop space Λ M, one obtains a handle decomposition of Λ M whose handles correspond to iterates of prime closed geodesics. When M admits a metric in Sec+(M), the Synge–Weinstein theorems force strong restrictions on the fundamental group and the rational homotopy type. The Morse inequalities for the energy functional then imply lower bounds on the number of distinct closed geodesics, which in turn constrain the possible diffeomorphism types of M. In particular, Grove’s symmetry program studies the action of a compact Lie group on M and uses equivariant Morse theory on the fixed‑point sets to classify positively curved manifolds with large symmetry rank.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Nonnegative Sectional Curvature: Advanced Aspects

For Sec≥ 0(M) the functional of interest is the Cheeger–Gromoll soul construction, which provides a deformation retraction onto a compact totally convex submanifold (the soul). The distance function to the soul is a Morse–Bott function on the open manifold; its critical manifolds are the soul itself and the normal spheres. The handle decomposition derived from this function shows that any open manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature is diffeomorphic to the total space of a vector bundle over its soul. When the soul is a point, the manifold is diffeomorphic to Rn. The Morse theory of the distance function also yields the soul conjecture (proved by Perelman): if there is a point where all sectional curvatures are positive, the soul is a point. In the compact case, the space of nonnegatively curved metrics is studied via the Ricci flow with surgery; the W-entropy again provides a Morse function whose critical points are gradient shrinking solitons with nonnegative curvature operator. The resulting stratification gives a handle decomposition of the moduli space of such metrics modulo diffeomorphism.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Scalar Curvature: Surgery and the α-Invariant

On a spin manifold Mn with n≥ 5, the Gromov–Lawson–Rosenberg conjecture (proved by Stolz) states that R+(M)≠varnothing iff the α-invariant α(M)∈ KOn(pt) vanishes. The proof uses a Morse‑theoretic analysis of the Dirac operator on the universal cover. One considers the space of metrics with a fixed spin structure and the functional D(g)=\|slashed{D}g\|-2, where slashed{D}g is the Dirac operator. Critical points correspond to harmonic spinors; the Morse index of a metric with a non‑trivial kernel is the spectral flow of the Dirac operator along a path of metrics. By constructing a handle decomposition of the space of metrics with α(M)=0 one shows that any two such metrics can be joined by a path avoiding metrics with harmonic spinors, which is equivalent to the existence of a positive scalar curvature metric. The surgery technique of Gromov–Lawson is interpreted as attaching handles of index ≤ n-2 to the space of metrics, preserving the non‑vanishing of the α-invariant.

  • Confusing the Morse index of a metric as a critical point of the Einstein–Hilbert functional with its index as a critical point of Perelman’s F or W entropy; the operators differ by lower‑order terms.
  • Assuming that every critical manifold in Ric+(M) is a single Einstein metric; many are orbits of the diffeomorphism group or families of solitons.
  • Neglecting the contribution of pure‑gauge (diffeomorphism) directions when counting negative eigenvalues; they are zero modes, not negative.
  • Applying the Morse inequalities for the energy functional on the loop space to Sec+(M) without verifying the Palais–Smale condition, which fails in general for non‑compact loop spaces.
  • Overlooking the role of the α-invariant in the spin case; the vanishing of α(M) is necessary and sufficient for R+(M)≠varnothing only in dimensions ≥ 5.
  • Treating the soul construction as a smooth Morse function on the whole manifold; it is only Morse–Bott and requires a smoothing of the distance function near the soul.
  • Believing that the handle decomposition of R+(M) yields a CW‑complex structure; the attaching maps are only continuous, not necessarily cellular.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Scalar Curvature: The Gromov–Lawson Relative Index Theorem

The Gromov–Lawson relative index theorem provides a Morse‑theoretic bridge between the topology of the space of positive scalar curvature metrics R+(M) and the index theory of the Dirac operator on a spin manifold M. Let M be a closed spin manifold of dimension n ≥ 5 and let g0, g1 be two metrics in R+(M). Choose a smooth path gt joining them. The family of Dirac operators Dt defines a Fredholm operator on the cylinder M × [0,1] with product metric near the ends. Its index, computed via the Atiyah–Patodi–Singer boundary correction, equals the spectral flow of the family Dt. Gromov and Lawson proved that this spectral flow coincides with the relative index of the two metrics in the K‑theory group KOn(pt). Consequently, the vanishing of the α‑invariant α(M) is not only necessary but also sufficient for R+(M) to be non‑empty, and the space of such metrics has the homotopy type of a CW‑complex whose cells correspond to handle attachments of index ≤ n−2. The Morse function used is the norm of the Dirac operator ‖Dg‖−2; its critical points are precisely metrics admitting harmonic spinors, and the Morse index at a critical metric equals the spectral flow of the Dirac operator along a descending gradient trajectory. This construction yields a handle decomposition of R+(M) that is compatible with the surgery operation of Gromov–Lawson: performing a surgery of codimension ≥ 3 corresponds to attaching a handle of index ≤ n−2, preserving the non‑vanishing of the α‑invariant. The theorem therefore translates a geometric surgery problem into an algebraic topology computation in real K‑theory, and it underlies Stolz’s proof of the Gromov–Lawson–Rosenberg conjecture for simply connected spin manifolds of dimension ≥ 5.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Ricci Curvature: The Cheeger–Gromoll Splitting and Soul Construction

For an open complete manifold M with nonnegative Ricci curvature, the Cheeger–Gromoll soul theorem asserts that M is diffeomorphic to the total space of a vector bundle over a compact totally convex submanifold S, called the soul. The distance function r(x)=dist(x,S) is a Morse–Bott function on MS; its critical manifolds are the soul itself (index 0) and the normal spheres of radius r (index equal to the codimension of the soul). By smoothing r near S one obtains a genuine Morse function whose handle decomposition exhibits M as a union of handles attached to S. When the soul is a point, M is diffeomorphic to Rn. In the compact case, the space Ric+(M) of metrics with positive Ricci curvature can be studied via Perelman’s W‑entropy functional. Critical points of W are gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with positive Ricci curvature. The Morse index of such a soliton equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the linearised operator ΔL+2Ric on symmetric 2‑tensors, modulo diffeomorphism invariance. The resulting handle decomposition of Ric+(M) is stratified by the dimension of the isometry group of the soliton. A key technical point is that the Palais–Smale condition holds for W on the space of metrics modulo diffeomorphism, because the entropy is bounded below and the Ricci flow provides a gradient‑like flow with compactness properties proved by Perelman. This Morse‑theoretic picture explains why Ric+(M) is often highly connected: the lowest index handles correspond to Einstein metrics, and higher index handles arise from solitons with nontrivial symmetry. The Cheeger–Gromoll splitting theorem for manifolds with a line (a complete geodesic without conjugate points) also admits a Morse‑theoretic proof: the Busemann function associated to the line is a convex Morse–Bott function whose critical set splits off an R factor, yielding the product structure M ≅ N × R.

Worked Example: Computing the Morse Index of a Gradient Shrinking Soliton
Let g be a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton on a closed 4‑manifold with potential function f satisfying Ric + Hess f = ½ g. The linearised operator on symmetric 2‑tensors h is L(h) = ΔLh + 2Rm(h) − ½ h − Lie∇fh. Show that the Morse index of g as a critical point of Perelman’s W‑entropy equals the number of negative eigenvalues of L on the subspace orthogonal to pure‑gauge directions LieXg.
The second variation of W at a critical metric g is given by δ²W(h,h) = ∫⟨h, L(h)⟩ e−f dvol. Because W is invariant under the diffeomorphism group, the Hessian has a kernel consisting of Lie derivatives LieXg. Restrict L to the L²(e−f)‑orthogonal complement of this kernel. The Morse index is the dimension of the maximal subspace on which the quadratic form is negative definite, i.e. the number of negative eigenvalues of L on that complement. In practice one computes the spectrum of L on the space of transverse‑traceless tensors (which are automatically orthogonal to pure‑gauge directions) and counts negative eigenvalues. For the round sphere S⁴ with its standard metric, L has no negative eigenvalues on transverse‑traceless tensors, so the Morse index is 0, reflecting that the round metric is a local minimum of W.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Morse index of a critical metric of an entropy functional, first identify the correct linearised operator (Einstein–Hilbert gives ΔL−2Ric, Perelman’s F gives ΔL+2Ric−½, W adds the Lie derivative term). Then remember to quotient out pure‑gauge directions; they contribute zero modes, not negative eigenvalues. A quick check: if the metric is Einstein with positive scalar curvature, the Einstein–Hilbert index is positive, but the W‑index may be zero because the soliton term shifts the spectrum.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Sectional Curvature: The Grove Symmetry Program and Equivariant Morse Theory

The Grove symmetry program investigates closed manifolds M admitting a metric of positive sectional curvature together with an effective isometric action of a compact Lie group G of large rank. The central tool is equivariant Morse theory applied to the energy functional E on the free loop space ΛM. Critical manifolds of E are the spaces of closed geodesics; when a G‑action is present, these critical manifolds inherit a G‑action and the Morse–Bott indices can be computed using the representation theory of the isotropy groups. Grove and collaborators showed that if the symmetry rank (the maximal dimension of a torus acting effectively by isometries) is at least log₂ n + 1 for an n‑dimensional manifold, then M is equivariantly diffeomorphic to a compact rank‑one symmetric space or a biquotient. The proof proceeds by analysing the fixed‑point set MT of a maximal torus T ⊂ G. The distance function to a component of MT is a T‑invariant Morse–Bott function whose critical manifolds are the components of MT and the normal spheres. The equivariant Morse inequalities then force strong restrictions on the Betti numbers of M and on the weights of the isotropy representations. In particular, the rational cohomology ring of M must be generated by classes of degree ≤ 2, which characterises the known positively curved examples. The program also uses the Morse theory of the action functional on the space of G‑invariant geodesics to bound the number of distinct closed geodesics, linking the topology of M to the dynamics of the geodesic flow.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Nonnegative Ricci Curvature: The Perelman Entropy and Ricci Flow Surgery

Perelman’s W‑entropy functional W(g,f,τ) = ∫M [τ(|∇f|² + R) + f − n] (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dvol provides a Morse function on the space of Riemannian metrics modulo diffeomorphism, where τ > 0 is a scale parameter and f satisfies the normalisation ∫ (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dvol = 1. Critical points are precisely gradient shrinking Ricci solitons satisfying Ric + Hess f = (2τ)−1 g. The Morse index of such a soliton equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the linearised operator L = ΔL + 2Rm − (2τ)−1 − Lie∇f on the space of symmetric 2‑tensors orthogonal to diffeomorphism directions. Perelman proved that the W‑entropy is non‑decreasing along the Ricci flow and satisfies a Palais–Smale condition after factoring out diffeomorphisms, which allows a Morse‑theoretic decomposition of the moduli space of metrics with nonnegative Ricci curvature. In the surgery construction for Ricci flow with R ≥ 0, one removes neck‑like regions modelled on Sn−1 × R and caps them off with standard caps. Each surgery corresponds to attaching a handle of index n to the space of metrics, and the entropy drops by a controlled amount. The resulting handle decomposition shows that the space of nonnegatively curved metrics modulo diffeomorphism is stratified by the number of surgeries performed, and each stratum has the homotopy type of a finite CW‑complex. This picture underlies the proof that the moduli space of nonnegatively curved metrics on a given manifold is compact in the Gromov–Hausdorff topology after suitable normalisation.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Bounded Geometry: The Cheeger–Gromov Compactness Theorem

The Cheeger–Gromov compactness theorem states that the set of pointed isometry classes of complete Riemannian manifolds with uniform bounds on sectional curvature |K| ≤ Λ, injectivity radius inj ≥ ι > 0, and dimension n is sequentially compact in the pointed C1,α topology. A Morse‑theoretic interpretation uses the energy functional E(γ) = ½ ∫ |γ̇|² on the path space of a fixed reference manifold. For a sequence of metrics gi satisfying the bounds, one can construct a common smooth manifold M and diffeomorphisms φi : M → Mi such that φi* gi converges in C1,α. The convergence is proved by applying the Morse lemma to the distance functions from a basepoint: the uniform curvature bounds give uniform control on the Hessian of the distance function, which yields uniform C1,α estimates for the exponential maps. The critical points of the distance function are the cut‑locus points; their indices are bounded by the dimension, and the Morse inequalities give a uniform bound on the topology of the cut‑locus. This uniform Morse theory is the analytic heart of the compactness theorem. In the context of the space of metrics with bounded geometry, one can define a Morse function by F(g) = ∫M |Rm|² dvol. Its critical points are metrics with harmonic curvature, and the Morse index relates to the number of negative eigenvalues of the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on the curvature operator. The handle decomposition induced by F provides a stratification of the moduli space of bounded‑geometry metrics, and the Cheeger–Gromov theorem guarantees that each stratum is compact.

  • Confusing the Morse index of a metric for the Einstein–Hilbert functional with its index for Perelman’s W‑entropy; the linearised operators differ by lower‑order terms involving the potential function.
  • Assuming every critical manifold in Ric+(M) consists of a single Einstein metric; many are orbits of the diffeomorphism group or families of solitons with continuous symmetry.
  • Neglecting to quotient out pure‑gauge (diffeomorphism) directions when counting negative eigenvalues; they contribute zero modes, not negative directions.
  • Applying the Morse inequalities for the energy functional on the free loop space to Sec+(M) without verifying the Palais–Smale condition, which fails in general for non‑compact loop spaces.
  • Overlooking the role of the α‑invariant in the spin case; the vanishing of α(M) is necessary and sufficient for R+(M) ≠ ∅ only in dimensions ≥ 5.
  • Treating the soul construction as a smooth Morse function on the whole manifold; it is only Morse–Bott and requires a smoothing of the distance function near the soul.
  • Believing that the handle decomposition of R+(M) yields a CW‑complex structure; the attaching maps are only continuous, not necessarily cellular.

Morse Theory for the Spectral Flow and the Maslov Index in Symplectic Floer Theory

The spectral flow of a continuous path of self-adjoint Fredholm operators provides the Morse index for the action functional on the loop space of a symplectic manifold. Let M be a closed symplectic manifold with symplectic form ω and let H : S1 × M → R be a time-dependent Hamiltonian. The action functional AH on the space of contractible loops ℒ0M is defined by AH(x) = −∫D2 ū*ω − ∫01 H(t, x(t)) dt, where ū : D2 → M extends x. Its critical points are the 1-periodic orbits of the Hamiltonian vector field XH. The Hessian of AH at a critical point x is a self-adjoint Fredholm operator on the space of vector fields along x given by Lx = −J0(t)d/dt − S(t), where J0 is an ω-compatible almost complex structure and S(t) is the linearisation of XH. The Conley-Zehnder index μCZ(x) equals the spectral flow of the path of operators Ls = −J0d/dt − sS(t) for s ∈ [0,1]. This index coincides with the Maslov index of the path of symplectic matrices obtained by linearising the Hamiltonian flow along x. The Maslov index counts intersections of the path with the Maslov cycle in the Lagrangian Grassmannian Λ(n). For a non-degenerate periodic orbit, the Morse index of AH equals the Conley-Zehnder index, and the Morse-Bott theory for degenerate orbits uses the spectral flow of the Hessian along a path of perturbations. The Floer chain complex CF*(H) is generated by the 1-periodic orbits graded by the Conley-Zehnder index, and the differential counts solutions of the Floer equation ∂su + J(t, u)(∂tu − XH(t, u)) = 0 with finite energy. The spectral flow provides the grading shift for the differential: a Floer trajectory connecting orbits x− and x+ has Fredholm index μCZ(x−) − μCZ(x+). The invariance of Floer homology under Hamiltonian isotopy follows from the homotopy invariance of the spectral flow. In the case of a symplectically aspherical manifold, the action functional is single-valued and the Morse theory is standard; for general symplectic manifolds one works on the universal cover of the loop space and the spectral flow computes the index of the linearised Cauchy-Riemann operator on the cylinder.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Kähler Metrics: The Mabuchi Functional and K-Stability

On a compact Kähler manifold X of complex dimension n with a fixed Kähler class [ω0], the space of Kähler metrics ℋ = {φ ∈ C∞(X) : ωφ = ω0 + i∂∂̄φ > 0} is an infinite-dimensional symmetric space with the Mabuchi metric gM(ψ1, ψ2) = ∫X ψ1ψ2 ωφn. The Mabuchi K-energy functional μ : ℋ → R is defined by its variation δμ(ψ) = −∫X ψ(R(ωφ) − R̄) ωφn, where R is the scalar curvature and R̄ its average. Critical points of μ are precisely constant scalar curvature Kähler (cscK) metrics. The second variation of μ at a cscK metric is given by the Lichnerowicz operator ΔL = Δ2 + Ric ⋅ ∇2 on functions orthogonal to the kernel of the linearised scalar curvature map. The Morse index of a cscK metric equals the number of negative eigenvalues of ΔL on the space of functions modulo the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields. Tian's α-invariant α(X) = sup{c > 0 : ∫X e−cφ ω0n < ∞ for all φ ∈ ℋ with sup φ = 0} controls the coercivity of μ. If α(X) > n/(n+1), then μ is proper and a cscK metric exists. The Donaldson-Futaki invariant DF(X, L) of a test configuration (X, L) provides an algebro-geometric analogue of the Morse index: a polarised manifold (X, L) is K-stable if DF(X, L) > 0 for all non-trivial test configurations, and K-polystable if equality holds only for product configurations. The Yau-Tian-Donaldson conjecture, proved by Chen-Donaldson-Sun, states that a Fano manifold admits a Kähler-Einstein metric if and only if it is K-polystable. In the Morse-theoretic picture, a test configuration corresponds to a ray in ℋ generated by a geodesic, and the Donaldson-Futaki invariant equals the asymptotic slope of μ along that ray. The Mabuchi functional is convex along geodesics in ℋ, and its Morse-Bott critical manifolds are the orbits of the automorphism group acting on cscK metrics. The handle decomposition of ℋ induced by μ is not known in general, but the existence of a cscK metric implies that the sublevel sets μc have the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex for all c. The space of Kähler metrics modulo the action of the Hamiltonian symplectomorphism group is the infinite-dimensional symmetric space of non-positive curvature studied by Mabuchi, Semmes, and Donaldson.

Worked Example: Conley-Zehnder Index of a Non-Degenerate Orbit
Let M = T2 = R2/Z2 with symplectic form ω = dp ∧ dq. Consider the Hamiltonian H(p, q) = ½(p2 + q2). The Hamiltonian flow is rotation by angle t. Compute the Conley-Zehnder index of the constant orbit x(t) ≡ (0,0) for the 1-periodic Hamiltonian H.
The linearised flow is Φ(t) = exp(tJ) where J = (0 −1; 1 0). The path of symplectic matrices is Φ(t) = (cos t −sin t; sin t cos t) for t ∈ [0,1]. The Maslov index of this path in Sp(2) ≅ SL(2,R) relative to the Lagrangian Grassmannian Λ(1) ≅ RP1 counts intersections with the train of the vertical line. The path rotates by angle 1 radian. Since 1 < π, the path does not cross the Maslov cycle. The Conley-Zehnder index for a path with no eigenvalue 1 is the Maslov index of the path of graphs of Φ(t) in Λ(2). For n=1, μCZ(Φ) = 0 because the rotation angle is less than π. Alternatively, the Hessian of the action functional is L = −Jd/dt − I on L2(S1, R2). Its eigenvalues are k − 1 for k ∈ Z. The negative eigenvalues correspond to k ≤ 0, giving infinitely many — but the Morse index is defined via spectral flow from the trivial path. The spectral flow of Ls = −Jd/dt − sI counts eigenvalues crossing zero. The eigenvalues of Ls are k − s. As s goes from 0 to 1, the eigenvalue for k=0 crosses from 0 to −1 (negative crossing, contributes −1), and the eigenvalue for k=1 crosses from 1 to 0 (positive crossing, contributes +1). Net spectral flow = 0. Thus μCZ = 0.
Exam Strategy: Spectral Flow vs Maslov Index
In questions asking for the Morse index of a periodic orbit in Floer theory, remember: (1) The Conley-Zehnder index equals the spectral flow of the Hessian path. (2) For a non-degenerate orbit in dimension 2n, the index is the Maslov index of the linearised flow path in Sp(2n). (3) The Maslov index can be computed by counting intersections with the Maslov cycle or by the winding number of the determinant line. (4) For a rotation by angle θ in Sp(2), the index is 2⌊θ/π⌋ + 1 if θ/π ∉ Z, and 2θ/π if θ/π ∈ Z (degenerate case). Memorise the formula for the standard quadratic Hamiltonian on R2n.

Morse Theory for the ADM Mass Functional and the Positive Mass Theorem

The ADM mass of an asymptotically flat Riemannian 3-manifold (M, g) with nonnegative scalar curvature is defined as mADM(g) = (1/16π) limr→∞ ∫Sr (∂jgij − ∂igjj) νi dA, where Sr are coordinate spheres. The space of asymptotically flat metrics with R ≥ 0 and fixed boundary data at infinity can be given a manifold structure modelled on weighted Sobolev spaces. The ADM mass functional mADM : ℳAF → R is differentiable, and its critical points are metrics satisfying the static vacuum Einstein equations: there exists a function V > 0 such that V Ric = Hess V and ΔV = 0. These are precisely the spatial slices of static vacuum spacetimes. The second variation of mADM at a static metric involves the linearised scalar curvature operator and the linearised constraint equations. Schoen and Yau's proof of the positive mass theorem uses minimal hypersurfaces and the stability inequality, which can be interpreted as a Morse index estimate: a stable minimal surface in a 3-manifold with R ≥ 0 has Morse index zero for the area functional. Witten's spinor proof uses the Dirac operator D on a spin manifold; the Lichnerowicz formula D2 = ∇*∇ + R/4 shows that if R ≥ 0, then D has no negative eigenvalues, so the Morse index of the Dirac energy functional is zero. The mass is expressed as a boundary term ∫∞ ⟨ψ, Dψ⟩, and positivity follows from the nonnegativity of the bulk integral. The rigidity case mADM = 0 implies the existence of a parallel spinor, forcing the metric to be flat. In the context of the space of metrics, the ADM mass is a Morse-Bott function whose critical manifolds are the orbits of the asymptotic symmetry group (the Poincaré group) acting on static solutions. The Morse index of the Schwarzschild metric gm = (1 + m/2r)4 δ as a critical point of mADM on the space of asymptotically flat metrics with fixed mass m is related to the number of negative modes of the linearised Einstein operator. For m > 0, the Schwarzschild metric is a local minimum of the mass among metrics with the same asymptotic mass, corresponding to Morse index zero. The positive mass theorem can be viewed as the statement that the sublevel set {g : mADM(g) < 0} is empty, so the mass functional has no critical points of negative mass. The Penrose inequality mADM ≥ √(A/16π), where A is the area of the outermost minimal surface, sharpens this: the mass functional is bounded below by a geometric quantity. The Riemannian Penrose inequality was proved by Huisken-Ilmanen (using inverse mean curvature flow) and Bray (using conformal flow), both of which can be interpreted as Morse-theoretic deformations of the metric that decrease the mass while preserving the horizon area.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Prescribed Scalar Curvature: The Kazdan-Warner Problem

Given a closed manifold M and a function f ∈ C∞(M), the Kazdan-Warner problem asks whether there exists a metric g conformal to a given background metric g0 such that the scalar curvature of g equals f. In the conformal class [g0], metrics are written as g = u4/(n−2) g0 for u > 0, and the scalar curvature transforms as Rg = u−(n+2)/(n−2) (−cn Δg0 u + R0 u), where cn = 4(n−1)/(n−2). The equation Rg = f becomes the semilinear elliptic PDE −cn Δ0 u + R0 u = f u(n+2)/(n−2). This is the Euler-Lagrange equation of the Yamabe-type functional E(u) = ∫M (cn |∇u|2 + R0 u2) dvol0 / (∫M f u2n/(n−2) dvol0)(n−2)/n on the positive cone of H1(M). Critical points of E correspond to solutions. The functional E is not bounded below in general; its Morse theory is governed by the sign of f and the Yamabe invariant Y(M, [g0]). If f changes sign, the problem is more subtle. Kazdan and Warner proved that on Sn, a necessary and sufficient condition for f to be a scalar curvature is that f is positive somewhere and satisfies the Kazdan-Warner obstruction: ∫Sn ∇f ⋅ X dvol = 0 for all conformal Killing fields X. This obstruction arises because the functional E is invariant under the conformal group, and the Morse-Bott critical manifolds are the orbits of this group. The Morse index of a solution u is the number of negative eigenvalues of the linearised operator L = −cn Δ0 + R0 − f(n+2)/(n−2) u4/(n−2). For the standard sphere, the solutions are classified by the Obata theorem: if f is constant, the solutions are the conformal factors of the round metric, forming a Morse-Bott manifold of dimension n+1. The Morse index of the constant solution for f = n(n−1) is zero (it is the global minimum of the Yamabe functional). For non-constant f, the Morse index can be computed via the spectral flow of the linearised operator along a path of functions. The space of solutions modulo the conformal group has a handle decomposition induced by the functional E, and the Morse inequalities give topological constraints on the space of prescribed scalar curvature metrics. In dimensions ≥ 3, the positive mass theorem and the solution of the Yamabe problem imply that every conformal class contains a metric of constant scalar curvature, which is a global minimum of the Yamabe functional. The Morse theory of the prescribed scalar curvature functional on the whole space of metrics (not just conformal) is much richer: the Einstein-Hilbert functional restricted to the slice of metrics with fixed volume has critical points at Einstein metrics, and its Morse index is given by the number of negative eigenvalues of the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on transverse traceless tensors.

Morse Theory for the Willmore Functional on the Space of Immersed Surfaces

The Willmore functional W(Σ) = ∫Σ H2 dA assigns to an immersed surface Σ ⊂ R3 (or a Riemannian 3-manifold) the integral of the squared mean curvature. Critical points are Willmore surfaces, satisfying the Euler-Lagrange equation ΔΣ H + 2H(H2 − K) = 0, where K is the Gaussian curvature. The space of immersions Imm(Σ, R3) is a Fréchet manifold, and W is invariant under the action of the Möbius group (conformal transformations of S3 = R3 ∪ {∞}). The second variation of W at a Willmore surface involves the Jacobi operator J = Δ2 + div(A∇) + ⟨∇H, ∇⟩ + 2|A|2(H2 − K) + 2H2(H2 − 2K), where A is the second fundamental form. The Morse index of a Willmore surface is the number of negative eigenvalues of J on normal variations modulo the Möbius group action. For the round sphere S2 ⊂ R3, H = 1, K = 1, and J = Δ2 + 2Δ. The eigenvalues on spherical harmonics Ylm are l(l+1)(l−1)(l+2). The negative eigenvalues occur for l = 0 (translation modes, zero due to Möbius invariance) and l = 1 (dilation modes, also zero). The first positive eigenvalue is for l = 2, so the Morse index of the round sphere is zero — it is a global minimum of W among all immersed spheres (Willmore's conjecture, proved by Marques-Neves). For the Clifford torus T2 = S1(1/√2) × S1(1/√2) ⊂ S3, H = 0, K = −1, and J = Δ2 − 2Δ. The eigenvalues are λk(λk + 2) where λk are eigenvalues of −Δ. The negative eigenvalues correspond to λk ∈ (0,2), which occur for certain modes. The Morse index of the Clifford torus in S3 is 5 (as computed by Montiel-Ros and Urbano). In R3, the Willmore functional is not bounded below due to the Möbius invariance: one can concentrate curvature at a point by a Möbius transformation, making W arbitrarily close to 4π. The compactness theorem for Willmore surfaces (Kuwert-Schätzle, Rivière) states that a sequence of Willmore surfaces with bounded energy and genus has a subsequence converging to a Willmore surface with possible bubbling. This bubbling corresponds to the failure of the Palais-Smale condition for W on the space of immersions modulo Möbius transformations. The Morse theory of W on the moduli space of immersed surfaces of fixed genus is complicated by the non-compactness of the Möbius group. However, if one fixes the conformal class of the immersion, the functional becomes the Liouville energy, and its critical points are constant mean curvature surfaces. The Willmore flow ∂tΣ = −(ΔH + 2H(H2 − K)) ν is the gradient flow of W, and its long-time behaviour is governed by the Morse indices of the critical points. For genus zero, the flow converges to a round sphere (index 0). For genus one, the flow can converge to the Clifford torus (index 5) or develop singularities. The handle decomposition of the space of immersions induced by W is not fully understood, but the min-max construction of Willmore spheres by Marques-Neves uses the Almgren-Pitts min-max theory for the area functional in the space of cycles, which is a Morse-theoretic construction in geometric measure theory.

  • Confusing the Conley-Zehnder index with the Maslov index of the linearised Hamiltonian flow; they coincide for non-degenerate orbits but differ by a correction term for degenerate orbits.
  • Assuming the Mabuchi functional is a Morse function on the space of Kähler metrics; it is Morse-Bott with critical manifolds given by automorphism group orbits.
  • Neglecting the role of the Möbius group in the Willmore functional; the functional is invariant, so critical points come in non-compact orbits, and the Morse index must be computed modulo this action.
  • Treating the ADM mass as a Morse function on the whole space of asymptotically flat metrics without fixing the asymptotic mass; the mass is not proper and its sublevel sets are not compact.
  • Overlooking the Kazdan-Warner obstruction when solving the prescribed scalar curvature problem on Sn; the obstruction is necessary and sufficient only for n = 2, but in higher dimensions it is only necessary.
  • Confusing the Morse index of a Willmore surface for normal variations with its index for all variations; tangential variations correspond to reparametrisations and contribute zero modes.
  • Assuming the Palais-Smale condition holds for the Willmore functional on the space of immersions modulo Möbius transformations; it fails due to bubbling, which corresponds to the formation of spheres with energy 4π.

Morse Theory for the Functional of the First Eigenvalue of the Dirac Operator on Spin Manifolds

Let (M,g) be a closed spin manifold of dimension n ≥ 2. The Dirac operator D_g acts on sections of the spinor bundle ΣM and its spectrum is real, discrete and symmetric about zero. The first positive eigenvalue λ1(g) defines a functional λ1 : Met(M) → ℝ on the space of Riemannian metrics. Critical points of λ1 are precisely those metrics for which there exists a non‑trivial eigenspinor ψ with D_g ψ = λ1(g) ψ that is also a harmonic spinor for the conformally related metric g̃ = λ1(g)2/(n-1) g. The Morse index of such a critical metric equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the Hessian of λ1 restricted to the slice transverse to the action of the diffeomorphism group and the conformal group. Hijazi’s inequality λ1(g) ≥ (n/2) (∫_M R_g dvol_g / vol(M))1/2 shows that the functional is bounded below by a scalar curvature term, and equality forces the metric to be Einstein with a Killing spinor. The second variation formula involves the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on symmetric 2‑tensors coupled to the spinor bundle; its kernel corresponds to infinitesimal deformations preserving the first eigenvalue. In dimension three, the work of Bär and Dahl relates the Morse index of λ1 to the spectral flow of a family of Dirac operators along a path of metrics, providing a bridge to Floer‑type invariants. For the round sphere S^n with its standard metric, λ1 = n/2 and the Morse index is zero, reflecting the fact that the round metric is a global minimiser of λ1 within its conformal class. On the other hand, on the flat torus T^n the first eigenvalue is zero and the functional is Morse‑Bott with critical manifolds given by the space of flat metrics modulo diffeomorphisms. The min‑max construction of metrics with prescribed λ1 uses the topology of the space of spin structures and the equivariant Morse theory of the λ1 functional under the action of the conformal group.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Scalar Curvature: The Stolz Positive Mass Theorem

Stolz’s positive mass theorem for spin manifolds with boundary asserts that if (M,g) is a compact spin manifold with boundary ∂M of positive scalar curvature and the Dirac operator on ∂M has non‑negative eigenvalues, then the ADM mass of any asymptotically flat extension of (M,g) is non‑negative, with equality only for the Euclidean metric. In the context of Morse theory on the space ℛ+(M) of positive scalar curvature metrics, this theorem translates into a statement about the topology of ℛ+(M): the inclusion of the subspace of metrics with non‑negative Dirac boundary spectrum induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups up to a certain range. The proof uses a Witten‑type deformation of the Dirac operator on a complete manifold obtained by attaching a cylindrical end to (M,g). The deformed operator D_t = D + t c(ν) (where ν is the outward normal) has a spectral gap for large t, and the index of D_t computes the relative η‑invariant of the boundary. The Morse function on ℛ+(M) is the spectral flow of the family D_t as t varies, and its critical points correspond to metrics for which the extended Dirac operator has a kernel. The handle decomposition of ℛ+(M) induced by this Morse function yields a filtration whose associated graded pieces are classified by the bordism groups of spin manifolds with positive scalar curvature. In particular, the Stolz theorem implies that the α‑invariant of a spin manifold, defined as the index of the Dirac operator on a closed spin manifold, vanishes if the manifold admits a metric of positive scalar curvature. This vanishing result is a cornerstone of the Gromov–Lawson–Stolz surgery classification of positive scalar curvature metrics in dimensions ≥ 5.

Worked Example: Computing the Morse Index of λ1 on S3
Consider the round 3‑sphere (S3, g0) with its standard spin structure. The first eigenvalue of the Dirac operator is λ1 = 3/2. Determine the Morse index of the functional λ1 at g0 within the space of metrics modulo diffeomorphisms and conformal transformations.
The round metric is Einstein with positive scalar curvature R = 6. By Hijazi’s inequality, λ1(g) ≥ (3/2) (∫ R / vol)1/2 = 3/2, with equality exactly for g0. The second variation of λ1 at g0 is given by the quadratic form Q(h) = ∫S3 ⟨h, L h⟩ dvol, where L is the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on symmetric 2‑tensors twisted by the spinor bundle. On S3, the representation theory of SO(4) shows that the space of transverse‑traceless tensors decomposes into irreducible components with eigenvalues of L all strictly positive. The conformal Killing tensors correspond to the zero modes of the conformal Laplacian and are removed by quotienting by the conformal group. Consequently, Q is positive definite on the tangent space to the slice, so the Morse index is zero. This matches the known fact that the round metric is a strict local minimum of λ1 on the moduli space of metrics.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Morse index of a spectral functional on a symmetric space, first identify the symmetry group and decompose the variation space into irreducible representations. The index equals the number of representations on which the Hessian is negative. For the round sphere, all relevant representations give positive eigenvalues, so the index is zero. Memorise the key inequality (Hijazi, Bär) that provides the lower bound and characterises equality cases; it often appears as a multiple‑choice distractor.

Morse Theory for the Chern–Simons Functional on 3‑Manifolds with Boundary and the Extended Topological Quantum Field Theory

Let Y be a compact oriented 3‑manifold with boundary Σ, and let G be a compact Lie group. The Chern–Simons functional CS : 𝒜(Y) → ℝ/ℤ is defined on the space of G‑connections modulo gauge transformations that are the identity on Σ. Its critical points are flat connections on Y, and the Hessian at a flat connection A is the operator *d_A on 1‑forms with values in the adjoint bundle, with boundary conditions given by the Lagrangian subspace of the symplectic space H1(Σ; ad P). The Morse index of a flat connection equals the spectral flow of the family of odd signature operators on Σ coupled to the restriction of A. In the extended topological quantum field theory of Freed–Hopkins–Teleman, the Chern–Simons functional is the action functional for a 3‑dimensional TQFT whose value on a closed 3‑manifold is the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant, and whose value on a surface Σ is the category of representations of the quantum group at a root of unity. The Morse complex of CS on Y with boundary Σ computes the Floer homology of the moduli space of flat connections on Σ, which is isomorphic to the space of conformal blocks of the associated Wess–Zumino–Witten model. The handle decomposition of the space of connections induced by CS corresponds to the surgery presentation of Y: each 2‑handle attachment adds a generator to the Morse complex, and the differential counts instantons on the 4‑manifold obtained by attaching a 2‑handle to Y × [0,1]. The non‑degeneracy of critical points requires that the restriction map H1(Y; ad P) → H1(Σ; ad P) be injective, a condition that fails precisely when the boundary holonomy lies in a singular stratum of the character variety. In that case the functional is Morse‑Bott, and the critical manifolds are tori parametrised by the centraliser of the holonomy. The resulting spectral sequence converges to the instanton Floer homology of the closed manifold obtained by gluing a handlebody to Y.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Ricci Curvature: The Hamilton–Perelman Surgery and the Canonical Neighborhoods

Hamilton’s Ricci flow ∂_t g = -2 Ric(g) defines a gradient‑like flow for the Perelman entropy functional ℱ(g,f) = ∫_M (R + |∇f|2) e-f dvol on the space of metrics modulo diffeomorphisms. The critical points of ℱ are gradient Ricci solitons, and the Morse index of a soliton equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the linearised Ricci flow operator L = Δ_L + 2 Ric on symmetric 2‑tensors, where Δ_L is the Lichnerowicz Laplacian. Perelman’s surgery procedure removes regions of high curvature that are modelled on κ‑solutions, which are ancient solutions with non‑negative curvature operator. The canonical neighborhood theorem asserts that at any point where the curvature is sufficiently large, the geometry is ε‑close to either a round cylinder S2 × ℝ, a capped cylinder, or a Bryant soliton. In Morse‑theoretic language, each surgery corresponds to attaching a handle of index equal to the Morse index of the corresponding κ‑solution. For the round cylinder, the linearised operator has exactly one negative eigenvalue (the neck‑pinching mode), so the surgery attaches a 1‑handle. The Bryant soliton has Morse index zero, so its removal does not change the homotopy type of the space of metrics. The flow with surgery therefore produces a handle decomposition of the original manifold M, and the number of surgeries of each index is bounded by topological invariants such as the Betti numbers. This decomposition underlies the proof of the geometrisation conjecture: the final extinct components are spherical space forms, and the remaining thick part admits a hyperbolic structure. The Morse theory of ℱ on the space of metrics with positive Ricci curvature is thus equivalent to the classification of 3‑manifolds via Ricci flow with surgery.

Morse Theory for the Volume Functional on the Space of Conformal Classes and the Yamabe Invariant

Given a closed manifold M of dimension n ≥ 3, the Yamabe invariant Y(M) = inf[g] (∫_M R_g dvol_g) / (vol(M))(n-2)/n is the infimum of the normalised total scalar curvature over all conformal classes. The functional whose critical points are constant scalar curvature metrics in a fixed conformal class is the Yamabe functional E(g) = ∫_M R_g dvol_g restricted to the conformal class. Its Morse index at a critical metric g equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the conformal Laplacian L_g = -4(n-1)/(n-2) Δ_g + R_g acting on functions, minus the dimension of the kernel (which corresponds to the conformal Killing fields). When the Yamabe invariant is positive, the minimiser of E in each conformal class is unique up to diffeomorphism and scaling, and its Morse index is zero. If Y(M) ≤ 0, the infimum is not attained in general, and the Palais–Smale condition fails due to bubbling phenomena analogous to those in the Willmore functional. The handle decomposition of the space of conformal classes induced by the Yamabe functional is related to the surgery classification of manifolds with positive scalar curvature: each conformal class that admits a metric of positive scalar curvature contributes a handle of index equal to the Morse index of the corresponding Yamabe metric. In dimension three, the work of Schoen and Yau shows that Y(M) > 0 if and only if M is a connected sum of spherical space forms and copies of S2 × S1. The Morse theory of the volume functional on the space of conformal classes therefore recovers the prime decomposition of 3‑manifolds and provides a variational proof of the geometrisation conjecture for manifolds with positive Yamabe invariant.

  • Confusing the Morse index of the Dirac eigenvalue functional with the index of the Dirac operator itself; the former counts negative directions of the eigenvalue as a function of the metric, the latter counts negative eigenvalues of the operator at a fixed metric.
  • Assuming the Stolz positive mass theorem holds without the spin condition; the theorem fails for non‑spin manifolds, and the α‑invariant is not defined.
  • Neglecting the boundary Lagrangian condition in the Chern–Simons Morse complex; the differential counts instantons only when the boundary values lie in the correct Lagrangian subspace of the character variety.
  • Treating the canonical neighborhood theorem as a purely local statement; it requires a global curvature scale and the κ‑noncollapsing condition from Perelman’s entropy.
  • Overlooking the role of the conformal Laplacian kernel in the Yamabe Morse index; zero modes correspond to conformal Killing fields and must be quotiented out before counting negative eigenvalues.
  • Believing that the Yamabe functional satisfies the Palais–Smale condition on all manifolds; bubbling occurs precisely when the Yamabe invariant is non‑positive, leading to loss of compactness.
  • These traps highlight the subtle points that frequently appear in examinations.

Morse Theory and the Topology of the Space of Metrics with Positive Scalar Curvature: The Schoen–Yau Minimal Hypersurface Technique

Schoen and Yau introduced a geometric Morse theory on the space of Riemannian metrics with positive scalar curvature by using stable minimal hypersurfaces as critical submanifolds of the area functional. Given a closed manifold M of dimension n ≥ 3, a metric g with R_g > 0 admits no stable minimal hypersurface of index zero; the second variation formula for area shows that any such hypersurface would force a non‑positive scalar curvature somewhere. Consequently, the space of positive scalar curvature metrics can be stratified by the Morse index of the area functional restricted to the space of embedded hypersurfaces. Each stratum corresponds to a handle attachment whose index equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the Jacobi operator L = Δ_Σ + |A|² + Ric(ν,ν) on the hypersurface Σ. The handle decomposition yields a filtration of the moduli space of positive scalar curvature metrics, and the number of handles of a given index is bounded by the Betti numbers of M. This approach recovers the Gromov–Lawson surgery theorem: a surgery of codimension at least three preserves the existence of a positive scalar curvature metric because the attached handle has index at least two, which does not create new components in the moduli space. The Schoen–Yau technique also provides a proof of the positive mass theorem for asymptotically flat manifolds by analysing the Morse index of the area functional on large coordinate spheres.

Morse Theory for the Einstein–Hilbert Functional on the Space of Metrics with Prescribed Ricci Curvature

The Einstein–Hilbert functional E(g) = ∫_M R_g dvol_g restricted to the slice of metrics with fixed volume has critical points exactly at Einstein metrics. When one further prescribes the Ricci tensor up to a constant factor, the functional becomes F(g) = ∫_M (R_g - 2Λ) dvol_g with Λ a Lagrange multiplier. The second variation of F at an Einstein metric g_E is given by the Lichnerowicz Laplacian Δ_L acting on transverse‑traceless symmetric 2‑tensors h: δ²F(h,h) = ∫_M ⟨h, Δ_L h⟩ dvol_g. The Morse index of g_E equals the number of negative eigenvalues of Δ_L on the space of TT‑tensors. Koiso showed that on a compact Einstein manifold with positive Einstein constant, the kernel of Δ_L consists precisely of infinitesimal Einstein deformations; the index is finite and can be computed via representation theory when the manifold is homogeneous. For example, on the round sphere Sⁿ the Lichnerowicz operator has exactly one negative eigenvalue corresponding to the volume‑changing mode, so the Morse index is one. On a Kähler–Einstein manifold with positive scalar curvature, the index equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the complexified Lichnerowicz operator on (1,1)‑forms, which is related to the Futaki invariant. The handle decomposition induced by the negative eigenspaces of Δ_L provides a stratification of the moduli space of Einstein metrics; each handle attachment corresponds to a bifurcation of Einstein metrics along a direction of negative curvature of the functional. This Morse‑theoretic picture underlies the proof that the space of Einstein metrics on a given manifold has finitely many connected components in dimensions ≥ 4.

Worked Example: Computing the Morse Index of the Round Sphere
