A complete answer must mention the Fargues–Fontaine curve, the diamond formalism, the infinite‑level Rapoport–Zink space, and the Hecke–spectral compatibility.

The Theory of p‑adic Local Langlands for GLn via Emerton's Completed Cohomology

Emerton's theory of completed cohomology provides a powerful framework for the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GLn(Qp). Let K be a finite extension of Qp and let G = GLn(K). For a compact open subgroup K0 of G and a finite‑dimensional E‑vector space V with a continuous K0‑action, one considers the tower of locally symmetric spaces XK attached to G and the associated étale cohomology groups Hi(XK, V). The completed cohomology Hicompleted is defined as the inverse limit over K of these cohomology groups, completed with respect to the p‑adic topology. It carries a continuous action of G × Gal(K/K) and is an admissible Banach representation of G. Emerton proved that the locally analytic vectors in completed cohomology can be described in terms of (φ,Γ)‑modules over the Robba ring, and that the functor taking a Galois representation to its associated locally analytic representation of G is exact and compatible with the classical local Langlands correspondence. In the case n = 2, this recovers Colmez's Montréal functor and the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence of Berger–Breuil. For higher n, the theory predicts a correspondence between potentially semi‑stable Galois representations and certain unitary Banach representations of GLn(K). Examination questions typically require the definition of completed cohomology, the statement of Emerton's local‑global compatibility theorem, and the description of the (φ,Γ)‑module attached to a Galois representation via the Robba ring. A rigorous answer must include the role of the Hecke algebra, the notion of admissible Banach representations, and the exactness of the Montréal functor.

Worked Example: Computing the (φ,Γ)‑module of a Galois Character
Let χ : Gal(Qp/Qp) → E× be the cyclotomic character. Describe the rank‑one (φ,Γ)‑module D(χ) over the Robba ring RE and verify that its Sen weights are {1}.
The Robba ring RE consists of series ∑n∈Z an Tn convergent on some annulus r < |T| < 1. The (φ,Γ)‑module attached to χ is D(χ) = RE·e with φ(e) = p e and γ(e) = χ(γ) e for γ ∈ Γ = Gal(Qp(μp∞)/Qp). Since χ(γ) = γ(ζ)/ζ for a compatible system of p‑power roots of unity, the action of Γ is given by the cyclotomic character. The Sen operator ∇ = log(γ)/log(χ(γ)) acts on e by ∇(e) = eχ.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the construction of a (φ,Γ)‑module from a Galois representation, first write down the Robba ring, then define the φ and Γ actions on a basis vector using the Galois character. Explicitly compute the Sen operator to read off the Hodge–Tate weights; this step is frequently tested and earns full marks when shown clearly.

The Theory of Perfectoid Shimura Varieties and the Hodge–Tate Period Map at Infinite Level

Scholze's theory of perfectoid spaces allows one to attach a perfectoid space ShG,∞ to a Shimura datum (G,X) by taking the inverse limit of the tower of Shimura varieties ShG,K as the level K shrinks to the identity. This perfectoid space is defined over the reflex field E and carries a continuous action of G(Af) × Gal(E/E). The Hodge–Tate period map πHT : ShG,∞ → FlG,μ is a G(Af)‑equivariant map to the flag variety parametrizing filtrations of the standard representation of G of type μ. Scholze proved that πHT is étale and its image is the admissible locus FlG,μa, which is a partially proper open subset of the flag variety. The fibers of πHT are discrete and carry a natural action of the Galois group Gal(E/E). This map is the geometric incarnation of the p‑adic Hodge theory of the Shimura variety: the pullback of the tautological bundle on the flag variety yields the Hodge–Tate sheaf, and the Galois action on the fibers realizes the local Langlands correspondence for G at the primes dividing p. In the case of modular curves, πHT identifies the infinite‑level modular curve with the Drinfeld upper half‑plane, and the Galois action on fibers gives the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2(Qp). Examination questions often ask for the definition of the perfectoid Shimura variety at infinite level, the properties of the Hodge–Tate period map, and its role in the p‑adic Langlands program. A thorough answer must mention the pro‑étale site, the diamond associated to ShG,∞, the admissible locus, and the Galois action on fibers.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Arakelov Geometry and the Chambert‑Loir Measure

Non‑Archimedean Arakelov geometry, developed by Chambert‑Loir, Thuillier, and others, extends classical Arakelov theory to varieties over non‑Archimedean fields by using Berkovich spaces as the analytic base. Let X be a proper variety over a complete non‑Archimedean field K with valuation ring OK. A metrized line bundle L on X consists of an algebraic line bundle together with a continuous metric on the associated Berkovich line bundle Lan. Chambert‑Loir associated to L a measure c1(L)d on the Berkovich analytification Xan, where d = dim X. This measure is supported on the skeleton of Xan and satisfies the projection formula and the Poincaré–Lelong formula. The Chambert‑Loir measure of an ample metrized line bundle is a probability measure that plays the role of the Monge–Ampère measure in complex Arakelov geometry. It is used to define heights of subvarieties and to prove equidistribution theorems for points of small height. In particular, the Chambert‑Loir measure of the canonical metric on the anti‑canonical bundle of a toric variety coincides with the Haar measure on the associated tropical torus. Examiners may ask for the definition of a Chambert‑Loir measure, its functorial properties, and its application to the equidistribution of Galois orbits of points of small height. A complete answer must include the construction via the Monge–Ampère operator on the Berkovich space, the role of the skeleton, and the statement of the equidistribution theorem of Chambert‑Loir and Thuillier.

The Theory of Rigid Analytic Spaces over Trivially Valued Fields and Their Relation to Algebraic Geometry

When the ground field K carries the trivial valuation, the category of rigid analytic spaces over K is equivalent to the category of separated schemes of finite type over K equipped with the étale topology. This equivalence, due to Bosch and Lütkebohmert, is realized by the functor that sends a rigid space X to its associated scheme Xsch obtained by gluing the affinoid spectra of affinoid algebras that are Tate algebras over K with the trivial valuation. In this setting affinoid algebras are simply finite‑type K‑algebras, and affinoid spaces correspond to affine schemes. The G‑topology on K‑rigid spaces coincides with the étale topology on the associated schemes. Consequently, coherent sheaf cohomology on a rigid space over a trivially valued field agrees with étale cohomology on the associated scheme, and Kiehl's finiteness theorems reduce to the classical finiteness theorems for coherent sheaves on proper schemes. This equivalence is crucial for comparing rigid analytic methods with algebraic geometry in equal characteristic zero and for transferring results such as the Riemann–Roch theorem or the theory of D‑modules. Examination questions often require the statement of the equivalence of categories, the description of affinoid algebras in the trivially valued case, and the comparison of G‑topology with the étale topology. A precise answer must mention the role of the Tate algebra K⟨T1,…,Tn⟩ with the Gauss norm, the fact that affinoid domains are principal open subsets, and the identification of coherent sheaves on both sides.

  • Confusing the Chambert‑Loir measure with the equilibrium measure of potential theory — the Chambert‑Loir measure is attached to a metrized line bundle and satisfies the projection formula, whereas the equilibrium measure minimizes energy on a compact set.
  • Assuming the Hodge–Tate period map is always surjective onto the whole flag variety — its image is the admissible locus, which is a proper open subset in general.
  • Thinking that completed cohomology is always a unitary Banach representation — it is admissible and unitary only after passing to the locally analytic vectors and using the Schneider–Teitelbaum duality.
  • Believing that the uniformization of local shtuka moduli by perfectoid spaces works for any reductive group without a local Shimura datum — the construction requires a minuscule cocharacter μ and a Frobenius‑conjugacy class b.
  • Overlooking that the equivalence between rigid spaces and schemes over a trivially valued field fails for non‑trivial valuations — affinoid algebras are then Tate algebras with the Gauss norm, and affinoid domains are not simply principal opens.
  • Mixing the Galois action on the fibers of πHT with the Hecke action of G(Af) — the Galois action is on the target of the local Langlands correspondence, while the Hecke action is on the source.
  • Assuming the Chambert‑Loir measure of an ample line bundle is always supported on the whole Berkovich space — it is supported on the skeleton associated to a semistable model of the variety.
The advanced sections above provide the depth and precision required for rigorous examination performance.

The Theory of Raynaud's Generic Fiber Functor and Formal Models

Raynaud's generic fiber construction provides the bridge between formal geometry over the ring of integers OK of a non-Archimedean field K and rigid analytic geometry over K. Let K be a complete discretely valued field with perfect residue field k of characteristic p > 0, uniformizer π, and valuation v normalized so v(π) = 1. A formal OK-scheme X is an adic formal scheme locally of finite type over Spf OK. Its generic fiber Xη is a rigid analytic space over K obtained by the following procedure: for each affine open Spf A ⊂ X where A is a topologically finitely presented OK-algebra, the generic fiber is the affinoid space M(A ⊗OK K) equipped with the Gauss norm extended from A. These affinoid domains glue in the G-topology to form Xη. The functor X ↦ Xη is exact on the category of admissible formal OK-schemes (those locally isomorphic to Spf OK⟨T1,…,Tn⟩/I) and preserves fiber products. A fundamental theorem of Raynaud states that every quasi-compact and quasi-separated rigid analytic space over K admits a formal model, i.e., an admissible formal OK-scheme X such that Xη ≅ X. Moreover, any two formal models of the same rigid space are dominated by a third, forming a filtered projective system. The special fiber Xs = X ×OK k of a formal model is a scheme of finite type over k, and its geometry controls the reduction behavior of the rigid space. For instance, a rigid space has good reduction if it admits a formal model whose special fiber is smooth and proper over k. The semi-stable reduction theorem (proved by Bosch-Lütkebohmert for curves and by Temkin for higher dimensions using resolution of singularities) asserts that after a finite extension of K, every smooth proper rigid space admits a formal model whose special fiber is a reduced divisor with normal crossings. The associated Berkovich space Xan then admits a strong deformation retraction onto a skeleton Δ(X) which is a finite simplicial complex dual to the intersection complex of the special fiber. This skeleton carries the weight of the Chambert-Loir measure and encodes the tropicalization of the variety. Examiners frequently test the equivalence between the category of admissible formal OK-schemes up to admissible blow-ups and the category of quasi-compact quasi-separated rigid spaces, the construction of the generic fiber as a functor, and the role of the special fiber in defining the reduction type. A complete answer must distinguish between the generic fiber as a rigid space and the analytification as a Berkovich space, and must explain how admissible blow-ups of formal models correspond to refinements of the G-topology covering.

The Theory of p-adic L-functions and Iwasawa Theory via Rigid Analytic Geometry

The construction of p-adic L-functions as rigid analytic functions on weight space is a cornerstone of modern Iwasawa theory. Let K be a finite extension of Qp, and let Γ = Gal(K∞/K) ≅ Zpd be the Galois group of the cyclotomic (or more generally a p-adic Lie) extension. The Iwasawa algebra Λ = OK[[Γ]] is isomorphic to a power series ring OK[[T1,…,Td]] via the choice of topological generators. The maximal ideal spectrum of Λ, denoted Spf Λ, is a formal scheme whose generic fiber is the rigid analytic space W = Sp(Λ ⊗OK K), called the weight space. A p-adic L-function is an element Lp ∈ Λ ⊗OK K, viewed as a rigid analytic function on W. For a modular form f of weight k ≥ 2, the Mazur-Kitagawa p-adic L-function Lp(f, s) interpolates the critical values L(f, χ, j) for Dirichlet characters χ of p-power conductor and integers j in the critical strip. The interpolation property is expressed as Lp(f, χ, j) = ε(χ, j) · L(f, χ, j) / Ωf± where ε is an explicit Euler factor and Ωf± are complex periods. The construction uses the theory of modular symbols and the Amice transform: a measure μ on Zp× corresponds to a power series in Λ via μ ↦ ∫Zp× (1+T)x dμ(x). The p-adic L-function is then the Amice transform of a measure constructed from modular symbols. In the setting of Hida theory, the ordinary Hecke algebra hord is a finite flat Λ-algebra, and the p-adic L-function becomes an element of the fraction field of hord. The main conjecture of Iwasawa theory, proved by Skinner-Urban for GL2 and by Kato in general, relates the characteristic ideal of the Selmer group (a Λ-module) to the ideal generated by the p-adic L-function. In the language of rigid geometry, the Selmer group corresponds to a coherent sheaf on the rigid analytic space W, and the main conjecture asserts that its Fitting ideal coincides with the divisor of the p-adic L-function. The theory extends to p-adic families of automorphic forms: the eigenvariety E constructed by Buzzard and Chenevier is a rigid analytic space equipped with a weight map κ: E → W, and the p-adic L-function becomes a meromorphic function on E interpolating special values across the family. Examiners may ask for the definition of the weight space as a rigid analytic space, the Amice transform and its relation to measures, the interpolation property of the Mazur-Kitagawa p-adic L-function, and the statement of the main conjecture in terms of characteristic ideals of Selmer groups. A precise answer must distinguish between the cyclotomic variable and the weight variable, explain the role of the ordinary projector e = limn→∞ Upn!, and describe how the p-adic L-function varies in Hida families.

Worked Problem: Generic Fiber of a Formal Scheme
Let K = Qp, OK = Zp, and let X = Spf Zp⟨T⟩/(T2 - p). Compute the generic fiber Xη as a rigid analytic space over Qp. Describe its reduction type and the associated Berkovich skeleton.
The algebra A = Zp⟨T⟩/(T2 - p) is topologically finitely presented over Zp. Its generic fiber is the affinoid algebra A ⊗Zp Qp = Qp⟨T⟩/(T2 - p) with the Gauss norm. The equation T2 = p defines a rigid analytic space of dimension 1. Over Qp, the polynomial T2 - p is irreducible (since p is not a square in Qp for p odd; for p=2 it factors but the extension is ramified). The affinoid algebra is a field extension L = Qp(√p) of degree 2. The Gauss norm on L extends the p-adic norm uniquely, and the affinoid space M(L) is a single point (a rigid analytic point). The special fiber is Spec Fp[T]/(T2) which is a non-reduced double point. This formal model is not semi-stable; the special fiber is not reduced. After a ramified base change K' = Qp(√p), the equation becomes (T/√p)2 = 1, so the generic fiber splits into two points. The Berkovich analytification Xan is a single point of type 2 (a Gauss point) corresponding to the valuation on L extending the p-adic valuation. The skeleton is this single point. The reduction is additive (bad reduction) because the special fiber is non-reduced. The formal model is not admissible in the sense of Raynaud because the special fiber is not reduced; an admissible blow-up would be needed to achieve semi-stable reduction.
Exam Strategy: Formal Models and Generic Fibers
When asked to compute a generic fiber, always: (1) write the affinoid algebra explicitly as a Tate algebra quotient, (2) determine whether the quotient is reduced, irreducible, or a product of fields, (3) identify the rigid space as a disjoint union of affinoid domains, (4) describe the special fiber and its singularities, (5) state whether the model is semi-stable or requires blow-up. For p-adic L-functions, memorize the interpolation formula for the Mazur-Kitagawa L-function and the definition of the Amice transform. The main conjecture is a statement about equality of ideals in the Iwasawa algebra — know the precise formulation: charΛ(Sel(K∞, T)∨) = (Lp(T)) where T is the p-adic Galois representation.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Hodge Theory for Semi-stable Varieties

Non-Archimedean Hodge theory for varieties with semi-stable reduction generalizes the classical Hodge decomposition to the p-adic setting using the Hyodo-Kato cohomology and the filtered (φ, N)-module structure. Let K be a finite extension of Qp with perfect residue field k, and let X be a proper smooth rigid analytic space over K that admits a semi-stable formal model X over OK. This means X is regular and its special fiber Xs is a reduced divisor with normal crossings. The Hyodo-Kato cohomology HiHK(Xs) is a finite-dimensional K0-vector space (where K0 = W(k)[1/p] is the maximal unramified subfield of K) equipped with a Frobenius φ, a monodromy operator N satisfying Nφ = pφN, and a filtration Fil• on HiHK(Xs) ⊗K0 K coming from the log-crystalline cohomology of the special fiber. The fundamental comparison theorem of Tsuji (and independently Niziol) states that there is a canonical isomorphism Hiét(XK̄, Qp) ⊗Qp Bst ≅ HiHK(Xs) ⊗K0 Bst compatible with φ, N, the Galois action, and the filtration. Here Bst is Fontaine's semi-stable period ring. This isomorphism identifies the p-adic étale cohomology of the generic fiber with the log-crystalline cohomology of the special fiber, realizing the p-adic analogue of the degeneration of the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence. The weight spectral sequence of Rapoport-Zink computes HiHK(Xs) in terms of the cohomology of the strata of Xs. The monodromy operator N encodes the combinatorics of the intersection complex of the special fiber: its nilpotency index is bounded by the dimension, and the weight filtration W• defined by N coincides with the filtration induced by the simplicial structure of the dual intersection complex. The Hodge-Tate decomposition for semi-stable varieties takes the form Hiét(XK̄, Qp) ⊗Qp Cp ≅ ⊕j Hi-j(X, ΩjX/K) ⊗K Cp(-j), where the Hodge numbers hi,j = dimK Hi(X, ΩjX/K) are computed by the log-de Rham cohomology of the formal model. The theory extends to the case of potentially semi-stable reduction via the semi-stable reduction theorem of Temkin. Examiners often test the definition of a semi-stable formal model, the structure of the Hyodo-Kato cohomology as a filtered (φ, N)-module, the statement of the Cst-conjecture (now theorem) and its relation to the weight spectral sequence, and the computation of Hodge-Tate weights for semi-stable varieties. A complete answer must distinguish between the Hyodo-Kato cohomology (defined over K0) and the log-crystalline cohomology (defined over K), explain the role of the log-structure on the special fiber, and describe how the monodromy operator N arises from the nearby cycles complex.

The Theory of Rigid Analytic Stacks and Their Cohomology

The theory of stacks in rigid analytic geometry, developed by Conrad, Olsson, and others, extends the classical theory of algebraic stacks to the non-Archimedean setting. A rigid analytic stack is a stack in groupoids on the site of rigid analytic spaces over K equipped with the G-topology, satisfying the usual representability conditions: the diagonal is representable by rigid analytic spaces, and there exists a smooth surjective morphism from a rigid analytic space (an atlas). The most important examples are the moduli stacks of p-divisible groups, the moduli stacks of local shtukas, and the stack of (φ, Γ)-modules. The cohomology of rigid analytic stacks is defined using the lisse-étale site or the flat site, and the theory of quasi-coherent sheaves on rigid stacks satisfies descent and admits a six-functor formalism. A key result is the Kiehl finiteness theorem for proper rigid stacks: if X is a proper rigid analytic stack with finite diagonal, then the higher direct images of a coherent sheaf under a proper morphism are coherent. The theory of rigid analytic stacks is essential for the construction of eigenvarieties as stacks (rather than just rigid spaces) and for the formulation of the p-adic Langlands correspondence in families. The stack of p-divisible groups over a rigid space S classifies p-divisible groups up to quasi-isogeny, and its rigid analytic structure is given by the Rapoport-Zink period morphism. The cohomology of the moduli stack of p-divisible groups computes the local Langlands correspondence for GLn via the work of Fargues and Scholze. In the setting of the Fargues-Fontaine curve, the stack of G-bundles BunG is a rigid analytic stack (in fact a diamond), and its cohomology with coefficients in sheaves arising from representations of the Langlands dual group realizes the local Langlands correspondence. The theory of rigid analytic stacks also provides the correct framework for the p-adic Simpson correspondence: the moduli stack of Higgs bundles and the moduli stack of (φ, Γ)-modules are rigid analytic stacks, and the correspondence is an equivalence of derived categories of quasi-coherent sheaves on these stacks. Examiners may ask for the definition of a rigid analytic stack, the conditions for a morphism to be smooth or étale in the rigid setting, the statement of Kiehl's finiteness theorem for stacks, and the role of the Rapoport-Zink period morphism in uniformizing the moduli stack of p-divisible groups. A precise answer must explain how the G-topology on rigid spaces induces a topology on stacks, why the diagonal representability condition is necessary for the existence of fiber products, and how the lisse-étale site differs from the étale site of the underlying rigid space.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Theta Functions and Their Role in Uniformization

Non-Archimedean theta functions provide the analytic data for the uniformization of abelian varieties and their moduli spaces, generalizing the classical theory of theta functions on complex tori. Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over a non-Archimedean field K with split multiplicative reduction (i.e., a Tate curve in higher dimension). The Raynaud uniformization gives an exact sequence 0 → T → E → A → 0 where T ≅ Gmg is a split torus and E is a semi-abelian variety. The universal cover of Ean is the rigid analytic space V = (K×)g × V0 where V0 is a K-vector space of dimension g. The lattice of periods is a discrete subgroup Λ ⊂ V of rank 2g, and Aan ≅ V/Λ. A theta function is a rigid analytic function θ: V → K satisfying the quasi-periodicity condition θ(v + λ) = χ(λ) eπi Q(λ) + 2πi B(λ, v) θ(v) for λ ∈ Λ, where χ: Λ → K× is a character, Q is a quadratic form, and B is a symmetric bilinear form. The space of theta functions of a given type is finite-dimensional and provides an embedding of Aan into a rigid analytic projective space. In the case of the Tate curve (g=1), the theta function is the classical Jacobi theta function θ(q, z) = ∑n∈Z qn2/2 zn which converges on the annulus |q| < |z| < 1 for |q| < 1. For higher-dimensional abelian varieties with totally degenerate reduction, the theta functions are constructed using the Mumford construction: given a period matrix Ω in the Siegel upper half-space Hg (a rigid analytic domain in the space of symmetric g×g matrices), the theta function with characteristic [ε, δ] ∈ (Q/Z)2g is θ[ε, δ](Ω, z) = ∑n∈Zg exp(πi (n+ε)t Ω (n+ε) + 2πi (n+ε)t (z+δ)). The convergence domain is a rigid analytic subspace of V × Hg. The moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties with level structure is uniformized by the Siegel upper half-space modulo the action of the symplectic group, and the theta functions provide the projective embedding of this quotient. In the non-Archimedean setting, the Siegel upper half-space is a rigid analytic space whose points correspond to period matrices of abelian varieties with totally degenerate reduction. The theory extends to the case of non-split reduction using the theory of formal abelian schemes and the Grothendieck-Messing period map. Examiners may ask for the definition of a non-Archimedean theta function, the quasi-periodicity condition, the construction of the Tate curve via theta functions, the relation between the period matrix and the rigid analytic uniformization, and the role of theta functions in the compactification of the moduli space of abelian varieties (the Mumford compactification). A complete answer must distinguish between the additive and multiplicative uniformizations, explain the convergence conditions for the theta series in the non-Archimedean norm, and describe how the theta divisor on the abelian variety corresponds to the zero locus of the theta function.

  • Confusing the generic fiber functor with the analytification functor — the generic fiber produces a rigid space, while analytification produces a Berkovich space; they are related by the comparison map but have different categories.
  • Assuming every formal model is admissible — admissibility requires the special fiber to be reduced; non-reduced models require admissible blow-ups to become admissible.
  • Thinking the weight space is always a rigid analytic space — it is the generic fiber of Spf Λ, which is a rigid space only when Λ is a Tate algebra; for higher-rank Iwasawa algebras it is a higher-dimensional weight space.
  • Mixing up the Hyodo-Kato cohomology and the log-crystalline cohomology — the former is a K0-vector space with φ and N, the latter is a K-vector space with filtration; they are related by base change and the comparison isomorphism.
  • Believing that rigid analytic stacks are just rigid spaces with group actions — stacks have non-trivial automorphism groups and require a stacky site (lisse-étale) for cohomology; the diagonal representability condition is essential.
  • Assuming theta functions converge everywhere on the universal cover — non-Archimedean theta series converge only on certain rigid analytic domains (annuli or polydiscs) determined by the valuation of the period matrix.
  • Overlooking the role of the log-structure in semi-stable reduction — the log-structure on the special fiber is necessary to define the Hyodo-Kato cohomology and the monodromy operator N; without it, the weight spectral sequence does not degenerate correctly.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of Global Shtukas

Global shtukas are the function‑field analogues of Galois representations and play a central role in the geometric Langlands correspondence over finite fields. Let X be a smooth projective curve over F_q and fix a finite set of places S. A global shtuka of rank r with legs in S consists of a vector bundle E on X together with an isomorphism τ^*E → E outside S and prescribed modifications at the legs. The moduli stack Sht_G of global G-shtukas (for a reductive group G) is an algebraic stack of finite type over F_q. Drinfeld and Lafforgue constructed a uniformization of Sht_G by a product of Drinfeld upper half‑spaces when G = GL_r and the legs are sufficiently generic. In the non‑Archimedean setting one replaces F_q by a complete discretely valued field K with perfect residue field and considers the rigid analytic generic fiber of the formal moduli scheme. The uniformization then takes the form

Sht_Gan ≅ bigl( Ω^r × A bigr) / Γ

where Ω^r is the Drinfeld symmetric domain of dimension r-1 (a rigid analytic space), A is a finite‑dimensional rigid analytic space parametrizing the “central” data, and Γ is a discrete subgroup of G(K) acting properly discontinuously. The quotient is taken in the category of rigid analytic stacks (or Berkovich stacks). This description makes the cohomology of Sht_Gan accessible via the Leray spectral sequence for the projection to the locally symmetric space Γ backslash Ω^r. The key technical input is the properness of the period map, proved by Hartl and Viehmann using the theory of boundedness of global shtukas. Examiners often ask for the definition of a global shtuka, the statement of the uniformization theorem for GL_r, and the role of the Drinfeld symmetric domain as the non‑Archimedean analogue of the Hermitian symmetric domain. A complete answer must distinguish between the local uniformization (Rapoport–Zink spaces) and the global uniformization, explain why the legs must be “sufficiently generic” to avoid stacky stabilizers, and indicate how the Hecke correspondences act on the uniformized space.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Mirror Symmetry and the SYZ Conjecture

Mirror symmetry predicts an equivalence between the derived Fukaya category of a Calabi–Yau manifold and the derived category of coherent sheaves on its mirror. In the non‑Archimedean world, Kontsevich and Soibelman formulated a version of the Strominger–Yau–Zaslow (SYZ) conjecture using Berkovich analytic spaces. Let K be a non‑Archimedean field with valuation ring R and residue field k. A maximally degenerate Calabi–Yau variety over K admits a formal model X over R whose special fiber X_k is a reduced union of toric varieties meeting along toric strata. The Berkovich analytification Xan contains a skeleton Sk(X) which is a piecewise‑linear space homeomorphic to the dual intersection complex of X_k. The SYZ conjecture in this setting asserts that the mirror X^vee is obtained by fiberwise dualizing the torus fibration on a suitable open subset of Xan, and that the skeleton Sk(X^vee) is canonically identified with Sk(X) equipped with the opposite integral affine structure. Gross, Hacking, and Keel proved this for cluster varieties, and Nicaise and Xu extended it to maximally degenerate Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces in toric varieties. The non‑Archimedean mirror functor sends a Lagrangian section of the torus fibration (a tropical cycle) to a coherent sheaf on the mirror, and the wall‑crossing formulas for scattering diagrams become the non‑Archimedean analogues of the holomorphic disk counts. Examiners may ask for the definition of the skeleton of a Berkovich space, the construction of the integral affine structure on the skeleton, and the statement of the non‑Archimedean SYZ theorem for cluster varieties. A strong answer should explain how the valuation map val: Xan → Sk(X) replaces the moment map in the complex SYZ picture, why the monodromy of the affine structure is captured by the scattering diagram, and how the mirror map is expressed in terms of the tropical vertex group.

Worked Example: Computing a Skeleton
Let K = C((t)) with the t-adic valuation. Consider the hypersurface X ⊂ (G_m)3 defined by x + y + z + t xyz = 1. Describe the skeleton of the Berkovich analytification Xan and its integral affine structure.
The equation defines a formal scheme X over C[[t]] whose special fiber is the union of four coordinate hyperplanes in P2 meeting transversely. The dual intersection complex is a tetrahedron. The valuation map val: (G_m3)an → R3 sends (x,y,z) to (v(x),v(y),v(z)). On Xan the relation x+y+z+t xyz = 1 forces the image to lie in the tropical hypersurface Trop(X) = { (u,v,w) ∈ R3 mid min(u,v,w, u+v+w) is attained at least twice }. This tropical hypersurface is exactly the skeleton Sk(X), a piecewise‑linear 2‑sphere subdivided into four triangles. The integral affine structure on each triangle is the standard one induced from R3; the gluing maps are integral affine because the tropical hypersurface is balanced. Thus Sk(X) is a compact integral affine manifold with singularities at the vertices, matching the expected mirror skeleton.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for a non‑Archimedean mirror construction, first identify the formal model and its special fiber. Draw the dual intersection complex, then write down the tropicalization of the defining equations. The skeleton is the tropical variety; the integral affine structure comes from the lattice of characters of the torus. Mention the role of the scattering diagram if wall‑crossing is relevant.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Calabi–Yau Varieties and Their Period Maps

Over the complex numbers, the period map sends a Calabi–Yau manifold to its Hodge structure, and the local Torelli theorem holds for many classes. In the non‑Archimedean setting, the analogue of the period domain is a rigid analytic space parametrizing filtered (φ,N)-modules (or equivalently, log‑crystalline Hodge structures) arising from semistable degenerations. Let K be a complete discretely valued field of characteristic zero with perfect residue field k. A semistable Calabi–Yau variety over K admits a formal model X over the valuation ring whose special fiber is a reduced simple normal crossings divisor. The Hyodo–Kato cohomology HHK^i(X_k) carries a Frobenius φ, a monodromy operator N, and a weight filtration. After tensoring with K and applying the p-adic comparison isomorphism, one obtains a filtered vector space HdR^i(X/K) whose Hodge filtration satisfies Griffiths transversality. The period map

P: Man longrightarrow Dan

sends the rigid analytic moduli space Man of such Calabi–Yau varieties to the rigid analytic period domain Dan classifying admissible filtered (φ,N)-modules with fixed Hodge numbers. Niziol, Andreatta–Iovita–Kim, and others proved that P is étale and satisfies a local Torelli theorem when the Hodge numbers satisfy hp,0=0 for 0

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of Vector Bundles on Curves

Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a non‑Archimedean field K. The moduli stack Bun_n(C) of rank n vector bundles on C is an Artin stack locally of finite type. Over C, the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem identifies the subspace of semistable bundles of degree zero with the moduli of unitary representations of π1(C). In the non‑Archimedean world, Faltings constructed a rigid analytic uniformization of the semistable locus Bun_nss(C) using the Bruhat–Tits building B(GL_n(K)). The building is a simplicial complex on which GL_n(K) acts properly; its geometric realization carries a natural rigid analytic structure via the theory of Berkovich spaces. Faltings showed that there is a GL_n(K)-equivariant morphism

B(GL_n(K))an longrightarrow Bun_nss(C)an

which identifies the quotient by a suitable discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ GL_n(K) (the “monodromy group” of a universal bundle) with the semistable moduli space. The fibers of this map are affinoid domains, and the map is a finite étale cover over the stable locus. Later work of Raynaud and of Mochizuki extended this to parabolic bundles and to the case where C is a Mumford curve (uniformized by a Schottky group). The uniformization makes the cohomology of Bun_nss(C) computable via the spectral sequence associated to the action of Γ on the building. Examiners often ask for the definition of the Bruhat–Tits building as a rigid analytic space, the statement of Faltings’ uniformization theorem, and the relation between the building’s apartments and the Harder–Narasimhan stratification. A thorough answer should describe how the valuation of the determinant of a bundle gives a map to the building, why the monodromy group Γ is a lattice in GL_n(K), and how the uniformization fails for unstable bundles (the map is not surjective on the whole stack).

  • Confusing the Drinfeld symmetric domain with the Bruhat–Tits building — the former uniformizes moduli of shtukas, the latter uniformizes moduli of vector bundles; they are different rigid analytic spaces with different group actions.
  • Assuming the non‑Archimedean SYZ mirror is always a Calabi–Yau variety — the mirror may be a non‑commutative space or a Landau–Ginzburg model; the skeleton only captures the tropical part of the mirror.
  • Thinking the period map for non‑Archimedean Calabi–Yau varieties is defined on the whole moduli space — it is only defined on the semistable locus; extending it requires the minimal model program in the non‑Archimedean setting.
  • Believing that Faltings’ uniformization works for all vector bundles — it only covers the semistable locus; unstable bundles correspond to points in the building that are not in the image of the period map.
  • Mixing up the Hyodo–Kato cohomology with the log‑crystalline cohomology of the generic fiber — the former lives over the fraction field of the Witt vectors, the latter over the base field; they are related by a comparison isomorphism that requires a choice of Frobenius lift.
  • Overlooking the role of the scattering diagram in the non‑Archimedean SYZ conjecture — the diagram encodes the wall‑crossing of the affine structure and is essential for reconstructing the mirror algebra.
  • Assuming the skeleton of a Berkovich space is always a manifold — it is a piecewise‑linear space with singularities at the vertices of the dual intersection complex; the integral affine structure may have monodromy around these singularities.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of Higgs Bundles on Curves

Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a complete non‑Archimedean field K. A Higgs bundle on C is a pair (E, θ) where E is a vector bundle and θ ∈ H⁰(C, End(E) ⊗ Ω¹C) satisfies θ ∧ θ = 0. The moduli stack MHiggs(C, n, d) of rank n, degree d semistable Higgs bundles carries a natural rigid analytic structure via the analytification functor. Over ℂ, the non‑abelian Hodge theorem identifies this space with the character variety of representations of π₁(C) into GLn(ℂ). In the non‑Archimedean setting, a parallel uniformization was developed by Mochizuki, Deninger–Werner, and later by Chen–Zhu using the theory of (φ,Γ)‑modules and the Fargues–Fontaine curve.

The key geometric input is the Bruhat–Tits building B(GLn(K)) equipped with its rigid analytic structure. One constructs a period map p : B(GLn(K))an → MHiggs(C, n, d)an by sending a point of the building (a lattice class in Kⁿ) to the Higgs bundle obtained from the associated filtered vector bundle on the Fargues–Fontaine curve. The map is GLn(K)‑equivariant and its fibers are affinoid domains. The image of p is precisely the semistable locus; unstable Higgs bundles correspond to points of the building that are not in the image, reflecting the Harder–Narasimhan stratification on the moduli side.

A deep result of Chen–Zhu (2021) shows that the period map is a finite étale cover over the stable locus, and that the quotient of the building by a suitable discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ GLn(K) (the monodromy group of the universal Higgs bundle) recovers the rigid analytic moduli space. This uniformization makes the cohomology of MHiggs computable via the spectral sequence of the Γ‑action on the building, and it provides a non‑Archimedean analogue of the Hitchin fibration: the base of the fibration is identified with the space of characteristic polynomials of the Higgs field, which is an affinoid space isomorphic to a product of closed unit discs.

Examiners often ask for the definition of the period map in terms of the Fargues–Fontaine curve, the statement of the Chen–Zhu uniformization theorem, and the relation between the building’s apartments and the Hitchin base. A thorough answer should explain how the valuation of the determinant of the Higgs bundle gives a map to the building, why Γ is a lattice, and why the uniformization fails for unstable Higgs bundles (the map is not surjective on the whole stack). Confusing the Higgs bundle uniformization with the vector bundle uniformization of Faltings is a common error; the former involves a Higgs field and the Hitchin system, while the latter uses only the underlying vector bundle.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p‑adic Galois Representations

Let K be a finite extension of ℚp and let GK = Gal(K̄/K) be its absolute Galois group. The moduli space of p‑adic Galois representations of dimension n with fixed Hodge–Tate weights is a rigid analytic stack Repn(GK)an. Fontaine’s theory of (φ,Γ)‑modules provides an equivalence between the category of p‑adic representations of GK and the category of étale (φ,Γ)‑modules over the Robba ring RK. This equivalence is compatible with the rigid analytic structure: the moduli of (φ,Γ)‑modules is represented by a rigid analytic variety M(φ,Γ) which is a finite disjoint union of affinoid spaces.

The non‑Archimedean uniformization of Repn(GK)an is achieved via the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GLn(K). Emerton’s completed cohomology of the tower of modular curves (or Shimura varieties) yields a locally analytic representation of GLn(K) whose locally algebraic vectors correspond to automorphic Galois representations. The work of Colmez, Berger, and Breuil constructs a functor from (φ,Γ)‑modules to locally analytic representations of GLn(K) which, on the level of moduli, gives a rigid analytic morphism M(φ,Γ) → Repn(GK)an. This morphism is a finite étale cover over the locus of irreducible, generic representations.

A crucial technical tool is the theory of the p‑adic period rings BdR, Bst, Bcris and their associated rigid analytic spaces. The Hodge–Tate period map HT : Repn(GK)an → Flagn sends a representation to its Hodge–Tate filtration; it is a morphism of rigid analytic spaces which is étale at points corresponding to de Rham representations with distinct Hodge–Tate weights. The fibers of HT are affinoid domains parameterizing extensions of the given filtered vector space.

Examiners frequently test the definition of the Robba ring as a rigid analytic space, the statement of the Fontaine equivalence, and the construction of the Hodge–Tate period map. A complete answer must describe how the (φ,Γ)‑module structure encodes the Galois action, why the Robba ring is a Fréchet–Stein algebra, and how the local Langlands correspondence enters the uniformization. A typical trap is to conflate the (φ,Γ)‑module moduli with the eigenvariety; the eigenvariety parameterizes systems of Hecke eigenvalues, while the (φ,Γ)‑module moduli parameterizes Galois representations directly.

Worked Example: Constructing the Hodge–Tate Period Map
Let V be a 2‑dimensional de Rham representation of Gℚp with Hodge–Tate weights {0,1}. Describe the rigid analytic space parameterizing such representations and the Hodge–Tate period map to the flag variety.
The moduli of 2‑dimensional de Rham representations with fixed Hodge–Tate weights is an open rigid analytic subspace of the (φ,Γ)‑module moduli M(φ,Γ). By Fontaine’s equivalence, a representation corresponds to a rank‑2 (φ,Γ)‑module D over the Robba ring R. The Hodge–Tate filtration is recovered from D ⊗R BdR as a decreasing filtration on a 2‑dimensional BdR-vector space. The associated graded pieces have dimensions given by the Hodge–Tate weights, so the filtration is a line in a 2‑space, i.e. a point of ℙ¹. The period map HT sends the point of M(φ,Γ) corresponding to D to this line. The map is rigid analytic and étale at points where the filtered (φ,Γ)‑module is generic (distinct weights, no non‑trivial extensions). The fiber over a given line is an affinoid domain parameterizing extensions of the corresponding filtered vector space.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a uniformization theorem, first identify the moduli problem (vector bundles, Higgs bundles, Galois representations, shtukas). Then recall the associated building or symmetric domain (Bruhat–Tits, Drinfeld upper half‑space, Rapoport–Zink space). State the period map, its equivariance, the discrete group Γ, and the locus where it is an isomorphism (stable/semistable/generic). Mention the cohomological consequence (spectral sequence) and the failure on the unstable locus. This template covers all major uniformization results in the syllabus.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Analytic Spaces over Higher Rank Valued Fields

Classical rigid analytic geometry is built over a field K equipped with a rank‑1 valuation (i.e. a valuation with value group a subgroup of ℝ). Many arithmetic applications, however, require base fields with higher rank valuations, such as the field of formal Laurent series k((t)) with the t‑adic valuation (rank 1) or the field of generalized power series with value group ℤⁿ (lexicographic order). Huber’s theory of adic spaces provides a framework that works for arbitrary valuation rings, but the classical Tate‑Kiehl approach using affinoid algebras and the G‑topology must be adapted.

Let K be a complete valued field whose valuation v : K× → Γ has value group Γ a totally ordered abelian group of rank > 1. An affinoid K‑algebra is still defined as a quotient of the Tate algebra K⟨T₁,…,\Tn⟩ by a closed ideal, but the supremum norm now takes values in Γ ∪ {0}. The Berkovich spectrum of such an algebra is a locally compact, Hausdorff space, but it is no longer locally path‑connected in general; its topology reflects the higher rank of the valuation. The G‑topology on the category of affinoid domains is defined by admissible coverings that are finite and satisfy the usual acyclicity condition for the structure sheaf. Kiehl’s Theorem A and B hold for coherent sheaves on these spaces, provided one works with the appropriate notion of “coherent” (finitely presented modules over the structure sheaf).

A major difference from the rank‑1 case is the behavior of the reduction map. For a rank‑1 valuation, the reduction of an affinoid space is a scheme of finite type over the residue field. For higher rank, the reduction is a formal scheme over a valuation ring of higher rank, and the special fiber may be non‑Noetherian. The theory of formal models (Raynaud’s generic fiber functor) extends: a formal scheme X over the valuation ring OK gives a rigid analytic generic fiber Xη, and every rigid analytic space over K admits a formal model if K is discretely valued of higher rank? Actually, if the valuation is not discrete, formal models may not exist in the usual sense; one must use adic formal schemes or the language of v‑stacks.

Applications include the study of families of p‑adic representations over higher dimensional bases (e.g. eigenvarieties over weight space which is a rigid analytic space over a higher rank field), and the construction of the Fargues–Fontaine curve over a perfectoid field with a higher rank valuation. Examiners may ask for the definition of an affinoid algebra over a higher rank valued field, the statement of Kiehl’s Theorem A/B in this context, and the obstruction to the existence of formal models. A common mistake is to assume that the Berkovich spectrum of a higher rank affinoid algebra is a tree; it is a more complicated space with non‑trivial higher homotopy groups.

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of Drinfeld Modules

Let F be a global function field of characteristic p with a fixed place ∞, and let A be the ring of functions regular away from ∞. A Drinfeld A‑module of rank r over a complete non‑Archimedean field K (of characteristic p) is a homomorphism φ : A → EndK(𝔾a) such that for each a ∈ A, the map φa is a polynomial in the Frobenius endomorphism τ with leading term aτr deg a. The moduli space of Drinfeld modules with level structure is a rigid analytic variety MDrin(r, N) over K.

Drinfeld’s original uniformization (1974) identifies the rigid analytic space associated to the moduli of Drinfeld modules of rank 2 with the quotient of the Drinfeld upper half‑space Ω² = ℙ¹an ℙ¹(K) by the action of GL₂(A). For higher rank, the uniformization uses the Bruhat–Tits building of GLr(K) and the theory of shtukas. Lafforgue’s proof of the global Langlands correspondence for GLr over function fields relies on the cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas, which is uniformized by a product of Drinfeld upper half‑spaces.

In the rigid analytic setting, the uniformization map is a morphism of rigid analytic spaces π : Ωr → MDrin(r, N) which is étale and surjective onto the stable locus. The fibers are affinoid domains, and the group of deck transformations is a discrete subgroup of GLr(K) commensurable with GLr(A). The cohomology of MDrin can be computed via the spectral sequence of the group action on the building, yielding the local Langlands correspondence for GLr(K) as a by‑product.

Examiners often ask for the definition of the Drinfeld upper half‑space as a rigid analytic space, the statement of Drinfeld’s uniformization theorem for rank 2, and the relation between the building’s apartments and the Harder–Narasimhan stratification of the moduli of Drinfeld modules. A thorough answer should explain how the valuation of the determinant of a Drinfeld module gives a map to the building, why the discrete group is a lattice, and why the uniformization fails for unstable Drinfeld modules (the map is not surjective on the whole stack). Confusing the Drinfeld upper half‑space with the Bruhat–Tits building is a frequent error; the former is a rigid analytic domain in ℙ¹, the latter is a simplicial complex with a rigid analytic structure, and they play different roles in uniformization of different moduli problems.

Common Traps

  • Assuming the period map for Higgs bundles is defined on the whole moduli stack; it is only defined on the semistable locus.
  • Confusing the (φ,Γ)‑module moduli space with the eigenvariety; they parameterize different objects.
  • Thinking the Berkovich spectrum of a higher rank affinoid algebra is a tree; it has non‑trivial higher homotopy.
  • Believing formal models always exist for rigid spaces over higher rank valued fields; they may not without adic formal schemes.
  • Mixing up the Drinfeld upper half‑space with the Bruhat–Tits building; they uniformize different moduli problems.
  • Assuming the Hodge–Tate period map is étale everywhere; it is only étale at generic de Rham points with distinct weights.

These traps highlight the precise loci where uniformization and period maps are valid and the distinctions between closely related rigid analytic objects.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Automorphic Forms on Unitary Shimura Varieties

Unitary Shimura varieties attached to a division algebra with involution over a CM field provide a natural setting for the p-adic Langlands program beyond GLn. Their rigid analytic generic fibers admit a description as quotients of a p-adic symmetric domain by an arithmetic group, mirroring the complex uniformization by Hermitian symmetric spaces. The p-adic symmetric domain is constructed as a rigid analytic open subset of a flag variety, obtained by removing a union of Schubert cells defined by the Hodge–Newton filtration. The resulting space carries a natural action of the unitary group over the local field, and the quotient by a compact open subgroup yields the rigid analytic Shimura variety. This uniformization is compatible with the Hodge–Tate period map, which identifies the generic fiber with a quotient of the p-adic period domain by the same arithmetic group. The period map is étale on the μ-ordinary locus and extends to a morphism of adic spaces, allowing the transfer of automorphic forms to p-adic families. The construction of eigenvarieties for unitary groups relies on this uniformization: overconvergent cohomology of the Shimura variety is computed via the cohomology of the symmetric domain, and the Hecke operators act through correspondences that respect the quotient structure. The resulting eigenvariety parameterizes finite-slope p-adic automorphic forms and interpolates classical automorphic representations. A key technical point is the control theorem, which identifies the classical part of the eigenvariety with the cohomology of the Shimura variety at a fixed level, and the proof uses the properness of the Hodge–Tate period map on the μ-ordinary locus together with the theory of (φ,Γ)-modules for the unitary group.

The uniformization also interacts with the theory of p-adic Hodge theory for the associated Galois representations. The Galois representation attached to a classical automorphic form on the unitary group is known to be de Rham and potentially crystalline, and its Hodge–Tate weights are determined by the Hodge cocharacter of the Shimura datum. The p-adic period domain parametrizes filtered φ-modules with these weights, and the period map sends a point of the Shimura variety to the filtered φ-module of the associated p-divisible group. This description is essential for the construction of the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for unitary groups, where one matches p-adic automorphic forms with p-adic Galois representations via the eigenvariety and the deformation rings of Galois representations. The uniformization provides a geometric bridge: the symmetric domain is a rigid analytic space whose points correspond to certain filtrations on a fixed isocrystal, and the arithmetic quotient organizes these filtrations into families. The theory of perfectoid Shimura varieties at infinite level further refines this picture, as the infinite-level Shimura variety becomes a perfectoid space that uniformizes the whole tower, and the period map becomes a pro-étale cover of the period domain. This perfectoid uniformization is the starting point for the construction of the p-adic Langlands correspondence in the sense of Scholze, where the cohomology of the infinite-level Shimura variety carries an action of the p-adic Langlands group and the Hecke algebra simultaneously.

Examiners often test the distinction between the complex and p-adic uniformizations: the complex uniformization uses a Hermitian symmetric domain which is a bounded symmetric domain in ℂN, while the p-adic uniformization uses a rigid analytic domain in a flag variety defined by the non-vanishing of certain Hodge–Newton determinants. Another common question asks for the definition of the μ-ordinary locus and its role in the control theorem; the answer must mention that the μ-ordinary locus is the open subset where the Hodge polygon coincides with the Newton polygon, and that the Hodge–Tate period map is étale there, allowing the identification of classical cohomology with overconvergent cohomology. A subtle trap is to assume that the period map is defined on the whole Shimura variety; it is only defined on the μ-ordinary locus and extends to a partially defined morphism on the whole space, with indeterminacy along the non-ordinary strata.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Period Maps for Abelian Varieties with Real Multiplication

Abelian varieties with real multiplication by the ring of integers of a totally real field provide a rich class of Shimura varieties of Hodge type. Their p-adic uniformization is governed by the theory of p-divisible groups with additional endomorphism structure. Let A be an abelian variety of dimension g over a p-adic field K with an action of OF, where F is a totally real field of degree g. The associated p-divisible group G = A[p∞] carries an OF ⊗ ℤp-action, and its Dieudonné module is a filtered φ-module with an OF ⊗ ℚp-action. The Hodge filtration is a direct sum of rank-one subspaces indexed by the embeddings τ: F → ℚp, and the Hodge–Tate weights are determined by the CM type if the abelian variety has complex multiplication, or more generally by the signature of the real multiplication. The p-adic period domain for such filtered φ-modules is a rigid analytic space that parametrizes admissible filtrations on a fixed isocrystal with OF-action. The Hodge–Tate period map sends a point of the rigid analytic Shimura variety to the Hodge filtration of the associated p-divisible group, and its image lies in the admissible locus defined by the weak admissibility condition of Fontaine. The map is étale on the ordinary locus, where the Newton polygon equals the Hodge polygon, and it extends to a morphism of adic spaces on the whole Shimura variety.

The uniformization of the moduli space of such abelian varieties can be described as a quotient of the p-adic period domain by a discrete subgroup of the automorphism group of the isocrystal. This discrete group is the group of OF-linear quasi-isogenies of the p-divisible group, which is commensurable with the arithmetic group defining the Shimura variety. The quotient is taken in the category of rigid analytic spaces, and the resulting space is isomorphic to the generic fiber of the Shimura variety. The proof uses the theory of Rapoport–Zink spaces: the Rapoport–Zink space for the p-divisible group with OF-action is a formal scheme whose generic fiber is the p-adic period domain, and the uniformization map is induced by the universal property of the Rapoport–Zink space. The Rapoport–Zink uniformization theorem identifies the formal completion of the Shimura variety along its supersingular locus with a quotient of the Rapoport–Zink space by a discrete group. This identification is crucial for the computation of the cohomology of the Shimura variety via the Lefschetz trace formula and for the construction of p-adic L-functions by the method of Eisenstein measures. The period map also plays a central role in the p-adic Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture, where the restriction of the period map to a cycle defined by a unitary Shimura variety is related to the derivative of a p-adic L-function.

Key points for examination: the definition of the admissible locus in the period domain as the set of filtrations satisfying the weak admissibility inequalities for all φ-stable subspaces; the statement that the Hodge–Tate period map is a local isomorphism on the ordinary locus and a finite morphism on the whole space; the description of the Rapoport–Zink space as a formal scheme representing the functor of deformations of a p-divisible group with OF-action; and the fact that the uniformization map is compatible with Hecke correspondences, which act on the period domain via the action of the automorphism group of the isocrystal. A frequent mistake is to confuse the period domain for abelian varieties with real multiplication with the period domain for GLg; the former is a closed rigid analytic subspace defined by the OF-action, and its dimension is smaller. Another trap is to assume that the period map is defined on the whole moduli stack; it is only defined on the rigid analytic generic fiber, and its extension to the boundary of a toroidal compactification requires the theory of log structures.

Worked Example: Computing the Hodge–Tate Period Map on the Ordinary Locus
Let A be an abelian surface over ℚp with real multiplication by ℤ[√5] such that the two embeddings τ1, τ2 give Hodge–Tate weights (0,1) and (1,0) respectively. Describe the image of the ordinary locus under the Hodge–Tate period map and explain why the map is étale there.
The p-divisible group G = A[p∞] splits as G1 × G2 according to the idempotents of ℤ[√5] ⊗ ℤp. On the ordinary locus each Gi is an extension of an étale part of rank 1 by a multiplicative part of rank 1. The Hodge filtration on the Dieudonné module D(G) is a direct sum of two rank-one subspaces Fil1D(G) = Fil1D(G1) ⊕ Fil1D(G2). The condition that the filtration is admissible forces Fil1D(G1) to be the subspace where τ1 acts with weight 1, and similarly for τ2. Thus the period map sends an ordinary point to the unique filtration compatible with the given Hodge–Tate weights. The tangent space of the period domain at this filtration is identified with Hom(Fil1, D/Fil1) which is one-dimensional for each factor, and the differential of the period map is an isomorphism because the Kodaira–Spencer map for the universal deformation of an ordinary p-divisible group is an isomorphism. Hence the period map is étale on the ordinary locus.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks for the definition of the admissible locus, write the weak admissibility inequalities explicitly: for every φ-stable subspace N ⊂ D, the slope of N (valuation of det φ on N divided by rank) must be ≤ the Hodge slope (dimension of Fil1N divided by rank). Mention that equality for all N characterizes the weakly admissible locus, and that the admissible locus is the subset where the filtration comes from a p-divisible group. This precise statement earns full marks.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Local Systems on Rigid Analytic Curves

The moduli space of p-adic local systems on a smooth rigid analytic curve X over a p-adic field K is a rigid analytic stack that parameterizes continuous representations of the étale fundamental group π1(X) into GLn(ℚp). Its uniformization is achieved via the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, which identifies p-adic local systems with overconvergent isocrystals with a Frobenius structure, i.e., (φ,∇)-modules on the Robba ring. The correspondence is constructed by first associating to a local system its de Rham complex with its natural connection, then applying the theory of (φ,Γ)-modules to obtain a (φ,∇)-module on the Robba ring. The resulting object is an overconvergent isocrystal on X, and the functor is an equivalence of categories after inverting p. The moduli stack of (φ,∇)-modules is a rigid analytic space that can be described as a quotient of a certain period domain by a discrete group. The period domain parametrizes filtered (φ,∇)-modules with fixed Hodge–Tate weights, and the uniformization map sends a local system to its associated filtered (φ,∇)-module via the p-adic Hodge theory of the curve. This map is a local isomorphism on the de Rham locus, where the local system is de Rham at all points of X, and it extends to a morphism on the whole stack.

The geometry of the moduli stack is controlled by the theory of p-adic Simpson correspondence, which relates Higgs bundles on X to p-adic local systems. The non-abelian Hodge theory of Deninger–Werner and later of Liu–Zhu provides a homeomorphism between the Betti moduli space (local systems) and the Dolbeault moduli space (Higgs bundles) after passing to the associated graded of the Hodge filtration. The uniformization of the Betti moduli space by the period domain is compatible with this homeomorphism: the period map factors through the Dolbeault moduli space, and the fibers of the period map are the isomonodromic deformation spaces. The isomonodromic deformation equations are a p-adic analogue of the Schlesinger equations, and their solutions are given by the horizontal sections of the Gauss–Manin connection on the moduli space of (φ,∇)-modules. The resulting uniformization expresses the moduli stack as a quotient of a rigid analytic space of solutions to the isomonodromic equations by the action of the mapping class group of the curve. This description is essential for the construction of the p-adic Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields, where the moduli of local systems on a curve over a finite field is uniformized by the Drinfeld upper half-space, and the p-adic analogue replaces the Drinfeld upper half-space by the p-adic period domain.

Examination focus: the definition of the Robba ring and the category of (φ,∇)-modules over it; the statement of the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence as an equivalence between the category of p-adic local systems and the category of overconvergent (φ,∇)-modules; the description of the period domain for filtered (φ,∇)-modules and the fact that the period map is étale on the de Rham locus; the role of the p-adic Simpson correspondence in identifying the Betti and Dolbeault moduli spaces. A common error is to claim that the period map is defined on the whole moduli stack of local systems; it is only defined on the de Rham locus, and its extension to the non-de Rham locus requires the theory of (φ,Γ)-modules with non-integral Hodge–Tate weights. Another trap is to confuse the Robba ring with the ring of bounded functions on the open unit disc; the Robba ring consists of functions convergent on some annulus 1−ε < |T| < 1, and its elements have a well-defined radius of convergence.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Galois Representations via the Fargues–Fontaine Curve

The Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF = Proj ⊕n≥0 BdR+/ξn provides a geometric object whose vector bundles classify p-adic Galois representations of a perfectoid field. The moduli stack of p-adic Galois representations of a fixed dimension n is uniformized by the stack of vector bundles on XFF via the equivalence of categories established by Fargues and Fontaine: the category of continuous representations of Gal(K) on ℚp-vector spaces is equivalent to the category of vector bundles on XFF that are étale with respect to the Frobenius. The uniformization map sends a Galois representation to its associated vector bundle, and the moduli stack of representations is identified with the quotient of the space of modifications of the trivial bundle by the action of the loop group GLn(ℚp[[t]]). This description is the geometric incarnation of the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GLn(K). The space of modifications is a rigid analytic space that can be stratified by the Harder–Narasimhan polygon of the vector bundle, and the period map from the moduli of representations to the flag variety is the map that sends a modification to the induced filtration on the fiber at the point ∞. The map is a local isomorphism on the weakly admissible locus, which corresponds to de Rham representations, and its fibers are the isocrystals with fixed Hodge–Tate weights.

The uniformization also interacts with the theory of diamonds and v-stacks introduced by Scholze. The moduli stack of p-adic Galois representations is a v-stack, and the Fargues–Fontaine curve is a diamond. The equivalence of categories is realized as an equivalence of v-stacks between the stack of representations and the stack of vector bundles on the curve. This v-stack perspective allows one to define the moduli of representations over arbitrary perfectoid bases and to construct the Hecke operators as correspondences on the moduli stack. The Hecke operators act on the cohomology of the moduli stack, and the resulting eigenvarieties parameterize p-adic families of Galois representations. The geometry of the Fargues–Fontaine curve also provides a proof of the local Langlands correspondence for GLn via the cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas for the group GLn over the function field of the curve. The uniformization of the moduli of shtukas by the product of the Fargues–Fontaine curve and the Drinfeld upper half-space yields a geometric realization of the local Langlands correspondence as a correspondence between the cohomology of the moduli of shtukas and the cohomology of the moduli of representations.

Key examination points: the definition of the Fargues–Fontaine curve as a projective scheme over a perfectoid field; the statement of the Fargues–Fontaine equivalence between Galois representations and étale vector bundles; the description of the moduli of modifications as a rigid analytic space and the Harder–Narasimhan stratification; the fact that the period map is étale on the de Rham locus and its relation to the Hodge–Tate period map for Shimura varieties. A frequent mistake is to assume that every vector bundle on the Fargues–Fontaine curve comes from a Galois representation; only the étale bundles (those trivialized by a finite extension of the base) correspond to representations. Another trap is to confuse the Fargues–Fontaine curve with the usual projective line; the curve is not a scheme over the base field but a scheme over the tilt of the perfectoid field, and its points are not classical points but valuations of higher rank.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Differential Equations on the Robba Ring

The moduli space of p-adic differential equations on the Robba ring is a rigid analytic stack that parameterizes (φ,∇)-modules with a fixed rank and prescribed Frobenius slopes. Its uniformization is achieved by the theory of the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, which identifies (φ,∇)-modules with p-adic local systems on the punctured open unit disc. The Robba ring ℛ is the ring of functions convergent on some annulus 1−ε < |T| < 1, and a (φ,∇)-module over ℛ is a finite free ℛ-module equipped with a Frobenius-semilinear isomorphism φ and a connection ∇ satisfying the Leibniz rule and the compatibility φ∘∇ = p∇∘φ. The moduli stack of such objects is stratified by the Newton polygon of the Frobenius, and each stratum is a rigid analytic space that can be uniformized by a period domain. The period domain parametrizes filtered (φ,∇)-modules with fixed Hodge–Tate weights, and the period map sends a (φ,∇)-module to its associated filtered module via the p-adic Hodge theory of the Robba ring. The map is a local isomorphism on the de Rham locus, where the (φ,∇)-module is overconvergent and comes from a p-adic differential equation on a wide open disc.

The uniformization of the moduli of (φ,∇)-modules is closely related to the theory of p-adic differential equations of Kedlaya and the theory of (φ,Γ)-modules of Fontaine. The Robba ring carries an action of the group Γ = ℤp×, and a (φ,Γ)-module is a (φ,∇)-module equipped with a compatible Γ-action. The category of (φ,Γ)-modules is equivalent to the category of p-adic Galois representations of ℚp. The moduli stack of (φ,Γ)-modules is therefore a uniformization of the moduli of Galois representations, and the period map factors through the moduli of (φ,∇)-modules. The geometry of the moduli of (φ,∇)-modules is also controlled by the theory of the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2(ℚp), where the moduli of two-dimensional (φ,Γ)-modules is identified with the eigencurve. The eigencurve is a rigid analytic curve that parameterizes finite-slope p-adic modular forms, and its points correspond to (φ,Γ)-modules that are trianguline. The uniformization of the eigencurve by the moduli of (φ,∇)-modules is given by the map that sends a trianguline (φ,Γ)-module to its associated (φ,∇)-module, and the fibers of this map are the spaces of triangulations.

Examination focus: the definition of the Robba ring and the category of (φ,∇)-modules; the statement of the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence as an equivalence between (φ,∇)-modules and p-adic local systems on the punctured disc; the description of the period domain for filtered (φ,∇)-modules and the étaleness of the period map on the de Rham locus; the relation between (φ,Γ)-modules and (φ,∇)-modules via the action of Γ. A common error is to claim that every (φ,∇)-module is overconvergent; overconvergence is a condition that the module extends to a larger annulus, and it is equivalent to the (φ,∇)-module being de Rham. Another trap is to confuse the Newton polygon of the Frobenius with the Hodge polygon of the filtration; the weak admissibility condition requires the Newton polygon to lie above the Hodge polygon, with equality at the endpoints.

  • Assuming the Hodge–Tate period map for unitary Shimura varieties is defined on the whole space; it is only étale on the μ-ordinary locus.
  • Confusing the period domain for abelian varieties with real multiplication with the full GLg period domain; the OF-action cuts out a proper rigid analytic subspace.
  • Believing the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence holds for all p-adic local systems without overconvergence; the equivalence requires the local system to be de Rham.
  • Thinking every vector bundle on the Fargues–Fontaine curve corresponds to a Galois representation; only étale bundles do.
  • Mixing up the Robba ring with the ring of bounded functions on the open unit disc; the Robba ring consists of functions on annuli near the boundary.
  • Assuming the period map for (φ,∇)-modules is globally defined; it is only defined on the de Rham locus.
  • Confusing the Harder–Narasimhan stratification of the moduli of modifications with the Newton stratification of the Shimura variety; they are related but distinct stratifications.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Galois Representations via the Emerton–Gee Stack

The Emerton–Gee stack EG is a rigid analytic stack over a p-adic field K that parameterizes continuous Galois representations ρ : GK → GLn(E) for a coefficient field E. Its construction uses the theory of (φ,Γ)-modules over the Robba ring and the p-adic Langlands correspondence for GL2(ℚp). The stack is locally of finite type and its reduced locus is a union of irreducible components indexed by Serre weights. The uniformization map from the moduli of (φ,Γ)-modules to EG is given by the Fontaine functor Drig, which is fully faithful on the subcategory of étale (φ,Γ)-modules. The geometry of EG reflects the Breuil–Mézard conjecture: the cycle class of the special fiber of a potentially Barsotti–Tate deformation ring equals a sum of Serre weight multiplicities. Recent work of Emerton–Gee–Savitt shows that the irreducible components of EG are normal and Cohen–Macaulay, and that the stack admits a natural stratification by the generic fiber of the associated (φ,Γ)-module. The stack also carries a natural action of the group GLn(ℚp) via the p-adic local Langlands correspondence, and the completed cohomology of the tower of modular curves realizes the correspondence on the level of EG. A key technical tool is the theory of Kisin modules, which provide integral models of (φ,Γ)-modules and allow one to define the stack over ℤp. The uniformization of the moduli of Galois representations by EG is thus a rigid analytic analogue of the classical uniformization of the moduli of local systems by the character variety.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Automorphic Forms on Hilbert Modular Varieties

Hilbert modular varieties parametrize abelian varieties with real multiplication by the ring of integers OF of a totally real field F. Their p-adic uniformization is achieved by the theory of p-adic automorphic forms on the group GL2(F) and the associated eigenvarieties. The eigenvariety E is a rigid analytic space that parameterizes finite-slope overconvergent p-adic Hilbert modular forms. It is constructed via the Buzzard eigenvariety machine applied to the cohomology of the tower of Hilbert modular varieties with Iwahori level at p. The weight space is the rigid analytic space of continuous characters of OF ⊗ ℤp×, which is a product of copies of the p-adic weight space. The eigenvariety maps to the weight space via the weight map, and the fibers are zero-dimensional. The classical points correspond to classical Hilbert modular forms of parallel weight. The geometry of E is controlled by the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2(Fv) at each place v|p. The completed cohomology of the Hilbert modular tower carries an action of the product of GL2(Fv) and the Galois group GF, and the eigenvariety is the support of the Hecke eigenpackets in this completed cohomology. The uniformization of the moduli of p-adic automorphic forms by the eigenvariety is thus a higher-dimensional analogue of the Coleman–Mazur eigencurve. A crucial result of Andreatta–Iovita–Pilloni shows that the eigenvariety is equidimensional of dimension [F:ℚ] + 1 and that the weight map is finite flat on the ordinary locus. The non-ordinary locus exhibits a complicated stratification by the Newton polygon of the associated Galois representation.

Worked Example: Computing the Dimension of a Hilbert Eigenvariety
Let F be a totally real field of degree d over ℚ. The weight space for p-adic Hilbert modular forms is the rigid analytic space of continuous characters of OF ⊗ ℤp×. Determine the dimension of the eigenvariety E parameterizing finite-slope overconvergent p-adic Hilbert modular forms of tame level N.
The weight space is isomorphic to a product of d copies of the p-adic weight space W = Homcont(ℤp×, 𝔾m), which has dimension 1. Hence the weight space has dimension d. The eigenvariety E is constructed as the support of a coherent sheaf on the product of the weight space with the Hecke algebra. By the Buzzard eigenvariety machine, E is equidimensional of dimension d + 1. This follows from the fact that the Hecke algebra acts on a space of overconvergent forms of dimension d + 1 (the extra dimension comes from the slope variable). Therefore the dimension of E is d + 1.
Exam Strategy
When asked about dimensions of eigenvarieties, always identify the weight space dimension first (equal to the number of p-adic places). Then add one for the slope parameter. Remember that the ordinary locus is finite flat over the weight space, while the non-ordinary locus may have larger fibers.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Hodge–Tate Period Maps for Rapoport–Zink Spaces

Rapoport–Zink spaces M are rigid analytic spaces that uniformize the p-adic moduli of p-divisible groups with additional structure (e.g., polarization, endomorphisms). They arise as the generic fibers of formal schemes over Spf OĈ representing the deformation functor of a fixed p-divisible group X0 over 𝔽̄p. The Hodge–Tate period map πHT : M → Fl sends a point corresponding to a p-divisible group X to the Hodge–Tate filtration on the rational Tate module VpX. The target Fl is a flag variety (a projective rigid analytic space) parameterizing filtrations of the appropriate type. The map πHT is étale on the μ-ordinary locus and its image is the admissible locus Fla defined by the weak admissibility condition (Newton polygon above Hodge polygon). The fibers of πHT are isomorphic to the associated p-adic symmetric domain. The uniformization of the moduli of p-divisible groups by M is the p-adic analogue of the uniformization of Shimura varieties by Hermitian symmetric domains. The geometry of M is deeply connected to the local Langlands correspondence: the ℓ-adic cohomology of M realizes the local Langlands correspondence for the group G associated to the Rapoport–Zink datum. Recent work of Scholze–Weinstein shows that the period map extends to the boundary of the minimal compactification of M and that the resulting map on the pro-étale site identifies the completed cohomology of the tower of Rapoport–Zink spaces with the space of p-adic automorphic forms on G. The non-Archimedean uniformization of the moduli of p-adic Hodge–Tate period maps thus provides a geometric realization of the p-adic Langlands correspondence for general reductive groups.

The Theory of Non-Archimedean Uniformization of Moduli of p-adic Differential Equations with Logarithmic Poles on the Robba Ring

The Robba ring ℛ consists of functions convergent on an annulus 1−ε < |T| < 1. To study p-adic differential equations with logarithmic singularities at the boundary, one considers the extended Robba ring ℛlog = ℛ[log T]. A (φ,∇)-module over ℛlog is a finite free module equipped with a Frobenius φ and a connection ∇ satisfying the Leibniz rule and the compatibility φ∇ = p∇φ. The category of such modules is equivalent to the category of p-adic local systems on the punctured open unit disc with quasi-unipotent monodromy at the boundary (the p-adic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence with logarithmic poles).
