Uniform Exponential Mixing of Geodesic Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G be a connected semisimple Lie group with finite centre, Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of G(ℤ), and X = ΓG/K the associated locally symmetric space. The geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of X is known to be exponentially mixing when Γ is a lattice. For thin subgroups the situation is more delicate: the spectral gap for the Laplacian on L²(ΓG/K) is not guaranteed by property (T) because thin groups never have property (T) in rank one. However, the superstrong approximation theorem of Bourgain–Gamburd (for SL₂) and of Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú (for higher rank) provides a uniform spectral gap for the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). This uniform gap translates, via the representation theory of G and the work of Mohammadi–Oh (2015), into a uniform exponential mixing estimate for the geodesic flow on X. Concretely, there exist constants c, η > 0 depending only on G and the generating set of Γ such that for any smooth compactly supported functions f₁, f₂ on the unit tangent bundle,

|∫ f₁·(f₂∘gᵗ) dμ − ∫ f₁ dμ ∫ f₂ dμ| ≤ c·e−ηt·‖f₁‖C¹·‖f₂‖C¹

for all t ≥ 0. The proof proceeds by lifting the flow to the homogeneous space G/Γ, expanding the correlation in terms of matrix coefficients of the unitary representation of G on L²₀(ΓG), and bounding the contribution of each irreducible component using the uniform spectral gap on the finite quotients. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument of Bourgain–Gamburd guarantees that the random walk on Γ/Γ(q) equidistributes at a rate independent of q, which is the key input for the uniform bound on matrix coefficients. This mixing result has immediate consequences for counting problems: it yields effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres and of closed geodesics on thin orbits, with error terms that are powers of the height parameter.

Quantitative Oppenheim Conjecture for Thin Subgroups

The classical Oppenheim conjecture, proved by Margulis (1987) using Ratner’s theorem, asserts that an indefinite integral quadratic form in at least three variables takes values arbitrarily close to any real number unless it is proportional to a rational form. For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ SO(Q)(ℤ) preserving a quadratic form Q, one asks for a quantitative version: given a target value t and a height bound T, how many orbit points γ·v with ‖γ‖ ≤ T satisfy |Q(γ·v) − t| < ε? The work of Gorodnik–Nevo (2010) and later of Einsiedler–Margulis–Venkatesh (2011) shows that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap on its congruence quotients (i.e. superstrong approximation holds), then the number of such points is asymptotic to the product of local densities times the volume of the corresponding region in the symmetric space, with an error term O(Tdim−δ) for some δ > 0. The proof uses the effective mixing of the diagonal flow on ΓG established in the previous section, together with a smoothing argument that replaces the sharp cutoff ‖γ‖ ≤ T by a smooth weight. The uniform spectral gap guarantees that the error term does not deteriorate as the level of congruence varies, which is essential when one applies the affine sieve to obtain almost‑prime values of Q on the thin orbit. In particular, for any Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of SO(Q)(ℤ) with rank Q ≥ 2, the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture holds with a power‑saving error term, and the affine sieve yields that Q takes infinitely many almost‑prime values on the orbit.

Worked Example: Applying the Affine Sieve to a Thin Orbit
Let Γ = ⟨A, B⟩ ⊂ SL₃(ℤ) be the subgroup generated by A = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] and B = [[1,0,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,1]]. Consider the polynomial f(γ) = γ1,1 + γ2,2 + γ3,3 (the trace). Show that f takes infinitely many values with at most R prime factors on the orbit Γ·e₁, where e₁ = (1,0,0)ᵗ.

1. Verify that Γ is Zariski‑dense in SL₃. The generators are unipotent elements whose Lie algebra spans the full 𝔰𝔩₃, so the Zariski closure is the whole group.

2. By Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú (2012), any Zariski‑dense, non‑virtually‑solvable subgroup of a simply connected absolutely almost simple algebraic group over a number field has property (τ). Hence the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) form an expander family for all square‑free q.

3. The uniform spectral gap gives a level of distribution θ > 0 for the sequence {f(γ·e₁) : γ ∈ Γ, ‖γ‖ ≤ T}. Concretely, for any q ≤ T^θ the reduction map Γ → Γ/Γ(q) equidistributes the values of f modulo q with error O(T−δ).

4. Apply the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2010). The polynomial f is non‑constant on Γ and the sieve dimension is κ = 1 (since f is linear). The expander mixing lemma yields the required upper bound for the sifted set.

5. The sieve produces an integer R depending only on the spectral gap and the degree of f such that infinitely many values of f on the orbit have at most R prime factors. In this concrete setting one can take R = 28 (the bound coming from the linear sieve with level of distribution θ = 1/30).

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “almost‑prime values on a thin orbit”, first check whether the subgroup is Zariski‑dense and non‑solvable. If yes, cite the Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú property (τ) theorem to obtain a uniform spectral gap. Then state the affine sieve input: non‑constant polynomial, sieve dimension, level of distribution from the expander mixing lemma. Finally, quote the resulting bound on the number of prime factors (often a concrete integer like 28 for linear forms in rank ≥ 2). This three‑step template covers the majority of exam problems on the topic.

Superstrong Approximation for Non‑Split Algebraic Groups

The original superstrong approximation theorems of Bourgain–Gamburd (for SL₂) and of Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú (for split simply connected groups) rely on the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type. For non‑split groups such as SUₙ or Spin(q) arising from quadratic forms over number fields, the same strategy works after replacing the finite quotients G(𝔽_q) by the corresponding finite groups of Lie type G(𝔽_q) where G is the quasi‑split inner form. The key technical input is the Breuillard–Green–Tao product theorem, which holds for all finite simple groups of Lie type, split or not. Salehi Golsefidy (2015) proved that if Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) is Zariski‑dense in a simply connected absolutely almost simple algebraic group G over a number field, and Γ is not virtually solvable, then the Cayley graphs of Γ/Γ(𝔮) form an expander family for all square‑free ideals 𝔮 of the ring of integers. The proof follows the same escape‑from‑subvarieties scheme: one shows that a random walk on Γ/Γ(𝔮) cannot concentrate on a proper subvariety of the algebraic group G defined over 𝔽_q. The non‑split case requires a careful analysis of the Bruhat–Tits building of G over the local fields to control the growth of the walk in the finite quotients. As a corollary, one obtains uniform diameter bounds diam(Γ/Γ(𝔮)) ≤ C (log N𝔮)^A and the affine sieve for polynomials on thin orbits of non‑split groups, for example the spinor norm on thin subgroups of Spin(q)(ℤ).

Expansion in Products of Finite Simple Groups and Thin Subgroups

A central tool in the proof of superstrong approximation is the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao (2012): for any finite simple group of Lie type G(𝔽_q) and any symmetric generating set S not contained in a proper subgroup, either S³ = G(𝔽_q) or |S³| ≥ |S|1+ε for an absolute constant ε > 0. When Γ is a thin subgroup, its reduction modulo q yields a subset S_q ⊂ G(𝔽_q). The product theorem forces rapid growth of S_q unless it is trapped in a proper subgroup. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument shows that for a Zariski‑dense Γ, the probability that the random walk lands in a fixed proper algebraic subgroup decays exponentially with the length of the walk, uniformly in q. Combining growth and escape gives a uniform spectral gap for the random walk operator on ℓ²(G(𝔽_q)). This method extends to products ∏i=1^k G_i(𝔽q_i) arising from the Chinese remainder theorem for square‑free levels. The resulting expander family is Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) where q = ∏ q_i. The uniformity across all square‑free q is precisely the superstrong approximation property. Recent work of Varjú (2020) sharpens the exponent A in the diameter bound to A = O(rank(G)) by using a refined product theorem that tracks the dependence on the rank of the ambient algebraic group.

Distribution of Integral Points on Homogeneous Varieties via Thin Groups

Let X ⊂ ℙ^N be a projective variety defined over ℚ and Γ ⊂ GLN+1(ℤ) a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup preserving X. For a base point v ∈ ℤN+1 one studies the set X(ℤ) ∩ Γ·v. The classical circle method gives an asymptotic for the number of integral points of height ≤ T on X when X is a quadric of dimension ≥ 3 or a complete intersection of high codimension. For thin orbits the major‑arc analysis still yields the product of local densities, but the minor arcs require cancellation in exponential sums over the orbit. The expander mixing lemma for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) provides exactly this cancellation: it implies that for any non‑trivial additive character ψ modulo q, the sum ∑γ∈Γ, ‖γ‖≤T ψ(f(γ·v)) is bounded by O(Tdim−δ) uniformly in q ≤ T^θ. Browning–Heath‑Brown (2015) executed this program for the number of representations of an integer by a ternary quadratic form restricted to a thin orbit of the orthogonal group. They obtained an asymptotic formula N(T) ∼ C·Tdim X/2 / (log T)^κ where κ is the sieve dimension of the polynomial map f. The uniformity of the spectral gap across all levels q is essential; without it the minor‑arc bound would deteriorate for large q and the circle method would fail. This result matches the Bateman–Horn prediction for the thin orbit and demonstrates that the affine sieve, powered by superstrong approximation, can replace the missing “large sieve” input in the classical Hardy–Littlewood method.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of Non‑Arithmetic Lattices

The spectral theory of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on hyperbolic surfaces uniformized by thin subgroups of SL₂(ℝ) differs fundamentally from the arithmetic case. For a Zariski‑dense, finitely generated subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) that is not commensurable with a congruence subgroup, the quotient Γ\ℍ is a finite‑area hyperbolic orbifold with infinite‑volume ends. The continuous spectrum starts at 1/4, and the discrete spectrum below 1/4 is finite. Bourgain and Gamburd (2008) proved that if Γ is Zariski‑dense and not virtually solvable, the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) form a family of expanders; this implies a uniform spectral gap λ₁ ≥ δ > 0 for the Laplacian on the associated congruence covers. Later, Magee (2015) showed that for Schottky subgroups the optimal gap can be expressed in terms of the Hausdorff dimension δ of the limit set: λ₁ ≥ δ(1−δ) when δ > 1/2, and λ₁ ≥ 1/4 otherwise. These results rely on the transfer operator method and the thermodynamic formalism for the geodesic flow, which replace the representation‑theoretic arguments available for arithmetic lattices.

A key mechanism is the Dolgopyat‑type estimate for the twisted transfer operator associated with the symbolic coding of the geodesic flow on the limit set. The estimate yields exponential mixing of the frame flow on the unit tangent bundle of Γ\ℍ, which in turn gives a power‑saving error term in the prime geodesic theorem for thin groups. The spectral gap is uniform across all congruence levels because the expansion constant depends only on the Zariski density of Γ and not on the level q. This uniformity is precisely the superstrong approximation property. In contrast, for non‑congruence subgroups the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture (λ₁ ≥ 1/4) remains open; the best known bound for general thin subgroups is λ₁ ≥ 3/16, obtained by adapting Selberg’s original argument to the congruence quotients of Γ.

The trace formula for thin groups must be modified because the group is not a lattice in the adelic sense. One works with the Selberg trace formula on each congruence cover Γ(q)\ℍ and then averages over q using the expander mixing lemma. The hyperbolic contribution is controlled by Weil bounds for Kloosterman sums, which are available because the congruence quotients are quotients of SL₂(𝔽_q). The elliptic and parabolic contributions are handled by the representation theory of SL₂(𝔽_q) and the fact that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup for all sufficiently large primes. This combination yields a uniform lower bound for the first non‑zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian on the congruence towers.

An important exception occurs when Γ is a thin subgroup of a higher‑rank algebraic group, for example a Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL₃(ℤ). In that setting Margulis property (T) gives a spectral gap for the full group, but the thin subgroup may fail to have property (T). The superstrong approximation theorem of Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varjú (2012) shows that a uniform spectral gap still holds for the congruence quotients of any Zariski‑dense subgroup of a simply connected, absolutely almost simple algebraic group over ℚ, provided the subgroup is not contained in a proper algebraic subgroup. The proof uses the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao and an escape‑from‑subvarieties argument that works uniformly in the level.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Schottky Surfaces

Schottky groups provide the most concrete examples of thin subgroups of SL₂(ℂ) and SL₂(ℝ). A classical Schottky group is generated by a finite set of Möbius transformations pairing disjoint circles in the Riemann sphere; the limit set is a Cantor set of Hausdorff dimension δ < 1. When the generators are chosen in SL₂(ℤ), the group is a thin subgroup of the modular group. The geometry of the associated hyperbolic surface Γ\ℍ is encoded in the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set, which is the unique conformal density of dimension δ. The critical exponent δ coincides with the abscissa of convergence of the Poincaré series and governs the asymptotic growth of orbit points: #{γ ∈ Γ : ‖γ‖ ≤ T} ∼ C T^δ.

The spectral gap for Schottky groups is intimately linked to the dimension δ. Naud (2005) proved that for convex co‑compact Schottky subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) the Laplacian on the convex core has a spectral gap λ₁ ≥ δ(1−δ) when δ > 1/2, and λ₁ ≥ 1/4 otherwise. This bound is sharp for certain symmetric Schottky groups. The proof uses the transfer operator for the Bowen–Series map on the limit set and a Dolgopyat‑type estimate that exploits the non‑lattice nature of the return times. The same method yields exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle, with a rate that depends only on δ and the minimal distance between the defining circles.

When the Schottky group is reduced modulo a prime p, the image is a subset of SL₂(𝔽_p) that generates a subgroup which is either the whole group or a proper subgroup. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument shows that the probability that a random word of length n lands in a fixed proper algebraic subvariety decays like exp(−c n) uniformly in p. Combined with the product theorem, this gives a uniform spectral gap for the random walk on the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(p), S). The resulting expander family has logarithmic diameter: diam(Γ/Γ(p)) ≤ C log p. This logarithmic bound is stronger than the polylogarithmic bound available for general thin groups and reflects the free‑group‑like structure of Schottky groups.

Applications of Schottky expanders include the affine sieve for polynomial maps on the orbit Γ·v. For example, the polynomial f(γ) = trace(γ) takes almost‑prime values infinitely often on a Schottky orbit, with a level of distribution that matches the sieve dimension. The uniformity of the spectral gap across all primes is essential; without it the minor‑arc estimates in the circle method would deteriorate for large moduli. Recent work of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2016) extended these results to thin subgroups of SL₂(𝔽_p[t]) in positive characteristic, showing that the same geometric methods apply over function fields.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap for a Schottky Subgroup
Show that a Zariski‑dense Schottky subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) generated by two hyperbolic elements with sufficiently large translation lengths yields a uniform spectral gap in its congruence quotients.
Let Γ = ⟨A, B⟩ where A, B ∈ SL₂(ℤ) are hyperbolic with translation lengths ℓ(A), ℓ(B) > L₀ for a large constant L₀. The group is a classical Schottky group because the axes of A and B can be separated by disjoint circles in the boundary ℝ∪{∞}. The limit set Λ is a Cantor set of Hausdorff dimension δ < 1. By the Patterson–Sullivan construction there exists a δ‑conformal measure μ on Λ. The transfer operator ℒ_s acting on Hölder functions on Λ is defined by (ℒ_s f)(x) = Σy: T y = x |T'(y)|-s f(y), where T is the Bowen–Series map. For s = δ the operator has spectral radius 1 and a simple eigenvalue at 1. Dolgopyat’s method gives a bound ‖ℒδ+it^n‖ ≤ C θ^n for |t| ≥ 1, with θ < 1 independent of the prime p. This implies exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on Γ\ℍ with rate θ. Reducing modulo p, the random walk operator on ℓ²(Γ/Γ(p)) inherits the same spectral gap because the escape‑from‑subvarieties estimate shows that the walk equidistributes on SL₂(𝔽_p) at exponential speed. Consequently the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(p), {A,B}) form a family of expanders with uniform spectral gap ε > 0, and the diameter satisfies diam ≤ C log p.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the role of the product theorem in superstrong approximation, focus on the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument and the uniform growth exponent ε; do not confuse it with Margulis property (T) which applies only in higher rank.

Thin Groups and the Dynamics of Diagonal Flows on Homogeneous Spaces

Diagonal flows on homogeneous spaces G/Γ, where G is a semisimple Lie group and Γ a thin subgroup, provide a dynamical framework for studying equidistribution of thin orbits. The classical setting is G = SL₂(ℝ) and Γ a lattice; the horocycle flow is unipotent and equidistributes by Ratner’s theorems. For thin subgroups, the quotient G/Γ has infinite volume, and the diagonal flow a_t = diag(e^t, e-t) acts on the space of lattices. Einsiedler, Katok, and Lindenstrauss (2006) proved that for any Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) the diagonal flow on the space of unimodular lattices modulo Γ is exponentially mixing with respect to the Haar measure on the finite‑volume part, provided Γ has a uniform spectral gap. The proof uses the representation theory of SL₂(ℝ) and the fact that the spectral gap for the Laplacian on Γ\ℍ implies a spectral gap for the unitary representation of G on L²₀(G/Γ).

In higher rank, say G = SL₃(ℝ), the diagonal subgroup A ≅ ℝ² acts on G/Γ. The work of Einsiedler and Lindenstrauss (2010) on measure rigidity for diagonal actions shows that any A‑invariant ergodic measure on G/Γ with positive entropy is algebraic. For thin subgroups, the lack of finite volume prevents a direct application of Ratner’s theorem, but the superstrong approximation property supplies a substitute: the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) are expanders, which yields effective equidistribution of A‑orbits on the finite‑volume quotients G/Γ(q). By a standard approximation argument, one obtains quantitative non‑divergence for A‑orbits on G/Γ: for any compact set K ⊂ G/Γ, the measure of {a_t x : t ≤ T} ∩ K is bounded by C T-η for some η > 0, uniformly for x in a compact subset of the finite‑volume part.

The connection to number theory appears through the correspondence between diagonal orbits and Diophantine approximation. For a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) acting on ℝ², the orbit of a vector v under the diagonal flow corresponds to the set of approximations of the slope of v by rationals with denominators in the projection of Γ. The uniform spectral gap implies a power‑saving error term in the counting of such approximations, which is a quantitative version of the Oppenheim conjecture for thin orbits. This was carried out by Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011) for the quadratic form Q(x,y) = x² − 2y² restricted to a thin orbit of the orthogonal group O_Q(ℤ). The result gives an asymptotic formula for the number of representations of an integer by Q on the thin orbit, with a level of distribution that matches the sieve dimension.

A subtle point is that the diagonal flow on G/Γ is not uniformly hyperbolic when Γ is thin; the presence of cusps of infinite volume creates regions where the flow is slowly mixing. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument controls the time spent in these regions by showing that the random walk on the congruence quotients avoids proper subvarieties exponentially fast. This yields a uniform bound on the measure of the set of points that stay in a cusp for a long time, which is the key input for the effective equidistribution theorem. The method extends to products of diagonal flows arising from the Chinese remainder theorem, giving superstrong approximation for the product of finite simple groups SL₂(𝔽p_i).

Thin Groups and the Arithmetic of Integral Points on Shimura Varieties

Shimura varieties are higher‑dimensional analogues of modular curves, attached to reductive algebraic groups over ℚ. Integral points on Shimura varieties correspond to special subvarieties such as CM points or abelian varieties with prescribed endomorphism structure. Thin subgroups arise naturally as the images of Galois representations attached to non‑CM elliptic curves or higher‑dimensional abelian varieties. For example, the adelic Galois representation ρ: Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → GL₂(ℤ̂) has open image by Serre’s open image theorem; the image of the restriction to a number field is a thin subgroup of GL₂(ℤ̂). The distribution of integral points on the associated Shimura variety can be studied via the dynamics of the thin group on the corresponding homogeneous space.

Clozel, Oh, and Ullmo (2001) proved equidistribution of Hecke orbits on Shimura varieties under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Later, unconditional results were obtained by using the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the locally symmetric space attached to the thin subgroup. The superstrong approximation theorem for thin subgroups of simply connected groups (Salehi‑Golsefidy, Varjú 2012) implies that the congruence quotients of the thin group form expanders. This gives a uniform level of distribution for the Hecke operators acting on automorphic forms, which is the analytic input needed for the circle method on thin orbits. As a consequence, one obtains asymptotic formulas for the number of integral points of bounded height on Shimura varieties that are cut out by thin group orbits, with a power‑saving error term.

A concrete application is the André–Oort conjecture for thin orbits. The conjecture predicts that a Zariski‑dense set of special points on a Shimura variety must be a special subvariety. When the special points are given by the orbit of a thin subgroup, the expander property provides the necessary equidistribution to show that the orbit cannot be contained in a proper special subvariety unless the thin subgroup itself is contained in a proper algebraic subgroup. This was used by Klingler and Yafaev (2014) to prove the André–Oort conjecture for certain Shimura curves uniformized by thin subgroups of SL₂(ℝ). The proof combines the spectral gap for the thin group with the Ax–Lindemann theorem for the uniformization map.

The main technical obstacle is that the thin subgroup is not a lattice in the adelic group, so the classical trace formula does not apply directly. One works instead with the trace formula on each congruence cover and uses the expander mixing lemma to average over levels. The hyperbolic contribution is controlled by the Weil bounds for Kloosterman sums on the finite quotients, which are available because the thin subgroup projects onto SL₂(𝔽_p) for almost all p. The elliptic and parabolic contributions are handled by the representation theory of the finite groups of Lie type. This yields a uniform spectral gap for the automorphic Laplacian on the tower of congruence covers, which is the engine behind the equidistribution results.

Thin Groups and the Distribution of Closed Geodesics on Hyperbolic Manifolds

The prime geodesic theorem for a hyperbolic manifold M = Γ\ℍ counts closed geodesics by length. For arithmetic lattices, the Selberg trace formula gives an exact formula with an error term O(e(1/2+ε)T) assuming the Ramanujan conjecture. For thin subgroups, the trace formula must be adapted because Γ is not a lattice in the adelic sense. The work of Lalley (1989) and later of Naud (2005) shows that for convex co‑compact thin groups the counting function π_Γ(T) = #{primitive closed geodesics of length ≤ T} satisfies π_Γ(T) = li(eδ T) + O(e(δ−η)T) for some η > 0, where δ is the critical exponent of Γ. The error term comes from the spectral gap of the transfer operator on the limit set, which is equivalent to the exponential mixing of the geodesic flow.

When Γ is a thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) that is not convex co‑compact (i.e., it has parabolic elements), the limit set is the whole circle and δ = 1. The prime geodesic theorem then has main term li(e^T) and the error term is governed by the spectral gap of the Laplacian on the congruence covers. Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011) proved that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap λ₁ ≥ ε > 0 on all congruence quotients, then the error term in the prime geodesic theorem for the congruence tower is O(e(1−η)T) for some η > 0 depending on ε. This is a direct consequence of the expander mixing lemma applied to the symbolic dynamics of the geodesic flow on the modular surface.

The distribution of closed geodesics in thin orbits also has arithmetic applications. For a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) and a polynomial map f: Γ → ℤ, the affine sieve counts the number of γ ∈ Γ with ‖γ‖ ≤ T such that f(γ) is almost prime. The sieve requires a level of distribution for the sequence f(γ) modulo q. The expander property of the congruence quotients gives exactly this level of distribution: for any non‑trivial additive character ψ modulo q, the exponential sum Σγ∈Γ, ‖γ‖≤T ψ(f(γ)) is bounded by O(T1−η) uniformly for q ≤ T^θ. This bound is proved by writing the sum as a matrix coefficient of the random walk operator on the expander graph and using the spectral gap. The resulting almost‑prime theorem matches the Bateman–Horn prediction for the thin orbit.

A limitation appears when the thin subgroup is contained in a proper algebraic subgroup of the ambient group. In that case the Zariski closure is smaller, and the product theorem does not apply because the generating set may be trapped in a proper subgroup modulo infinitely many primes. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument fails, and the spectral gap can collapse. This is why the hypothesis of Zariski density is essential in all superstrong approximation theorems. Another limitation is that the spectral gap for thin subgroups of higher‑rank groups is not known to be uniform across all levels without assuming the subgroup is not contained in a proper normal subgroup of the ambient algebraic group. Recent work of Varjú (2020) has removed some of these restrictions for simply connected groups, but the general case remains open.

  • Assuming that every thin subgroup automatically inherits the Selberg 3/16 bound; the bound holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for non‑arithmetic lattices with the Ramanujan bound for arithmetic quotients; the former is typically weaker and depends on the geometry of the limit set.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)^A with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Forgetting that the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument uses the Zariski density of the original subgroup; if the subgroup is not Zariski dense the exponential decay of hitting proper subvarieties fails.

Thin Groups and the Langlands Correspondence for Non‑Arithmetic Subgroups

The Langlands program predicts a deep relationship between automorphic representations of a reductive algebraic group G over a global field and Galois representations into the Langlands dual group ^L G. For arithmetic lattices Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) the correspondence is realized through the trace formula and the theory of automorphic forms on the adelic quotient G(ℚ)G(𝔸). Thin subgroups, by definition, are Zariski‑dense but of infinite index in the ambient arithmetic group; they do not arise as the rational points of an algebraic subgroup and therefore do not support a natural adelic quotient. Consequently the classical Langlands correspondence does not apply directly. Recent work has focused on spectral transfer: given a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) with a uniform spectral gap on its congruence quotients, one can compare the spectrum of the Laplacian on Γ\ℍ with the spectrum on the modular surface SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ. The transfer operator associated to the geodesic flow on the limit set of Γ provides a dynamical analogue of the Hecke operators. Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak (2011) showed that the expander property of the Cayley graphs Γ/Γ(q) implies a Selberg‑type eigenvalue bound λ₁ ≥ 3/16 − ε for the congruence covers, which in turn yields a spectral gap for the transfer operator. This gap allows one to prove a prime geodesic theorem with power‑saving error term for Γ, a result that mirrors the consequences of the Ramanujan conjecture for arithmetic quotients. In higher rank, the work of Oh and Winter (2016) on the spectral gap for thin subgroups of SLₙ(ℤ) (n ≥ 3) uses the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to establish uniform expansion, and they conjecture that the resulting spectral data should match the functorial lift of automorphic representations from the ambient group to the thin subgroup. The main obstruction remains the lack of a Hecke algebra acting on the thin quotient; the expander graphs provide a combinatorial substitute, but a full Langlands functoriality statement for non‑arithmetic thin groups is still open.

Thin Groups and the Arithmetic of Integral Points on Flag Varieties

Flag varieties G/P, where P is a parabolic subgroup of a semisimple algebraic group G, parametrize nested sequences of subspaces and carry a natural projective embedding via the Plücker coordinates. Integral points on G/P correspond to lattices in a fixed representation satisfying certain incidence relations. When a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) acts on G/P(ℤ), the orbit Γ·x₀ is a thin set of integral points. Counting such points with height ≤ T is a central problem in arithmetic geometry. Eskin, Mozes and Shah (1996) proved that for any lattice Γ in a higher‑rank group the number of integral points in a Γ‑orbit on a flag variety grows like c·T^δ where δ is the critical exponent of Γ; for thin subgroups the same asymptotic holds provided Γ has a uniform spectral gap on congruence quotients. The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak can be applied to polynomial functions on the orbit, yielding almost‑prime values for the Plücker coordinates. A key technical input is the level of distribution for the sequence of reductions modulo q, which follows from the expander mixing lemma on the Cayley graphs Γ/Γ(q). In the rank‑one case (G = SL₂) the flag variety is ℙ¹ and the orbit is a set of rational numbers; the work of Kontorovich and Oh (2011) gives an explicit error term O(T1−η) for the counting function, with η depending on the spectral gap. For higher rank, the recent results of Gorodnik and Nevo (2020) on effective equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on homogeneous spaces provide the necessary quantitative mixing to run the sieve. An important limitation appears when the stabilizer of x₀ is not reductive; then the orbit may accumulate on a proper subvariety and the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument fails, causing the spectral gap to collapse for infinitely many levels. This phenomenon explains why the affine sieve works for generic points on flag varieties but can break down for special points with large stabilizers.

Applying the Affine Sieve to Flag Variety Orbits
Let Γ ⊂ SL₃(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup with a uniform spectral gap λ₁ ≥ ε > 0 on all congruence quotients. Consider the action of Γ on the flag variety of lines in ℚ³, identified with ℙ²(ℚ). For a generic integral point x₀ ∈ ℙ²(ℤ) with primitive coordinates, define the height H(γ·x₀) = max{|coordinates of γ·x₀|}. Show that the number of γ ∈ Γ with H(γ·x₀) ≤ T such that the first Plücker coordinate is an almost prime (product of at most two primes) is ≫ Tδ−η for some η > 0 depending on ε.
The orbit Γ·x₀ is a thin set of integral points on ℙ². The height function is comparable to the word norm on Γ, so counting points of height ≤ T is equivalent to counting group elements of word length ≤ c·log T. The uniform spectral gap on Γ/Γ(q) implies, via the expander mixing lemma, that for any non‑trivial additive character ψ modulo q the exponential sum ∑‖γ‖≤L ψ(f(γ)) is bounded by O(e(1−η)L) uniformly for q ≤ eθL. Here f(γ) is the first Plücker coordinate of γ·x₀, a polynomial map on Γ. This level of distribution allows the linear sieve of dimension 1 to be applied. The sieve dimension equals the degree of f, which is 1 for a coordinate function. The fundamental lemma of the sieve yields a lower bound ≫ (L / log L) for the number of γ with f(γ) having at most two prime factors. Translating back to height gives ≫ Tδ / log T, which is ≫ Tδ−η for any η > 0 after adjusting constants. The crucial steps are: (1) uniform expansion gives the required exponential sum bound; (2) the polynomial f is non‑constant on Γ because x₀ is generic; (3) the sieve dimension is 1, so the almost‑prime bound follows from the standard linear sieve.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for an almost‑prime result on a thin orbit, first verify that the subgroup is Zariski‑dense and that a uniform spectral gap is known (cite Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak for SL₂, Varju for higher rank). Then identify the polynomial map and its degree; the sieve dimension equals that degree. Finally, state the level of distribution obtained from the expander mixing lemma and invoke the linear or combinatorial sieve. Do not forget to mention the genericity condition on the base point to avoid stabilizer obstructions.

Thin Groups and the Dynamics of Horospherical Flows on Homogeneous Spaces

Horospherical flows are the actions of one‑parameter unipotent subgroups on homogeneous spaces G/Γ. For arithmetic quotients, Ratner’s theorems guarantee that orbit closures are homogeneous and that the flow is uniquely ergodic on each invariant measure. When Γ is a thin subgroup of G(ℤ), the quotient G/Γ is not a finite‑volume homogeneous space; it is a non‑compact orbifold with infinite volume. Nevertheless, the work of Margulis and Tomanov (1994) on the Oppenheim conjecture extends to thin subgroups provided the subgroup is Zariski‑dense and the horospherical subgroup is not contained in a proper normal subgroup of G. The key dynamical input is the exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of ΓG/K, which follows from the uniform spectral gap on congruence covers. Using the spectral gap, one can prove effective equidistribution of horospherical orbits: for a compactly supported test function φ on G/Γ, the average (1/T)∫₀ᵀ φ(g·u_t x) dt converges to the integral of φ against the Haar measure with an error O(T−η). This quantitative mixing is the engine behind the affine sieve on thin orbits, because the level of distribution for reductions modulo q is exactly the matrix coefficient decay for the horospherical flow on the finite quotients Γ/Γ(q). In rank one, the horospherical flow is the horocycle flow on the modular surface; the work of Flaminio and Forni (2003) gives a precise description of the Sobolev norms controlling the decay of correlations. For thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) the same Sobolev estimates hold with constants depending only on the spectral gap, yielding uniform polynomial decay of correlations across the congruence tower. In higher rank, the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao provides the necessary expansion to obtain a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence quotients, which in turn implies exponential mixing of the diagonal flow and polynomial mixing of the horospherical flow. A subtle point is that the horospherical subgroup must be generated by the unipotent elements that appear in the Iwasawa decomposition of G; if the thin subgroup misses some root subgroups, the flow may not be ergodic and the equidistribution fails. This explains why the Zariski‑density hypothesis is essential: it guarantees that the projection of Γ onto each simple factor is non‑elementary and that all root subgroups are represented modulo infinitely many primes.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of Non‑Compact Arithmetic Quotients

The spectral theory of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a non‑compact arithmetic quotient ΓG/K decomposes into a discrete spectrum (cusp forms) and a continuous spectrum spanned by Eisenstein series. For congruence subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) the Selberg trace formula gives an exact expression for the trace of the heat kernel, and the Ramanujan conjecture predicts that all non‑trivial eigenvalues satisfy λ ≥ 1/4. For thin subgroups the quotient has infinite volume, so the continuous spectrum fills the whole half‑line [1/4, ∞) and there is no discrete spectrum in the usual sense. However, the congruence covers Γ(q)G/K have finite volume, and their spectra can be studied via the trace formula adapted to the thin group. The work of Lalley (1989) and Naud (2005) shows that the transfer operator associated to the geodesic flow on the limit set of a convex co‑compact thin group has a spectral gap; this gap is equivalent to a Dolgopyat‑type estimate for the Ruelle resonances. In the presence of parabolic elements (so the limit set is the whole boundary) the critical exponent δ equals the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set, which is 1 for subgroups of SL₂(ℤ). The Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for non‑congruence subgroups predicts a uniform lower bound λ₁ ≥ 3/16 for the first eigenvalue on all congruence covers of a fixed thin group. Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak proved that if the thin group has a uniform spectral gap on the family of Cayley graphs Γ/Γ(q), then the Laplacian on the congruence covers satisfies λ₁ ≥ 3/16 − ε. The proof uses the expander mixing lemma to bound the matrix coefficients of the regular representation of Γ on ℓ²(Γ/Γ(q)), which translates into a bound on the Eisenstein series via the Selberg transform. A major open problem is whether the same bound holds for thin subgroups of higher‑rank groups such as SLₙ(ℤ) with n ≥ 3. The product theorem gives expansion for the Cayley graphs, but the trace formula for higher‑rank groups involves a much more complicated continuous spectrum (Eisenstein series attached to all parabolic subgroups). Recent work of Oh and Winter (2016) establishes a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence quotients of thin subgroups of SLₙ(ℤ) assuming the subgroup is not contained in a proper normal subgroup; the bound they obtain is λ₁ ≥ c/n² for some absolute constant c > 0, which is far from the conjectured Ramanujan bound λ₁ ≥ (n−1)²/4. Closing this gap would require a deeper understanding of the Langlands functoriality for thin groups, as discussed in the first section.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs in Higher Rank

Expander graphs are finite graphs with strong connectivity properties quantified by a uniform spectral gap of the normalized adjacency operator. For a finitely generated group Γ and a family of finite quotients Γ/Γ_i, the Cayley graphs form an expander family if the second eigenvalue of the adjacency operator is bounded away from 1 uniformly in i. In the setting of thin subgroups of higher‑rank semisimple groups, the breakthrough of Bourgain and Gamburd (2008) for SL₂(𝔽_p) was extended by Breuillard, Green and Tao (2011) to all finite simple groups of Lie type via the product theorem: any approximate subgroup of a finite simple group of Lie type is either very small or contained in a proper subgroup. Varju (2012) used this to prove that for any Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) (n ≥ 3) the Cayley graphs of Γ modulo p form an expander family for all sufficiently large primes p. The proof proceeds by showing that the random walk on Γ/Γ(p) flattens rapidly: after O(log p) steps the distribution is close to uniform in ℓ² norm. The flattening lemma relies on the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument, which uses the Zariski density of Γ to guarantee that the walk does not concentrate on any proper algebraic subvariety of SLₙ modulo p. Once flattening is established, the spectral gap follows from the standard connection between mixing time and eigenvalue gap. A quantitative version gives an explicit bound on the diameter: diam(Γ/Γ(p)) ≤ C (log p)^A with A = O(n²). This logarithmic diameter bound is the combinatorial analogue of the strong approximation property with effective error terms. For thin subgroups that are not arithmetic lattices, the same method works provided the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; otherwise the walk may be trapped in a proper subgroup and expansion fails. The expander property has immediate applications: it yields a level of distribution for the affine sieve on thin orbits, it implies the superstrong approximation theorem (the closure of Γ in the profinite completion is open), and it gives quantitative equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on homogeneous spaces via the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence quotients. An important limitation is that the product theorem requires the finite quotients to be simple groups of Lie type; for non‑split groups or for groups with non‑trivial center the argument needs additional work, and the uniform spectral gap is not known in full generality.

  • Assuming that every thin subgroup automatically inherits the Selberg 3/16 bound; the bound holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for non‑arithmetic lattices with the Ramanujan bound for arithmetic quotients; the former is typically weaker and depends on the geometry of the limit set.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)^A with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Forgetting that the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument uses the Zariski density of the original subgroup; if the subgroup is not Zariski dense the exponential decay of hitting proper subvarieties fails.

These traps highlight the precise hypotheses needed for each major theorem in the theory of thin groups and superstrong approximation.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets and Patterson–Sullivan Measures

The limit set of a thin subgroup Γ of a semisimple Lie group G is the set of accumulation points of a Γ‑orbit on the Furstenberg boundary G/P. For Zariski‑dense thin groups the limit set is typically a fractal of Hausdorff dimension strictly between 0 and the dimension of the boundary. Patterson (1976) and Sullivan (1979) constructed a family of conformal measures supported on the limit set, now called Patterson–Sullivan measures, which are eigenfunctions of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the associated locally symmetric space. The exponent of convergence of the Poincaré series equals the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set and coincides with the bottom of the L²‑spectrum of the Laplacian on the quotient ΓG/K. For thin subgroups of SL₂(ℝ) this dimension is known to be > 1/2 by work of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011), and the Patterson–Sullivan measure is ergodic for the geodesic flow. In higher rank the limit set lives in a flag variety and its dimension is governed by the growth exponent of Γ; recent results of Quint (2010) and Benoist–Quint (2016) give a variational formula for the dimension in terms of the Lyapunov spectrum of the random walk on Γ.

These geometric objects are central to the spectral theory of thin groups because the spectral gap of the Laplacian on congruence quotients is directly related to the dimension of the limit set. When the limit set has dimension less than the critical exponent of the ambient lattice, the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture fails for the corresponding non‑congruence covers. The Patterson–Sullivan measure also provides the natural reference measure for the affine sieve on thin orbits, as the sieve weights are built from the decay of matrix coefficients against this measure.

An important open problem is to compute the exact Hausdorff dimension for explicit thin groups such as the Apollonian group or the thin subgroups generated by two parabolic elements in SL₂(ℤ). Numerical experiments suggest dimensions around 1.3057 for the Apollonian packing, but a rigorous proof remains out of reach. Progress on this question would simultaneously advance the spectral gap estimates for the associated congruence quotients and the level of distribution in the affine sieve.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Automorphic Forms on Non‑Arithmetic Quotients

Classical automorphic forms are functions on arithmetic quotients ΓG where Γ is a congruence subgroup. For thin subgroups the quotient ΓG is non‑arithmetic and typically has infinite volume. The spectral decomposition of L²(ΓG) then contains a continuous spectrum coming from Eisenstein series attached to all proper parabolic subgroups, together with a discrete spectrum that may be empty or very sparse. Work of Lax and Phillips (1982) on scattering theory for convex co‑compact hyperbolic manifolds shows that the resonances of the Laplacian correspond to poles of the Eisenstein series, and the distribution of these resonances controls the error term in the lattice point counting problem for Γ‑orbits.

In higher rank the theory is far less developed. Lindenstrauss and Venkatesh (2007) proved a quantitative non‑divergence theorem for unipotent flows on homogeneous spaces, which can be applied to thin orbits when the stabiliser is a unipotent subgroup. Their method yields effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres in ΓG provided Γ satisfies a Diophantine condition that is known to hold for Zariski‑dense subgroups with a uniform spectral gap. More recently, Einsiedler, Lindenstrauss, and Michel (2015) established a measure classification theorem for invariant measures of diagonal actions on ΓG when Γ is a thin subgroup of SLₙ(ℤ) with n ≥ 3, assuming the subgroup is not contained in a proper normal algebraic subgroup. This result is a thin‑group analogue of the celebrated Ratner theorems for arithmetic quotients.

A major obstacle is the absence of a Hecke algebra acting on L²(ΓG) for non‑arithmetic Γ. Without Hecke operators one cannot use the standard trace formula to relate spectral data to geometric data such as lengths of closed geodesics. The emerging programme of “spectral transfer” attempts to bypass this by comparing the spectrum of ΓG with that of a suitable arithmetic lattice via the Langlands functoriality conjectures for thin groups, but at present this remains largely conjectural.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap from Limit Set Dimension
Let Γ be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) whose limit set Λ has Hausdorff dimension δ = 0.75. Using the Patterson–Sullivan construction, the bottom of the L²‑spectrum of the Laplacian on the hyperbolic surface Γ\ℍ is λ₀ = δ(1−δ). Compute λ₀ and explain why this implies a spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) when q is square‑free.
The formula λ₀ = δ(1−δ) gives λ₀ = 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875. For a congruence quotient Γ/Γ(q) the Laplacian on the finite graph has eigenvalues related to the continuous spectrum via the Selberg trace formula. A uniform lower bound λ₁ ≥ λ₀ on the continuous spectrum transfers to a uniform spectral gap for the family of Cayley graphs of Γ/Γ(q) because the discrete spectrum of the finite quotients interlaces with the continuous spectrum of the infinite cover. Hence the Cayley graphs form an expander family with spectral gap at least 0.1875.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the spectral gap of a thin‑group congruence quotient, first identify the limit set dimension δ (often given or computable from the growth exponent). Then apply λ₀ = δ(1−δ) for rank‑one groups; for higher rank use the known bound λ₁ ≥ c/n² from Oh–Winter (2016). Remember that the expander property requires the generating set to project onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Covers of Hyperbolic Manifolds

For a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) are finite graphs whose normalized adjacency operators have a second eigenvalue λ₁(q). The superstrong approximation theorem of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011) asserts that there exists ε > 0 such that λ₁(q) ≤ 1 − ε for all square‑free q. The proof combines the product theorem of Breuillard, Green, and Tao (2011) with an escape‑from‑subvarieties argument that uses the Zariski density of Γ. The constant ε depends on the generating set and on the dimension of the limit set; explicit bounds have been obtained by Salehi Golsefidy and Varju (2012) who showed that one can take ε ≍ 1/(log q)⁰ for a suitable power depending on the rank.

In higher rank the situation is more delicate. For Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) with n ≥ 3, Varju (2012) proved that the Cayley graphs of Γ modulo p form an expander family for all sufficiently large primes p, provided the projection of the generating set is non‑elementary. The spectral gap obtained is uniform in p but the quantitative bound on the diameter is diam(Γ/Γ(p)) ≤ C (log p)ᴬ with A = O(n²). This logarithmic diameter bound is the combinatorial counterpart of effective strong approximation. For non‑split groups or groups with non‑trivial centre the product theorem does not apply directly, and the uniform spectral gap is known only under additional hypotheses such as the subgroup being “strongly dense” in the sense of Breuillard–Gelander (2007).

Recent work of Oh and Winter (2016) established a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence quotients of thin subgroups of SLₙ(ℤ) assuming the subgroup is not contained in a proper normal subgroup; the bound they obtain is λ₁ ≥ c/n² for some absolute constant c > 0, which is far from the conjectured Ramanujan bound λ₁ ≥ (n−1)²/4. Closing this gap would require a deeper understanding of the Langlands functoriality for thin groups.

Thin Groups and the Distribution of Hecke Eigenvalues in Thin Families

When a thin subgroup Γ arises as the monodromy group of a family of algebraic varieties, the Frobenius traces at good primes give rise to a sequence of Hecke eigenvalues. For arithmetic groups the Sato–Tate conjecture (proved by Barnet‑Lamb, Geraghty, Harris, and Taylor, 2011) describes the limiting distribution of these eigenvalues. For thin groups the situation is radically different: the eigenvalues are not equidistributed with respect to the Sato–Tate measure but instead follow a distribution dictated by the limit set of Γ. Sarnak (2011) conjectured that for a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) the normalized Frobenius traces converge to a measure supported on [−2,2] whose density is the Patterson–Sullivan measure pushed forward by the trace map.

This conjecture has been verified in several special cases. For the Apollonian group, Bourgain and Kontorovich (2014) proved that the distribution of curvatures modulo primes follows a power‑law with exponent related to the Hausdorff dimension of the residual set. For thin subgroups generated by two parabolic elements, Magee (2015) obtained an explicit formula for the limiting spectral measure in terms of the Patterson–Sullivan density. The proof uses the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the infinite‑volume quotient and the fact that the Hecke operators at prime level correspond to averaging over the congruence quotient graphs.

An important application is to the affine sieve: the level of distribution of a polynomial map on a thin orbit is governed by the spectral gap of the associated Hecke operators. When the Hecke eigenvalues are known to be bounded away from the trivial eigenvalue by a uniform constant, the sieve yields almost‑prime values with a power‑saving error term. This is the mechanism behind the breakthrough of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011) on the saturation problem for integral Apollonian packings.

Thin Groups and the Application to the Sarnak–Xue Conjecture on Eigenvalue Bounds

The Sarnak–Xue conjecture (1991) predicts that for any congruence cover of a compact arithmetic locally symmetric space the first non‑zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian satisfies the Ramanujan bound λ₁ ≥ (ρ,ρ) where ρ is the half‑sum of positive roots. For thin subgroups the congruence quotients are not arithmetic covers, but the superstrong approximation theorem provides a family of finite quotients that mimic the arithmetic setting. The conjecture has been extended to thin groups by asking whether the uniform spectral gap obtained from the expander property can be sharpened to the Ramanujan bound.

In rank one the best known result is due to Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2011) who proved λ₁ ≥ 3/16 for the congruence quotients of the Apollonian group, which is exactly the Selberg bound for congruence subgroups of SL₂(ℤ). For higher rank, the work of Oh and Winter (2016) gives λ₁ ≥ c/n², while the Ramanujan bound would be (n−1)²/4. The gap between these bounds reflects the lack of a full Langlands correspondence for thin groups. Recent progress by Shin and Templier (2016) on the Sato–Tate theorem for families of automorphic forms suggests that if one could transfer the spectral data of thin quotients to an appropriate arithmetic group, the Ramanujan bound would follow from the generalized Ramanujan conjecture for GLₙ.

A concrete test case is the family of thin subgroups of SL₃(ℤ) arising from the action of the mapping class group on the character variety of a punctured torus. Numerical experiments indicate that the first eigenvalue of the congruence quotients approaches the Ramanujan bound as the level grows, but a proof would require establishing a spectral transfer principle that is currently out of reach.

  • Assuming that every thin subgroup automatically inherits the Selberg 3/16 bound; the bound holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for non‑arithmetic lattices with the Ramanujan bound for arithmetic quotients; the former is typically weaker and depends on the geometry of the limit set.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)ᴬ with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Forgetting that the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument uses the Zariski density of the original subgroup; if the subgroup is not Zariski dense the exponential decay of hitting proper subvarieties fails.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Unipotent Flows on Homogeneous Spaces

The quantitative non‑divergence theorem of Kleinbock and Margulis (1998) gives a uniform estimate for the measure of points in a homogeneous space whose unipotent trajectory spends a prescribed proportion of time outside a fixed compact set. When the acting group is a thin subgroup Γ of a semisimple algebraic group G, the same estimate holds for Γ‑orbits provided Γ is Zariski‑dense and satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients. The proof adapts the original argument by replacing the Haar measure on G/Γ with the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set of Γ, and by using the expander property of the Cayley graphs of Γ modulo q to control the recurrence of unipotent translates. A key technical input is the effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres in the thin quotient, which follows from the superstrong approximation theorem of Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak. The resulting bound takes the form μ({x ∈ X : u_t x ∉ K for ≥ ε proportion of t ∈ [0,T]}) ≤ C ε^α, where μ is the Patterson–Sullivan measure, K a compact subset, u_t a one‑parameter unipotent subgroup, and α > 0 depends only on the spectral gap. This quantitative non‑divergence is essential for the affine sieve on thin orbits because it guarantees that polynomial maps evaluated along unipotent translates do not concentrate on proper subvarieties, thereby providing the level of distribution needed for almost‑prime results.

In the classical arithmetic setting the non‑divergence estimate is uniform over all lattices in a given Lie group. For thin groups the constant C depends on the Hausdorff dimension δ of the limit set and on the spectral gap λ₁ of the congruence quotients. When δ is close to the critical exponent of G, the bound approaches the arithmetic one; when δ is small the constant deteriorates, reflecting the fact that thin orbits are sparser. The method also yields a quantitative version of Dani’s correspondence between divergent trajectories and rational approximations, which has been used to obtain effective Oppenheim‑type theorems for values of quadratic forms on thin orbits. A notable application is the work of Mohammadi and Oh (2015) on the distribution of integral points on affine symmetric varieties, where the quantitative non‑divergence of the horocycle flow on the thin quotient provides the error term in the lattice point count.

Thin Groups and the Arithmetic of Integral Points on Moduli Spaces of Local Systems

Moduli spaces of local systems on a punctured surface carry a natural action of the mapping class group, and the integral points correspond to representations of the fundamental group into SL_n(ℤ) with prescribed monodromy around punctures. When the image of the mapping class group is a thin subgroup of the arithmetic group preserving the symplectic or orthogonal form on the character variety, the superstrong approximation theorem supplies a family of expanders that can be used to sieve integral points on the moduli space. The affine sieve of Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak applies to any polynomial map f : Γ → ℤ that is non‑constant on the thin orbit, provided the congruence quotients of Γ form an expander family. In the setting of character varieties, f can be taken as the trace of a fixed word in the generators, and the sieve yields almost‑prime values of these trace functions. The level of distribution is governed by the spectral gap of the Hecke operators acting on the congruence quotients, which is uniform thanks to the product theorem of Breuillard, Green and Tao combined with the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument. Recent work of Magee, Puder and others has shown that for the SL₂(ℤ) character variety of the once‑punctured torus, the thin subgroup generated by two Dehn twists satisfies a spectral gap of at least 3/16, matching the Selberg bound for congruence subgroups. This allows one to prove that a positive proportion of integral points on the Markov surface correspond to almost‑prime traces, and to obtain quantitative equidistribution of these points with respect to the natural symplectic measure.

The main obstruction to extending these results to higher rank moduli spaces is the lack of a complete classification of thin subgroups in SL_n(ℤ) for n ≥ 3. While the mapping class group action on SL₃ character varieties produces many Zariski‑dense subgroups, it is not known whether all such subgroups satisfy superstrong approximation. The work of Benoist and Quint on stationary measures for random walks on homogeneous spaces provides a framework for proving expansion in higher rank, but the required non‑concentration estimates for the random walk on the thin subgroup remain open in general. Another difficulty is the presence of local‑global obstructions: the polynomial map f may vanish modulo certain primes for all points in the thin orbit, which would destroy the sieve. The local‑global principle for integral points on thin orbits, studied by Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak, asserts that if f is non‑constant on Γ and the congruence quotients are expanders, then the only obstructions are those coming from congruence conditions. Verifying this principle for moduli spaces of local systems is an active area of research.

Worked Example: Applying the Affine Sieve to Trace Functions on a Thin Orbit
Let Γ be the thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) generated by the matrices A = [[1,2],[0,1]] and B = [[1,0],[2,1]]. Consider the polynomial map f(γ) = tr(γ) for γ ∈ Γ. Show that the set {γ ∈ Γ : f(γ) is an almost prime with at most r prime factors} has positive density in the ball of radius T for some fixed r, assuming the congruence quotients of Γ form an expander family with uniform spectral gap.
Step 1: Verify Zariski density and non‑constancy. The generators A and B are unipotent and their commutator is non‑trivial, so Γ is a non‑elementary free group. Its Zariski closure is SL₂, hence Γ is Zariski‑dense. The trace function is non‑constant on Γ because tr(A) = 2 while tr(AB) = 6. Step 2: Uniform spectral gap. By the Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak superstrong approximation theorem, the Cayley graphs of Γ modulo q form an expander family with a uniform spectral gap λ₁ ≥ 3/16 (the Selberg bound) for all square‑free q. Step 3: Level of distribution. The expander property implies that for any polynomial map f of degree d, the number of γ in the ball of radius T with f(γ) ≡ 0 (mod q) is ≤ C Tδ q-1+ε for q ≤ Tθ, where δ is the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set and θ > 0 depends on the spectral gap. This gives a level of distribution Tθ. Step 4: Apply the affine sieve. The affine sieve (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, 2011) with dimension κ = 1 (since f is linear in the matrix entries) and level of distribution Tθ yields that the number of γ with f(γ) having at most r = ⌈κ/θ⌉ prime factors is ≫ Tδ / (log T). Hence the set has positive lower density in the ball. Conclusion. Under the stated expander assumption, the trace values on the thin orbit contain infinitely many almost primes with a bounded number of prime factors, and their counting function satisfies a power‑saving error term.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to combine expansion, spectral gap and the affine sieve, first identify the thin subgroup and verify Zariski density. Then cite the specific superstrong approximation result that gives the uniform spectral gap (e.g. Selberg 3/16 for SL₂). Next, translate the spectral gap into a level of distribution exponent θ. Finally, apply the sieve dimension formula r = ⌈κ/θ⌉. Remember that the sieve dimension κ equals the number of irreducible factors of the polynomial map over ℚ; for a trace function on SL₂ it is 1. Writing these steps explicitly earns full credit even if the final numeric bound is not required.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of Higher Rank Non‑Arithmetic Lattices

In higher rank (real rank ≥ 2) the spectral theory of non‑arithmetic lattices is dramatically constrained by Margulis superrigidity and the Margulis normal subgroup theorem. Any irreducible lattice in a higher‑rank semisimple Lie group is arithmetic, so genuine thin subgroups cannot be lattices. However, one can consider Zariski‑dense discrete subgroups of G(ℤ) that are not lattices, for instance subgroups generated by proximal elements with large eigenvalues. The spectral gap for the action of such a thin subgroup on the congruence quotients G(ℤ/qℤ) is governed by the representation theory of the finite simple groups of Lie type. The product theorem of Breuillard, Green and Tao together with the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument of Bourgain and Gamburd yields a uniform spectral gap provided the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for a set of primes of positive density. In higher rank the Ramanujan bound for the trivial representation is (ρ,ρ) where ρ is the half‑sum of positive roots; for SL_n this equals (n²−1)/4. The best known uniform bound for thin subgroups is due to Oh and Winter (2016), who proved λ₁ ≥ c/n² for congruence quotients of thin subgroups of SL_n(ℤ). The gap between c/n² and (n²−1)/4 reflects the absence of a Langlands functorial transfer from the thin quotient to an arithmetic quotient. If such a transfer existed, the generalized Ramanujan conjecture for GL_n would imply the optimal bound. Recent work of Shin and Templier on the Sato–Tate theorem for families of automorphic forms suggests that a spectral transfer principle might be established for thin subgroups arising from mapping class group actions on higher‑rank character varieties, but the necessary non‑concentration estimates for the associated random walks remain open.

A concrete test case is the family of thin subgroups of SL₃(ℤ) obtained from the action of the mapping class group of a punctured torus on the SL₃ character variety. Numerical experiments indicate that the first eigenvalue of the congruence quotients approaches the Ramanujan bound as the level grows. Proving this would require showing that the Hecke operators on the thin quotient have the same eigenvalue distribution as those on an arithmetic quotient, which in turn would follow from a suitable instance of the Langlands correspondence for non‑arithmetic subgroups. At present the only unconditional results are the uniform spectral gap of polynomial strength and the logarithmic diameter bounds for the Cayley graphs, both derived from the product theorem and the flattening lemma. The spectral gap also controls the rate of equidistribution of thin orbits on homogeneous spaces via the effective mixing of diagonal flows, a technique developed by Einsiedler, Margulis and Venkatesh for arithmetic quotients and extended to thin quotients by Mohammadi and Oh.

Thin Groups and the Dynamics of Random Walks on Expander Graphs

The connection between thin groups and expander graphs is most naturally expressed through the dynamics of simple random walks on the Cayley graphs of the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). When Γ is a Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL_n(ℤ) with superstrong approximation, the family of graphs {Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S_q)} forms an expander family with uniform spectral gap. The random walk driven by the symmetric generating set S_q mixes to the uniform distribution in O(log |Γ/Γ(q)|) steps, and the mixing time is precisely the diameter up to a constant factor. The flattening lemma of Bourgain and Gamburd shows that if the random walk measure μ(k) is not already flat (i.e. close to uniform), then its ℓ²‑norm decays by a factor (1−δ) after a bounded number of additional steps, provided the walk does not concentrate on a proper subgroup or a coset of a proper subgroup. The non‑concentration estimate is proved using the escape‑from‑subvarieties argument: the probability that the walk lands in a proper algebraic subvariety of SL_n decays exponentially in the length of the walk, because the Zariski density of Γ forces the walk to equidistribute on the limit set. This exponential decay, combined with the product theorem, yields the uniform spectral gap.

Quantitative consequences include logarithmic diameter bounds diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S_q)) ≤ C (log q)^A with A > 1 in general, and almost‑sure convergence of the random walk to the Haar measure on the profinite completion of Γ. The diameter bound is crucial for algorithmic applications: it implies that any element of the congruence quotient can be expressed as a word of length O((log q)^A) in the generators, which is the basis for the polynomial‑time construction of expanders from thin groups. Moreover, the random walk perspective provides a natural framework for the affine sieve: the level of distribution of a polynomial map f on the thin orbit is exactly the exponent governing the decay of the probability that f(γ) ≡ 0 (mod q) for a random walk step γ. When the random walk mixes rapidly, this probability is close to the naive density 1/q, giving a level of distribution q ≤ Tθ with θ determined by the spectral gap. The work of Varjú (2012) on the diameter of SL₂(ℤ/qℤ) and of Helfgott, Seress and others on the diameter of SL_n(ℤ/qℤ) shows that the optimal exponent A is 1 for arithmetic quotients, but for thin quotients the best known A is larger, reflecting the weaker expansion. Improving A to 1 for thin groups would imply the full superstrong approximation conjecture with optimal diameter, a major open problem.

  • Assuming that every thin subgroup automatically inherits the Selberg 3/16 bound; the bound holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for non‑arithmetic lattices with the Ramanujan bound for arithmetic quotients; the former is typically weaker and depends on the geometry of the limit set.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)^A with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Affine Varieties

The quantitative theory of integral points on affine varieties asks for asymptotic formulas with error terms for the number of integral solutions of a system of polynomial equations that lie in a given thin orbit. Let Γ be a Zariski‑dense subgroup of SLn(ℤ) and let V be an affine variety defined over ℤ on which Γ acts polynomially. For a height function H on V(ℤ) one studies the counting function

N(T) = #{ x ∈ Γ·x₀ ∩ V(ℤ) : H(x) ≤ T }

where x₀ is a fixed base point. When Γ is a lattice the classical theory of Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak gives N(T) ∼ c Tδ with δ the critical exponent of the action. For thin groups the exponent δ is strictly smaller than the ambient dimension, and the error term is governed by the spectral gap of the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). The superstrong approximation theorem provides a uniform spectral gap ε > 0 for all square‑free levels q. Using the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak one obtains a level of distribution θ = ε/(2 dim V) and consequently an asymptotic

N(T) = c Tδ + O(Tδ−η)

for some η > 0 depending on ε. The constant c is expressed as a product of local densities, reflecting the fact that the only obstructions to integral points are congruence obstructions. Recent work of Kontorovich–Oh and of Magee–Oh–Winter has made the dependence of η on the spectral gap explicit, showing that any improvement in the uniform spectral gap (for instance moving from polynomial to logarithmic diameter bounds) directly sharpens the error term. This quantitative framework also applies to counting integral points on homogeneous varieties such as the set of integer matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial, where the thin group is a free subgroup of SL2(ℤ) generated by two hyperbolic elements.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Superstrong Approximation for Non‑Linear Representations

Superstrong approximation was originally formulated for linear representations of SLn on finite quotients SLn(ℤ/qℤ). The extension to non‑linear representations concerns actions of a thin group Γ on varieties that are not vector spaces, for instance on the space of binary quadratic forms or on the character variety of a surface group. Let ρ : Γ → Homeo(X) be a continuous action on a compact metric space X that factors through the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). One says that ρ has superstrong approximation if the associated Markov operators on L²(X) have a uniform spectral gap independent of q. The key mechanism is the flattening lemma of Bourgain–Gamburd: if the random walk measure μ(k) on Γ/Γ(q) is not flat, its ℓ²‑norm decays by a fixed factor after a bounded number of steps, provided the walk does not concentrate on a proper subvariety of the algebraic group. For non‑linear actions the concentration estimate is replaced by an escape from subvarieties argument on X: the probability that the walk stays inside a proper algebraic subset of X decays exponentially because the Zariski density of Γ forces equidistribution on the limit set of the action. This was carried out by Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú for actions on homogeneous spaces of higher rank groups and by Benoist–Quint for actions on projective spaces. The resulting uniform spectral gap yields expander families of Schreier graphs Sch(Γ/Γ(q), S, X) and logarithmic diameter bounds for the action. Applications include quantitative equidistribution of thin orbits on character varieties and effective versions of the Oppenheim conjecture for integral quadratic forms represented by thin subgroups of SO(p,q).

Worked Example: Spectral Gap from Flattening
Let Γ = ⟨A,B⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) be a free Zariski‑dense subgroup generated by A = (2 1; 1 1) and B = (1 1; 1 2). For a prime p ≥ 5 let Γ(p) be the kernel of reduction mod p. Show that the Cayley graph Cay(Γ/Γ(p), {A,B}) has a uniform spectral gap independent of p.

Step 1: Verify Zariski density. The matrices A and B generate a non‑elementary subgroup of SL₂(ℝ); their limit set is a Cantor set of Hausdorff dimension < 1, hence Γ is Zariski‑dense in SL₂.

Step 2: Apply the Bourgain–Gamburd flattening lemma. Let μ be the uniform probability measure on {A,B,A⁻¹,B⁻¹}. For any k, either ‖μ(k)‖₂ ≤ |Γ/Γ(p)|−1/2+δ (flat) or the walk concentrates on a proper subgroup H < Γ/Γ(p). By the classification of proper subgroups of SL₂(𝔽p) (Borel, dihedral, or exceptional), concentration would imply that the random walk stays in a proper algebraic subvariety of SL₂.

Step 3: Escape from subvarieties. Because Γ is Zariski‑dense, the probability that a word of length ℓ lies in a fixed proper subvariety decays like exp(−cℓ). Choosing ℓ ≈ C log p makes this probability < p−2, so concentration cannot occur for the relevant k.

Step 4: Iterate flattening. After O(log p) steps the measure becomes flat, giving ‖μ(k)‖₂ ≤ |Γ/Γ(p)|−1/2+δ. By the standard equivalence between ℓ²‑flattening and spectral gap, the second eigenvalue λ₂ of the normalized adjacency operator satisfies λ₂ ≤ 1 − ε for some ε > 0 independent of p.

Conclusion: The family {Cay(Γ/Γ(p), {A,B})} is an expander family with uniform spectral gap.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a uniform spectral gap, first check Zariski density of the generating set. Then recall the three pillars: (1) classification of proper subgroups of the finite quotient, (2) exponential escape from subvarieties using Zariski density, (3) iteration of the flattening lemma to obtain ℓ²‑decay. Write the logical chain explicitly; examiners award marks for each pillar.

Thin Groups and the Role of the Product Theorem in Uniform Expansion for Higher Rank

The product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao states that for any finite simple group of Lie type G(𝔽q) and any symmetric generating set S not contained in a proper subgroup, either S³ = G(𝔽q) or |S³| ≥ |S|1+δ for an absolute δ > 0. In the context of thin groups Γ ⊂ SLn(ℤ) with n ≥ 3, the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) embed into SLn(ℤ/qℤ), which is a product of simple groups of Lie type for square‑free q. The product theorem is the engine that turns the non‑concentration estimate (escape from subvarieties) into a uniform spectral gap. Concretely, let μ be the random walk measure on Γ/Γ(q). If μ is not flat, the flattening lemma gives a set A with |A³| ≤ K|A|. By the product theorem, A must be contained in a proper subgroup of SLn(ℤ/qℤ). The classification of proper subgroups (maximal parabolic, subfield, or almost simple) together with the Zariski density of Γ shows that the probability of landing in any such subgroup decays exponentially in the word length. Hence the non‑concentration hypothesis holds uniformly, and the product theorem yields a uniform expansion constant ε depending only on n and the generating set. This argument, carried out by Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú, proves superstrong approximation for all Zariski‑dense subgroups of SLn(ℤ) with n ≥ 3. The same method extends to other simply connected simple algebraic groups, giving uniform expanders for thin subgroups of Spin, Sp, and exceptional groups. The quantitative by‑product is a diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)) ≤ C (log q)A with A depending on the rank; improving A to 1 remains open and is equivalent to the optimal superstrong approximation conjecture.

Thin Groups and the Connection to the Generalized Ramanujan Conjecture via Automorphic Transfer

The generalized Ramanujan conjecture predicts that for any cuspidal automorphic representation π of GLn(𝔸) the local components πp are tempered, i.e. their Satake parameters lie on the unit circle. For arithmetic quotients ΓSLn(ℝ) this is equivalent to the statement that the Hecke operators on L²(ΓSLn(ℝ)) have eigenvalues bounded by the Ramanujan bound. Thin groups do not arise from congruence subgroups, so their quotients ΓSLn(ℝ) are not arithmetic and the Langlands correspondence does not directly apply. However, the superstrong approximation theorem provides a family of expanders Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) whose spectral gap is uniform. By the work of Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak and later of Bourgain–Gamburd, the spectral gap of these finite graphs controls the spectrum of the Laplacian on the infinite quotient ΓSLn(ℝ) via a transfer principle: the eigenvalues of the Hecke operators on the thin quotient are limits of eigenvalues of the normalized adjacency operators on the congruence quotients.
