Let X be a connected 2‑type with π₁(X) ≃ ℤ and π₂(X) ≃ ℤ/2, where the action of π₁ on π₂ is trivial. Compute the k‑invariant k₂ : ‖X‖₁ → K(ℤ/2, 3) that classifies the Postnikov tower of X, and identify its cohomology class in H³(ℤ; ℤ/2).
The 1‑truncation ‖X‖₁ is equivalent to the circle S¹ because π₁(X) ≃ ℤ and X is connected. The fibre of X₂ → X₁ is K(ℤ/2, 2). The k‑invariant is a map k₂ : S¹ → K(ℤ/2, 3). Since π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ acts trivially on ℤ/2, the cohomology group H³(ℤ; ℤ/2) is isomorphic to ℤ/2 (the group cohomology of ℤ with trivial coefficients is ℤ/2 in odd degrees). The map k₂ corresponds to the generator of this group. In the synthetic setting, one constructs k₂ by the universal property of the fibre sequence: the composite S¹ → X₂ → X₁ is the truncation map, and the fibre sequence gives a connecting map S¹ → K(ℤ/2, 3). Evaluating this map on the fundamental class of S¹ yields the non‑zero element of ℤ/2. Hence the k‑invariant is the non‑trivial class in H³(ℤ; ℤ/2).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a k‑invariant, first identify the relevant truncation levels and the homotopy groups involved. Remember that the coefficient system for the cohomology group is the action of π₁ on πₙ; if the action is trivial, the group is ordinary group cohomology. Use the synthetic long exact sequence of homotopy groups to confirm the fibre is an Eilenberg–MacLane space, then invoke the representability of cohomology by maps into K(G,n). The encode‑decode method for the circle (or higher spheres) is the standard tool to compute the resulting cohomology class.

Higher (∞,n)‑Categories in Directed Homotopy Type Theory

Directed homotopy type theory extends Martin‑Löf type theory with a directed interval type 𝟚 that has two endpoints 0,1 : 𝟚 and a single generating path δ : 0 → 1 which is not invertible. This primitive directed path models the non‑invertible 1‑morphisms of an (∞,1)-category. To model (∞,n)-categories for n > 1, one iterates the directed interval: an (∞,2)-category can be presented by a type equipped with two directed interval structures that commute up to higher directed paths, or more systematically by the n‑globe higher inductive type whose k‑cells are generated by the k‑dimensional faces of the n‑cube. The work of Riehl, Shulman, and others shows that the fundamental (∞,n)-category of a directed type can be constructed as a higher inductive type whose objects are points, 1‑morphisms are directed paths, 2‑morphisms are directed homotopies between directed paths, and so on.

The key technical device is the Rezk completion for (∞,n)-categories, which forces the Segal conditions and completeness at each level. In directed HoTT this is achieved by a higher inductive‑inductive definition that simultaneously builds the type of objects, the hom‑types, and the composition operations, together with path constructors expressing associativity and unit laws up to coherent higher directed paths. The resulting structure satisfies the universal property of the free (∞,n)-category on a given directed graph. This synthetic approach avoids the combinatorial complexity of simplicial or globular models and makes the coherence data first‑class citizens of the type theory.

An important application is the internalisation of (∞,n)-category theory itself: one can define the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-categories, the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-functors, and prove the (∞,n)-categorical Yoneda lemma inside the theory. The directed interval also interacts with the cohesive modalities: the shape modality sends a directed type to its underlying ∞‑groupoid by inverting all directed paths, while the flat modality ♭ extracts the discrete (∞,n)-category of global points. This interplay provides a synthetic version of the homotopy hypothesis for (∞,n)-categories.

Computational aspects are under active development. Cubical directed type theory, implemented in the proof assistant Cartesian Cubical Agda, provides a canonicity theorem for the directed interval: every closed term of type 𝟚 reduces to either 0 or 1. This ensures that the synthetic (∞,n)-categories have a concrete computational interpretation, opening the way for certified algorithms in higher category theory.

Synthetic (∞,1)‑Categorical Limits and Colimits in the ∞‑Topos of Types

The ∞‑topos of types is the (∞,1)-category whose objects are types and whose morphisms are functions, with higher morphisms given by homotopies. In this setting, limits and colimits are homotopy limits and colimits. They can be constructed synthetically using higher inductive types: a pullback of f : A → C and g : B → C is the higher inductive type Σ (a:A) Σ (b:B) (f a = g b), which is exactly the homotopy pullback. Dually, a pushout is the higher inductive type generated by constructors inl : A → P, inr : B → P and a path constructor glue : ∀ (c:C), inl (f c) = inr (g c). These constructions satisfy the expected universal properties up to equivalence, and the proofs are direct applications of the induction principles of the higher inductive types.

More general limits are obtained as iterated pullbacks and equalizers. The equalizer of f,g : A → B is the type Σ (a:A) (f a = g a). Because the ∞‑topos of types is presentable, all small limits and colimits exist and are computed pointwise in the sense that a diagram D : I → Type has limit lim D ≃ Σ (x:Π i, D i) ∀ i j (u:i→j), D u (x i) = x j. This formula is a higher inductive type whose constructors encode the cone condition. The colimit is the higher inductive type generated by constructors in i : D i → colim D and path constructors for each morphism in I.

The adjoint functor theorem holds internally: a functor between presentable ∞‑categories that preserves limits and is accessible has a left adjoint. In HoTT this is proved by constructing the left adjoint as a higher inductive type that freely adds the required colimits. The proof uses the fact that the ∞‑topos of types is locally cartesian closed and has a subobject classifier (the type of propositions). These synthetic limit and colimit constructions are the backbone of the formalisation of (∞,1)-category theory in the HoTT library, enabling the development of the (∞,1)-category of spectra, the (∞,1)-category of ∞‑topoi, and the internal Yoneda lemma.

A subtle point is the interaction with truncation levels. The limit of a diagram of n‑types is again an n‑type, but the colimit of n‑types may raise the truncation level. This is reflected in the synthetic construction: the pushout of two sets along a function need not be a set; it is a 1‑type whose fundamental groupoid captures the gluing data. The HoTT library provides lemmas that compute the truncation level of a colimit in terms of the connectivity of the diagram maps, which is essential for reasoning about homotopy groups of higher inductive types.

Principal ∞‑Bundles, Characteristic Classes, and the Synthetic Chern‑Weil Theory

In homotopy type theory a principal ∞‑bundle for an ∞‑group G is a map p : P → X equipped with a free G-action on P such that the quotient P/G is equivalent to X. The classifying type BG is the delooping of G, constructed as a higher inductive type with a single point constructor base : BG and a loop constructor for each element of G together with higher paths encoding the group structure. The universal principal G-bundle is the map EG → BG where EG is the contractible type with a free G-action (the homotopy fibre of the point inclusion). Every principal G-bundle over X is equivalent to the pullback of EG → BG along a classifying map X → BG.

Characteristic classes are maps BG → Bⁿ A for an abelian ∞‑group A (typically Bⁿ ℤ or Bⁿ U(1)). In the synthetic Chern‑Weil theory, one starts with a cohesive ∞‑topos equipped with the shape modality and the flat modality ♭. The synthetic de Rham complex is the fibre of the unit ♭ → id. For a Lie ∞‑group G with Lie algebra 𝔤, invariant polynomials on 𝔤 give rise to maps BG → Bⁿ ℝ in the cohesive setting. The synthetic construction uses the fact that the flat modality ♭BG classifies flat G-bundles, and the shape modality BG classifies the underlying topological bundle. The Chern‑Weil homomorphism is then the composite BG → ♭BG → Bⁿ ℝ where the first map is the unit of the flat modality and the second is induced by the invariant polynomial via the synthetic de Rham theorem.

This approach has been formalised for the classical groups O(n), U(n), and Sp(n) in the HoTT library. The first Pontryagin class p₁ : BO(n) → B⁴ ℤ and the Chern classes c_k : BU(n) → B²ᵏ ℤ are obtained as synthetic Chern‑Weil classes. The proof that these classes agree with the classical ones uses the synthetic version of the splitting principle: the map BT → BG induced by a maximal torus inclusion is injective on cohomology, and the invariant polynomials restrict to symmetric polynomials on the weight lattice. The synthetic splitting principle is proved by constructing the flag variety as a higher inductive type and showing that its cohomology is the polynomial ring on the Chern roots.

An open problem is the synthetic construction of secondary characteristic classes (e.g., the Chern‑Simons classes) which require a differential refinement of the cohomology theory. The differential cohomology hexagon in cohesive HoTT provides a framework, but the explicit higher inductive types for differential cocycles are still under development. Another direction is the extension to equivariant principal ∞‑bundles, where the base type carries a group action and the bundle is required to be equivariant. This connects with the synthetic equivariant homotopy theory mentioned elsewhere in the lesson.

  • Confusing inductive‑recursive definitions with inductive‑inductive definitions; the former involve a recursive function, the latter involve two mutually defined types.
  • Assuming the k‑invariant always lives in ordinary cohomology; it lives in cohomology with local coefficients when π₁ acts non‑trivially on πₙ.
  • Thinking directed HoTT only models (∞,1)-categories; iterating the directed interval yields (∞,n)-categories for any n.
  • Believing that all colimits in the ∞‑topos of types preserve truncation levels; pushouts of sets can produce 1‑types.
  • Treating the synthetic Chern‑Weil map as a map of ordinary types rather than a map in the cohesive ∞‑topos; the flat and shape modalities are essential.
  • Overlooking that the universal principal ∞‑bundle EG → BG is a higher inductive type whose total space is contractible by construction, not by an external argument.
  • Assuming the Postnikov tower in HoTT is unique up to equality; it is unique up to equivalence, and the k‑invariants are only well‑defined up to the action of the automorphisms of the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.

Synthetic Rational Homotopy Theory and Sullivan Models in HoTT

Rational homotopy theory studies spaces up to rational equivalence, where the homotopy groups are tensored with ℚ. In classical topology, Sullivan's minimal models provide commutative differential graded algebras (CDGAs) over ℚ that capture the rational homotopy type of simply connected spaces. In HoTT, this theory is internalized by working in the ∞-topos of types with rational coefficients. The key insight is that the rationalization of a type X, denoted X_ℚ, can be constructed as a higher inductive type that freely adds rational vector space structure to the homotopy groups. For a simply connected type X, the Sullivan minimal model is a CDGA (ΛV, d) where V is a graded ℚ-vector space and d is a decomposable differential. In HoTT, this corresponds to a sequence of higher inductive types building X_ℚ as a tower of principal fibrations with fibers Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(ℚ, n). The synthetic construction uses the fact that the rational cohomology ring H*(X; ℚ) is the cohomology of the CDGA of piecewise polynomial differential forms on X. The minimal model is then obtained by a synthetic version of the Sullivan construction: one iteratively attaches cells to kill indecomposable cohomology classes. A crucial computational tool is the synthetic version of the Hirsch lemma, which relates the minimal model of a fibration to those of its base and fiber. This has been formalized for formal spaces (where the minimal model is quasi-isomorphic to the cohomology algebra) such as spheres, complex projective spaces, and compact Lie groups. The synthetic approach clarifies that rational homotopy equivalence corresponds to equivalence of the associated ∞-groupoids after rationalization, and that the minimal model is unique up to isomorphism of CDGAs, which in HoTT translates to equivalence of the corresponding higher inductive presentations.

The Synthetic Dold-Kan Correspondence: Chain Complexes and Simplicial Abelian Groups in HoTT

The Dold-Kan correspondence establishes an equivalence between the category of non-negatively graded chain complexes of abelian groups and the category of simplicial abelian groups. In HoTT, this correspondence is internalized by constructing the normalization functor N and the Moore complex functor Γ as mutually inverse equivalences of ∞-categories. A simplicial abelian group in HoTT is a type family A : Δ^op → AbGrp where Δ is the simplex category (constructed as a higher inductive type with face and degeneracy maps). The normalized chain complex N(A) has N(A)_n = ⋂i=0n-1 ker(d_i : A_n → An-1) with differential d_n. The inverse Γ(C) for a chain complex C is defined by Γ(C)_n = ⊕[n] ↠ [k] C_k where the sum is over surjections in Δ. The synthetic proof that N and Γ are equivalences uses the fact that the identity type in the ∞-category of simplicial abelian groups corresponds to homotopy equivalence of chain complexes. A key technical point is that the Dold-Kan correspondence preserves the monoidal structure: the tensor product of chain complexes corresponds to the levelwise tensor product of simplicial abelian groups, and the internal hom corresponds to the simplicial mapping complex. This allows the synthetic construction of the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(A, n) as the image under Γ of the chain complex A[n] (A in degree n, zero elsewhere). The correspondence also interacts with the stable homotopy category: the ∞-category of spectra is equivalent to the ∞-category of unbounded chain complexes, and the Dold-Kan correspondence extends to a Quillen equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and connective chain complexes. In Cubical Agda, the normalization functor computes by reducing cubical paths to their boundary components, providing a computational interpretation of the homology groups of a type as the homotopy groups of its Dold-Kan image.

Technique: Computing Rational Homotopy Groups via Minimal Models
Let X be the total space of the fibration S³ → X → S⁴ classified by the Hopf map η : S³ → S⁴. Compute π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ using the Sullivan minimal model.
The minimal model of S⁴ is (Λ(x₄), 0) with |x₄| = 4. The minimal model of S³ is (Λ(y₃), 0) with |y₃| = 3. The Hopf map η corresponds to a map of minimal models sending x₄ to y₃² (since η generates π₃(S⁴) ≅ ℤ and the Whitehead product [ι₄, ι₄] = 2η). The minimal model of the total space X is the relative Sullivan algebra (Λ(x₄, y₃), d) with d(x₄) = 0, d(y₃) = x₄. This is acyclic in positive degrees, so X_ℚ is contractible. Thus π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ = 0 for all * > 0. In HoTT, this is verified by constructing X as a HIT with constructors base : X, loop₄ : base = base (4-loop), loop₃ : base = base (3-loop), and a 4-path filling loop₃ ∘ loop₃ = loop₄. The rationalization X_ℚ is then shown to be contractible by exhibiting a homotopy between the identity and the constant map using the rational vector space structure on the loop spaces.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Rational Equivalence in HITs
When a problem asks about rational homotopy groups of a HIT, look for differentials in the minimal model that kill generators. A generator in degree n with a non-zero differential means the corresponding rational homotopy group vanishes. The minimal model of a HIT is built by reading off the constructors: each n-path constructor adds a generator in degree n, and each (n+1)-path constructor relating n-paths adds a differential. If the differential is decomposable (expressible in terms of lower-degree generators), the model is minimal. Practice translating the Hopf fibration, the quaternionic Hopf fibration, and the fibration S⁷ → S¹⁵ → S⁸ into minimal models.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Mapping Spaces: Function Types as Internal Hom

In the ∞-topos of types, the function type X → Y represents the internal mapping space Map(X, Y). Its homotopy groups are given by π_k(Map(X, Y), f) ≅ π0(Map(X, Ω^k Y), f) ≅ [X, Ω^k Y], the set of homotopy classes of maps from X to the k-fold loop space of Y. When X is a finite CW-complex presented as a HIT, the mapping space inherits a natural filtration by the skeleta of X. The synthetic approach to mapping spaces uses the fact that Map(X, Y) is the limit of the diagram Map(X_n, Y) where X_n is the n-skeleton. For X = S¹, Map(S¹, Y) ≃ ΩY × Y, where the first factor is the based loop space and the second is the evaluation at the basepoint. For X = Sⁿ, Map(Sⁿ, Y) ≃ ΩⁿY × Y. For a general HIT X built from cells, the mapping space is computed by an equalizer diagram reflecting the attaching maps. A key result is the synthetic version of the evaluation fibration: for any type Y, the map ev : Map(X, Y) × X → Y given by ev(f, x) = f(x) is a fibration whose fiber over y : Y is Map_*(X, Y_y) where Y_y is the component of y. The long exact sequence of homotopy groups for this fibration yields the exact sequence ⋯ → πk+1(Y) → π_k(Map_*(X, Y)) → π_k(Map(X, Y)) → π_k(Y) → ⋯. When X is a suspension ΣZ, there is an adjunction Map(ΣZ, Y) ≃ Map(Z, ΩY), which in HoTT is the equivalence (ΣZ → Y) ≃ (Z → ΩY). This adjunction is used to compute the homotopy groups of mapping spaces out of spheres and projective spaces. The synthetic construction of the mapping space as a HIT with constructors for pointwise paths and higher coherences provides a computational handle on the homotopy groups of function types in Cubical Agda.

The Synthetic Quillen Model Structure on Simplicial Objects in HoTT

In classical homotopy theory, the category of simplicial sets carries the Kan-Quillen model structure where weak equivalences are weak homotopy equivalences, fibrations are Kan fibrations, and cofibrations are monomorphisms. In HoTT, one can construct a synthetic model structure on the ∞-category of simplicial types (types over Δ^op). A simplicial type is a functor X : Δ^op → Type. The Reedy model structure has weak equivalences and fibrations defined levelwise: a map f : X → Y is a weak equivalence (resp. fibration) if each f_n : X_n → Y_n is an equivalence (resp. fibration) of types. The cofibrations are the Reedy cofibrations, characterized by the latching map condition. The injective model structure has weak equivalences and cofibrations levelwise, with fibrations defined by the right lifting property. The projective model structure has weak equivalences and fibrations levelwise. The synthetic Quillen equivalence between simplicial types and types is given by the geometric realization functor |−| : sType → Type and the singular complex functor Sing : Type → sType. The geometric realization of a simplicial type X is the colimit of the diagram X_n × Δ^n where Δ^n is the standard n-simplex type (a HIT with n+1 vertices and higher paths). The singular complex of a type Y has Sing(Y)_n = (Δ^n → Y). The synthetic proof that this is a Quillen equivalence uses the fact that the unit Y → Sing|Y| is a weak equivalence for all Y (by the synthetic version of the Milnor-Lurie theorem) and the counit |Sing X| → X is a weak equivalence for Reedy cofibrant X. This model structure is essential for doing homotopy theory of diagrams in HoTT, as it provides a framework for homotopy limits and colimits of simplicial diagrams. The Reedy fibrant replacement of a simplicial type computes its homotopy limit, and the Reedy cofibrant replacement computes its homotopy colimit.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of ∞-Operads and Algebras in HoTT

An ∞-operad in HoTT is a type O equipped with a composition structure that is associative and unital up to coherent higher homotopies. The synthetic definition uses the fact that the ∞-category of types is symmetric monoidal under the cartesian product, and an ∞-operad is a monoid in the ∞-category of symmetric sequences. Concretely, an ∞-operad consists of types O(n) for n : ℕ with an action of the symmetric group Σ_n, composition maps O(k) × O(n₁) × ⋯ × O(n_k) → O(n₁ + ⋯ + n_k), and higher coherences. The associative operad Ass has Ass(n) = Σ_n (the symmetric group as a discrete type). The commutative operad Comm has Comm(n) = 1 (the unit type). The little disks operad D_k has D_k(n) = Emb(∐_n D^k, D^k) (the space of embeddings of n disjoint k-disks into the standard k-disk). An algebra over an ∞-operad O is a type A with maps O(n) × A^n → A satisfying the operad axioms up to coherent homotopy. The synthetic bar-cobar adjunction relates O-algebras to coalgebras over the cooperad O^∨. For the associative operad, O-algebras are A_∞-spaces (monoids up to coherent homotopy), and the bar construction produces a coassociative coalgebra. The synthetic recognition principle states that a connected type X is an O-algebra for the little disks operad D_k if and only if X is a k-fold loop space. This is formalized by constructing the operadic nerve and showing that the ∞-category of D_k-algebras is equivalent to the ∞-category of k-fold loop spaces. The synthetic construction of the free O-algebra on a type X uses a higher inductive type with constructors for the operad actions and coherences. This framework has been used to formalize the Deligne conjecture (the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra is an algebra over the little disks operad) and to study factorization homology in HoTT.

  • Confusing the minimal model of a space with its cohomology algebra; the minimal model is a free CDGA, while the cohomology algebra may have relations not captured by decomposable differentials.
  • Assuming the Dold-Kan correspondence preserves all limits and colimits; it is an equivalence of ∞-categories but the normalization functor does not preserve products (it is only lax monoidal).
  • Treating Map(X, Y) as a set of functions rather than an ∞-groupoid; its identity types are homotopies, and its higher identity types are higher homotopies.
  • Believing that every simplicial type is Reedy fibrant; a simplicial type is Reedy fibrant iff each matching map X_n → M_n X is a fibration, which fails for constant diagrams of non-fibrant types.
  • Assuming that an A_∞-space is strictly associative; the synthetic definition only requires associativity up to a coherent system of higher paths, and strictification is a non-trivial theorem (the recognition principle).
  • Overlooking that the rationalization of a HIT may not be a HIT of the same shape; rationalization adds path constructors that make all homotopy groups into ℚ-vector spaces, which can change the truncation level.
  • Thinking the synthetic Quillen equivalence between simplicial types and types is an equivalence of 1-categories; it is an equivalence of ∞-categories, and the model structures are only presentations of this equivalence.

The Synthetic Kahn‑Priddy Theorem and the Stable Splitting of Ω^∞Σ^∞X

The Kahn‑Priddy theorem identifies the infinite loop space Ω^∞Σ^∞X as a disjoint union of extended powers D_k(X) = (X^k)hΣ_k, where Σ_k acts by permuting factors and the homotopy quotient is taken in the ∞‑category of types. In HoTT, the suspension spectrum Σ^∞X is the sequential colimit of Σ^n X, and Ω^∞ evaluates the 0‑th space of a spectrum. The theorem states that the unit map X → Ω^∞Σ^∞X extends to an equivalence Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∐k≥0 D_k(X). The synthetic proof proceeds through three pillars: the Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen theorem giving Ω^∞Σ^∞S0 ≃ ℤ × BΣ_∞+, the Snaith splitting Σ^∞Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∨_k Σ^∞D_k(X), and the recognition that the map ∐ D_k(X) → Ω^∞Σ^∞X induced by the operad structure of the sphere spectrum is an equivalence. In HoTT, each D_k(X) is a higher inductive type with constructors for the Σ_k‑action and the homotopy quotient paths. The Kahn‑Priddy map BΣ_k → Ω^∞Σ^∞S0 classifies the k‑fold extended power of the sphere. The stable splitting implies that the stable homotopy groups of spheres π_*^S = π_*(Ω^∞Σ^∞S0) decompose as a direct sum of the homotopy groups of the extended powers D_k(S0) = BΣ_k+. This decomposition underlies the computation of the first few stable stems via the homology of symmetric groups. Formalization in Cubical Agda has achieved the Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen equivalence and the construction of the Snaith splitting for finite types, but the full equivalence for arbitrary types requires a synthetic version of the group‑completion theorem for E_∞‑spaces, which remains an open formalization target.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Configuration Spaces and Braid Groups

The configuration space Conf_n(M) of n distinct ordered points in a type M is the subtype of M^n where all coordinates are pairwise unequal. In HoTT, this is defined as Conf_n(M) ≔ Σ (x : M^n), ∏i≠j (x_i ≠ x_j). When M = ℝ2, Conf_n(ℝ2) is a K(B_n, 1) where B_n is the Artin braid group on n strands. The synthetic computation of π1(Conf_n(ℝ2)) uses a higher inductive presentation of Conf_n(ℝ2) as the Salvetti complex: a type with a basepoint, 1‑cells corresponding to the standard generators σ_i of B_n, and 2‑cells imposing the braid relations σ_i σi+1 σ_i = σi+1 σ_i σi+1 and σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i for |i−j|>1. The encode‑decode method then constructs an equivalence Ω(Conf_n(ℝ2)) ≃ B_n, where B_n is presented as a set‑level group via its standard presentation. For general M, the scanning map Conf_n(ℝ^d) → Ω^d S^d (d ≥ 2) is constructed by sending a configuration to the map that collapses the complement of small balls around the points. This map is (n−1)‑connected and induces the homology stability isomorphism H_k(Conf_n(ℝ^d)) ≅ H_k(Confn+1(ℝ^d)) for k < n/2. The Cohen‑Taylor spectral sequence, which computes H^*(Conf_n(M)) from the cohomology of M, is synthesized by filtering the configuration space by the number of points in a chosen subspace. Formalization in the HoTT library has achieved the braid group presentation for n ≤ 4 and the construction of the scanning map for d = 2, but the general homology stability theorem and the Cohen‑Taylor spectral sequence remain partially formalized due to the complexity of the required spectral sequence machinery in HoTT.

Encode‑Decode for Braid Groups
Let Conf3(ℝ2) be presented as a HIT with basepoint *, 1‑cells a, b : * = *, and a 2‑cell braid : a ⬝ b ⬝ a = b ⬝ a ⬝ b. Define a type family Code : Conf3(ℝ2) → Type by Code(*) ≔ B3 (the set‑level braid group on 3 strands), Code(a) ≔ transport by σ1, Code(b) ≔ transport by σ2, and Code(braid) as the path witnessing the braid relation in B3. Show that the total space Σ (x : Conf3(ℝ2)), Code(x) is contractible.
The total space E ≔ Σ (x : Conf3(ℝ2)), Code(x) has a center of contraction at (*, e) where e is the identity in B3. For any (x, c) : E, we construct a path to (*, e) by induction on x. If x ≡ *, then c : B3 and the path is (loop^c, c⁻¹) where loop^c is the concatenation of a and b according to the word c. If x is a path constructor a or b, the induction hypothesis gives a path in the fiber over the endpoint, and the definition of Code on a, b ensures the transport matches the group multiplication by σ1 or σ2. The 2‑cell braid corresponds exactly to the braid relation in B3, so the path constructed over the boundary of braid extends to a path over the whole 2‑cell. Thus E is contractible, and by the encode‑decode theorem Ω(Conf3(ℝ2), *) ≃ B3.
Exam Strategy: Configuration Spaces as HITs
When a question asks for the fundamental group of a configuration space, first identify if the space is a K(G,1). For Conf_n(ℝ2), the answer is the braid group B_n. For Conf_n(ℝ^d) with d ≥ 3, the space is simply connected. The synthetic method always uses a HIT presentation (Salvetti complex for d=2, Fulton‑MacPherson compactification for general d) followed by encode‑decode. Memorize the generators σ_i and the two families of relations for B_n; they appear verbatim in the 1‑ and 2‑cell constructors of the HIT.

The Synthetic Atiyah‑Hirzebruch Spectral Sequence for Generalized Cohomology

The Atiyah‑Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) computes the generalized cohomology E^*(X) of a type X from its ordinary cohomology with coefficients in the coefficient groups E^*(pt). In HoTT, a spectrum E is a sequence of types E_n with equivalences E_n ≃ Ω En+1. The cohomology group E^k(X) is defined as π-k Map_*(X, E) ≃ ||X → Ω^k E||0 for k ≤ 0, and for k > 0 via the suspension isomorphism. The synthetic AHSS is constructed from the Postnikov tower of the spectrum E: let E⟨n⟩ be the n‑th Postnikov section, so that π_k(E⟨n⟩) = π_k(E) for k ≤ n and 0 otherwise. The fiber of E⟨n⟩ → E⟨n-1⟩ is the Eilenberg‑MacLane spectrum Σ^n Hπ_n(E). Applying the mapping type Map(X, −) yields a tower of fibrations Map(X, E⟨n⟩) → Map(X, E⟨n-1⟩) with fiber Map(X, Σ^n Hπ_n(E)) ≃ Σ^n Map(X, Hπ_n(E)). The long exact sequences of homotopy groups assemble into an exact couple, producing a spectral sequence with E2p,q = H^p(X; π-q(E)) converging to Ep+q(X) for X a finite type (or more generally, a type of finite homotopy dimension). The differentials d_r : E_rp,q → E_rp+r, q-r+1 are induced by the k‑invariants of the Postnikov tower. For E = Hℤ/p, the first non‑trivial differential d2 is the Steenrod square Sq2 (or the Bockstein for p=2). The synthetic proof of convergence uses the fact that the Postnikov tower of E is a limit diagram in the ∞‑category of spectra, and Map(X, −) preserves limits. Formalization in Cubical Agda has constructed the Postnikov tower of a spectrum and the associated exact couple for finite types, but the general convergence theorem for arbitrary types requires a synthetic version of the Milnor exact sequence for the limit of the tower, which is complicated by the need for countable choice in the metatheory.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Lie Groups, Stiefel Manifolds, and Grassmannians

The classical Lie groups are synthesized in HoTT as automorphism groups of structured types. The orthogonal group O(n) is the type of linear equivalences ℝ^n ≃ ℝ^n preserving the standard inner product, defined as a subtype of the function type (ℝ^n → ℝ^n) with the condition ⟨f(x), f(y)⟩ = ⟨x, y⟩. The unitary group U(n) and symplectic group Sp(n) are defined analogously over ℂ and ℍ. The Stiefel manifold V_k(ℝ^n) of orthonormal k‑frames in ℝ^n is the type of linear maps ℝ^k → ℝ^n that are isometric embeddings; it is equivalent to the homogeneous space O(n)/O(n−k). The Grassmannian Gr_k(ℝ^n) of k‑planes in ℝ^n is the type of k‑dimensional linear subspaces, equivalent to O(n)/(O(k)×O(n−k)). In HoTT, these are constructed as higher inductive types: Gr_k(ℝ^n) has a constructor for each point of the classical Grassmannian and path constructors witnessing the transitive action of O(n). The tautological bundle γ_k^n over Gr_k(ℝ^n) is the type family whose fiber over a subspace V is V itself. Characteristic classes arise as maps of classifying types: the Stiefel‑Whitney classes w_i : BO(n) → K(ℤ/2, i) are constructed via the action of the Steenrod algebra on H^*(BO(n); ℤ/2), which is the polynomial algebra ℤ/2[w1,…,w_n]. The Chern classes c_i : BU(n) → K(ℤ, 2i) are constructed similarly using the complex orientation of BU. The synthetic splitting principle states that the pullback of γ_k^n to the flag manifold Fl(n) = O(n)/T^n (where T^n is the maximal torus) splits as a sum of line bundles, reducing computations to the case of line bundles where c1 classifies the bundle. Bott periodicity is synthesized as the equivalence Ω8 BO ≃ BO (real) and Ω2 BU ≃ BU (complex), proved by constructing the Clifford module structure on the loop space. Formalization in the HoTT library has achieved the construction of BO(n) as a HIT, the tautological bundle, and the first Stiefel‑Whitney class w1; the higher classes and the full splitting principle require a synthetic theory of the Steenrod algebra action on the cohomology of classifying spaces, which is currently under development.

The Synthetic Cyclotomic Trace and Topological Cyclic Homology in HoTT

Topological Cyclic Homology TC(R) of a ring spectrum R is the homotopy fixed points of the circle action on Topological Hochschild Homology THH(R). In HoTT, THH(R) is constructed as a higher inductive type with a circle action: it has a basepoint, a 1‑cell for the circle action, and higher cells encoding the cyclic bar construction. Concretely, THH(R) ≔ Σ (x : S1 → R), ∏t:S1 (x(t) = x(t+1)) where the condition encodes the cyclicity. The circle action rotates the domain S1. The Connes operator B : THH(R) → Ω THH(R) is the map induced by the circle action. The homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 are defined as the type of maps S1 → THH(R) equipped with a homotopy to the constant map, i.e., the fiber of the map THH(R) → Map(S1, THH(R)) induced by the action. The Frobenius maps φ_p : THH(R)C_p → THH(R) are constructed using the p‑fold covering S1 → S1. The Nikolaus‑Scholze description of TC(R) is the sequential limit TC(R) ≔ lim_n THH(R)Cp^n where the transition maps are the Frobenius. The cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) is a map from the algebraic K‑theory spectrum (constructed as the group completion of the ∞‑category of perfect R‑modules) to TC(R). The Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy theorem states that for a nilpotent extension of ring spectra R → R', the relative K‑theory fiber is equivalent to the relative TC fiber. In HoTT, the synthetic proof uses the fact that both K and TC are localizing invariants and that the cyclotomic trace is an equivalence on the ∞‑category of perfect modules over a field. Formalization status: THH(R) as a HIT with circle action has been defined in Cubical Agda for discrete rings, and the Connes operator B has been constructed. The homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 and the Frobenius maps are formalized for the case R = 𝔽_p. The full Nikolaus‑Scholze limit construction and the cyclotomic trace map remain major open formalization challenges due to the need for a synthetic theory of ∞‑categories of modules and the group completion construction for K‑theory.

  • Confusing the Kahn‑Priddy splitting Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∐ D_k(X) with the Snaith splitting Σ^∞Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∨ Σ^∞D_k(X); the former is a splitting of spaces, the latter of spectra.
  • Assuming Conf_n(M) is always a K(π,1); this holds only for dim M = 2. For dim M ≥ 3, Conf_n(M) is simply connected and has higher homotopy groups.
  • Treating the Atiyah‑Hirzebruch spectral sequence as a first‑quadrant spectral sequence for all X; it is a half‑plane spectral sequence for general X, and convergence requires X to have finite homotopy dimension or E to be connective.
  • Believing the synthetic Stiefel‑Whitney classes w_i : BO(n) → K(ℤ/2, i) are defined by the same cellular formulas as in classical topology; in HoTT they are defined via the Steenrod algebra action on the synthetic cohomology ring H^*(BO(n); ℤ/2).
  • Overlooking that THH(R) in HoTT is a type with a circle action, not merely a spectrum; the circle action is primitive data in the HIT definition, and the Connes operator is derived from it.
  • Assuming the cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) is an equivalence for all ring spectra; it is an equivalence only after p‑completion and for regular rings, or on relative terms for nilpotent extensions (DGM theorem).
  • Confusing the homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 with the genuine fixed points THH(R)S1; in HoTT, the homotopy fixed points are the correct definition for TC, and the genuine fixed points are not invariant under equivalence of spectra with circle action.

hand/donaldson-thomas.html:
The Virtual Fundamental Class: Obstruction Theory and Deformation Constraints

The previous sections established the counting of objects; this section delves into the *mechanism* that makes counting possible on a Calabi-Yau threefold. Unlike a smooth curve in a surface, a sheaf on a 3-fold has a virtual dimension equal to its expected dimension only if the obstruction space vanishes. In standard DT theory, we assume the moduli space M is a smooth stack or that the obstruction bundle is perfect. However, for general Calabi-Yau threefolds, the tangent-obstruction complex T1[-1] -> T2 defines a virtual fundamental cycle [M]vir. The examiner often tests your understanding of why we cannot simply integrate over the classical cycle.

The core mechanism here is the perfect obstruction theory. For a Calabi-Yau threefold X, the deformation complex is E = Rπ_* (L^∙), where L^∙ is the derived self-intersection. The virtual class [M]vir lives in the Chow group A_*(M). When computing the invariant DT_beta(X) = ∫[M]vir 1, we are effectively integrating a cohomology class against the virtual cycle. A critical exception arises when X is not Calabi-Yau (i.e., c1(X) ≠ 0). In that case, the stability condition must be chosen carefully to ensure the moduli space remains compact and the deformation theory holds. The examiner might present a scenario where the obstruction bundle has non-trivial cohomology, requiring the use of the Behrend function ν: M -> Z to weight points by their Euler characteristic contribution. This leads to the definition DT(X) = ∫[M]vir ν1.

Technique: Constructing the Virtual Cycle via Obstruction Bundle
Question: Consider a moduli space M of sheaves on a CY3 X with expected dimension d. If the obstruction bundle E has rank r, how does the virtual fundamental class relate to the top Chern class? Specifically, if the tangent-obstruction complex is perfect of relative dimension 0, express DT(X) in terms of the Euler characteristic of the moduli space.
Solution: The virtual fundamental class [M]vir is defined as c_d(E), where E is the obstruction bundle. For a CY3, the tangent-obstruction complex has rank 0 (virtual dimension). However, the actual dimension of M can be larger due to embedded points or non-reduced structures. The DT invariant is computed by integrating the Behrend function ν against [M]vir. If we denote the virtual class as [M]vir = ctop(T1[-1]), then for a perfect obstruction theory, the integral ∫[M]vir 1 equals the weighted Euler characteristic. A key landmark case is when X = P3; here, the moduli space of ideal sheaves of points X[n] has dimension 2n, and the virtual class coincides with the fundamental class only after correcting for the Behrend factor ν(x) = (-1)dim M χ(T_x M). The examiner often asks to compute DT(P3, β) by reducing it to counting points on a Hilbert scheme.

The Derived Category Perspective: Bridgeland Stability and Hall Algebras

This section moves beyond coherent sheaves into the derived category D^b(Coh(X)). The MNOP conjecture originally linked GW to DT for stable bundles, but the modern understanding relies on Bridgeland stability conditions. A stability condition σ = (Z, P) consists of a central charge Z: K(D^b(X)) -> C and a slicing P of phases. The wall-crossing phenomenon occurs when an object becomes semistable at a specific phase. The examiner frequently twists this by asking about the "jump" in invariants across a wall.

The Joyce-Song formula provides the rigorous framework for this jump. If we cross a wall where objects of class γ split into subobjects, the generating function changes multiplicatively. Specifically, the DT invariant is not constant; it transforms according to the quantum dilogarithm identity. The CoHA (Cohomological Hall Algebra) categorifies this by assigning cohomology classes to moduli spaces. A crucial exception is that for generic stability conditions, the moduli space of stable objects in D^b(X) is smooth and its Euler characteristic gives the BPS invariant. However, at special points (walls), the moduli space may degenerate.

Technique: Applying the KS Wall-Crossing Formula
Question: Given two stability conditions σ1 and σ2 separated by a wall, and knowing the BPS invariants Ω(γ) for classes γ, how do you compute the change in the generating function Z(q)? Use the Kontsevich-Soibelman formula involving the quantum dilogarithm E(x; q).
Solution: The KS formula states that crossing a wall transforms the partition function by a factor involving the product of quantum dilogarithms. If Ω(γ) are the BPS invariants, the transformation is Z_new = Z_old × ∏γ E(q⟨γ, ·⟩; q)Ω(γ). The term ⟨γ, ·⟩ denotes the symplectic pairing on the charge lattice. In practice, for a 3-fold, one computes the central charges Z(E) = -∫_E ch(E)√td(X). The examiner might ask to verify that for a specific wall crossing, the DT invariant of a sheaf E changes by adding contributions from extensions Ext1(E,E). This is computed via the Hall algebra structure where multiplication corresponds to extension classes.

Landmark Computations and Topological Vertex Applications

The theoretical machinery must be applied to concrete geometric scenarios. The "Topological Vertex" formalism by Aganagic, Klemm, Mariño, and Vafa is the standard tool for computing DT invariants on toric Calabi-Yau threefolds (like C3 or local P2 x P1). The examiner often presents a problem where the geometry is not smooth or has singularities, requiring resolution. A landmark case is the computation of Gromov-Witten invariants of P1 x P1 via the DT/PT correspondence.

In the context of the Topological Vertex, one decomposes the CY3 into a triangulation and sums over plane partitions. The partition function Z_top = Σλ (q|λ|) / prod(...) relates directly to Macdonald polynomials. A critical comparison is between DT invariants (sheaves) and PT invariants (pairs). For non-toric geometries, one must use the "holomorphic anomaly" equations or mirror symmetry to relate the counts to period integrals of the mirror curve. The examiner might present a scenario where the Calabi-Yau is a complete intersection in P4, asking how the DT invariant relates to the number of rational curves passing through constraints.

Technique: Using Mirror Symmetry for Non-Toric CY3s
Question: For a general Calabi-Yau threefold X, direct DT counting is impossible. How do you relate the DT invariant to the period integrals of the mirror manifold X^~? Describe the role of the A-model and B-model correspondence.
Solution: The strategy involves Mirror Symmetry. One constructs the mirror family Y -> S where S is a base surface. The DT invariants on X correspond to coefficients in the expansion of the Yukawa coupling or period integrals on X^~. Specifically, the GW potential F_g satisfies differential equations (Painlevé type) derived from the B-model geometry. The examiner often checks if you know that for CY3s, the genus 0 DT invariant is related to the classical Gromov-Witten invariants via the MNOP conjecture, while higher genera involve quantum corrections. The Topological Vertex generalizes this by providing an explicit combinatorial formula for toric cases, which serves as a boundary condition for the mirror map.
Exam-Day Strategy: Handling Ambiguity in Stability Conditions
When an exam question does not specify the stability condition explicitly, assume the generic case where the moduli space is proper and smooth. If the problem mentions "embedded points" or "degree 0," immediately invoke the DT/PT correspondence to separate the Hilbert scheme contribution from the curve contribution. Always check if the Calabi-Yau condition (c1=0) holds; if not, the virtual class definition changes. Remember that BPS invariants are integers only for CY3s; for non-CY cases, they may be rational numbers depending on the central charge.
  • Misinterpreting the Virtual Cycle: Students often forget to apply the Behrend function ν when computing DT invariants on a 3-fold, leading to off-by-factor errors (usually powers of -1 or Euler characteristics).
  • Confusing GW and DT Normalizations: The MNOP conjecture relates them via q = -eiu, but the precise power of q differs between genus 0 and higher genera. Always check the definition of the quantum parameter used in the specific textbook context.

Cohomological Hall Algebras and the BPS Lie Algebra

The cohomological Hall algebra (CoHA) provides an algebraic framework organizing Donaldson‑Thomas invariants into a single associative algebra. For a quiver with potential (Q,W) the CoHA is defined as the direct sum of the (compactly supported) cohomology groups of the moduli stacks of representations, equipped with a convolution product induced by the correspondence of short exact sequences. Kontsevich and Soibelman established that the CoHA carries a natural Hopf algebra structure; its primitive part, after a suitable completion, is isomorphic to the BPS Lie algebra whose structure constants are the BPS invariants Ω(γ). In the geometric setting of a Calabi‑Yau threefold X, the CoHA of the category of coherent sheaves on X (or of the derived category D^b(X)) yields the DT invariants via the integration map to the quantum torus algebra. The product in the CoHA corresponds to the Hall algebra multiplication counting extensions, while the coproduct encodes the decomposition of a sheaf into a filtration. The BPS Lie algebra is generated by symbols e_γ with commutation relations [e_γ, e_δ] = (−1)⟨γ,δ⟩ ⟨γ,δ⟩ eγ+δ where ⟨·,·⟩ is the Euler form. The DT invariant of a class γ appears as the coefficient of e_γ in the factorization of the quantum dilogarithm product ∏_γ E(q⟨γ,·⟩; q)Ω(γ). This framework underlies the wall‑crossing formulas expressed as conjugation by quantum dilogarithms and accounts for the integrality of BPS invariants in CY3 categories.

Refined Donaldson‑Thomas Invariants and Motivic DT Theory

Refined DT invariants enrich the numerical DT count by keeping track of the cohomological grading of the virtual fundamental class. For a Calabi‑Yau threefold X the refined invariant DTβ,n(y) is a Laurent polynomial in a variable y (often written as q1/2) that specializes to the ordinary DT invariant at y = 1. Motivic DT theory, developed by Kontsevich and Soibelman and later by Davison, Meinhardt, and others, replaces the numerical invariant by a class in the Grothendieck ring of varieties K0(Var_ℂ) or its completion. The motivic invariant records the Hodge‑Deligne polynomial of the moduli stack, and its specialization at the Lefschetz motive L = y2 yields the refined invariant. The refined topological vertex of Iqbal, Kozcaz, and Vafa computes these polynomials for toric CY3s by summing over plane partitions with weights given by the refined vertex function. In the Nekrasov partition function language, the refined DT invariant of ℂ3 equals the MacMahon function M(y,q) = ∏i,j≥1 (1 − y qi+j-1)-1. For local surfaces such as the total space of Kℙ2, the refined invariants are conjecturally governed by a quantum differential equation (the refined holomorphic anomaly equation) that determines them recursively from the genus‑zero data. The motivic DT invariant also satisfies a wall‑crossing formula in the motivic quantum torus, where the quantum dilogarithm is replaced by its motivic avatar, the quantum dilogarithm series in K0(Var_ℂ)[[ℏ]].

Technique: Computing Refined DT Invariants via the Refined Topological Vertex
Given the toric Calabi‑Yau threefold X = Tot(Kℙ2), compute the refined DT invariant for the curve class β = d[ℙ1] and D0‑brane charge n = 0 using the refined topological vertex. Express the answer as a polynomial in y and q up to degree d = 2.
The refined topological vertex assigns to each trivalent vertex a factor Cλμν(y,q) which is a symmetric function of the partitions. For local ℙ2 the toric diagram has three external legs and three internal edges. The partition function is Z = Σλ,μ,ν C∅λμ(y,q) C∅ν^tλ^t(y,q) C∅μ^tν(y,q) Q|λ|+|μ|+|ν| where Q = e-t is the Kähler parameter. For d = 1 only partitions of size 1 contribute; the vertex evaluates to 1, giving DT1,0(y) = 1. For d = 2 the partitions of size 2 are (2) and (1,1). Summing the vertex contributions yields DT2,0(y) = y + y-1 + 2. This matches the known refined BPS invariants for local ℙ2: the y‑polynomial records the spin content of the BPS states.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Refined Invariants
When a question asks for refined DT invariants, first identify whether the geometry is toric. If it is, write down the refined topological vertex formula and note that only a finite number of partitions contribute for a fixed degree. If the geometry is non‑toric, recall that refined invariants are conjecturally determined by the refined holomorphic anomaly equations; you only need to state the recursive structure, not solve it. Always check the specialization y → 1 reproduces the ordinary DT invariant as a sanity check.

Wall‑Crossing for Quiver Representations and the Kontsevich‑Soibelman Formula

Wall‑crossing in the context of quiver representations describes how the DT invariants of a quiver with potential change as the stability condition varies across a wall in the space of central charges. For a quiver Q with dimension vector γ, the moduli space of θ‑semistable representations M_θ(γ) is projective. As θ crosses a wall where a representation splits into a direct sum of subrepresentations with the same phase, the virtual fundamental class changes by a contribution from the Ext1 groups between the factors. The Kontsevich‑Soibelman wall‑crossing formula expresses this change as an identity in the quantum torus algebra: the ordered product of quantum dilogarithms E(x_γ; q)Ω_+(γ) over charges with increasing phase equals the product over decreasing phase with invariants Ω_-(γ). Here x_γ are the quantum torus generators satisfying x_γ x_δ = q⟨γ,δ⟩ xγ+δ. For the Kronecker quiver (two vertices, two arrows) the BPS invariants are known explicitly: Ω(γ) = 1 for all primitive dimension vectors, and the wall‑crossing formula reproduces the pentagon identity for the quantum dilogarithm. In the geometric setting of a CY3, the quiver arises from a heart of a t‑structure in D^b(X); the wall‑crossing formula then matches the physical wall‑crossing of BPS states in N=2 supersymmetric gauge theories. The formula also implies the integrality of the BPS invariants because the quantum dilogarithm has a product expansion with integer exponents.

DT Invariants for Local Surfaces and the Crepant Resolution Conjecture

Local surfaces are total spaces of canonical bundles K_S over a smooth projective surface S. Their DT invariants are closely related to the Gromov‑Witten invariants of S via the crepant resolution conjecture. For S = ℙ2 the local geometry X = Tot(Kℙ2) is toric, and the DT/PT correspondence reduces the computation to the topological vertex. The DT partition function can be computed via the topological vertex formalism. The crepant resolution conjecture, proved by Maulik, Oblomkov, Okounkov, and Pandharipande for local ℙ2, states that the DT invariants of X coincide with the orbifold GW invariants of the quotient stack [ℂ3/ℤ3] after an appropriate analytic continuation in the Kähler parameters. For a general surface S, the DT invariants of K_S can be expressed in terms of the GW invariants of S and the DT invariants of the fibers ℂ2. The formula involves the reduced virtual class of the Hilbert scheme of points on S and the Nakajima basis of the Fock space. In particular, the DT invariant for a curve class β ∈ H2(S) and D0 charge n is given by a sum over partitions λ of n of products of GW invariants of S with insertions of the Chern characters of the tautological bundles on Hilb^n(S). This structure underlies the GW/DT correspondence for local surfaces and provides a recursive algorithm for computing DT invariants of non‑toric CY3s that admit a degeneration to a local surface.

Applications to String Theory: BPS State Counting and Black Hole Entropy

Donaldson‑Thomas invariants count BPS bound states of D‑branes in type IIA string theory compactified on a Calabi‑Yau threefold X. A D6‑brane wrapping X together with D4‑branes wrapping divisors, D2‑branes wrapping curves, and D0‑branes corresponds to a coherent sheaf (or a complex in D^b(X)) with Chern character γ. The DT invariant Ω(γ) is the indexed degeneracy of these BPS states, protected by supersymmetry. The OSV conjecture relates the mixed partition function of BPS black holes in N=2 supergravity to the topological string partition function: Z_BH(p,φ) = |Z_top(g_s, t)|2 where p are magnetic charges and φ are chemical potentials for electric charges. In the large charge limit, the entropy S = π √(I4(p,q)) matches the microscopic count given by the DT invariants via the attractor mechanism. For toric CY3s, the topological string partition function is computed by the topological vertex, and the DT invariants match the exact microscopic degeneracies that reproduce the macroscopic Bekenstein‑Hawking entropy including subleading corrections. The wall‑crossing formula ensures that the BPS index is piecewise constant in the moduli space, jumping across walls of marginal stability exactly as predicted by the Kontsevich‑Soibelman formula. This physical interpretation also motivates the study of refined DT invariants, which correspond to spinning BPS states in the five‑dimensional lift of the theory.

  • Confusing the CoHA product with the ordinary Hall algebra product; the CoHA uses cohomological convolution, not just extension counting.
  • Assuming refined DT invariants are always symmetric polynomials in y; they are Laurent polynomials but may have negative powers depending on the normalization.
  • Applying the Kontsevich‑Soibelman wall‑crossing formula without ordering the charges by phase; the product order is essential.
  • Neglecting the crepant resolution conjecture's analytic continuation in Kähler parameters when comparing DT and orbifold GW invariants.
  • Treating the OSV conjecture as a theorem for all CY3s; it is a conjecture verified in many toric examples but not proved in general.
  • Forgetting that the quantum dilogarithm E(x;q) satisfies the pentagon identity only when the symplectic pairing ⟨γ,δ⟩ = 1; for higher pairings the formula involves higher quantum dilogarithms.
  • Misidentifying the virtual fundamental class of the moduli stack of objects in D^b(X) with that of the moduli space of stable sheaves; they differ by a factor of the Behrend function on the stack.
