The collection of vanishing cycles for all singular fibres forms a directed A∞‑subcategory whose homotopy category is equivalent to the derived category of representations of the associated quiver with relations. This quiver is precisely the one appearing in the mirror construction via the Gross–Siebert program.

The SYZ transform intertwines the open‑closed string map with the microlocal index formula: the image of the fundamental class of a Lagrangian under the open‑closed map corresponds to the Euler characteristic of the associated constructible sheaf. Moreover, the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of the singular fibres is equivalent to the category of sheaves on the base with singular support away from the discriminant, providing a categorical version of the statement that the mirror of a punctured Calabi–Yau is obtained by removing the divisor corresponding to the singular fibres.

In the presence of a B‑field, the SYZ transform is modified by twisting the constructible sheaf category with a local system determined by the B‑field holonomy around the singular fibres. This twisted equivalence matches the expectation from mirror symmetry that the B‑field on the symplectic side corresponds to a deformation of the complex structure on the mirror. The categorical framework also accommodates non‑exact Lagrangians by passing to the curved A∞‑category of branes with bounding cochains, whose microlocal image is a category of ind‑constructible sheaves with a curvature term.

  • Confusing the curved A∞‑structure from bulk deformations with the twisted A∞‑structure from local systems; the former adds an m₀ term, the latter modifies the differential by holonomy.
  • Assuming every Lagrangian correspondence is composable without checking transversality of the fibre product; non‑transverse composition requires a derived fibre product and introduces higher homotopies.
  • Treating the SYZ transform as an equivalence of the whole Fukaya category without restricting to the subcategory of Lagrangians with appropriate singular support.
  • Neglecting the role of the sectorial cover in defining wrapped Floer cohomology for non‑compact branes; different choices of stop can give non‑quasi‑equivalent categories if the cover condition fails.
  • Overlooking the necessity of a grading and relative spin structure on Lagrangian cobordisms to define the A∞‑operations; without them the moduli spaces are not oriented and the signs in the A∞‑relations are ambiguous.
  • Believing that the categorical mirror symmetry for Fano varieties follows directly from the equivalence for the ambient toric variety; the restriction to the critical locus of the superpotential introduces a matrix factorisation category that is not a subcategory of the toric Fukaya category.

These advanced topics illustrate how cobordisms, correspondences, cluster structures, Landau–Ginzburg models, and singular fibrations enrich the Fukaya category and its mirror symmetry predictions.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Manifolds with Lagrangian Skeleta and Stop Removal Functors

A Liouville manifold X admits a Lagrangian skeleton 𝕃 ⊂ X, a closed Lagrangian subset onto which X deformation retracts. The wrapped Fukaya category W(X) can be defined using a stop — a contact hypersurface at infinity or a Legendrian submanifold in the contact boundary — which controls the wrapping Hamiltonian. When the stop is the entire contact boundary, one recovers the fully wrapped category; when the stop is empty, one obtains the compact Fukaya category of the Liouville domain. The stop removal functor W(X, f) → W(X, ∅) and its adjoint, the stop creation functor, form a Verdier localisation sequence. For a Weinstein manifold, the skeleton 𝕃 is a union of Lagrangian discs attached along their boundaries; the wrapped category is generated by the cocores of these discs. The stop removal functor sends a cocore to the corresponding compact Lagrangian in the skeleton, and its kernel consists of objects supported near the stop. This framework, developed by Ganatra–Pardon–Shende, provides a categorical interpretation of the surgery exact triangle: attaching a Weinstein handle corresponds to a categorical gluing along a stop. The sectorial cover condition ensures that the wrapped category is independent of the choice of stop up to quasi-equivalence; failure of this condition leads to distinct categories, as seen in the case of the punctured torus versus the annulus. The stop removal functor intertwines the open-closed string map with the map on symplectic cohomology induced by the inclusion of the stop, and it identifies the Hochschild cohomology of W(X, f) with the symplectic cohomology of the pair (X, f).

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Grassmannians and Homogeneous Spaces

Homological mirror symmetry for Grassmannians Gr(k, n) and more general homogeneous spaces G/P has been established through the work of Rietsch–Williams, Abouzaid–Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono, and others. The mirror of Gr(k, n) is a Landau–Ginzburg model (Y, W) where Y is an open subvariety of the Langlands dual Grassmannian Gr(n−k, n) and W is a superpotential given by a sum of Plücker coordinates. The Fukaya–Seidel category FS(Y, W) is generated by a collection of Lagrangian thimbles associated to the critical points of W, which correspond to the Schubert cells of Gr(k, n). The equivalence DπFS(Y, W) ≃ DbCoh(Gr(k, n)) sends the thimble of the unique critical point of index zero to the structure sheaf 𝒪, and the thimbles of higher index to the Schubert sheaves. The A∞-structure on the thimble category is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on the thimbles; these counts match the structure constants of the quantum cohomology ring of Gr(k, n), which is isomorphic to the Jacobian ring of W. For general homogeneous spaces G/P, the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model on the dual group G∨ with superpotential given by the sum of fundamental characters. The categorical equivalence is constructed via the Rietsch–Williams mirror, which identifies the quantum cohomology of G/P with the Jacobian ring of the superpotential. The wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model is equivalent to the category of matrix factorisations of W, and the stop removal functor recovers the compact Fukaya category of the Fano variety. This program extends to partial flag varieties and to the categorical mirror symmetry for the quantum cohomology of G/P as the Hochschild cohomology of the wrapped category.

Worked Example: Stop Removal on the Cotangent Bundle of the Circle
Let X = T*S1 ≅ S1 × ℝ with the standard Liouville form λ = p dq. The contact boundary is two circles at p = ±∞. Take the stop f to be the circle at p = +∞. Describe the stop removal functor W(X, f) → W(X, ∅) on generators.
The wrapped category W(X, f) is generated by the zero-section L0 = S1 × {0} (a compact Lagrangian) and the cocore L1 = {q0} × [0, ∞) (a non-compact Lagrangian with boundary on the stop). The stop removal functor sends L0 to itself (now viewed as an object in the fully wrapped category) and sends L1 to the compact Lagrangian L1' = {q0} × ℝ, which is a fibre of the cotangent bundle. In the fully wrapped category W(X, ∅), the objects L0 and L1' generate, and their morphism spaces are HW*(L0, L0) ≅ H*(S1), HW*(L1', L1') ≅ H*(S1), and HW*(L0, L1') ≅ k in degree 0. The functor is fully faithful on the subcategory generated by L0 and identifies the kernel with the subcategory generated by L1 (which becomes zero after stop removal because its boundary lies on the stop).
Exam Strategy: Stop Removal and Localisation
When a question asks about the effect of removing a stop, recall the Verdier localisation sequence: the kernel of the stop removal functor is the subcategory of objects supported near the stop. The functor is essentially surjective onto the compact Fukaya category of the Liouville domain. For computations, identify the cocores of the Weinstein handles that intersect the stop — these become zero in the quotient. The sectorial cover condition is the key technical hypothesis for invariance; if a problem mentions "different choices of stop give non-equivalent categories", the sectorial cover condition has failed.

Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Manifolds with Legendrian Fillings and the Augmentation Category

Given a Legendrian submanifold Λ in the contact boundary of a Liouville manifold X, an exact Lagrangian filling is an exact Lagrangian submanifold L ⊂ X with ∂L = Λ. The augmentation category Aug(Λ) is the category of augmentations of the Chekanov–Eliashberg differential graded algebra CE*(Λ), which counts rigid pseudoholomorphic discs with boundary on Λ in the symplectisation. There is a functor from the wrapped Fukaya category W(X) to Aug(Λ) sending a Lagrangian L with boundary on Λ to the augmentation induced by counting discs with boundary on L ∪ Λ. When X is the symplectisation of the contact manifold, this functor is an equivalence onto the subcategory of Aug(Λ) generated by augmentations coming from exact fillings. For a Legendrian link Λ in the standard contact S3, the augmentation category is equivalent to the category of representations of the cord algebra, and the functor from the Fukaya category of the 4-ball with stops at the conormal lifts of the link components recovers the Shende–Treumann–Williams–Zaslow equivalence with constructible sheaves on the link complement. The Lagrangian filling of a Legendrian knot corresponds to a microlocal sheaf on the knot complement, and the augmentation category encodes the knot contact homology. The cord algebra is the endomorphism algebra of the generator of the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of the conormal Lagrangian, and its representations are the augmentations. This framework extends to higher-dimensional Legendrians and to the relative Fukaya category of a Liouville domain with Legendrian boundary, where the objects are Lagrangians with boundary on the Legendrian and the morphisms are given by relative Floer cohomology.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Hypertoric Varieties

Hypertoric varieties are hyperkähler analogues of toric varieties, constructed as hyperkähler quotients of ℂ2n by a torus action. They admit a holomorphic symplectic form and a family of Kähler forms. The categorical mirror symmetry for hypertoric varieties, established by Braden–Licata–Proudfoot–Webster and extended by Kuwagaki, relates the derived category of coherent sheaves on a hypertoric variety Y to the Fukaya category of its mirror, which is a hypertoric Landau–Ginzburg model — a hypertoric variety X equipped with a superpotential W given by a sum of exponential functions of the moment map coordinates. The Fukaya–Seidel category FS(X, W) is generated by a collection of Lagrangian thimbles associated to the critical points of W, which correspond to the fixed points of the torus action on Y. The equivalence DπFS(X, W) ≃ DbCoh(Y) sends the thimble of a critical point to the structure sheaf of the corresponding fixed point. The A∞-structure on the thimble category is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on the thimbles; these counts match the Ext groups between structure sheaves of fixed points, which are controlled by the hypertoric category 𝒪 of Braden–Licata–Proudfoot–Webster. The hypertoric category 𝒪 is a highest-weight category whose simple objects correspond to the fixed points, and its projective objects correspond to the thimbles. The categorical equivalence intertwines the hypertoric convolution algebra with the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror. The hypertoric mirror symmetry also admits a 3d mirror symmetry interpretation: the Higgs branch of a 3d N = 4 gauge theory is a hypertoric variety, and its Coulomb branch is the mirror hypertoric variety; the categorical equivalence exchanges the category of boundary conditions in the A-model with the category of boundary conditions in the B-model.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Higgs Bundles

The moduli space ℳH(G, C) of G-Higgs bundles on a Riemann surface C is a hyperkähler manifold that plays a central role in the geometric Langlands program. The SYZ conjecture for ℳH predicts a dual special Lagrangian torus fibration given by the Hitchin fibration h : ℳH → B, where B is the space of spectral curves. The mirror of ℳH(G, C) is the moduli space ℳH(G∨, C) of G∨-Higgs bundles, where G∨ is the Langlands dual group. The categorical mirror symmetry equivalence DbCoh(ℳH(G, C)) ≃ W(ℳH(G∨, C)) has been established in the case G = GLn by Hausel–Thaddeus and extended to the categorical setting by Arinkin–Gaitsgory, Donagi–Pantev, and others. The Fukaya category of ℳH(G∨, C) is generated by the Lagrangian sections of the Hitchin fibration, which correspond to the Hecke eigensheaves on the moduli stack of G-bundles. The spectral data of a Higgs bundle — a spectral curve Σ ⊂ T*C and a line bundle on Σ — determines a Lagrangian submanifold of ℳH via the Abel–Jacobi map. The wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of the singular fibres of the Hitchin fibration is equivalent to the category of perverse sheaves on the base B with singular support on the discriminant, following the Nadler–Zaslow correspondence for singular Lagrangian fibrations. The open-closed string map in this setting recovers the Hitchin Hamiltonians as elements of the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category. The categorical equivalence intertwines the Hecke operators on the B-model side with the spherical twists around the vanishing cycles of the singular fibres on the A-model side, providing a geometric realisation of the geometric Langlands correspondence for G = GLn.

  • Confusing the stop removal functor (a Verdier localisation) with the sectorial cover functor (a quasi-equivalence); the former changes the category, the latter compares categories defined by different stops satisfying the sectorial condition.
  • Assuming every Lagrangian filling of a Legendrian induces an augmentation; only exact fillings with appropriate grading and spin structures give well-defined augmentations in the Chekanov–Eliashberg algebra.
  • Treating the hypertoric category 𝒪 as equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the hypertoric variety; 𝒪 is a highest-weight category that is equivalent to the category of perverse sheaves on the moment map fibres, not to DbCoh.
  • Overlooking the role of the B-field in the SYZ transform for the Hitchin fibration; the B-field holonomy around the singular fibres twists the constructible sheaf category and corresponds to a choice of gerbe on the moduli stack of bundles.
  • Believing that the categorical mirror symmetry for Grassmannians follows directly from the toric case; the Grassmannian is not toric, and the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model on an open subvariety of the dual Grassmannian, not a toric variety.
  • Neglecting the grading and relative spin structure on Lagrangian thimbles in the Fukaya–Seidel category; without them the A∞-operations are not well-defined and the equivalence with matrix factorisations fails.
  • Confusing the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model with the category of matrix factorisations of the superpotential; they are equivalent only after passing to the split-closed derived category and imposing the sectorial cover condition on the stop.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Nakajima Quiver Varieties

Nakajima quiver varieties provide a geometric construction of moduli spaces of representations of quivers with relations, equipped with a natural hyperkähler structure. For a quiver Q and dimension vectors v, w, the Nakajima quiver variety M(v, w) is a symplectic resolution of an affine variety M₀(v, w). The categorical mirror symmetry conjecture for these varieties, formulated by Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima, posits an equivalence between the derived category of coherent sheaves on M(v, w) and the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror symplectic manifold M(w, v), where the roles of the dimension vectors are exchanged. This exchange reflects the 3d mirror symmetry of the corresponding N = 4 supersymmetric gauge theories: the Higgs branch of a theory with gauge group ∏ U(vᵢ) and flavor group ∏ U(wᵢ) is M(v, w), while its Coulomb branch is M(w, v). The equivalence is constructed via the Coulomb branch algebra, which acts on the category of modules over the quantized affine Grassmannian, and matches the convolution algebra of the affine Grassmannian for the Langlands dual group. On the A-model side, the wrapped Fukaya category of M(w, v) is generated by Lagrangian thimbles associated to the critical points of a superpotential on the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model. The A∞-structure is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on these thimbles, and the resulting category is equivalent to the category of modules over the Coulomb branch algebra. The open-closed string map identifies the quantum cohomology of M(v, w) with the Hochschild cohomology of the wrapped Fukaya category of M(w, v), and the quantum connection matches the KZ connection on the space of conformal blocks. This equivalence has been proven for type A quivers by Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima, and extended to other types by Weekes and others. The categorical equivalence intertwines the spherical twists around the exceptional collections on the B-model side with the monodromy of the quantum connection on the A-model side, providing a geometric realization of the 3d mirror symmetry at the categorical level.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Parabolic Higgs Bundles

The moduli space M_par(G, C, D) of parabolic G-Higgs bundles on a Riemann surface C with parabolic structure along a divisor D is a hyperkähler manifold that generalizes the moduli space of Higgs bundles. The parabolic structure consists of a flag in the fiber at each point of D together with a weight α ∈ [0, 1)ʳ. The Hitchin fibration h: M_par → B_par is a completely integrable system whose generic fibers are abelian varieties, and the SYZ conjecture predicts a dual torus fibration on the mirror moduli space M_par(G∨, C, D). The categorical mirror symmetry equivalence DᵇCoh(M_par(G, C, D)) ≃ W(M_par(G∨, C, D)) has been established for G = GLₙ by Hausel, Mellit, and others, using the non-abelian Hodge correspondence and the geometry of the Hitchin fibration. The wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of the singular fibers is generated by Lagrangian sections of the Hitchin fibration, which correspond to parabolic Hecke eigensheaves on the moduli stack of parabolic G-bundles. The spectral data of a parabolic Higgs bundle — a spectral curve Σ ⊂ T*C with ramification at D and a line bundle on Σ with parabolic structure — determines a Lagrangian submanifold via the Abel–Jacobi map. The open-closed string map recovers the parabolic Hitchin Hamiltonians as elements of the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category. The categorical equivalence intertwines the parabolic Hecke operators on the B-model side with spherical twists around the vanishing cycles of the singular fibers on the A-model side. The B-field holonomy around the singular fibers, determined by the parabolic weights, twists the constructible sheaf category and corresponds to a choice of gerbe on the moduli stack of parabolic bundles. This equivalence provides a geometric realization of the geometric Langlands correspondence for parabolic bundles, and the categorical structure encodes the fusion rules of the associated conformal field theory.

Worked Example: Parabolic Weights and B-field Holonomy
Let C = P¹ with parabolic divisor D = {0, 1, ∞} and G = GL₂. Suppose the parabolic weights at each point are α = (0, 1/2). Compute the B-field holonomy around a singular fiber of the Hitchin fibration and explain its effect on the constructible sheaf category on the base B_par.
The parabolic weights α = (0, 1/2) at each of the three points determine a B-field B ∈ H²(B_par, ℝ/ℤ) whose holonomy around a loop γ encircling a singular fiber is exp(2πi ∫_γ B). For GL₂, the singular fibers correspond to spectral curves with a node. The B-field holonomy is given by the sum of the parabolic weights modulo 1: at each point the weight difference is 1/2, so the total holonomy is exp(2πi × 3 × 1/2) = exp(3πi) = -1. This non-trivial holonomy means the constructible sheaf category on B_par is twisted by a ℤ/2-gerbe. On the mirror side, this corresponds to a choice of spin structure on the Lagrangian sections, and the wrapped Fukaya category is defined with coefficients in a local system of rank 2 with monodromy -1 around the singular fibers. The categorical equivalence DᵇCoh(M_par) ≃ W(M_par∨) intertwines this twist with the gerbe on the moduli stack of parabolic bundles.
Exam Strategy: Parabolic vs. Non-Parabolic HMS
When comparing parabolic and non-parabolic HMS, focus on three differences: (1) the base B_par has a discriminant locus of higher codimension due to parabolic singularities; (2) the B-field is determined by parabolic weights and is absent in the non-parabolic case; (3) the Hecke operators are replaced by parabolic Hecke operators that modify the flag at D. Examiners often test whether you know the B-field is trivial when all weights are zero — this reduces to the non-parabolic case.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Wild Character Varieties and Irregular Singularities

Wild character varieties are moduli spaces of meromorphic connections on a Riemann surface C with irregular singularities at a divisor D. They are symplectic manifolds that arise as the de Rham moduli spaces in the non-abelian Hodge correspondence for irregular singularities. The mirror of a wild character variety M_B^wild(G, C, D) is another wild character variety M_B^wild(G∨, C, D) for the Langlands dual group, where the irregular type (the formal normal form of the connection) is exchanged with the parabolic weight data. The categorical mirror symmetry equivalence DᵇCoh(M_B^wild(G, C, D)) ≃ W(M_B^wild(G∨, C, D)) has been formulated by Boalch and others, and proven in special cases using the theory of isomonodromic deformations and the geometry of the wild Hitchin fibration. The wild Hitchin fibration h: M_B^wild → B_wild is a completely integrable system whose fibers are affine tori, and the SYZ conjecture predicts a dual torus fibration on the mirror. The wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of the singular fibers is generated by Lagrangian sections corresponding to irregular Hecke eigensheaves. The irregular type determines a Stokes filtration on the local system, and the categorical equivalence intertwines the Stokes data with the parabolic weights on the mirror side. The open-closed string map recovers the wild Hitchin Hamiltonians, which include the isomonodromic deformation parameters, as elements of the Hochschild cohomology. The categorical structure encodes the fusion rules of the associated irregular conformal blocks, and the spherical twists around the vanishing cycles correspond to the braid group action on the Stokes matrices. This equivalence provides a geometric realization of the wild geometric Langlands correspondence, and the A∞-structure on the Fukaya category is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on Lagrangian thimbles associated to the critical points of the irregular superpotential.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Hilbert Schemes of Points on ALE Spaces

The Hilbert scheme Hilbⁿ(X) of n points on an ALE space X (a minimal resolution of ℂ²/Γ for a finite subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℂ)) is a symplectic resolution of the symmetric product Symⁿ(X). The categorical mirror symmetry for Hilbⁿ(X) relates the derived category of coherent sheaves DᵇCoh(Hilbⁿ(X)) to the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, which is a quotient of the Hilbert scheme of points on the mirror ALE space X∨ by a group action. The mirror X∨ is the minimal resolution of ℂ²/Γ∨, where Γ∨ is the dual group under the McKay correspondence. The equivalence is constructed via the categorical McKay correspondence, which identifies DᵇCoh(Hilbⁿ(X)) with the category of Γ-equivariant coherent sheaves on Hilbⁿ(ℂ²), and the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror with the category of modules over the Cherednik algebra at a specific parameter. The A∞-structure on the Fukaya category is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on Lagrangian thimbles associated to the fixed points of the torus action on the mirror. The open-closed string map identifies the quantum cohomology of Hilbⁿ(X) with the spherical subalgebra of the Cherednik algebra, and the quantum connection matches the KZ connection on the space of conformal blocks for the affine Lie algebra associated to Γ. The categorical equivalence intertwines the Nakajima operators on the B-model side with the spherical twists around the exceptional Lagrangian spheres on the A-model side, providing a geometric realization of the affine Lie algebra action on the cohomology of Hilbⁿ(X). This equivalence has been established by Maulik and Okounkov for X = ℂ², and extended to ALE spaces by Bezrukavnikov, Finkelberg, and others using the geometry of the affine Grassmannian and the Coulomb branch algebra.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Framed Sheaves on Projective Space

The moduli space M_fr(r, n) of framed rank r sheaves on ℙ² with second Chern class n is a symplectic manifold that arises as a Nakajima quiver variety for the Jordan quiver with dimension vectors v = n, w = r. The categorical mirror symmetry for M_fr(r, n) relates the derived category of coherent sheaves DᵇCoh(M_fr(r, n)) to the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, which is the moduli space of framed sheaves on the mirror ℙ² with exchanged rank and Chern class. The mirror is the moduli space M_fr(n, r) of framed rank n sheaves with second Chern class r. The equivalence is a special case of the 3d mirror symmetry for the U(r) gauge theory with n flavors, where the Higgs branch is M_fr(r, n) and the Coulomb branch is M_fr(n, r). The wrapped Fukaya category of M_fr(n, r) is generated by Lagrangian thimbles associated to the fixed points of the torus action, which correspond to the torus-fixed framed sheaves. The A∞-structure is computed by counting holomorphic polygons with boundary on these thimbles, and the resulting category is equivalent to the category of modules over the Coulomb branch algebra, which is the spherical subalgebra of the rational Cherednik algebra of type A. The open-closed string map identifies the quantum cohomology of M_fr(r, n) with the Hochschild cohomology of the wrapped Fukaya category of M_fr(n, r), and the quantum connection matches the KZ connection on the space of conformal blocks for the affine Lie algebra ŝl_r. The categorical equivalence intertwines the Nakajima operators on the B-model side with the spherical twists around the exceptional Lagrangian spheres on the A-model side, and the spherical twists generate an action of the braid group on n strands. This equivalence has been proven by Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima using the geometry of the affine Grassmannian and the Coulomb branch algebra, and provides a geometric realization of the 3d mirror symmetry at the categorical level for this class of quiver varieties.

  • Confusing the Nakajima quiver variety M(v, w) with its affine quotient M₀(v, w); the categorical equivalence requires the symplectic resolution, and the wrapped Fukaya category of the mirror is defined on the smooth locus of M(w, v).
  • Assuming the B-field in parabolic HMS is always trivial; it is determined by the parabolic weights and is non-trivial whenever the weights are not all zero, twisting the constructible sheaf category by a gerbe.
  • Treating wild character varieties as ordinary character varieties; the irregular type introduces Stokes data that has no analogue in the regular singular case, and the mirror exchanges irregular type with parabolic weights.
  • Overlooking the role of the Cherednik algebra in HMS for Hilbert schemes of points on ALE spaces; the quantum cohomology matches the spherical subalgebra, not the full Cherednik algebra, and the parameter is determined by the McKay correspondence.
  • Believing the mirror of M_fr(r, n) is M_fr(r, n) itself; the mirror exchanges rank and Chern class, giving M_fr(n, r), and the equivalence is a non-trivial instance of 3d mirror symmetry.
  • Neglecting the grading and spin structures on Lagrangian thimbles in the Fukaya–Seidel category for quiver varieties; without them the A∞-operations are not well-defined and the equivalence with modules over the Coulomb branch algebra fails.
  • Confusing the spherical twists in the Fukaya category with the braid group action on the B-model side; they correspond under the equivalence, but the spherical twists act on the wrapped Fukaya category while the braid group acts on the derived category of coherent sheaves via the Nakajima operators.

The Essential Role of Grading, Spin Structures, and Orientations in Fukaya Categories

The definition of the Fukaya category, F(X), relies on counting pseudoholomorphic polygons with boundaries on Lagrangian submanifolds. For these counts to yield well-defined integer (or Z₂-coefficient) invariants, several geometric structures must be imposed on the Lagrangian submanifolds and the ambient symplectic manifold X. These structures are crucial for resolving sign ambiguities and ensuring the coherence of the A∞-operations.

Firstly, grading is indispensable. A Lagrangian submanifold L in a symplectic manifold (X, ω) is called graded if it is equipped with a choice of a lift of its tangent bundle TL to the universal cover of the Lagrangian Grassmannian. This corresponds to a map from L to the space of Lagrangian subspaces in R²ⁿ. More concretely, a grading is a choice of a continuous path of Lagrangian subspaces starting from a fixed reference Lagrangian subspace. This grading allows us to assign a degree to intersection points between Lagrangians, which is essential for defining the Z-graded Floer cohomology groups. Without a consistent grading, Floer cohomology would only be Z₂-graded, losing significant algebraic structure. The Maslov index of a disc with boundary on L is an integer, and the grading ensures that the degrees of intersection points are well-defined modulo the Maslov index.

Secondly, spin structures are often required. A spin structure on a Lagrangian submanifold L is a lift of its tangent bundle TL to a spin bundle. This is necessary when the dimension of L is greater than 1 and the first Stiefel-Whitney class w₁(L) is zero, but the second Stiefel-Whitney class w₂(L) might be non-zero. The existence of a spin structure on L allows for the definition of a canonical orientation on the moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic discs with boundary on L. Without this, the counts of pseudoholomorphic discs would be defined only up to sign, making the A∞-operations ill-defined over Z. The choice of a spin structure on L induces an orientation on the determinant line bundle of the Cauchy-Riemann operator, which is crucial for defining the signs in the Floer differential and the higher A∞-operations. For example, if X is a Calabi-Yau manifold, then a spin structure on X induces spin structures on all Lagrangian submanifolds, simplifying the requirements.

Thirdly, orientations on the Lagrangian submanifolds themselves are fundamental. For any pair of transverse Lagrangian submanifolds L₀ and L₁, their intersection points L₀ ∩ L₁ are isolated. To define the Floer chain complex CF(L₀, L₁), we need to orient the intersection points. This is achieved by choosing an orientation for each Lᵢ. The orientation of an intersection point p ∈ L₀ ∩ L₁ is then determined by comparing the orientation of TₚL₀ with TₚL₁ within TₚX. The symplectic form ω provides a canonical orientation on TₚX, allowing for a consistent definition. For the higher A∞-operations, which involve moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic polygons, we need to orient these moduli spaces. The orientations on the Lagrangians, combined with the spin structures (if required) and the grading, provide the necessary data to orient these moduli spaces, ensuring that the counts of polygons are signed integers. The choice of orientations for the Lagrangians and the ambient manifold must be consistent across all operations to ensure the associativity and other properties of the A∞-category.

These geometric structures are not merely technicalities; they are integral to the algebraic richness of the Fukaya category. They ensure that Floer cohomology groups are Z-graded vector spaces (or modules over a ring) and that the A∞-operations satisfy their defining relations, such as the Stasheff associator identities. Without them, the Fukaya category would be a much coarser invariant, lacking the precision required for applications like Homological Mirror Symmetry.

Lagrangian Surgery and the Gluing of Fukaya Categories

Lagrangian surgery is a powerful geometric technique used to construct new Lagrangian submanifolds from existing ones, or to understand how the Fukaya category changes under symplectic surgeries of the ambient manifold. It provides a crucial link between the topology of Lagrangians and the algebraic structure of their associated Fukaya categories. The fundamental idea involves modifying a Lagrangian submanifold locally by "cutting" and "regluing" in a controlled manner, analogous to Morse surgery in topology.

The simplest form of Lagrangian surgery is a Lagrangian handle attachment. Consider a Lagrangian L in a symplectic manifold (X, ω). If we have a Lagrangian sphere Sᵏ embedded in L, we can perform a surgery along Sᵏ to obtain a new Lagrangian L'. This involves removing a tubular neighborhood of Sᵏ in L and replacing it with a "Lagrangian handle." More precisely, we consider a Lagrangian sphere Sᵏ in L, which is the boundary of a Lagrangian disk Dᵏ⁺¹ in X. The surgery replaces a neighborhood of Sᵏ in L with a copy of Sᵏ × D¹ (a cylinder) where the ends are glued to L - N(Sᵏ). This operation is often performed in a Weinstein manifold, where the handle attachment corresponds to adding a critical point to the Weinstein potential.

The categorical consequence of Lagrangian surgery is profound. When a Lagrangian L is modified by surgery, its Floer cohomology with other Lagrangians, and thus its role in the Fukaya category, changes predictably. For instance, if a Lagrangian L' is obtained from L by a Lagrangian surgery, there is often a surgery exact triangle in the Fukaya category, relating the Floer cohomology of L and L' to the Floer cohomology of the "attaching sphere" or related Lagrangians. This is a direct analogue of the exact triangles in derived categories arising from distinguished triangles.

A key example is the Lagrangian sphere surgery. If L₀ and L₁ are two Lagrangian submanifolds intersecting transversely, and we perform a surgery on L₀ along a Lagrangian sphere Sᵏ that is disjoint from L₁, the resulting Lagrangian L'₀ will have its Floer cohomology with L₁ related to CF(L₀, L₁) by an exact sequence. This is particularly relevant in the context of symplectic blow-ups, where exceptional Lagrangian spheres appear, and their surgery properties dictate how the Fukaya category of the blown-up manifold relates to the original one. The "Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Blow-ups and the Exceptional Lagrangian Spheres" section hints at this, but a deeper dive into the mechanism of surgery on Lagrangians is distinct.

More generally, the concept of Lagrangian correspondence plays a role in understanding surgery. A Lagrangian correspondence between (X₁, ω₁) and (X₂, ω₂) is a Lagrangian submanifold in (X₁ × X₂, ω₁ ⊕ -ω₂). Surgeries can be viewed as composing with specific Lagrangian correspondences. This perspective allows for a more functorial understanding of how the Fukaya category transforms under geometric operations.

The gluing of Fukaya categories, as mentioned in "Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Sums and the Gluing Formula" and "Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Cuts and the Surgery Exact Triangle," often relies on understanding how Lagrangians behave across the gluing boundary. Lagrangian surgery provides the microscopic tool to analyze these changes. For example, when performing a symplectic sum of two manifolds X₁ and X₂ along a common symplectic divisor, the Lagrangians in the resulting manifold X₁ # X₂ are often constructed by gluing Lagrangians from X₁ and X₂ along their intersection with the divisor. The Floer theory across this glued region is then understood via a combination of relative Floer theory and surgery techniques. This interplay between local Lagrangian modifications and global categorical structures is central to advanced applications of Fukaya categories.

Applying Grading and Spin Structures in Floer Homology
Consider two transverse Lagrangian submanifolds L₀ and L₁ in a symplectic manifold (X, ω). The Floer chain complex CF(L₀, L₁) is a free Z-module generated by the intersection points p ∈ L₀ ∩ L₁. The differential ∂: CF(L₀, L₁) → CF(L₀, L₁) counts pseudoholomorphic discs with boundary on L₀ ∪ L₁ and specific boundary conditions. If L₀ and L₁ are not graded or do not possess compatible spin structures, explain why the Floer differential might not be well-defined as a Z-linear map and what issues arise.
Without proper grading, the degree of an intersection point p ∈ L₀ ∩ L₁ is only defined modulo 2 (Z₂-graded). The Floer differential maps elements of degree k to elements of degree k-1. If the grading is only Z₂, then all elements effectively have the same degree, and the differential cannot distinguish between degrees, making the Z-grading of Floer cohomology impossible. The Maslov index of a pseudoholomorphic disc, which determines the degree shift in the differential, is an integer. A Z-grading on Lagrangians ensures that this integer shift translates into a well-defined degree change in the chain complex. Without compatible spin structures (when required by dimension/topology), the moduli spaces of pseudoholomorphic discs between L₀ and L₁ lack a canonical orientation. When counting these discs to define the coefficients of the differential, the counts would be defined only up to sign. This means the differential ∂ would be defined only as a map over Z₂ coefficients, or as a map whose coefficients are integers but with arbitrary signs. This ambiguity would prevent the Floer cohomology groups from being well-defined Z-modules and would break the associativity relations of the A∞-category, which crucially depend on precise sign conventions. The spin structures provide the necessary coherent orientation for these moduli spaces, ensuring that the counts are signed integers and the differential is a well-defined Z-linear map.
Mastering the Abstract: Focus on "Why"
When encountering highly abstract mathematical concepts like Fukaya categories, it's easy to get lost in the definitions. For competitive exams, instead of just memorizing definitions, focus on the "why" behind each component. Why are gradings needed? Why spin structures? Why A∞-categories instead of just categories? Understanding the underlying problems these structures solve will deepen your comprehension and allow you to reason through complex scenarios, even if you don't recall every specific detail. Connect each technical requirement to its functional purpose in the overall theory.

The Fukaya Category and the Symplectic Homology of Liouville Domains

The relationship between the wrapped Fukaya category of a Liouville domain and its symplectic homology (SH) is a cornerstone of modern symplectic geometry, providing a deep connection between A-model invariants and a specific algebraic invariant of the symplectic manifold. A Liouville domain W is a compact exact symplectic manifold (W, dλ) with boundary ∂W, such that the Liouville vector field Z (defined by ι_Z dλ = dλ) points strictly outwards along ∂W. The completion of W, denoted Ŵ, is a non-compact exact symplectic manifold obtained by attaching a cylindrical end ∂W × [0, ∞).

The wrapped Fukaya category W(Ŵ) of the Liouville completion Ŵ is an A∞-category whose objects are exact Lagrangian submanifolds L ⊂ Ŵ that are "wrapped" in the cylindrical end. The morphisms are given by wrapped Floer cohomology groups, which are defined by counting pseudoholomorphic strips that extend into the cylindrical end. This category is particularly rich because it captures information about the global structure of the Liouville domain, not just compact Lagrangians.

Symplectic homology SH(Ŵ) is an invariant of the Liouville completion Ŵ, defined as the Floer homology of the Hamiltonian flow on Ŵ. It is a Z-graded vector space (or module) that measures the existence and properties of periodic orbits of certain Hamiltonian vector fields. SH(Ŵ) can be thought of as a generalization of Morse homology for the action functional on the loop space of Ŵ. It has a rich algebraic structure, including a product (the pair-of-pants product) and a Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) operator.

The profound connection lies in the fact that the Hochschild cohomology of the wrapped Fukaya category, HH*(W(Ŵ)), is isomorphic to the symplectic homology SH(Ŵ). This is a fundamental result, often referred to as the "open-closed string map" in this context. The open-closed string map, in general, relates the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category (an "open string" invariant) to the quantum cohomology of the ambient manifold (a "closed string" invariant). For Liouville domains, the quantum cohomology is replaced by symplectic homology.

This isomorphism is not merely a coincidence; it arises from counting pseudoholomorphic curves. The elements of HH*(W(Ŵ)) are constructed from Floer cohomology groups, which are defined by counting open pseudoholomorphic polygons. The product in HH* involves composing these operations. On the other hand, SH(Ŵ) is defined by counting closed pseudoholomorphic curves (periodic orbits of Hamiltonian vector fields). The open-closed map itself is realized by counting pseudoholomorphic discs with one boundary component on a Lagrangian L and one interior marked point, which maps to a closed curve in X.

This correspondence is crucial for Homological Mirror Symmetry. On the mirror B-model side, for a Landau-Ginzburg model (Y, W), the derived category of matrix factorizations of W (or a related category of coherent sheaves) has its Hochschild cohomology isomorphic to the Jacobian algebra of W. The mirror symmetry conjecture then implies that the symplectic homology of the A-model Liouville domain should correspond to the Jacobian algebra of the mirror Landau-Ginzburg potential. This provides a powerful tool for computing and understanding these invariants. The structure of SH(Ŵ) as a BV algebra is mirrored by the structure of HH*(W(Ŵ)). The BV operator on SH(Ŵ) corresponds to a specific operator on HH*(W(Ŵ)) derived from counting pseudoholomorphic discs with a single boundary component on a Lagrangian and a marked point in the interior.

Constructing the Mirror Functor: From Fukaya Categories to Derived Categories of Sheaves

The core of Homological Mirror Symmetry (HMS) is the assertion of a categorical equivalence between the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold (the A-model) and the derived category of coherent sheaves on a complex manifold (the B-model). While the existence of such an equivalence is a grand conjecture, its explicit construction, known as the mirror functor, is a major technical challenge and a central focus of research. This section delves into the conceptual steps involved in building such a functor.

Let F(X) be the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold X and DᵇCoh(Y) be the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a mirror complex manifold Y. The mirror functor, denoted Φ: F(X) → DᵇCoh(Y), must map objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms, respecting the A∞-structure.

The first step is to define the action of Φ on objects. An object in F(X) is a Lagrangian submanifold L ⊂ X. The mirror functor must associate to L a coherent sheaf (or a complex of sheaves) F(L) on Y. This is often the most challenging part. In many cases, particularly for Calabi-Yau manifolds, the mirror manifold Y is also a Calabi-Yau, and the Lagrangians L are special Lagrangian submanifolds. For example, in the case of a torus T²ⁿ, a Lagrangian torus L corresponds to a point on the mirror torus (or a skyscraper sheaf at that point). More generally, for a Lagrangian L, F(L) might be a complex of coherent sheaves supported on a subvariety of Y, or even a more abstract object like a matrix factorization in the context of Landau-Ginzburg models. The SYZ conjecture provides a geometric intuition: if X has a Lagrangian torus fibration, then a fiber L maps to a point on the base of the mirror fibration.

The second step is to define the action of Φ on morphisms. Given two Lagrangian submanifolds L₀, L₁ ∈ F(X), the morphisms are given by their Floer cohomology group HF*(L₀, L₁). The mirror functor must map this to the Ext group between their images in DᵇCoh(Y): Φ: HF*(L₀, L₁) → Ext*(F(L₀), F(L₁)). This map must be an isomorphism of graded vector spaces. The construction of this map typically involves counting pseudoholomorphic discs with boundaries on L₀ and L₁. These counts are then related to the Ext groups via a geometric construction on the B-model side. For instance, the elements of HF*(L₀, L₁) correspond to intersection points between L₀ and L₁. On the mirror side, these intersection points might correspond to generators of the Ext algebra.

Crucially, the mirror functor must be an A∞-functor. This means it must not only preserve the composition of morphisms (m₀) but also the higher A∞-operations (m₁, m₂, m₃, ...). Specifically, the A∞-structure on F(X) is given by counting pseudoholomorphic polygons. The mirror functor must translate these polygon counts into the corresponding higher compositions of morphisms in DᵇCoh(Y). This is often expressed as a sequence of maps Φₖ: HF(L₀, L₁) ⊗ ... ⊗ HF(Lₖ₋₁, Lₖ) → Ext(Φ(L₀), Φ(Lₖ)), satisfying coherence conditions. The m₂ operation in F(X) (composition of Floer cohomology classes) must map to the composition of Ext classes in DᵇCoh(Y). The higher operations m₃, m₄, etc., must be preserved by the higher components of the A∞-functor.

The construction of Φ often relies on specific geometric setups. For toric varieties, the mirror functor can be constructed using Laurent polynomials and their associated Landau-Ginzburg models. For Fano varieties, the mirror is often a Landau-Ginzburg model, and the functor maps Lagrangians to matrix factorizations. In many cases, the construction involves intricate analytical techniques, such as constructing specific families of pseudoholomorphic curves, and algebraic techniques, such as constructing derived categories of modules over specific algebras. The PSS map ("Exact Functors and the PSS Map: Bridging Cohomology and Floer Theory") is an example of such a functor, relating Floer cohomology to quantum cohomology, which is a component of the larger HMS picture.

Beyond Compact Lagrangians: Exact and Non-Exact Lagrangians in the Wrapped Fukaya Category

The Fukaya category, in its most basic formulation, often considers compact Lagrangian submanifolds. However, in many important contexts, particularly for non-compact symplectic manifolds or Liouville domains, the objects of interest are non-compact Lagrangians, leading to the concept of the wrapped Fukaya category. Within this framework, the distinction between exact and non-exact Lagrangians becomes paramount, influencing the algebraic structure of the category, specifically whether the A∞-algebra is curved or not.

A Lagrangian submanifold L in an exact symplectic manifold (X, dλ) is called exact if the restriction of the primitive λ to L is an exact 1-form, i.e., λ|L = df for some function f: L → R. If λ|L is not exact, L is called non-exact. This distinction is crucial because the Floer differential and higher A∞-operations involve integrals of λ over pseudoholomorphic discs. If L is exact, these integrals simplify significantly.

For a wrapped Fukaya category W(X) of a Liouville manifold X (which is exact by definition), the objects are typically exact Lagrangian submanifolds that are "wrapped" into the cylindrical end of X. The condition of being exact ensures that the Floer cohomology groups are well-defined over fields of characteristic zero (e.g., C) without needing to introduce a formal parameter t (which would be used to track the symplectic area of discs). The A∞-algebra associated with a collection of exact Lagrangians in W(X) is typically uncurved, meaning the m₀ operation (which counts discs with no boundary marked points) vanishes. This reflects a fundamental property: exact Lagrangians are "Floer-theoretically trivial" in a certain sense, as they don't generate non-trivial m₀ terms.

However, the situation changes dramatically when non-exact Lagrangians are considered, as explored in "Fukaya Categories of Symplectic Manifolds with Non‑Exact Lagrangians and the Curved A∞-Algebra." If we include non-exact Lagrangians as objects in the Fukaya category, the associated A∞-algebra becomes curved. A curved A∞-algebra is a generalization where the m₀ operation is non-zero. This m₀ term, often called the "curvature element," counts pseudoholomorphic discs with boundary on a single Lagrangian and no marked points. For a non-exact Lagrangian L, the integral of λ over such a disc is generally non-zero, leading to a non-zero m₀ term. The curvature element acts as an obstruction to forming an ordinary A∞-algebra and modifies the standard A∞-relations.

The presence of curvature has significant implications. It means that the standard definition of Floer cohomology (where ∂² = 0) needs to be modified. Instead, one considers a "curved differential" and a more general notion of cohomology. The curvature element itself can be interpreted geometrically as the "energy" of the Lagrangian. In the context of Homological Mirror Symmetry, the mirror of a non-exact Lagrangian in the A-model might correspond to a complex of sheaves on the B-model whose endomorphism algebra is a curved A∞-algebra. This happens, for instance, when the mirror category is a derived category of matrix factorizations for a Landau-Ginzburg potential, where the potential itself induces curvature.

The choice of including exact or non-exact Lagrangians, and the resulting uncurved or curved A∞-structure, depends on the specific problem and the properties of the symplectic manifold. For instance, in compact Calabi-Yau manifolds, all special Lagrangians are exact (up to Hamiltonian isotopy), leading to uncurved algebras. In contrast, for general symplectic manifolds or when considering Lagrangians with local systems, non-exact Lagrangians and curved algebras are a natural and necessary part of the theory, providing a richer and more flexible framework for understanding symplectic geometry.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the necessity of grading with the necessity of spin structures; grading ensures Z-degrees for intersection points and Maslov index, while spin structures ensure consistent signs for counting pseudoholomorphic curves, particularly when w₂(L) ≠ 0.
  • Assuming all A∞-algebras in Fukaya categories are uncurved; this is only true for exact Lagrangians in exact symplectic manifolds (or when considering specific coefficients). Non-exact Lagrangians naturally lead to curved A∞-algebras where the m₀ operation is non-zero.
  • Overlooking the specific conditions for Lagrangian surgery; it requires a Lagrangian sphere (or more generally, a Lagrangian submanifold with specific properties) as the "cutting" locus, and the resulting manifold or Lagrangian must remain symplectic and Lagrangian, respectively.
  • Believing that symplectic homology is simply the Hochschild cohomology of any Fukaya category; it is specifically the Hochschild cohomology of the wrapped Fukaya category of a Liouville domain, and the isomorphism is a deep result, not a general identity.
  • Simplifying the construction of the mirror functor to a mere dictionary lookup; the explicit construction of the A∞-functor requires defining maps on objects and all higher A∞-operations, satisfying intricate coherence conditions, which is a major analytical and algebraic undertaking.
  • Ignoring the role of the Liouville vector field in defining Liouville domains and their completions; its outward-pointing property at the boundary is fundamental for defining the wrapped Fukaya category and symplectic homology.
  • Assuming that the mirror functor Φ always maps a Lagrangian L to a single coherent sheaf F(L); often, F(L) is a complex of sheaves, or even a more general object like a matrix factorization, especially in Landau-Ginzburg models.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Sheaves on K3 Surfaces

The homological mirror symmetry conjecture for K3 surfaces relates the Fukaya category of a symplectic K3 surface to the derived category of coherent sheaves on its mirror, which is another K3 surface. This case is distinguished by the fact that both sides are Calabi–Yau categories of dimension two, and the equivalence is expected to be induced by a Fourier–Mukai transform whose kernel is a universal sheaf on the product of the two K3 surfaces. The symplectic K3 surface carries a hyperkähler structure, and its Fukaya category can be defined using graded Lagrangian spheres and their Dehn twists. The mirror K3 surface is determined by the period domain: if the symplectic K3 has complexified Kähler class in the positive cone of its Néron–Severi lattice, the mirror is the K3 whose transcendental lattice is orthogonal to that class. The equivalence of categories must respect the Bridgeland stability conditions on both sides. On the B-model side, stability conditions on the derived category of a K3 surface are described by the space of stability conditions Stab(D^b(Coh(X))), which is a covering of a domain in the complexified ample cone. On the A-model side, stability conditions on the Fukaya category are constructed via the central charge given by the period integral of the holomorphic volume form over Lagrangian cycles. The HMS equivalence identifies these stability manifolds, and the autoequivalence groups on both sides — the symplectic mapping class group generated by Dehn twists on the A-side, and the derived autoequivalence group generated by spherical twists and Fourier–Mukai transforms on the B-side — are matched. A key technical tool is the use of the spherical twist functors associated to Lagrangian spheres, which correspond under HMS to spherical twists associated to spherical objects in the derived category. The proof of HMS for K3 surfaces with high Picard rank often proceeds by degeneration to a union of rational surfaces, where the Fukaya category can be computed via the wrapped Fukaya category of the complement of an anticanonical divisor, and the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model whose category of matrix factorizations is equivalent to the derived category of the K3 surface. The categorical Torelli theorem for K3 surfaces states that an equivalence of derived categories induces a Hodge isometry of the Mukai lattices, and the HMS conjecture implies that the symplectic mapping class group maps onto the group of Hodge isometries preserving the orientation of the positive cone.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Sheaves on Abelian Varieties

For an abelian variety A equipped with a principal polarization, the mirror is the dual abelian variety Â, and the homological mirror symmetry equivalence is the classical Fourier–Mukai transform with kernel the Poincaré line bundle on A × Â. The Fukaya category of A, when A is viewed as a real torus T2n with a constant symplectic form, has objects given by Lagrangian subtori with flat unitary connections, and morphisms given by Floer cohomology which reduces to the cohomology of the intersection points. The A∞-structure is formal in this case: the higher products m_k for k ≥ 3 vanish on the nose for a suitable choice of almost complex structure, and the category is quasi-equivalent to the category of local systems on the Lagrangian torus fibration. The mirror functor sends a Lagrangian torus with a flat connection to a skyscraper sheaf on the dual torus, and more generally, a Lagrangian section of the fibration corresponds to a line bundle on Â. The HMS equivalence extends to the derived categories, where the Fukaya category of the abelian variety is equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the dual abelian variety. This equivalence is compatible with the action of the symplectic group Sp(2n, Z) on the Fukaya category and the action of the derived autoequivalence group on the derived category, which is generated by translations, tensor products with line bundles, and the Fourier–Mukai transform. The categorical mirror symmetry for abelian varieties is the foundational case that generalizes to the SYZ conjecture for Calabi–Yau manifolds with Lagrangian torus fibrations. In the presence of a B-field, the Fukaya category is twisted by a gerbe, and the mirror is a non-commutative torus; the equivalence then relates the twisted Fukaya category to the derived category of modules over the non-commutative torus. The homological mirror symmetry for abelian varieties also provides a categorical interpretation of the classical theta functions: the space of sections of a line bundle on Â corresponds to the Floer cohomology of the corresponding Lagrangian section with the zero section. The higher genus generalization involves the Fukaya category of the moduli space of flat connections on a Riemann surface, which is mirror to the derived category of the moduli space of Higgs bundles, a case covered by the non-abelian Hodge correspondence.

Worked Example: Fourier–Mukai Kernel for T2
Let X = T2 = R2 / Z2 with symplectic form ω = dx ∧ dy. Its mirror is the dual torus ̂X = T2 with complex structure τ = i. Describe the Fourier–Mukai kernel P on X × ̂X and compute the image of the structure sheaf O_x of a point x ∈ X under the transform Φ_P.
The Poincaré line bundle P on X × ̂X has fibre over (x, ̂x) equal to the one-dimensional vector space of homomorphisms from the trivial line bundle on X to the line bundle on X corresponding to ̂x. Explicitly, if ̂X = Hom(X, U(1)), then P(x, ̂x) = ̂x(x). The Fourier–Mukai transform Φ_P: D^b(Coh(X)) → D^b(Coh(̂X)) sends a sheaf F to Rπ̂X*(π_X^*F ⊗ P). For F = O_x, the skyscraper sheaf at x, we have π_X^*O_x = O_{{x} × ̂X}. Tensoring with P restricts P to {x} × ̂X, which is the line bundle on ̂X whose fibre at ̂x is ̂x(x). This is precisely the line bundle L_x on ̂X corresponding to the point x under the duality X ≅ ̂̂X. Since π̂X is the projection, the pushforward is just L_x itself (concentrated in degree 0). Thus Φ_P(O_x) = L_x, a line bundle on the dual torus. This matches the symplectic picture: the Lagrangian point x in X (with trivial local system) corresponds to the Lagrangian section of the dual fibration given by the graph of the translation by x, whose mirror is the line bundle L_x.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Formality in Toric Cases
When a question asks about the Fukaya category of a torus or a toric variety, check whether the symplectic form is constant (or the moment polytope is Delzant with standard symplectic structure). In these cases, the A∞-structure is often formal: all higher products m_k for k ≥ 3 vanish. This means the Fukaya category is quasi-equivalent to its cohomology category, which is a dg-category with only m1 and m2 non-zero. This simplification is a standard exam shortcut — if you can argue formality (e.g., by choosing a Morse function with no gradient flow lines of length > 1, or by using the fact that the moment map is a toric fibration with no holomorphic discs), you can compute morphisms as ordinary cohomology groups and composition as cup product. Always state the formality theorem you are invoking (e.g., Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono for toric manifolds, or Abouzaid for the standard torus).

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps and Quantum Cohomology

The relationship between the Fukaya category and quantum cohomology is mediated by the open-closed string map, which is a morphism of A∞-algebras from the Fukaya category to the Hochschild cochain complex of the quantum cohomology ring. For a symplectic manifold X, the quantum cohomology QH^*(X) is a deformation of the ordinary cohomology ring by genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants, and it carries a Frobenius manifold structure. The closed-open string map goes in the opposite direction, from quantum cohomology to the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category, and is part of the structure of a Calabi–Yau A∞-category. The categorical mirror symmetry for moduli spaces of stable maps asserts that the Fukaya category of X is equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the mirror Y, and under this equivalence, the quantum cohomology ring of X is isomorphic to the Hochschild cohomology of the derived category of Y, which by the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem is the polyvector fields on Y. The genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants of X correspond to the Yukawa couplings on Y, which are the third derivatives of the prepotential. The open-closed map can be used to define the quantum product on Floer cohomology: for Lagrangians L0, L1, the quantum product on HF^*(L0, L1) is induced by counting pseudoholomorphic triangles with one interior marked point mapping to a cycle in X. This structure makes the Fukaya category into a module over the quantum cohomology ring. In the case of Fano varieties, the quantum cohomology is semisimple at the large radius limit, and the Fukaya category splits into a direct sum of categories corresponding to the idempotents. The mirror of this splitting is the decomposition of the derived category of the Landau–Ginzburg model into categories of matrix factorizations for each critical point of the superpotential. The Dubrovin connection on the quantum cohomology, which encodes the variation of the quantum product with the Kähler parameters, corresponds under mirror symmetry to the Gauss–Manin connection on the cohomology of the fibres of the superpotential. The categorical enumeration of stable maps is captured by the cyclic homology of the Fukaya category, which is isomorphic to the symplectic cohomology of X, and this isomorphism is the closed-open string map at the level of homology.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Curves and Tautological Rings

The moduli space of curves M_g carries a rich tautological ring generated by the κ and ψ classes, and its cohomology is governed by the Witten–Kontsevich theorem, which identifies the generating function of intersection numbers of ψ classes with the τ-function of the KdV hierarchy. The categorical mirror symmetry for M_g relates the Fukaya category of the moduli space of curves (or more precisely, of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces with marked points) to the derived category of a certain Landau–Ginzburg model or to the category of representations of the Virasoro algebra. The A-model side involves the symplectic geometry of the moduli space of curves, which can be approached via the Teichmüller space with the Weil–Petersson symplectic form, or via the moduli space of flat connections on a surface (the character variety) with the Goldman symplectic form. The Fukaya category of the character variety is related to the representation theory of the mapping class group, and the spherical twists in the Fukaya category correspond to Dehn twists in the mapping class group. The B-model side involves the derived category of coherent sheaves on the moduli space of curves, or more generally on the moduli stack of curves. The tautological ring maps to the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category via the open-closed string map, and the Virasoro constraints on the Gromov–Witten potential of a point correspond to the action of the Virasoro algebra on the Hochschild cohomology. The categorical mirror symmetry for M_g is closely related to the geometric Langlands correspondence: the Fukaya category of the moduli space of Higgs bundles on a curve is equivalent to the derived category of D-modules on the moduli space of bundles, and the restriction to the nilpotent cone gives a relation to the moduli space of curves. The tautological classes on M_g correspond to certain characteristic classes of the universal curve, and their intersection numbers are computed by the ELSV formula, which expresses Hurwitz numbers in terms of Hodge integrals. The categorical version of the ELSV formula relates the Hochschild homology of the Fukaya category of the moduli space of curves to the cohomology of the moduli space of stable maps to a point.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Matrix Factorizations and the Orlov Equivalence

For a Landau–Ginzburg model (Y, W) where Y is a smooth variety and W: Y → C is a regular function (the superpotential), the B-model category is the category of matrix factorizations MF(Y, W), which is a triangulated category equivalent to the singularity category of the critical locus of W. The mirror A-model is the Fukaya–Seidel category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, whose objects are Lagrangian thimbles (vanishing cycles) associated to the critical points of W. The Orlov equivalence states that for a hypersurface X = {f = 0} in a weighted projective space, the derived category of coherent sheaves on X is equivalent to the category of graded matrix factorizations of f. Under homological mirror symmetry, the Fukaya category of the mirror Calabi–Yau manifold is equivalent to the derived category of the hypersurface, and the Fukaya–Seidel category of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model is equivalent to the category of matrix factorizations. The A∞-structure on the Fukaya–Seidel category is defined by counting pseudoholomorphic polygons with boundary on the thimbles, and the curvature term m0 is given by the value of the superpotential at the critical points. The mirror functor sends a thimble to the corresponding matrix factorization, and the higher A∞-products correspond to the higher products in the dg-category of matrix factorizations. The categorical mirror symmetry for matrix factorizations is the key to proving HMS for Fano varieties, where the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model. The superpotential W on the mirror is constructed from the counts of Maslov index two discs with boundary on the Lagrangian torus fibre, and its critical points correspond to the eigenvalues of the quantum product by the anticanonical class. The Orlov equivalence is realized geometrically by the Knörrer periodicity, which relates matrix factorizations of W to matrix factorizations of W + x2 + y2, and this corresponds on the A-side to the stabilization of the Fukaya category by taking products with T^*S2. The Hochschild cohomology of the category of matrix factorizations is the Jacobian ring of W, which under mirror symmetry is isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of the Fano variety.

  • Confusing the Fourier–Mukai transform for abelian varieties (which is an exact equivalence of derived categories) with the general HMS functor for Calabi–Yau manifolds (which is only conjectural and requires A∞-enhancements); the abelian variety case is formal and does not involve higher A∞-products.
  • Assuming the quantum cohomology ring is always isomorphic to the Hochschild cohomology of the Fukaya category; this holds for the wrapped Fukaya category of a Liouville domain, but for the compact Fukaya category the open-closed map lands in the Hochschild cohomology of the quantum cohomology, not the other way around.
  • Overlooking the grading shift in the Orlov equivalence: the category of graded matrix factorizations of a polynomial of degree d is equivalent to the derived category of a Calabi–Yau of dimension d−2, so the Calabi–Yau dimension shifts by two.
  • Treating the moduli space of curves M_g as a smooth symplectic manifold for Fukaya category purposes; it is an orbifold (or stack) with finite quotient singularities, and its Fukaya category must be defined using orbifold Lagrangians or by passing to a smooth cover.
  • Neglecting the role of the B-field in the mirror symmetry for abelian varieties: a non-trivial B-field deforms the Fukaya category by a gerbe, and the mirror becomes a non-commutative torus, not a commutative dual abelian variety.
  • Confusing the category of matrix factorizations MF(Y, W) with the derived category of the critical locus Crit(W); they are related by the Knörrer periodicity and the equivalence of singularity categories, but MF(Y, W) is a dg-enhancement of the singularity category of the zero fibre, not of the critical locus itself.
  • Assuming the tautological ring of M_g is the full cohomology ring; it is a proper subring for g ≥ 3, and the Virasoro constraints only govern the intersection theory of tautological classes, not the full Gromov–Witten theory of M_g.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs and Pandharipande–Thomas Invariants on Calabi–Yau Threefolds

The Pandharipande–Thomas (PT) stable pair invariants count curves on a Calabi–Yau threefold X by studying the moduli space P_n(X, β) of stable pairs (F, s) where F is a pure one-dimensional sheaf with Chern character (0, 0, β, n) and s: O_X → F is a section with zero-dimensional cokernel. The PT invariants Pn,β are defined as the weighted Euler characteristic of this moduli space with respect to the Behrend function. Under homological mirror symmetry, the generating series of PT invariants is conjecturally equal to the generating series of Donaldson–Thomas (DT) invariants, which count ideal sheaves of curves. The categorical mirror symmetry for stable pairs identifies the category of stable pairs on X with a category of Lagrangian branes on the mirror Y. Specifically, the derived category of coherent sheaves on the moduli space of stable pairs is expected to be equivalent to a Fukaya-type category on the mirror. The PT/DT correspondence, proved by Bridgeland and Toda using wall-crossing in the space of stability conditions on D^b(Coh(X)), implies that the two theories are related by a universal change of variables. The categorical version of this correspondence involves the Joyce–Song theory of generalized DT invariants for Calabi–Yau categories and the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall-crossing formula. The moduli space of stable pairs carries a symmetric obstruction theory, and its virtual fundamental class is used to define the invariants. The categorical mirror symmetry for stable pairs is closely related to the categorical DT/PT correspondence, which states that the category of matrix factorizations of the superpotential on the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model is equivalent to the category of stable pairs on X. The superpotential is constructed from counts of holomorphic discs with boundary on the Lagrangian torus fibre, and its critical points correspond to stable pairs. The higher A∞-structure on the Fukaya category encodes the wall-crossing formulas for PT invariants across chambers in the space of stability conditions. The categorical mirror symmetry for stable pairs has been verified for local Calabi–Yau threefolds such as the resolved conifold and local P2, where the moduli space of stable pairs can be described explicitly using quiver representations with potential.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for the Space of Bridgeland Stability Conditions and the Mirror Conjecture for Stab

Bridgeland's space of stability conditions Stab(D) on a triangulated category D is a complex manifold that parametrizes stability conditions (Z, P) where Z: K(D) → C is a central charge and P is a slicing. For a Calabi–Yau category of dimension d, Stab(D) carries a natural holomorphic symplectic structure. The mirror symmetry conjecture for stability conditions, formulated by Bridgeland and others, asserts that for a Calabi–Yau variety X and its mirror Y, there is an isomorphism Stab(D^b(Coh(X))) ≅ Stab(Fuk(Y)) that intertwines the natural group actions by autoequivalences and the complex structure on the moduli space. In particular, the connected component Stab^†(D^b(Coh(X))) containing geometric stability conditions is conjectured to be isomorphic to the universal cover of the complexified Kähler moduli space of Y, while the space of stability conditions on the Fukaya category is related to the complex moduli space of X. The wall-and-chamber structure of Stab(D) corresponds to the wall-crossing of DT/PT invariants on the A-side and the variation of Hodge structure on the B-side. The autoequivalence group Aut(D) acts on Stab(D) by deck transformations, and the quotient Stab(D)/Aut(D) is the moduli space of stability conditions. For the derived category of a K3 surface, Stab(D) is a connected complex manifold of dimension 22, and the mirror conjecture relates it to the period domain of the mirror K3. For the Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold, stability conditions are defined using the central charge Z(L) = ∫_L Ω where Ω is the holomorphic volume form on the mirror. The categorical mirror symmetry for stability conditions implies that the wall-crossing formula for DT invariants (Kontsevich–Soibelman) is equivalent to the wall-crossing for the counts of pseudoholomorphic polygons in the Fukaya category. The space Stab(D) also carries a natural metric (the generalized Donaldson metric) and a hyperkähler structure in certain cases. The conjecture has been verified for elliptic curves, where Stab(D^b(Coh(E))) ≅ C × H (H the upper half-plane), and for certain quiver categories with potential. The categorical mirror symmetry for Stab provides a framework for understanding the analytic continuation of the Fukaya category across walls in the Kähler moduli space.

Worked Example: Wall-Crossing for Stable Pairs on the Resolved Conifold
Consider the resolved conifold X = Tot(O(-1) ⊕ O(-1) → P1). The moduli space of stable pairs P_n(X, β) for β = d[P1] is isomorphic to the Hilbert scheme of d points on C2. Compute the PT invariant Pn,d for d=1 and explain its relation to the DT invariant via the wall-crossing formula.
For d=1, the moduli space P_n(X, [P1]) parametrizes stable pairs (F, s) where F is a sheaf supported on the zero section P1 with χ(F) = n. Since the zero section is a rational curve, F must be a torsion sheaf on P1 of degree n. The section s: O_X → F factors through OP1 → F, so the moduli space is isomorphic to the space of quotients OP1 → F with F a torsion sheaf of length n. This is the symmetric product Sym^n(P1) ≅ P^n. The virtual fundamental class coincides with the fundamental class because the obstruction theory is trivial (the normal bundle is O(-1)⊕O(-1)). The Behrend function is constant 1, so Pn,1 = χ(P^n) = n+1. The DT invariant DTn,1 counts ideal sheaves I_C of curves C with χ(O_C) = n. For d=1, the only curve is the zero section with multiplicity n, so the moduli space is also P^n and DTn,1 = n+1. The PT/DT correspondence states that the generating series are related by ∑ Pn,β q^n = ∑ DTn,β (-q)^n / (1-q)χ(X). For the conifold, χ(X)=2, and the formula holds termwise for d=1: Pn,1 = DTn,1 because the wall-crossing factor (1-q)-2 contributes only for higher degrees. The categorical mirror symmetry identifies the category of stable pairs with the category of matrix factorizations of the superpotential W = x + y + 1/(xy) on the mirror (C^*)2, where the critical points correspond to the zero section.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Wall-Crossing in Categorical Mirror Symmetry
When a question asks about the relationship between DT and PT invariants, or about the variation of stability conditions across a wall, identify the central charge Z and the phase of the objects involved. The wall is defined by Im(Z(E1)/Z(E2)) = 0 for two objects E1, E2. The wall-crossing formula for the generating series of invariants is governed by the Kontsevich–Soibelman product of symplectomorphisms of the torus associated to the charge lattice. In the Fukaya category, this corresponds to the mutation of the exceptional collection or the change in the A∞-structure under a change of Kähler form. Memorize the universal DT/PT change of variables: P(q) = DT(-q) / (1-q)χ(X) for the resolved conifold, and the general formula involving the plethystic exponential. For stability conditions, recall that Stab(D) is a complex manifold and the wall-crossing is a piecewise linear transformation on the space of central charges.

Fukaya Categories and the Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Moduli Spaces of Perverse Sheaves on the Hitchin Base and the Geometric Langlands Correspondence

The geometric Langlands correspondence, as formulated by Beilinson and Drinfeld, predicts an equivalence between the derived category of D-modules on the moduli stack Bun_G of G-bundles on a curve C and the derived category of coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSys^L G of ^L G-local systems, where ^L G is the Langlands dual group. Kapustin and Witten realized this correspondence as a mirror symmetry between two topological twists of N=4 super Yang–Mills theory: the A-model on the Hitchin moduli space M_H(G) (the moduli space of Higgs bundles) and the B-model on M_H(^L G). The Hitchin fibration h: M_H(G) → A (where A is the Hitchin base, an affine space of dimension (g-1)dim G) is an integrable system whose generic fibres are abelian varieties (Prym varieties). The SYZ conjecture applied to this fibration suggests that the mirror of M_H(G) is M_H(^L G) with the dual fibration. The categorical mirror symmetry for the Hitchin system identifies the Fukaya category of M_H(G) (with respect to the holomorphic symplectic form Ω = ω_I + i ω_J) with the derived category of coherent sheaves on M_H(^L G). The objects of the Fukaya category are Lagrangian submanifolds that are sections or multisections of the Hitchin fibration, or more generally, Lagrangian branes supported on the fibres. The morphisms are given by Floer cohomology, which computes the Ext groups of the corresponding sheaves on the mirror. The perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base A arise from the decomposition theorem applied to the Hitchin fibration: R h_* QM_H is a direct sum of shifted perverse sheaves on A. The support of these perverse sheaves corresponds to the singular fibres of the Hitchin fibration, and their stalks encode the topology of the fibres. Under mirror symmetry, the category of perverse sheaves on A is equivalent to the category of Lagrangian branes on M_H(G) that are invariant under the Hamiltonian torus action. The categorical geometric Langlands correspondence for the Hitchin system is closely related to the work of Arinkin and Gaitsgory on the categorical Langlands correspondence for GL_n, and to the work of Nadler and Yun on the categorical Langlands correspondence for general reductive groups using the microlocal sheaf theory on the Hitchin base.
