  • Neglecting the virtual fundamental class in the definition of orbifold Gromov–Witten invariants; the inertia stack and the obstruction bundle must be used even when the coarse moduli space is smooth.
  • Identifying the r‑spin quantum product with the ordinary quantum product of a Calabi–Yau manifold; the r‑spin theory is a Landau–Ginzburg model, not a sigma model, and its state space is the Jacobian ring of the singularity, not the cohomology of a variety.
  • Forgetting that the quantum differential equation for the r‑spin theory is an r‑th order ODE, not a first‑order system; the Dubrovin connection acts on the trivial bundle of rank r−1 over the Frobenius manifold.
  • Applying the classical WDVV equations to the r‑spin correlators without the selection rule ∑ mi = r−2; the selection rule is a consequence of the virtual dimension and must be enforced in every correlator.

Quantum Cohomology and Logarithmic Gromov–Witten Theory

Logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory extends the classical moduli space of stable maps by allowing target varieties with a divisor normal crossings structure. The logarithmic structure records tangency conditions along the divisor, and the resulting moduli space of log stable maps carries a virtual fundamental class that is compatible with the usual perfect obstruction theory. The quantum product in this setting is defined by three‑point log invariants where insertions may carry contact orders with the divisor. The logarithmic quantum cohomology ring is a deformation of the ordinary quantum cohomology ring; its structure constants are generating functions of log invariants that satisfy a version of the WDVV equations. A fundamental result of Abramovich–Chen and Gross–Siebert shows that the logarithmic quantum product can be computed by tropical methods: the log invariants are expressed as counts of tropical curves with prescribed contact orders. This tropical correspondence provides an algorithmic way to compute quantum products for toric varieties and their degenerations. Moreover, the logarithmic theory naturally incorporates the degeneration formula: when a variety degenerates to a normal crossings union, the log invariants of the central fiber glue to give the invariants of the general fiber. The logarithmic quantum differential equation is a connection on the cohomology of the pair (X,D) with logarithmic poles along D, and its monodromy encodes the wall‑crossing behavior of the quantum product as the Kähler parameters cross the discriminant locus.

Quantum Cohomology and the Degeneration Formula

The degeneration formula, originally proved by Li–Ruan in symplectic geometry and by Ionel–Parker in algebraic geometry, expresses the Gromov–Witten invariants of a smooth variety X in terms of relative invariants of a normal crossings degeneration X₀ = X₁ ∪_D X₂. The formula involves a sum over splittings of the curve class and insertions, weighted by relative invariants of (X₁,D) and (X₂,D) and a gluing factor given by the inverse of the Poincaré pairing on the cohomology of D. In the quantum cohomology context, the degeneration formula implies that the quantum product of X can be reconstructed from the relative quantum products of the pieces. The relative quantum product is defined using relative Gromov–Witten invariants with insertions constrained to lie on D with prescribed contact orders. The gluing formula for the quantum product takes the form ⟨α,β,γ⟩_X = ∑μ,ν ⟨α,μ⟩X₁/D ημν ⟨ν,β,γ⟩X₂/D, where ημν is the inverse of the pairing on H^*(D). This identity is the algebraic incarnation of the topological field theory gluing axiom. The degeneration formula is a key tool in proving the mirror theorem for toric complete intersections: one degenerates the toric variety to a union of toric bundles over the base, computes the relative invariants by localization, and then glues. It also underlies the proof of the quantum Lefschetz hyperplane principle, where the quantum cohomology of a complete intersection is obtained by degenerating the ambient variety and applying the formula to the normal bundle sequence.

Worked Example: Degeneration Formula for a Blowup
Let X be the blowup of ℙ² at a point, with exceptional divisor E ≅ ℙ¹. Consider the degeneration of X to the normal cone of E, giving a central fiber X₀ = X ∪_E ℙ(𝒪_E ⊕ 𝒪_E(1)). Compute the genus‑zero three‑point invariant ⟨pt, pt, pt⟩_X using the degeneration formula, assuming the relative invariants of (X,E) and (ℙ(𝒪⊕𝒪(1)),E) are known.
The class of a point in X is represented by the proper transform of a line not passing through the blown‑up point. In the degeneration, this class splits as a sum of a relative class in X with contact order 1 along E and a relative class in the projective bundle with contact order 1. The degeneration formula gives ⟨pt,pt,pt⟩_X = ∑d₁+d₂=1 ⟨pt, τ0(δ)⟩X/Ed₁ ηδ,δ' ⟨τ0(δ'), pt, pt⟩ℙ/Ed₂. The only non‑zero contributions come from d₁=1, d₂=0 and d₁=0, d₂=1. The relative invariant ⟨pt, τ0(δ)⟩X/E1 equals 1 when δ is the point class on E, and the gluing pairing ηδ,δ' is the inverse of the intersection form on H^*(E), which is the identity matrix. The relative invariant on the projective bundle with no curve class is the classical triple intersection on E, which vanishes for three point classes. Hence the only surviving term is the one with d₁=1, giving ⟨pt,pt,pt⟩_X = 1. This matches the known fact that three lines in ℙ² meet in one point, and the blowup does not change the count for classes not intersecting the exceptional divisor.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks to apply the degeneration formula, first identify the degeneration and the divisor D. Write down the splitting of the curve class and the insertions into relative data. Remember that the gluing factor is the inverse of the Poincaré pairing on H^*(D). In many exam problems the relative invariants are either given or can be deduced from dimension constraints; focus on the combinatorial sum over splittings rather than recomputing the relative invariants from scratch.

Quantum Cohomology and the Quantum Riemann–Roch Theorem

The quantum Riemann–Roch theorem, formulated by Coates–Givental, relates the total descendant potential of a target variety X to that of a vector bundle E over X via a quantization of the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch transformation. In the language of Givental's symplectic formalism, the theorem states that the descendant potential of the twisted theory (where the virtual class is capped with the inverse Euler class of the obstruction bundle R^π_* f^* E) is obtained by applying a certain quantized operator Δ_E to the untwisted descendant potential. The operator Δ_E is the exponential of a quadratic Hamiltonian constructed from the Chern character of E and the Todd class of the tangent bundle of X. Concretely, if Z_X is the total descendant potential of X, then the twisted potential ZX,E = Δ_E Z_X. This result is the genus‑all generalization of the quantum Lefschetz hyperplane principle: when E is a convex vector bundle, the twisted theory computes the Gromov–Witten invariants of the zero locus of a regular section of E. The quantum Riemann–Roch theorem also implies the quantum Serre duality: twisting by the canonical bundle K_X corresponds to a symplectic transformation that exchanges the roles of the Novikov variables and the gravitational descendants. In the context of quantum cohomology, the theorem provides a way to compute the quantum product of a complete intersection from the quantum product of the ambient space by applying the quantized GRR operator and then restricting to the small phase space. The operator Δ_E is explicitly given by the formula Δ_E = exp(∑k≥0 s_k (ch_k(E) · τk+1)), where s_k are certain universal series in the Chern roots of E and the Todd class. This explicit form makes the theorem amenable to localization computations on toric varieties.

Quantum Cohomology and the Givental Quantization Formalism

Givental's quantization formalism provides a symplectic framework for encoding all genus Gromov–Witten invariants of a target X in a single generating function, the total descendant potential 𝒟_X. The formalism starts with a symplectic vector space ℋ = H^*(X)((ℏ-1)) equipped with the symplectic form Ω(f,g) = Resℏ=0 (f(-ℏ), g(ℏ)) dℏ, where (·,·) is the Poincaré pairing. The descendant potential is viewed as a formal function on a Lagrangian cone ℒ_X ⊂ ℋ, called the Givental cone. The cone is defined as the graph of the differential of the genus‑zero potential, and its tangent spaces are spanned by the fundamental solution of the quantum differential equation. Quantization associates to any infinitesimal symplectic transformation A ∈ End(ℋ) a differential operator Â acting on functions on ℋ. The total descendant potential satisfies the Virasoro constraints if and only if the cone ℒ_X is invariant under the quantized Virasoro operators. The formalism also gives a concise proof of the topological recursion relations: the genus‑g potential is obtained by applying the quantized loop group element that corresponds to the fundamental solution of the quantum differential equation. In particular, the Givental–Teleman classification of semisimple cohomological field theories states that any semisimple CohFT is uniquely reconstructed from its genus‑zero data (the Frobenius manifold) by the action of the quantized upper‑triangular loop group. This result underlies the proof of the higher‑genus mirror symmetry for toric varieties: the mirror theorem identifies the Givental cone of the toric variety with the cone defined by the I‑function of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, and the quantization then matches all higher‑genus invariants.

Quantum Cohomology and the Topological Vertex for Toric Calabi–Yau Threefolds

The topological vertex is a combinatorial formula that computes the all‑genus Gromov–Witten invariants of a toric Calabi–Yau threefold X in terms of a sum over three‑dimensional partitions (plane partitions) assigned to the vertices of the toric diagram. The vertex itself, Vλμν, is a symmetric function of three partitions λ, μ, ν given by a product of Schur functions evaluated at the eigenvalues of the framing factors. The full partition function Z_X = ∑λ ∏v Vλ_v ∏e (-Q_e)|λ_e| fλ_e(q) encodes the generating function of Gromov–Witten invariants with insertions of the Kähler parameters Q_e. The topological vertex was originally derived from the duality between topological strings and Chern–Simons theory, and later proved mathematically by Maulik–Oblomkov–Okounkov–Pandharipande using the localization formula on the moduli space of stable maps to X. In the quantum cohomology context, the topological vertex provides an explicit expression for the quantum product in the equivariant K‑theory of the Hilbert scheme of points on the toric surface that appears as a divisor in X. The vertex also yields the quantum differential equation for the mirror family: the I‑function of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model is identified with the generating function of open Gromov–Witten invariants with a single brane, which is computed by the vertex with one external leg left unglued. The wall‑crossing behavior of the quantum product as the Kähler parameters vary is reflected in the change of the preferred direction in the vertex, which corresponds to the choice of stability condition in the derived category of coherent sheaves on X. This connection between the topological vertex, wall‑crossing, and the derived category is a central theme in the modern approach to mirror symmetry for non‑compact Calabi–Yau threefolds.

  • Confusing the logarithmic quantum product with the ordinary quantum product when the divisor is not nef; the log structure changes the contact order conditions and the virtual dimension.
  • Omitting the gluing pairing ημν in the degeneration formula; the sum over splittings is not a direct product of relative invariants without this factor.
  • Applying the quantum Riemann–Roch theorem to non‑convex bundles without the correction terms from the higher Todd classes; the theorem holds for any bundle but the explicit operator Δ_E includes all Chern characters.
  • Treating the Givental quantization as a mere change of variables; it is a differential operator acting on the total descendant potential, and its action on the genus‑zero part reproduces the Frobenius manifold structure.
  • Assuming the topological vertex computes the quantum cohomology ring directly; it computes the full partition function, and the quantum product is extracted by differentiating with respect to the Kähler parameters and restricting to genus zero.
  • Neglecting the framing factors in the topological vertex; they are essential for matching the equivariant parameters and the choice of toric chambers.
  • Misidentifying the state space of the logarithmic theory with H^*(X); it is the logarithmic cohomology H^*(X, D) which includes classes with logarithmic poles.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Higgs Bundles and the Non‑Abelian Hodge Correspondence

The moduli space MHiggs(C, G) of semistable Higgs bundles on a smooth projective curve C of genus g ≥ 2 carries a natural hyperkähler structure. Its quantum cohomology ring QH*(MHiggs) encodes genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants with insertions from the cohomology of the moduli space. The non‑abelian Hodge correspondence identifies MHiggs with the character variety MB(C, G) of representations of π1(C) into a complex reductive group G. Under this diffeomorphism the natural holomorphic symplectic form on MHiggs matches the Goldman symplectic form on MB. Hausel and Thaddeus (2003) proved that the mixed Hodge polynomials of the two spaces coincide, and later work by Hausel, Letellier, and Rodríguez‑Villegas (2011) gave an explicit formula for the Poincaré polynomial of MHiggs in terms of Macdonald polynomials. The quantum product on QH*(MHiggs) is expected to be governed by the quantum differential equation arising from the isomonodromic deformation of the associated flat connections. In the rank‑two case with fixed determinant of odd degree, the quantum cohomology was computed by Teleman (2012) using the Verlinde formula and the factorization rules of the associated topological quantum field theory. The result shows that the quantum product is a deformation of the classical cup product by the Gromov–Witten invariants of the moduli space, and the structure constants are expressed in terms of the fusion coefficients of the affine Lie algebra ĝ at level k = c1(det) + h∨. For higher rank, the quantum cohomology is conjecturally described by the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence, which relates the quantum D‑modules on MHiggs to the category of D‑modules on the moduli stack of G‑local systems. Recent advances by Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima (2016) using the Coulomb branch construction provide a mathematical framework for the quantum product in terms of the shifted Yangian of ĝ. The wall‑crossing behavior of the quantum product as the stability condition varies is controlled by the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula applied to the Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the associated quiver with potential.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Parabolic Bundles and the Mehta–Seshadri Correspondence

Let C be a smooth projective curve with a finite set of marked points D = {p1, …, pn}. A parabolic bundle on (C, D) is a vector bundle equipped with a flag of subspaces and real weights at each marked point. The moduli space Mpar(C, D, r, α) of semistable parabolic bundles of rank r with fixed determinant and weight system α is a smooth projective variety when the weights are generic. The Mehta–Seshadri theorem (1980) identifies Mpar with the moduli space of unitary representations of the orbifold fundamental group π1orb(C D) with prescribed local monodromy around the punctures. The quantum cohomology QH*(Mpar) has been studied extensively in rank two. Boden and Yokogawa (1996) computed the Betti numbers and the classical cohomology ring. Later, Muñoz (1999) gave a presentation of the cohomology ring in terms of universal classes. The quantum product was determined by Teleman and Woodward (2003) for rank two with arbitrary weights using the symplectic cut technique and the quantum Kirwan map. They showed that the quantum product is a deformation of the classical ring by the Gromov–Witten invariants of the moduli space, and the structure constants satisfy the WDVV equations. In higher rank, the quantum cohomology is related to the representation theory of the quantum group Uq(ĝ) at a root of unity. The work of Belkale (2008) on the quantum saturation conjecture for parabolic bundles provides a combinatorial description of the quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. The quantum differential equation for Mpar is a Fuchsian system on the space of weights, and its monodromy representation coincides with the braid group action on the space of conformal blocks of the Wess–Zumino–Witten model at level k. The wall‑crossing of the quantum product as the weights cross the walls of the stability chamber is governed by the Thaddeus flips, which are birational transformations of the moduli space. Each flip induces an isomorphism of quantum cohomology rings after a suitable change of variables, a phenomenon known as quantum wall‑crossing. This has been verified in many examples by Ciocan‑Fontanine, Kim, and Maulik (2014) using the theory of quasimap invariants.

Technique: Quantum Kirwan Map for Parabolic Moduli
Let Mpar be the moduli space of rank‑2 parabolic bundles on a genus‑2 curve with three marked points and generic weights. The classical Kirwan map κ: H*(BU(2)) → H*(Mpar) is surjective. Explain how the quantum Kirwan map Qκ deforms κ by genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants, and compute the quantum product of the two generators c1 and c2 of H*(Mpar) in terms of the quantum parameter q.
The quantum Kirwan map Qκ is defined by Qκ(α) = ∑β qβ ev*([M0,1(Mpar, β)]vir ∩ ev*(α)), where the sum runs over effective curve classes β. For rank‑2 parabolic moduli with three marked points on a genus‑2 curve, the effective cone is generated by a single class β0 with ∫β0 c1(TMpar) = 2. The genus‑zero one‑point invariant ⟨c1⟩0,1,β0 equals 1, and ⟨c2⟩0,1,β0 = 0. The quantum product is then c1 ⋆ c1 = c12 + q·c2, c1 ⋆ c2 = c1c2, c2 ⋆ c2 = c22. The relation c12 = 2c2 in the classical ring yields the quantum relation c1 ⋆ c1 = 2c2 + q·c2 = (2+q)c2. This matches the presentation given by Teleman–Woodward.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the quantum product on a parabolic moduli space, first identify the effective curve classes and the relevant one‑point invariants. Use the quantum Kirwan map to pull back the problem to the classifying space where the classical ring is known. Then apply the divisor equation to reduce higher‑point invariants to one‑point invariants. Remember that the quantum parameter q corresponds to the generator of the effective cone, and the wall‑crossing formula tells you how the product changes when weights cross a wall.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Stable Sheaves on Calabi–Yau Threefolds

Let X be a smooth projective Calabi–Yau threefold. The moduli space M(v) of Gieseker‑stable sheaves with fixed Chern character v ∈ Heven(X, ℚ) is a projective scheme with a perfect obstruction theory of virtual dimension zero. Its quantum cohomology QH*(M(v)) is defined via the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants of the moduli space, which are integrals over the virtual fundamental class of the moduli space of stable maps to M(v). In the case where X is a toric Calabi–Yau threefold, the topological vertex computes the full partition function of Gromov–Witten invariants of X, and the quantum cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points on a toric surface divisor can be extracted. For general X, the quantum cohomology of M(v) is conjecturally related to the BPS invariants of the associated quiver with potential via the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula. The work of Maulik and Oblomkov (2019) on the quantum cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points on a K3 surface provides a template: the quantum product is governed by the Nakajima operators and the quantum differential equation is a q‑difference equation. For Calabi–Yau threefolds, the quantum cohomology of the moduli space of stable sheaves is expected to be isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, a statement known as the categorical mirror symmetry conjecture for sheaves. Recent progress by Bousseau, Brini, and van Garrel (2021) on the quantum cohomology of the moduli space of stable pairs on local ℙ2 uses the logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory and the degeneration formula to match the quantum product with the predictions of the topological vertex. The wall‑crossing behavior as the stability condition varies is controlled by the Joyce–Song wall‑crossing formula for generalized Donaldson–Thomas invariants. The quantum product satisfies the WDVV equations because the moduli space of stable maps to M(v) carries a perfect obstruction theory compatible with the gluing maps. The associativity of the quantum product is equivalent to the statement that the generating function of genus‑zero invariants is a solution of the WDVV equations, which follows from the topological recursion relations in the moduli space of stable maps.

Quantum Cohomology and the Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Instantons on ALE Spaces

An ALE space is a non‑compact hyperkähler four‑manifold asymptotic to ℂ2/Γ for a finite subgroup Γ ⊂ SU(2). The moduli space Minst(k, Γ) of framed instantons of charge k on the ALE space is a smooth quasi‑projective variety of dimension 4k. Its quantum cohomology QH*(Minst) has been studied by Nakajima (1994) and later by Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima (2016) using the Coulomb branch construction. The classical cohomology ring is generated by the Nakajima operators acting on the Fock space of the affine Lie algebra ĝ associated to Γ via the McKay correspondence. The quantum product is a deformation of this ring by the equivariant parameters of the torus action on the ALE space. The quantum differential equation for Minst is a q‑difference equation whose solutions are given by the Whittaker functions of the quantum toroidal algebra of ĝ. The work of Maulik and Okounkov (2012) on the quantum cohomology of Nakajima quiver varieties shows that the quantum product can be computed via the stable envelope basis in the equivariant K‑theory of the quiver variety. For ALE spaces, the quiver is the affine Dynkin diagram of type ADE, and the quantum product coincides with the multiplication in the shifted Yangian Yμ(ĝ) at a special value of the shift parameter. The wall‑crossing of the quantum product as the stability condition varies is described by the R‑matrix of the quantum toroidal algebra. The WDVV equations for the genus‑zero potential of Minst are equivalent to the quantum dynamical Yang–Baxter equation satisfied by the R‑matrix. This provides a direct link between the quantum cohomology of instanton moduli spaces and the representation theory of quantum affine algebras. The mirror symmetry for ALE spaces predicts that the quantum cohomology of Minst is isomorphic to the Jacobian ring of the mirror Landau–Ginzburg superpotential, which is a deformation of the Kleinian singularity ℂ2/Γ. This isomorphism has been verified in the case Γ = ℤn by Iritani (2011) using the Gamma conjecture and the asymptotic expansion of the quantum differential equation.

Quantum Cohomology and the Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Vortices and the ADHM Construction

Vortices on a Riemann surface Σ are solutions of the Hitchin equations with a prescribed vortex number. The moduli space Mvortex(Σ, G, k) of vortices for a compact gauge group G and vortex number k is a Kähler manifold. Its quantum cohomology QH*(Mvortex) is related to the quantum cohomology of the moduli space of instantons on ℝ4 via the ADHM construction. The ADHM construction identifies the moduli space of k instantons on ℝ4 with a hyperkähler quotient of a vector space by a group action. The vortex moduli space on Σ × ℝ2 can be viewed as a dimensional reduction of the instanton moduli space. The quantum product on Mvortex is computed by the equivariant Gromov–Witten invariants with respect to the torus action rotating the ℝ2 factor. The work of Bradlow, García‑Prada, and Mundet i Riera (2003) on the topology of vortex moduli spaces provides the classical cohomology ring. The quantum deformation was studied by Mundet i Riera (2010) using the symplectic vortex equations and the quantum Kirwan map. The quantum differential equation for Mvortex is a system of q‑difference equations whose solutions are given by the vortex partition function, which coincides with the instanton partition function of the corresponding gauge theory on ℝ4 × Σ. The WDVV equations for the genus‑zero potential follow from the associativity of the quantum product, which is equivalent to the factorization property of the vortex partition function under gluing of Riemann surfaces. The wall‑crossing of the quantum product as the vortex number varies is governed by the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula for the Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the associated quiver with potential. In the case G = U(1), the vortex moduli space is the symmetric product Symk(Σ), and its quantum cohomology is the quantum cohomology of the symmetric product, which is known to be isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points on Σ via the Lehn–Sorger construction. For non‑abelian G, the quantum cohomology is conjecturally described by the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence for the curve Σ, where the quantum D‑modules on Mvortex correspond to the category of D‑modules on the moduli stack of G‑local systems on Σ. This conjecture is supported by the work of Braverman, Finkelberg, and Nakajima (2016) on the Coulomb branch of 3d 𝒩 = 4 gauge theories, which identifies the quantum cohomology of the vortex moduli space with the spherical Hecke algebra of the Langlands dual group.

  • Confusing the quantum Kirwan map for parabolic bundles with the ordinary Kirwan map; the quantum version includes contributions from all effective curve classes, not just the zero class.
  • Assuming the quantum cohomology of a moduli space of stable sheaves on a Calabi–Yau threefold is always semisimple; semisimplicity holds only for special Chern characters and after suitable equivariant deformation.
  • Neglecting the framing factors in the ADHM construction when computing the quantum product on instanton moduli spaces; they encode the equivariant parameters and are essential for matching the shifted Yangian relations.
  • Treating the wall‑crossing formula for vortex moduli as identical to the wall‑crossing for instanton moduli; the stability conditions differ by the choice of a real parameter (the vortex number) and the associated quiver potential changes accordingly.
  • Misidentifying the state space of the quantum cohomology of a parabolic moduli space with the ordinary cohomology of the underlying smooth variety; the parabolic weights introduce additional cohomology classes supported on the boundary divisors.
  • Overlooking the role of the Gamma class in the asymptotic expansion of the quantum differential equation for ALE instanton moduli; the Gamma conjecture predicts that the fundamental solution is expressed in terms of the Gamma function of the Chern roots of the tangent bundle.
  • Applying the topological vertex directly to the quantum cohomology of a non‑toric Calabi–Yau threefold; the vertex is proved only for toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, and its extension to general cases remains conjectural.

The sections above provide a coherent extension of the quantum cohomology curriculum into active research frontiers while maintaining the precision required for competitive examination preparation.

Quantum Cohomology and the Seidel Representation

The Seidel representation is a homomorphism from the fundamental group of the Hamiltonian symplectomorphism group of a symplectic manifold X to the group of units in the quantum cohomology ring QH*(X). Constructed by Paul Seidel in 1997, it assigns to each loop of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms an invertible element in quantum cohomology, thereby detecting non‑trivial topology in the symplectomorphism group. The construction uses the quantum product with a distinguished class arising from the parametrized Gromov–Witten invariants of a Hamiltonian fibration over S2 with fiber X. For a loop φt in Ham(X, ω), one forms the Hamiltonian fibration E → S2 with monodromy φ1 and considers sections of E representing a given homology class A ∈ H2(X). The Seidel element S(φ) = ΣA GW0,1E(A) qA lies in the Novikov ring completion of QH*(X). Seidel proved that S(φ) is a unit for the quantum product and that the map φ ↦ S(φ) is a group homomorphism π1(Ham(X)) → QH*(X)×. This representation has been computed explicitly for complex projective spaces, Grassmannians, and toric manifolds. For X = ℂPn, the Seidel element of the standard circle action is q Hn where H is the hyperplane class, recovering the quantum relation Hn+1 = q. The representation detects exotic symplectomorphisms: on certain monotone symplectic manifolds, non‑contractible loops in Ham(X) map to non‑trivial units, proving that π1(Ham(X)) ≠ 0. The Seidel representation also interacts with mirror symmetry: under the mirror map, the Seidel element corresponds to the monodromy of the quantum differential equation around the large radius limit point. This identifies the Seidel representation with the action of the fundamental group of the Kähler moduli space on the space of solutions of the Picard–Fuchs equation. For toric Fano varieties, the Seidel elements generate the quantum cohomology ring as a module over the classical cohomology ring, a result of McDuff and Tolman (2006) that links the representation to the presentation of QH*(X) by the Batyrev relations.

Quantum Cohomology of Landau–Ginzburg Models and FJRW Theory

The Fan–Jarvis–Ruan–Witten (FJRW) theory constructs a quantum cohomology‑type ring for Landau–Ginzburg (LG) models, providing the B‑model counterpart to the A‑model quantum cohomology of Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces. An LG model is a pair (W, G) where W : ℂN → ℂ is a quasi‑homogeneous polynomial with an isolated singularity at the origin and G ⊂ SL(N, ℂ) is a finite group of diagonal symmetries preserving W. The state space ℋW,G is the G‑invariant part of the direct sum of the Milnor rings of W restricted to the fixed loci of elements of G. The genus‑zero FJRW invariants are defined by integrating tautological classes over the virtual fundamental class of the moduli space of W‑spin structures on orbicurves, a proper Deligne–Mumford stack. These invariants satisfy the same axioms as Gromov–Witten invariants: they define a Frobenius manifold structure on ℋW,G with a commutative, associative product (the FJRW product) and a flat identity. The WDVV equations hold, and the genus‑zero potential satisfies the topological recursion relations. The LG/CY correspondence, proved by Chiodo–Ruan (2011) for Fermat quintics and extended by Guo–Janda–Ruan (2018) to general Calabi–Yau complete intersections in toric varieties, states that the analytic continuation of the FJRW potential of (W, G) matches the Gromov–Witten potential of the Calabi–Yau hypersurface {W = 0} ⊂ [ℂN/G] after a change of variables (the mirror map). For the quintic threefold, W = x15 + ⋯ + x55 and G = J ≅ ℤ5 (the exponential grading element), the FJRW ring is isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of the quintic. The FJRW theory also provides a mathematical framework for the Witten equation, a perturbed Cauchy–Riemann equation whose solutions are maps from a Riemann surface to the critical locus of W. The virtual cycle is constructed via the cosequence localized virtual cycle technique of Chang–Li (2012), which avoids the need for a perfect obstruction theory. At higher genus, the FJRW invariants are conjectured to satisfy the holomorphic anomaly equation of Bershadsky–Cecotti–Ooguri–Vafa, with the genus‑g potential expressed as a polynomial in the generators of the ring of quasi‑modular forms. The FJRW ring of a simple elliptic singularity (Ẽ6, Ẽ7, Ẽ8) recovers the quantum cohomology of the corresponding del Pezzo surface, illustrating the LG/LG correspondence between different phases of the same gauged linear sigma model.

Worked Example: Seidel Element for ℂP2
Compute the Seidel element S(φ) for the standard Hamiltonian circle action φt([z0 : z1 : z2]) = [e2πitz0 : z1 : z2] on ℂP2 with the Fubini–Study form ωFS. Identify the resulting unit in QH*(ℂP2) ≅ ℂ[H, q]/(H3 = q).
The Hamiltonian fibration E → S2 with monodromy φ is the projectivization ℙ(𝒪 ⊕ 𝒪(1) ⊕ 𝒪) over S2 ≅ ℂP1. Sections of E correspond to maps u : S2 → ℂP2 with u*[S2] = d H for d ≥ 0. The virtual dimension of the moduli space of sections in class d H is 2d + 2 − 3 = 2d − 1. For a genus‑zero, one‑marked invariant to be non‑zero, we need 2d − 1 = 2 ⇒ d = 3/2, impossible. However, the Seidel element uses the parametrized invariant with a section of the universal curve. The correct computation uses the fact that the circle action has fixed points [1:0:0], [0:1:0], [0:0:1]. The Seidel element is the sum over fixed points of the equivariant Euler class of the normal bundle. For the standard action, the weights at [1:0:0] are (1, 0) on the fiber, giving contribution q H2. The other fixed points contribute zero because the action is not semi‑free there. Thus S(φ) = q H2. In the quantum ring H3 = q, so q H2 = H3 H2 = H5 = q H2 (consistent). The inverse is H because (q H2) ⋆ H = q H3 = q2 = 1 in the Novikov ring after rescaling. Hence S(φ) = q H2 is a unit, generating the quantum relation.
Exam Strategy: Seidel vs. FJRW
When a question asks for a unit in quantum cohomology arising from a Hamiltonian loop, the answer is the Seidel element. When the context is a Landau–Ginzburg model (W, G) and the state space is a Milnor ring, the theory is FJRW. The LG/CY correspondence matches the analytic continuation of the FJRW potential to the GW potential of the Calabi–Yau hypersurface. Do not confuse the Seidel representation (symplectic topology, A‑model) with the FJRW product (singularity theory, B‑model). The Seidel element lives in QH*(X); the FJRW product lives in ℋW,G. Both satisfy WDVV and define Frobenius manifolds, but their geometric origins differ.

Quantum Cohomology and the Quantum Kirwan Map for Symplectic Quotients

The quantum Kirwan map, introduced by Martin (2000) and developed by Woodward (2005) and others, relates the equivariant quantum cohomology of a Hamiltonian G‑manifold X to the quantum cohomology of its symplectic quotient X//G at a regular value of the moment map. Let G be a compact Lie group acting Hamiltonianly on a symplectic manifold X with moment map μ : X → 𝔤*. For a regular value ξ ∈ 𝔤*, the symplectic quotient is X//ξG = μ−1(ξ)/G. The classical Kirwan map κ : HG*(X) → H*(X//ξG) is surjective with kernel generated by the ideal of the moment map. The quantum Kirwan map κq : QHG*(X) → QH*(X//ξG) is a ring homomorphism for the quantum products, defined by counting G‑equivariant stable maps to X that descend to stable maps to the quotient. The domain curve carries a principal G‑bundle, and the map is a section of the associated bundle XP → C. The virtual localization formula of Graber–Pandharipande reduces the computation to fixed loci of a maximal torus T ⊂ G. The quantum Kirwan map is not surjective in general; its image is the subring generated by the quantum characteristic classes of the universal bundle over the quotient. For X = ℂN with the standard U(r) action, the quotient is the Grassmannian Gr(r, N). The quantum Kirwan map identifies the equivariant quantum cohomology of ℂN (a polynomial ring in Chern roots) with the quantum cohomology of the Grassmannian presented by the quantum Giambelli formula. The kernel is generated by the quantum elementary symmetric polynomials ek(λ1, …, λr) for k > N − r, which become the quantum relations σk = 0 for k > N − r in QH*(Gr(r, N)). For non‑abelian quotients, the quantum Kirwan map involves the quantum Martin relations, which are the quantum analogues of the relations in the classical cohomology of the quotient coming from the non‑abelian localization formula of Jeffrey–Kirwan. The map is compatible with the wall‑crossing of the symplectic quotient as ξ varies: the quantum cohomology rings of different quotients are related by the quantum wall‑crossing formula of Woodward (2010), which expresses the difference of the quantum Kirwan maps as a sum over wall‑crossing terms indexed by unstable strata. This provides a quantum version of the Kirwan–Ness stratification and the Morse theory of the moment map norm square.

Quantum Cohomology of Homogeneous Spaces G/P and the Quantum Schubert Calculus

The quantum cohomology of generalized flag varieties G/P, where G is a complex semisimple Lie group and P a parabolic subgroup, extends the quantum Schubert calculus of Grassmannians to all homogeneous spaces. The classical cohomology H*(G/P) has a basis of Schubert classes σw indexed by minimal coset representatives w ∈ WP of the Weyl group W modulo the parabolic subgroup WP. The quantum product is σu ⋆ σv = Σw, d Nu, vw, d qd σw, where d ∈ H2(G/P, ℤ) ≅ ℤr (r = rank of G/P) and Nu, vw, d are three‑point genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants. The quantum Chevalley formula of Fulton–Woodward (2004) and Mihalcea (2006) gives the product of a divisor class σsi (simple reflection) with any Schubert class: σsi ⋆ σw = Σ cw, vi σv + Σ qα σw, where the first sum is over classical Chevalley terms and the second sum is over quantum corrections indexed by simple roots α such that w−1(α) < 0. The quantum Giambelli formula expresses any Schubert class as a polynomial in the divisor classes using the quantum product, generalizing the classical determinantal formula. For cominuscule G/P (Grassmannians, quadrics, Lagrangian Grassmannians, spinor varieties, Cayley plane), the quantum Schubert calculus is governed by the quantum = classical principle of Buch–Kresch–Tamvakis (2003): a quantum Littlewood–Richardson coefficient Nu, vw, d is non‑zero only if the corresponding classical coefficient is non‑zero for a related triple in a smaller cominuscule variety. This reduces quantum computations to classical ones. The presentation of QH*(G/P) as a quotient of the polynomial ring in the divisor classes by the quantum ideal is given by the quantum Schubert polynomials of Fomin–Gelfand–Postnikov (1997) for Grassmannians and by the quantum Monk formula for general G/P. The quantum cohomology ring is semisimple at generic values of the quantum parameters, and its idempotents are given by the eigenvectors of quantum multiplication by the first Chern class c1(T(G/P)). The eigenvalues are the critical values of the Landau–Ginzburg superpotential on the mirror torus, which for G/P is the Givental superpotential W = Σi=1r eyi + q1 e−Σ aij yj + ⋯, where aij are the Cartan matrix entries. The quantum differential equation is the G/P quantum Toda lattice, and its solutions are given by the J‑function of G/P, which satisfies the quantum differential equations of the Dubrovin connection.

Quantum Cohomology and Symplectic Field Theory

Symplectic Field Theory (SFT), introduced by Eliashberg–Givental–Hofer (2000), is a topological field theory that generalizes Gromov–Witten theory to symplectic manifolds with contact boundary and to cobordisms between contact manifolds. The SFT Hamiltonian is a formal power series in variables corresponding to Reeb orbits of the contact boundary, with coefficients given by counts of punctured holomorphic curves in the symplectization. The genus‑zero part of SFT for a symplectic manifold X with contact boundary Y = ∂X defines a deformation of the quantum cohomology of X called the symplectic contact homology algebra. When X is closed, SFT reduces to the Gromov–Witten potential of X. The SFT gluing formula expresses the Hamiltonian of a symplectic cobordism as a composition of the Hamiltonians of its ends, providing a functorial structure. The linearized contact homology of Y is the homology of the chain complex generated by good Reeb orbits with differential counting rigid holomorphic cylinders in the symplectization ℝ × Y. The full contact homology includes multiple covers and is defined via the SFT Hamiltonian. The relation to quantum cohomology appears in the Bourgeois–Oancea (2009) isomorphism between the symplectic homology of a Liouville domain X and the linearized contact homology of its boundary Y, which identifies the quantum cohomology of the completion of X with a subalgebra of the contact homology of Y. For a Fano variety X with an anticanonical divisor D, the complement X D is a Liouville domain whose symplectic homology is isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of X (Ritter, 2013). The SFT framework also produces the Legendrian contact homology of Legendrian submanifolds in Y, which is related to the open Gromov–Witten invariants of Lagrangian fillings in X. The SFT Hamiltonian satisfies the master equation {H, H} = 0 with respect to the Poisson bracket on the space of functions on the symplectization, which is the SFT analogue of the WDVV equations. The quantization of SFT, developed by Cieliebak–Latschev (2009), produces a chain complex whose homology is the symplectic homology, and the quantum product on symplectic homology is induced by the pair‑of‑pants product in SFT. The SFT compactness theorem (Bourgeois–Eliashberg–Hofer–Wysocki–Zehmisch, 2003) describes the boundary of the moduli space of punctured holomorphic curves as broken curves with levels in the symplectization and the cobordism, providing the analytical foundation for the algebraic relations in the SFT Hamiltonian.

  • Confusing the Seidel representation (a homomorphism from π₁(Ham(X)) to units in QH*(X)) with the quantum Kirwan map (a ring homomorphism from equivariant QH*(X) to QH*(X//G)); they operate on different domains and serve different purposes.
  • Assuming the FJRW state space ℋW,G is always the Milnor ring of W; it is the G‑invariant part of the direct sum of Milnor rings of W restricted to fixed loci of G, which can be larger than the Milnor ring of W itself.
  • Treating the quantum Chevalley formula for G/P as identical to the classical Chevalley formula; the quantum formula includes extra terms proportional to the quantum parameters qα indexed by simple roots α with w⁻¹(α) < 0.
  • Believing the quantum Kirwan map is always surjective; its image is the subring generated by quantum characteristic classes, and the cokernel measures the failure of the quantum Martin relations to generate all relations in QH*(X//G).
  • Confusing the SFT Hamiltonian (a formal power series in Reeb orbit variables satisfying {H,H}=0) with the Gromov–Witten potential (a function on H*(X) satisfying WDVV); SFT reduces to GW theory only when the contact boundary is empty.
  • Assuming the quantum = classical principle of Buch–Kresch–Tamvakis holds for all homogeneous spaces G/P; it is proved only for cominuscule G/P (Grassmannians, quadrics, Lagrangian Grassmannians, spinor varieties, Cayley plane).
  • Neglecting the role of the Novikov ring in the Seidel element computation; the Seidel element S(φ) = ΣA GW0,1E(A) qA lives in the Novikov completion, and its invertibility is a statement in that completed ring, not in the polynomial ring ℂ[H].

Equivariant Quantum Cohomology and the Atiyah–Bott Localization Formula

Equivariant quantum cohomology extends the ordinary quantum product to a setting where a torus T acts on a symplectic manifold X with isolated fixed points and one‑dimensional orbits. The equivariant quantum product *T deforms the equivariant cup product in HT*(X) by genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants with insertions of equivariant cohomology classes. Concretely, for α, β ∈ HT*(X) one defines

α *T β = ΣA ∈ H2(X) qA ev3*(ev1*α ∪ ev2*β ∪ [M0,3(X,A)]vir)

where the pushforward is taken in equivariant cohomology and the virtual fundamental class is the T‑equivariant one. The Atiyah–Bott localization formula expresses any equivariant integral over the moduli space M0,n(X,A) as a sum over T‑fixed loci. These fixed loci are indexed by decorated graphs whose vertices correspond to fixed points of X and edges to T‑invariant rational curves connecting them. The contribution of each graph is a product of vertex, edge, and flag factors involving the equivariant weights of the tangent spaces at the fixed points and the normal bundles to the invariant curves.

This combinatorial description yields completely explicit formulas for the equivariant quantum product on toric varieties, Grassmannians, flag varieties, and more general homogeneous spaces G/P. For example, the equivariant quantum cohomology of Pn is generated by the hyperplane class H and the equivariant parameters λ0,…,λn with the relation (H−λ0) *T … *T (H−λn) = q. The localization formula also underlies the proof of the quantum Chevalley formula for G/P, where the product of a Schubert class with a divisor class is expressed as a sum over Schubert classes indexed by quantum Bruhat graph edges.

The equivariant J‑function JT(τ,z) satisfies a system of equivariant quantum differential equations (the equivariant Dubrovin connection). Its non‑equivariant limit recovers the ordinary J‑function. The ring structure can be presented via a quantum Giambelli formula expressing arbitrary Schubert classes as polynomials in the divisor classes with coefficients in the equivariant parameter ring ℂ[λ1,…,λr]. For toric varieties, Givental’s mirror theorem identifies the equivariant J‑function with a hypergeometric series on the mirror torus, providing a powerful computational tool. The virtual localization formula of Graber–Pandharipande extends the Atiyah–Bott method to the virtual fundamental class, making it the standard technique for concrete Gromov–Witten computations in enumerative geometry.

Twisted Quantum Cohomology and the Quantum Lefschetz Theorem for Non‑Convex Vector Bundles

Twisted quantum cohomology arises when the Gromov–Witten theory of a smooth projective variety X is coupled to a vector bundle E → X via an invertible multiplicative characteristic class c(·) (the twist). The twisted genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants are defined by inserting the inverse of the Euler class of the obstruction bundle R1π*f*E into the virtual fundamental class of M0,n(X,A). The twisted quantum product *tw deforms the ordinary cup product by these twisted invariants. When E is convex — i.e. H1(C, f*E) = 0 for every stable map f : C → X — the quantum Lefschetz theorem asserts that the twisted quantum cohomology of X is isomorphic to the ordinary quantum cohomology of a smooth complete intersection Y ⊂ X cut out by a regular section of E. The isomorphism identifies the twisted J‑function of X with the J‑function of Y after a change of variables known as the mirror map.

For non‑convex bundles the theorem fails: the obstruction bundle does not vanish, and correction terms appear. These corrections are captured by the theory of quasimap invariants (Ciocan‑Fontanine–Kim) or by the I‑function of the total space Tot(E). The twisted J‑function satisfies a twisted quantum differential equation whose coefficients involve the Chern classes of E and the twist c(·). Coates–Givental’s mirror theorem for twisted theories expresses the twisted J‑function as a hypergeometric series on the mirror of Tot(E). Applications include the quantum cohomology of complete intersections in toric varieties (where E is a sum of line bundles), the quantum cohomology of Grassmannians via the quantum Lefschetz for the tautological bundle, and the computation of Gromov–Witten invariants of Calabi–Yau complete intersections. In the non‑convex case the correction terms are governed by the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants of Tot(E), leading to a quantum Lefschetz hyperplane theorem with explicit error terms. The theory also connects to quantum K‑theory of Tot(E), where the twist is replaced by the K‑theoretic Euler class.

Worked Example: Twisted J‑function for a Convex Bundle
Let X = P3 and E = O(2) ⊕ O(2). Compute the twisted J‑function Jtw(τ,z) for the twist c(E) = e(E) (the Euler class) and verify that it matches the J‑function of the quartic K3 surface Y ⊂ P3 after the mirror map.
The twisted J‑function is defined by Jtw(τ,z) = eτH/z (1 + Σd>0 qd ev*( [M0,1(P3,d)]vir / (z(z−ψ)) ∪ e−1(R1π*f*E) ) ). Because E is convex, R1π*f*E = 0 and the twist reduces to the ordinary Euler class of E on X. The hypergeometric expression from the mirror theorem gives Jtw = eτH/z Σd≥0 qd ∏k=1d (H+ kz)4 / ∏k=12d (2H+ kz)2. The mirror map is τ = log q + 2 Σd>0 (−1)d (2d−1)!/(d!2) qd. Substituting this into Jtw and expanding in z−1 yields the J‑function of the quartic K3, confirming the quantum Lefschetz isomorphism.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the twisted J‑function of a convex bundle, write the hypergeometric series directly from the mirror theorem; do not attempt to compute virtual localization graphs unless explicitly required. Remember that the quantum Lefschetz isomorphism holds only for convex bundles — if the problem states H1(C, f*E) ≠ 0, you must mention the correction terms from the total space Tot(E) or the quasimap I‑function.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to a Curve and the Double Ramification Cycle

The moduli space Mg,n(C, β) of stable maps from genus‑g curves with n marked points to a smooth projective curve C carries a virtual fundamental class of dimension g + n − 3 + deg β. Although the target has dimension one, the Gromov–Witten invariants of C encode rich combinatorial data: they are equivalent to Hurwitz numbers counting branched covers of C. The double ramification cycle DRg(d1,…,dn) is a cohomology class on Mg,n defined as the pushforward of the virtual class of the moduli space of stable maps to P1 with prescribed ramification profiles (d1,…,dn) satisfying Σ di = 0. This cycle provides a geometric realization of the Hamiltonians of the integrable hierarchies governing the Gromov–Witten theory of curves.

For C = P1, the generating series of genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants is the tau‑function of the KdV hierarchy (Witten’s conjecture, proved by Kontsevich). The double ramification cycle satisfies Pixton’s relations, which give a complete set of tautological relations in the cohomology of Mg,n. The DR/DZ equivalence (Buryak–Rossi) identifies the double ramification hierarchy with the Dubrovin–Zhang hierarchy of the target curve. The J‑function for a curve target is essentially the generating function of Hurwitz numbers; its quantum differential equation reduces to the KdV (for P1) or Toda (for elliptic curves) hierarchy. The quantum Riemann–Roch theorem expresses the total descendant potential of C in terms of the Givental quantization of the R‑matrix derived from the Hodge bundle. The double ramification cycle also appears in the formula for the virtual class of the moduli space of stable maps to a curve with relative conditions, linking it to the degeneration formula and logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to a Surface and the Yau–Zaslow Formula

For a target surface S, the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants are classical intersection numbers because the virtual dimension of M0,n(S, β) equals n − 1 + ∫β c1(TS), matching the expected dimension of the space of maps. Consequently the quantum product on H*(S) receives no quantum corrections from genus‑zero invariants unless ∫β c1 > 0. For del Pezzo surfaces (e.g. blow‑ups of P2 at up to eight points) there are non‑trivial quantum corrections, and the quantum cohomology ring can be computed via the quantum Lefschetz theorem or by localization on the toric model.

The Yau–Zaslow formula gives a spectacular closed form for the generating function of genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants of a K3 surface. For a primitive curve class β with β2 = 2g−2, the formula states Σg≥0 N0,β qg = 1/Δ(q), where Δ(q) = q ∏n≥1 (1−qn)24 is the discriminant modular form. For non‑primitive classes the generating series involves Hecke operators acting on 1/Δ. Higher genus Gromov–Witten invariants of surfaces are conjecturally governed by the Gopakumar–Vafa invariants and the holomorphic anomaly equation of Bershadsky–Cecotti–Ooguri–Vafa. The quantum cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points S[n] is related to that of S via the Nakajima construction: the Maulik–Okounkov quantum product on H*(S[n]) is expressed in terms of the quantum product on S and the geometry of the Hilbert–Chow morphism. This connection underlies the computation of quantum cohomology for moduli spaces of stable sheaves on surfaces.

Quantum Cohomology of Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps with Level Structure and the Modular Properties of the J‑Function

A level structure on a stable map f : C → X is additional discrete data such as a choice of basis for the homology of the source curve, a framing of the map, or a marking of points with values in a finite group. The moduli space Mg,n(X, β; Γ) with level structure Γ carries a natural action of the mapping class group, and its quantum cohomology inherits a modular structure. The J‑function JΓ(τ, z) for a target with level structure satisfies a system of modular differential equations reflecting the action of the modular group on the space of conformal blocks. For instance, the J‑function of P1 with full level structure at three points is identified with the hypergeometric solutions of the Picard–Fuchs equation of the mirror family, and its monodromy yields the modular group representation.

The modular properties of the J‑function are central to the Gamma conjecture, which predicts that the asymptotic expansion of JΓ at the large radius limit is governed by the Gamma class Γ̂X of the target. The level structure also appears in the quantum cohomology of moduli spaces of curves with marked points, where the J‑function is a section of the Hodge bundle over Mg,n. The modular differential equations are derived from the action of the Virasoro operators on the total descendant potential, and they coincide with the equations of the topological recursion of Eynard–Orantin when the spectral curve is the mirror curve. The choice of level structure corresponds to the choice of a symplectic basis of cycles on the spectral curve, and the resulting J‑function provides the generating series of intersection numbers on Mg,n twisted by the level data.

  • Assuming the quantum Lefschetz theorem holds for any vector bundle; it requires convexity, and for non‑convex bundles one must use the twisted I‑function of the total space or quasimap invariants.
  • Treating the double ramification cycle as a class on the moduli space of stable maps rather than on Mg,n; it is defined by pushing forward the virtual class of maps to P1 with prescribed ramification.
  • Believing the Yau–Zaslow formula applies to all surfaces; it is specific to K3 surfaces (or more generally to hyperkähler manifolds) and primitive curve classes.
  • Neglecting the role of the level structure in the modular differential equations for the J‑function; the level structure determines the monodromy representation and the precise form of the Gamma class asymptotics.
