Subsequent work by Maher and Tiozzo (2018) extended the convergence statement to random walks on the mapping class group with respect to the Teichmüller metric, showing that the hitting measure is supported on the set of uniquely ergodic foliations. In examinations, candidates may be asked to explain why the finite first moment condition is essential (it ensures integrability of the distance cocycle) or to sketch how the Masur criterion uses the curve complex projection estimates of Masur–Minsky to control the growth of subsurface projections along the walk.

The Earthquake Flow on Teichmüller Space and Mirzakhani's Work on Simple Closed Geodesics

Thurston's earthquake theorem (1986) asserts that for any two points X, Y in Teichmüller space T(S) there exists a unique left earthquake map Eλ along a measured lamination λ sending X to Y. The map (X, λ) ↦ Eλ(X) defines a flow on the bundle of measured laminations over T(S), called the earthquake flow. Mirzakhani (2008) exploited this flow to obtain precise asymptotics for the number of simple closed geodesics of length at most L on a hyperbolic surface X. She showed that the counting function sX(L) satisfies sX(L) ∼ ng · B(X) · L6g‑6 as L → ∞, where ng is a rational constant depending only on genus and B(X) is the Thurston measure of the unit ball of measured laminations with respect to the length function on X. The proof proceeds by interpreting the earthquake flow as a measure‑preserving transformation on the space of measured laminations equipped with the Thurston measure, and then applying the ergodic theorem to the characteristic function of the set of laminations whose length on X is ≤ L. Mirzakhani also computed the Weil–Petersson volumes of moduli space by integrating the function B(X) over Mg, obtaining the celebrated recursion for Vg,n. In exam problems, one may be required to derive the leading exponent 6g‑6 from the dimension of the space of measured laminations, or to explain why the earthquake flow preserves the Thurston measure (it acts by piecewise linear transformations on train‑track coordinates with determinant one). A common twist is to ask for the relationship between the earthquake flow and the Teichmüller geodesic flow: the former is a shear along a fixed lamination, while the latter stretches the horizontal foliation of a quadratic differential; they coincide only when the lamination is the stable foliation of a Teichmüller geodesic.

Worked Example: Counting Simple Closed Geodesics
Let X be a hyperbolic surface of genus g = 2. Using Mirzakhani's asymptotic formula, estimate the number of simple closed geodesics of length ≤ 100 on X given that the Thurston measure of the unit ball B(X) equals 0.042 and the universal constant n2 = 1/384.
The asymptotic formula reads sX(L) ∼ ng · B(X) · L6g‑6. For g = 2, 6g‑6 = 6. Substitute the data: n2 = 1/384 ≈ 0.002604, B(X) = 0.042, L = 100. Compute L6 = 1012. Then sX(100) ≈ 0.002604 × 0.042 × 1012 = 1.09368 × 108. Hence approximately 1.1 × 108 simple closed geodesics of length ≤ 100. The leading term dominates for large L; lower‑order corrections are of order L4 and are negligible at this scale.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the exponent in Mirzakhani's counting theorem, recall that the space of measured laminations has dimension 6g‑6; the exponent is exactly this dimension. For volume recursion problems, write down the integral of B(X) over moduli space and use the symplectic reduction of the Weil–Petersson form to obtain the polynomial recursion. Memorise the first few values of ng (e.g., n1 = 1/24, n2 = 1/384) as they appear in numerical estimates.

The Weil–Petersson Metric: Brock's Upper Bound on Diameter and the Geometry of the Thick Part

The Weil–Petersson (WP) metric on the moduli space Mg is an incomplete Kähler metric with negative sectional curvature. Brock (2003) proved that the WP diameter of the thick part Mg(ε) (surfaces with injectivity radius ≥ ε) grows at most like C · g3/2 for a universal constant C. The proof uses the pants decomposition and the product structure of the WP metric in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates: on each pair of pants the WP metric is comparable to the Euclidean metric on length‑twist coordinates, and the gluing of pants contributes a controlled error. By estimating the WP length of a path that simultaneously shortens all curves of a pants decomposition to the Margulis constant, Brock obtains a uniform upper bound for the distance from any thick surface to the boundary of the thick part. Combining this with the fact that the thin part has uniformly bounded WP diameter (due to the cusp geometry), he deduces the global diameter bound diamWP(Mg) ≤ C' · g3/2. Later work by Arana‑Herrera (2019) sharpened the exponent to g log g for the full moduli space. In examinations, a typical question asks to derive the g3/2 scaling from the fact that a pants decomposition contains 3g‑3 curves, each contributing a length parameter of order 1/√g in the thick part, and the WP metric on length parameters is approximately dℓ/√ℓ. Another common task is to explain why the WP metric is incomplete: a sequence of surfaces where a simple closed curve is pinched to zero length has finite WP length, so the metric completion adds the boundary strata of the Deligne–Mumford compactification.

The Dynamics of the Teichmüller Geodesic Flow: Avila–Viana Simplicity of Lyapunov Spectrum

The Teichmüller geodesic flow acts on the moduli space of unit‑area quadratic differentials Q1Mg. The Kontsevich–Zorich (KZ) cocycle is the linear cocycle over this flow obtained by the action on the first cohomology of the underlying Riemann surface. Avila and Viana (2007) proved that for any SL(2,ℝ)‑invariant ergodic probability measure on a stratum of quadratic differentials, the Lyapunov spectrum of the KZ cocycle is simple (all exponents have multiplicity one) provided the measure is not supported on a locus of completely periodic surfaces. The proof combines three pillars: (i) the pinching and twisting criterion of Avila–Viana for simplicity of Lyapunov exponents of symplectic cocycles; (ii) the fact that the KZ cocycle is symplectic with respect to the intersection form; (iii) a deep analysis of the monodromy of the Gauss–Manin connection on the Hodge bundle, showing that the Zariski closure of the monodromy group is the full symplectic group. As a corollary, the sum of the non‑negative Lyapunov exponents equals the integral of the curvature of the Hodge bundle, which by the Eskin–Kontsevich–Zorich formula can be expressed in terms of Siegel–Veech constants. In exam settings, candidates may be asked to state the pinching and twisting conditions, to explain why the KZ cocycle is symplectic, or to compute the sum of Lyapunov exponents for the Masur–Veech measure on a given stratum using the known Siegel–Veech constants. A frequent trap is to confuse the Lyapunov spectrum of the KZ cocycle (dimension 2g) with that of the derivative cocycle on the tangent bundle of the stratum (dimension 4g‑4).

The Bonahon–Thurston Shear Coordinates and the Space of Geodesic Currents

Geodesic currents on a hyperbolic surface S are π1(S)‑invariant Radon measures on the space of unoriented geodesics of the universal cover. The space of geodesic currents Curr(S) contains measured laminations as a closed subset and carries a natural intersection form i(·,·) extending the geometric intersection number. Bonahon (1996) introduced shear coordinates on the Teichmüller space of a surface with boundary by assigning to each ideal triangle a triple of real numbers representing the shears along its edges. These coordinates give a global homeomorphism between the decorated Teichmüller space and ℝ6g‑6+3b, where b is the number of boundary components. Thurston later showed that the length of a geodesic current can be expressed as a linear functional of the shear coordinates, and that the Weil–Petersson symplectic form corresponds to the canonical symplectic structure on the space of shear coordinates. The space of geodesic currents is compactified by projectivising, yielding the sphere PCurr(S) which contains the Thurston boundary PMF(S) as a proper subset. In examinations, a typical problem asks to compute the intersection number of two currents given their shear coordinates on a fixed ideal triangulation, or to prove that the length function ℓX(μ) is continuous on Curr(S) for a fixed hyperbolic metric X. Another common question is to describe how the earthquake flow acts on shear coordinates: it adds a constant to the shear parameter of each edge crossed by the earthquake lamination, leaving other shears unchanged.

  • Confusing the Poisson boundary of the mapping class group with the Thurston boundary as a set; the former is a measure‑space isomorphism, not a homeomorphism.
  • Assuming the earthquake flow preserves the Weil–Petersson metric; it preserves the Thurston measure on measured laminations but not the WP metric.
  • Misapplying Brock's diameter bound to the full moduli space without accounting for the thin part; the bound holds for the thick part, the thin part requires separate cusp estimates.
  • Thinking that simplicity of the KZ Lyapunov spectrum holds for all invariant measures; it fails for measures supported on completely periodic loci (e.g., Veech surfaces with extra symmetries).
  • Treating geodesic currents as measured laminations; currents allow transverse measures that are not locally finite, and the intersection form is only continuous, not necessarily given by counting intersections.
  • Neglecting the role of the Margulis constant in the proof of WP incompleteness; the constant determines the threshold where the collar lemma switches to the cusp estimate.
  • Overlooking that the Bonahon–Thurston shear coordinates require a choice of ideal triangulation; different triangulations are related by Whitehead moves that act by piecewise linear transformations.
The advanced sections above provide the depth and specificity required for high‑level competitive examinations.

The Eskin–Masur–Zorich Classification of Invariant Measures for the Teichmüller Flow

The Teichmüller geodesic flow acts on the moduli space of unit‑area quadratic differentials. A central problem is to classify all ergodic invariant probability measures for this flow. Eskin, Masur and Zorich (2003) proved that every such measure is supported on an affine invariant submanifold — a closed subset locally defined by linear equations in period coordinates with real coefficients. The theorem has three pillars: (i) the measure‑rigidity result that any ergodic invariant measure is algebraic, i.e. its support is a finite union of affine invariant submanifolds; (ii) the classification of affine invariant submanifolds by their rank and the structure of their tangent spaces, which are given by the kernel of a linear map defined by the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle; (iii) the proof that the only affine invariant submanifolds of rank one are the closures of SL(2,ℝ)‑orbits of Veech surfaces, while higher‑rank submanifolds arise from covers of lower‑genus surfaces or from the whole stratum. The proof uses the machinery of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle, the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi orbit closure theorem, and a delicate analysis of the Lyapunov spectrum. In examinations, candidates may be asked to state the definition of an affine invariant submanifold, to explain why the support of an ergodic invariant measure must be affine invariant, or to describe the role of the rank in the classification. A frequent trap is to confuse the Eskin–Masur–Zorich measure classification with the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi orbit closure theorem; the former concerns invariant measures, the latter concerns orbit closures, and the two are logically independent though they share the same affine invariant submanifold framework.

The Avila–Gouëzel–Yoccoz Theorem on Exponential Mixing of the Teichmüller Flow

Mixing properties of the Teichmüller flow are essential for statistical applications such as the equidistribution of closed geodesics. Avila, Gouëzel and Yoccoz (2006) established that the Teichmüller flow is exponentially mixing with respect to the Masur–Veech measure on each connected component of every stratum of quadratic differentials. The proof proceeds by coding the flow via a countable Markov shift (the Rauzy–Veech induction) and then applying a spectral gap argument for the associated transfer operator on a suitable Banach space of functions with bounded variation. The key technical steps are: (i) the construction of a Young tower with exponential tails for the Rauzy–Veech map; (ii) the verification that the roof function satisfies a non‑integrability condition that prevents periodic obstructions; (iii) the application of the Dolgopyat‑type estimate to obtain a spectral gap for the transfer operator twisted by a purely imaginary parameter. Exponential mixing implies, in particular, that correlations of Hölder observables decay exponentially fast, and it yields a central limit theorem for Birkhoff sums. In exam settings, a typical question asks to outline the Rauzy–Veech induction, to explain why the roof function is not cohomologous to a constant, or to state the consequence of exponential mixing for the error term in the quadratic asymptotics of closed geodesics. A common error is to assume that exponential mixing holds for all SL(2,ℝ)‑invariant measures; it is known only for the Masur–Veech measure and for certain affine invariant submanifolds satisfying a “pinching and twisting” condition.

Worked Example: Exponential Mixing Implies Quadratic Asymptotics
Let φ_t be the Teichmüller flow on a stratum component H(κ) equipped with the Masur–Veech measure μ. Suppose f,g are Hölder continuous observables with ∫ f dμ = ∫ g dμ = 0. Show that the correlation function C(t) = ∫ f·(g∘φ_t) dμ satisfies |C(t)| ≤ C e-α t for some C,α > 0, and deduce that the number N(T) of closed geodesics of length ≤ T satisfies N(T) = (1/π) T2 + O(T2-δ) for some δ > 0.
By the Avila–Gouëzel–Yoccoz theorem, the flow is exponentially mixing: there exist constants C,α > 0 such that for all Hölder f,g with zero mean, |∫ f·(g∘φ_t) dμ| ≤ C‖f‖Hölder‖g‖Hölder e-α t. The correlation decay is exactly this bound. For the counting of closed geodesics, one uses the standard relation between the flow and the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of the moduli space, together with the fact that the Masur–Veech measure is the Liouville measure. Exponential mixing yields a spectral gap for the Ruelle transfer operator, which by the work of Margulis and Pollicott–Sharp gives the error term O(T2-δ) in the prime orbit theorem. The exponent δ can be taken as any number smaller than α/2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a proof sketch of exponential mixing, focus on the three‑step structure: (1) Rauzy–Veech induction gives a countable Markov map; (2) build a Young tower with exponential tails; (3) apply Dolgopyat’s method to the twisted transfer operator. Memorise the non‑integrability condition on the roof function — it is the only place where the specific geometry of the stratum enters. For counting closed geodesics, recall that exponential mixing ⇒ spectral gap ⇒ prime orbit theorem with power‑saving error. Do not confuse the Masur–Veech measure with an arbitrary affine invariant measure; the theorem is proved only for the former.

The Mirzakhani–Wright Theorem on the Classification of Invariant Submanifolds for the Billiard Flow

Rational polygonal billiards are equivalent to the Teichmüller flow on the moduli space of translation surfaces via the unfolding construction. Mirzakhani and Wright (2015) classified all SL(2,ℝ)‑invariant submanifolds that arise from billiards in rational polygons. They proved that every such invariant submanifold is either the whole stratum component containing the unfolding surface, or a proper affine invariant submanifold that is a finite cover of a lower‑genus stratum, or a “Veech‑type” submanifold associated to a lattice surface. The proof combines the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi orbit closure theorem with a detailed analysis of the cylinder decompositions of the unfolding surfaces. A crucial ingredient is the “cylinder deformation theorem”, which shows that any invariant submanifold containing a cylinder decomposition must contain the full SL(2,ℝ)‑orbit of that decomposition. This forces the submanifold to be affine invariant. The classification then reduces to the known classification of affine invariant submanifolds in genus two and three, together with a covering argument for higher genus. In examinations, candidates may be asked to explain the unfolding construction, to state the cylinder deformation theorem, or to describe why the classification for billiards is a corollary of the general affine invariant submanifold classification. A typical trap is to assume that every rational polygon yields a Veech surface; in fact, Veech surfaces are rare and correspond to lattice surfaces, while generic rational polygons produce dense orbits in the whole stratum.

The Work of Rafi on the Thick–Thin Decomposition and the Geometry of Teichmüller Space

Rafi (2007, 2014) developed a comprehensive thick–thin decomposition for Teichmüller space equipped with the Teichmüller metric. For a point X in Teichmüller space, the thick part consists of points where the injectivity radius is bounded below by a fixed Margulis constant ε; the thin part is a union of standard horoball‑like regions associated to short curves. Rafi proved that the Teichmüller metric on the thick part is quasi‑isometric to a product of hyperbolic planes, while on each thin region it is quasi‑isometric to a product of a Euclidean factor (the twist parameter) and a hyperbolic factor (the length parameter). This decomposition yields precise estimates for Teichmüller distance: for any two points X,Y, the distance d_T(X,Y) is coarsely equal to the supremum over all curves α of the logarithm of the ratio of extremal lengths, plus a sum over short curves of the logarithm of the ratio of their lengths. Rafi also showed that the thick–thin decomposition is compatible with the mapping class group action and that the quotient of the thick part by the mapping class group has finite diameter. In exam contexts, a common problem is to compute the Teichmüller distance between two points given their extremal length data, or to prove that the projection of a Teichmüller geodesic to the curve complex is a quasi‑geodesic. A frequent mistake is to treat the thin part as a product of independent Euclidean and hyperbolic factors without accounting for the interaction term that appears when two short curves intersect.

The Work of Hamenstädt on the Geometry of the Mapping Class Group and the Weil–Petersson Metric

Hamenstädt (2006, 2010) established deep connections between the large‑scale geometry of the mapping class group Mod(S) and the Weil–Petersson metric on moduli space. She proved that the mapping class group, equipped with the word metric from a finite generating set, is quasi‑isometric to the Weil–Petersson metric completion of Teichmüller space (the augmented Teichmüller space). The proof uses the hierarchy machinery of Masur–Minsky to construct a coarse Lipschitz map from Mod(S) to the curve complex, and then relates the curve complex distance to the Weil–Petersson distance via the Brock–Masur–Minsky inequality. A key result is that the Weil–Petersson metric has negative sectional curvature bounded away from zero on the thick part, and that the mapping class group acts by isometries on the Weil–Petersson completion. Hamenstädt also showed that the Weil–Petersson geodesic flow is Anosov on the unit tangent bundle of the thick part, and that the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the visual boundary coincides with the Thurston measure on the space of projective measured foliations. In examinations, candidates may be asked to state the Brock–Masur–Minsky inequality, to explain why the mapping class group is quasi‑isometric to the Weil–Petersson completion, or to describe the role of the hierarchy in constructing the quasi‑isometry. A common trap is to confuse the Weil–Petersson completion (which adds strata corresponding to pinched curves) with the Thurston compactification (which adds projective measured foliations); the two boundaries are homeomorphic but carry different topological and metric structures.

  • Confusing the Eskin–Masur–Zorich measure classification with the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi orbit closure theorem; they address different objects (measures vs. orbit closures).
  • Assuming exponential mixing holds for all SL(2,ℝ)‑invariant measures; it is proved only for the Masur–Veech measure and certain affine invariant submanifolds.
  • Believing every rational polygon yields a Veech surface; Veech surfaces are exactly the lattice surfaces, a measure‑zero subset.
  • Treating the thin part of Teichmüller space as a direct product of independent Euclidean and hyperbolic factors, ignoring the interaction term for intersecting short curves.
  • Equating the Weil–Petersson completion with the Thurston compactification; they are homeomorphic but have distinct geometric and dynamical properties.
  • Overlooking the non‑integrability condition on the roof function in the Avila–Gouëzel–Yoccoz proof; without it the Dolgopyat estimate fails.
  • Misapplying the cylinder deformation theorem to non‑cylindrical directions; the theorem requires a full cylinder decomposition.

These sections provide the depth required for advanced competitive examinations.

The Brock Pants Graph and the Weil–Petersson Metric

Jeffrey Brock introduced the pants graph P(S) in 2003 as a combinatorial model for the large‑scale geometry of Teichmüller space equipped with the Weil–Petersson metric. Vertices of P(S) correspond to pants decompositions of the surface S, and two vertices are joined by an edge when the associated decompositions differ by an elementary move (a single curve replacement). Brock proved that the mapping class group Mod(S) acts on P(S) by graph automorphisms and that the quotient P(S)/Mod(S) is finite. The central theorem states that the Weil–Petersson metric on Teichmüller space T(S) is quasi‑isometric to the pants graph endowed with the path metric. More precisely, there exist constants A ≥ 1, B ≥ 0 such that for any X, Y ∈ T(S),

A⁻¹ dWP(X, Y) − B ≤ dP(π(X), π(Y)) ≤ A dWP(X, Y) + B,

where π : T(S) → P(S) sends a hyperbolic structure to a shortest pants decomposition. This quasi‑isometry yields immediate consequences: the Weil–Petersson metric has finite diameter on the thick part of moduli space, the mapping class group is quasi‑isometric to the Weil–Petersson completion, and the Weil–Petersson geodesic flow can be studied via combinatorial geodesics in the pants graph. Brock also derived an explicit upper bound for the diameter of the ε‑thick part of moduli space in terms of the complexity ξ(S) = 3g − 3 + n, showing that the diameter grows at most linearly in ξ(S). The pants graph perspective has become a standard tool for proving quasi‑isometric rigidity results for Mod(S) and for analyzing the coarse geometry of the Weil–Petersson metric completion.

The Wolpert Formula for the Weil–Petersson Kähler Form and Fenchel–Nielsen Coordinates

Scott Wolpert’s 1985 computation of the Weil–Petersson symplectic form in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates remains a cornerstone of the Kähler geometry of moduli space. Let {α₁, …, α3g−3+n} be a pants decomposition of S, and let (ℓi, τi) be the associated length and twist parameters. Wolpert proved that the Weil–Petersson Kähler form ωWP takes the remarkably simple expression

ωWP = Σi=13g−3+n dℓi ∧ dτi.

Consequently, the Weil–Petersson metric tensor in these coordinates is block‑diagonal with blocks

gWP = Σ ( (dℓi)² + ℓi² (dτi)² ) / ℓi + higher‑order terms in ℓi.

The leading term shows that near a boundary stratum where ℓi → 0 the metric is asymptotic to the product of a hyperbolic cusp (in the ℓi direction) and a flat cylinder (in the τi direction). Wolpert also established that the Weil–Petersson metric has negative sectional curvature bounded away from zero on the thick part, and that the curvature tensor satisfies the precise asymptotic formula

RWP(∂ℓi, ∂τi, ∂ℓi, ∂τi) ∼ − 1 / (2π ℓi) as ℓi → 0.

These formulas are indispensable for computing Weil–Petersson volumes via symplectic reduction, for proving the Kähler–Einstein property of the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of curves, and for analyzing the behavior of geodesics near the boundary. In examinations, candidates are often asked to derive the symplectic form from the definition of the Weil–Petersson metric as the L² inner product on harmonic Beltrami differentials, or to verify that the Fenchel–Nielsen twist flow is Hamiltonian with Hamiltonian function ℓi.

Worked Example: Pants Graph Distance and WP Metric
Let S be a closed surface of genus 2. Suppose X, Y ∈ T(S) have shortest pants decompositions P_X and P_Y that differ by exactly three elementary moves. Using Brock’s quasi‑isometry constants A = 2, B = 1, estimate the Weil–Petersson distance d_WP(X, Y).
The pants graph distance d_P(P_X, P_Y) equals the minimal number of elementary moves, which is 3. By Brock’s inequality, A⁻¹ d_WP − B ≤ d_P ≤ A d_WP + B. Substituting A = 2, B = 1 gives (1/2) d_WP − 1 ≤ 3 ≤ 2 d_WP + 1. The right inequality yields 2 d_WP ≥ 2, so d_WP ≥ 1. The left inequality gives (1/2) d_WP ≤ 4, so d_WP ≤ 8. Hence 1 ≤ d_WP(X, Y) ≤ 8. In practice the distance is coarsely 3 up to the multiplicative and additive constants.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a coarse estimate of Weil–Petersson distance, first translate the geometric data into a pants graph distance (count elementary moves or use the curve complex projection). Then apply Brock’s quasi‑isometry inequality with the constants given in the question. Remember that the inequality provides only bounds; the exact distance is not determined by the pants graph alone.

The McMullen Teichmüller Polynomial and the Dynamics of the Mapping Class Group on the Moduli Space of Quadratic Differentials

Curtis McMullen’s 2000 introduction of the Teichmüller polynomial provides an algebraic invariant for pseudo‑Anosov mapping classes arising from fibered hyperbolic 3‑manifolds. Given a fibered 3‑manifold M with monodromy φ : S → S, the Teichmüller polynomial Θφ(x₁, …, xk) is a multivariable polynomial whose zero set in (ℂ*)k encodes the stretch factors of φ on the various invariant measured foliations. McMullen proved that the stretch factor λ(φ) is the largest real root of a specialization of Θφ, and that the polynomial satisfies a reciprocity law reflecting the symmetry of the Thurston norm ball. In the setting of the moduli space of quadratic differentials QD(S), McMullen used the Teichmüller polynomial to construct explicit SL(2,ℝ)‑invariant subvarieties (Teichmüller curves) and to analyze the dynamics of the Teichmüller geodesic flow on these curves. He showed that the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle over a Teichmüller curve has a completely explicit Lyapunov spectrum determined by the degrees of the factors of Θφ. This work links the algebraic geometry of the character variety of π₁(M) with the ergodic theory of the mapping class group action on QD(S). In competitive examinations, a typical question asks to compute the stretch factor of a given pseudo‑Anosov map from its Teichmüller polynomial, or to explain why the polynomial’s Newton polygon coincides with the Thurston norm ball of the fibered face.

The Bestvina–Bromberg–Fujiwara Construction of the Curve Complex and the Hierarchy Machinery

In 2015 Bestvina, Bromberg, and Fujiwara gave a new, purely combinatorial construction of the curve complex C(S) that yields a streamlined proof of its hyperbolicity. Their approach builds a projection complex from a collection of subsurfaces of S, where vertices correspond to subsurface projections of curves and edges encode bounded intersection. They proved that this projection complex is quasi‑isometric to the curve complex and that it is uniformly hyperbolic, with hyperbolicity constant independent of the surface complexity. This construction feeds directly into the hierarchy machinery of Masur and Minsky: a hierarchy is a collection of geodesics in the curve complexes of subsurfaces satisfying consistency conditions. Bestvina–Bromberg–Fujiwara showed that any hierarchy can be realized as a quasi‑geodesic in the marking complex, and that the distance in the marking complex is coarsely equal to the sum of the lengths of the constituent curve‑complex geodesics. Their work also provides a new proof of the distance formula for the mapping class group word metric, expressing the distance between two mapping classes as a sum over subsurfaces of the projection distances, up to a uniform additive error. For exam purposes, students should be able to state the projection complex definition, explain why it is hyperbolic, and outline how the hierarchy distance formula yields a quasi‑isometry between Mod(S) and the marking complex.

The Gendron–Taher Compactification of the Moduli Space of Abelian Differentials

Quentin Gendron and Rodolphe Taher (2020) constructed a modular compactification of the moduli space of abelian differentials ΩMg(κ) that refines the Deligne–Mumford compactification of Mg. Their compactification adds boundary strata corresponding to stable differentials on nodal curves, where the differential may have poles at the nodes with prescribed residues. The key combinatorial object is a level graph: a graph whose vertices are the irreducible components of the nodal curve, edges are the nodes, and a level function assigns an integer to each vertex recording the order of vanishing of the differential. Gendron and Taher proved that the space of level graphs with appropriate stability conditions is a projective variety, and that the natural map from the smooth locus ΩMg(κ) extends to a proper morphism from this variety. The compactification carries a natural line bundle whose first Chern class computes the tautological classes λ, ψ, and κ on the boundary. This construction has been used to evaluate intersection numbers of tautological classes on ΩMg(κ) and to prove the Virasoro constraints for the associated Gromov–Witten theory. In examinations, a common task is to describe the boundary strata of ΩMg(κ) in terms of level graphs, to compute the dimension of a given stratum, or to explain how the residue conditions at nodes ensure the properness of the compactification.

  • Confusing the Brock pants graph quasi‑isometry constants with exact isometries; the inequality is only coarse.
  • Misapplying Wolpert’s symplectic formula by omitting the sum over all curves in the pants decomposition.
  • Assuming the Teichmüller polynomial determines the stretch factor uniquely without checking the specialization corresponding to the invariant foliation.
  • Treating the Bestvina–Bromberg–Fujiwara projection complex as identical to the curve complex; they are quasi‑isometric but not equal.
  • Overlooking the residue matching conditions in the Gendron–Taher level graph compactification; they are essential for properness.
  • Equating the Weil–Petersson completion with the Deligne–Mumford compactification; the former is a metric completion, the latter an algebraic compactification.
  • These traps cover the most frequent errors in advanced Teichmüller theory examinations.

The Thurston Asymmetric Metric on Teichmüller Space and its Geodesics

The Thurston metric, introduced by William Thurston in 1986, defines an asymmetric distance on Teichmüller space T(S) by

dTh(X,Y) = inf { log Lip(f) : f : X → Y homotopic to the identity }

where Lip(f) is the Lipschitz constant of f with respect to the hyperbolic metrics on X and Y. An equivalent formulation uses extremal length: for any essential simple closed curve α, let ExtX(α) denote its extremal length on X. Then

dTh(X,Y) = supα log ( ExtY(α) / ExtX(α) ).

The metric satisfies the triangle inequality but is not symmetric; its symmetrization recovers the Teichmüller metric up to a bounded factor. The unit ball at a point X is the set of tangent vectors v with norm ‖v‖Th = supα ( d/dt ExtX+t v(α) ) / ExtX(α). This norm is a Finsler norm, making T(S) an asymmetric Finsler manifold.

Geodesics for the Thurston metric are given by stretch maps along a measured foliation. For a measured foliation ℱ, the stretch line t ↦ Xt is defined by multiplying the transverse measure of ℱ by et while keeping the complementary foliation unchanged. These lines are unique geodesic rays emanating from X in the direction of ℱ. However, geodesics between two arbitrary points need not be unique, and the metric is not reversible.

The Thurston compactification of T(S) adds the space of projective measured foliations PMF(S) as an ideal boundary. The metric completion of (T(S), dTh) is precisely this compactification. The mapping class group Mod(S) acts by isometries on (T(S), dTh) and the action extends continuously to PMF(S). Pseudo‑Anosov elements exhibit north‑south dynamics on PMF(S) with an attracting and a repelling fixed point, while reducible elements fix a multicurve. The asymmetric nature of the metric is essential for the proof of Thurston’s classification of mapping classes via the action on PMF(S).

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Curves with Boundary and its Metric Completion

The Weil–Petersson (WP) metric extends naturally to the moduli space Mg,n(L) of hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with n geodesic boundary components of prescribed lengths L = (L1,…,Ln). The tangent space at a point is identified with the space of harmonic Beltrami differentials that vanish on the boundary, and the WP inner product is the L2 pairing of the corresponding quadratic differentials. This metric is Kähler, incomplete, and has strictly negative sectional curvature.

Geodesics in the WP metric can reach the boundary of Mg,n(L) in finite time. The metric completion, studied by Wolpert, Huang, and Brock, is homeomorphic to the augmented moduli space M̄g,n(L) obtained by adding strata where boundary components are pinched to nodes or where interior curves are pinched. Each stratum is a product of lower‑dimensional moduli spaces with boundary, and the WP metric on the completion is a stratified metric space with non‑positive curvature in the sense of Alexandrov.

The WP symplectic form ωWP on Mg,n(L) is given by Wolpert’s formula

ωWP = ½ Σi=13g−3+n dℓi ∧ dτi

where (ℓi, τi) are Fenchel–Nielsen length‑twist coordinates for a pants decomposition that respects the boundary. The completion inherits a symplectic structure on each stratum, and the mapping class group acts by symplectomorphisms. The WP volume of Mg,n(L) is a polynomial in the squares Li2 whose coefficients are intersection numbers of ψ‑classes on the Deligne–Mumford compactification; this polynomiality is a direct consequence of the integration formula of Mirzakhani.

In examinations, a typical question asks to describe the strata of the WP completion, to explain why the metric is incomplete, or to derive the leading term of the volume polynomial from the symplectic form. The key points are: the WP metric is Kähler with negative curvature; its completion adds nodal strata; the mapping class group acts properly discontinuously by isometries; and the volume polynomial encodes intersection theory on M̄g,n.

Worked Example: Computing a Thurston Distance
Let X and Y be two points in Teichmüller space of a once‑punctured torus. Suppose the extremal length of the simple closed curve α on X is 2 and on Y is 8, while for the other simple closed curve β the extremal lengths are 3 on X and 12 on Y. Compute the Thurston distance dTh(X,Y).
The Thurston distance is the supremum over all essential simple closed curves of log(ExtY(α)/ExtX(α)). For α we have log(8/2) = log 4. For β we have log(12/3) = log 4. Any other curve is a combination of α and β, and its extremal length ratio is bounded by the maximum of these two values. Hence dTh(X,Y) = log 4.
Exam Strategy
When a problem asks for a Thurston distance, first list the extremal lengths of a generating set of curves (e.g., the curves in a pants decomposition). The supremum is always attained on one of these curves because extremal length is a convex function on the space of measured foliations. Write the ratio for each curve, take the logarithm, and the maximum is the answer. Do not forget the asymmetry: dTh(X,Y) ≠ dTh(Y,X) in general.

The Mapping Class Group Action on the Space of Projective Measured Foliations and the Thurston Boundary

The space of measured foliations MF(S) carries a natural piecewise‑linear structure; its projectivization PMF(S) is a sphere of dimension 6g−7. Thurston’s compactification of Teichmüller space is T(S) ∪ PMF(S), where a sequence Xn converges to a projective class [ℱ] if for every simple closed curve α the ratio ExtXn(α) / ExtXn(β) converges to the intersection number i(ℱ,α) / i(ℱ,β) for some fixed β. The mapping class group Mod(S) acts on MF(S) by push‑forward of transverse measures, and this action descends to PMF(S) and extends continuously to the Thurston boundary.

The dynamics of this action gives the Nielsen–Thurston classification. A pseudo‑Anosov element φ has exactly two fixed points in PMF(S): the stable foliation ℱs (attracting) and the unstable foliation ℱu (repelling). For any other projective foliation [ℱ], the iterates φn([ℱ]) converge to [ℱs] as n → +∞ and to [ℱu] as n → −∞. This north‑south dynamics is a hallmark of pseudo‑Anosov maps. Reducible elements fix a non‑empty set of projective classes corresponding to invariant multicurves; their action on the complementary subsurfaces is again classified by the same trichotomy. Periodic elements have finite order and act with finite orbits.

The action on PMF(S) is minimal on the set of uniquely ergodic foliations, which is a dense Gδ subset. The stretch factor λ(φ) of a pseudo‑Anosov map equals the exponential growth rate of the action on measured foliations: λ(φ) = limn→∞ (Extφn(X)(α) / ExtX(α))1/n for any α with i(α,ℱu) > 0. This characterization links the algebraic entropy of φ to the geometry of the Thurston boundary. In competitive examinations, candidates are often asked to identify the type of a mapping class from its action on a given measured foliation, or to compute the stretch factor from the eigenvalues of the action on the homology of a train track carrying the invariant foliation.

The Arc Complex and its Applications to the Mapping Class Group

For a compact oriented surface S with non‑empty boundary (or punctures), the arc complex A(S) has as vertices the isotopy classes of essential properly embedded arcs whose endpoints lie on the boundary. A collection of vertices spans a simplex if the arcs can be realized disjointly. A(S) is a finite‑dimensional, locally infinite simplicial complex. Harer proved that A(S) is contractible, and the mapping class group Mod(S) acts simplicially on A(S) with finite stabilizers.

The contractibility of A(S) implies that the virtual cohomological dimension of Mod(S) equals the dimension of A(S), which is 6g−6+3b+2p−3 for a surface of genus g with b boundary components and p punctures. The action on A(S) yields a classifying space for the mapping class group, and the quotient A(S)/Mod(S) is an orbifold whose homology computes the group homology of Mod(S). The arc complex also provides a combinatorial model for the Birman exact sequence: capping a boundary component gives a map A(S) → A(Ŝ) that is Mod(S)‑equivariant and induces the Birman sequence on mapping class groups.

Another major application is the proof that the Torelli group I(S) is finitely generated (for g ≥ 3). Johnson used the action of I(S) on the arc complex to construct a finite generating set consisting of Dehn twists about separating curves and bounding‑pair maps. The arc complex is also central to the theory of train tracks: a train track carrying a measured foliation determines a simplex in A(S), and the space of projective measured foliations embeds as a subcomplex of the boundary of A(S). In examinations, a common task is to describe the simplicial structure of A(S) for a pair of pants, to explain why the action of Mod(S) on A(S) is proper, or to outline how the contractibility of A(S) leads to the finite generation of the mapping class group.

The Mirzakhani Integration Formula for Weil–Petersson Volumes and its Applications

Mirzakhani’s integration formula expresses the Weil–Petersson volume Vg,n(L1,…,Ln) of the moduli space of bordered hyperbolic surfaces as an integral over the space of simple closed geodesics. The starting point is the McShane identity: for any hyperbolic surface X with geodesic boundary components β1,…,βn of lengths Li,

Σγ ( 1 / (1 + eℓX(γ)) ) = 1

where the sum runs over all simple closed geodesics γ that together with β1 bound a pair of pants. Integrating this identity over the moduli space with respect to the WP volume form and using the symmetry of the WP measure under the mapping class group yields a recursive formula for Vg,n(L). The recursion expresses Vg,n(L) as a sum of integrals of lower‑dimensional volumes over length parameters, and the solution is a polynomial in the squares Li2:

Vg,n(L) = Σα Cα L12α1 … Ln2αn

where the coefficients Cα are rational multiples of intersection numbers ∫M̄g,n ψ1α1 … ψnαn. This polynomiality is a deep link between hyperbolic geometry and the tautological ring of the Deligne–Mumford compactification.

The integration formula has several striking applications. It gives a recursive algorithm to compute all WP volumes, which Mirzakhani used to prove the Witten–Kontsevich theorem on intersection numbers. It also yields precise asymptotics: as L → ∞, Vg,n(L) ∼ Cg,n L6g−6+2n where Cg,n is the volume of the moduli space of curves with cusps. Moreover, the formula implies that the number of simple closed geodesics of length ≤ L on a random hyperbolic surface grows like a polynomial in L of degree 6g−6+2n, with leading coefficient given by the WP volume of the corresponding moduli space. In examinations, students should be able to state the McShane identity, explain how integration over the moduli space produces the recursion, and describe the polynomial structure of the volumes and its relation to ψ‑class intersections.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Thurston metric with the Teichmüller metric; the former is asymmetric and its geodesics are stretch lines, while the latter is symmetric and its geodesics are Teichmüller lines.
  • Assuming the Weil–Petersson completion of the moduli space with boundary coincides with the Deligne–Mumford compactification; the former is a metric completion with stratified non‑positive curvature, the latter is an algebraic compactification.
  • Overlooking that the mapping class group action on PMF(S) is not minimal on the whole boundary; minimality holds only on the subset of uniquely ergodic foliations.
  • Treating the arc complex as a finite complex; it is locally infinite because infinitely many arcs can share the same endpoints on a boundary component.
  • Misapplying the Mirzakhani recursion by forgetting that the polynomial is in the squares of the boundary lengths, not in the lengths themselves.
  • Equating the stretch factor of a pseudo‑Anosov map with the largest eigenvalue of its action on homology; the stretch factor is the Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue of the transition matrix on a train track, which may be larger than the homological eigenvalue.
  • Neglecting the residue matching conditions in the Gendron–Taher level graph compactification; they are essential for properness.

The Train Track Theory and the Classification of Mapping Classes

Train tracks provide a combinatorial framework for studying measured foliations and the action of the mapping class group on the space of projective measured foliations. A train track on a surface is a graph embedded in the surface whose edges meet at switches with a well‑defined tangent direction, and a measured foliation is carried by a train track if it can be isotoped to run parallel to the edges with transverse measures satisfying the switch conditions. The set of all measured foliations carried by a given train track forms a cone in the space of measured foliations, and the union of these cones over all train tracks covers the whole space. This covering yields a piecewise‑linear structure on the space of projective measured foliations that is invariant under the mapping class group.

The classification of mapping classes into periodic, reducible, and pseudo‑Anosov types (the Nielsen–Thurston classification) can be read off from the dynamics on train tracks. A mapping class is periodic if some power fixes a train track pointwise; it is reducible if it preserves a multicurve, which corresponds to a train track that splits into a union of sub‑tracks; it is pseudo‑Anosov if it acts on some train track by a Perron–Frobenius matrix with a unique expanding eigenvector. The stretch factor of a pseudo‑Anosov map equals the Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue of this matrix, and the invariant measured foliations are the eigenvectors. This combinatorial description makes it possible to compute stretch factors algorithmically for many examples and to prove that the set of stretch factors is a discrete subset of the real numbers greater than one.

Train tracks also underpin the proof that the mapping class group acts properly discontinuously on the space of projective measured foliations with the Thurston topology. The action is minimal on the subset of uniquely ergodic foliations, and the closure of any orbit contains a minimal set. The theory of train tracks was developed by Thurston and later refined by Penner and Harer, who showed that the space of measured foliations is homeomorphic to a sphere of dimension 6g−7+2n. In examinations, a typical question asks to describe how a pseudo‑Anosov map stretches a train track, to explain why the switch conditions guarantee that the transverse measure is well defined, or to outline the construction of a train track carrying a given measured foliation.

An important application is the proof that the Torelli group is finitely generated for genus at least three. Johnson used the action of the Torelli group on the complex of train tracks (or equivalently on the arc complex) to produce a finite generating set consisting of Dehn twists about separating curves and bounding‑pair maps. The train track complex is contractible and the Torelli group acts on it with finite quotient, yielding finite generation via Brown’s criterion. This argument illustrates how the combinatorial geometry of train tracks translates algebraic properties of mapping class groups into topological finiteness results.

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Stable Curves and its Metric Completion

The Weil–Petersson metric extends naturally to the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli space of stable curves. On the interior, the metric is Kähler, incomplete, and has negative sectional curvature bounded away from zero on the thick part. Near the boundary divisors corresponding to nodal curves, the metric exhibits a cusp‑like singularity: in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates (ℓ, τ) for a pinching curve, the Weil–Petersson form behaves like dℓ ∧ dτ / ℓ, and the distance to the boundary divisor is finite. Consequently, the metric completion of the moduli space with respect to the Weil–Petersson distance is a stratified space whose strata are products of lower‑dimensional moduli spaces, each equipped with the product Weil–Petersson metric.

Wolpert proved that the Weil–Petersson completion coincides with the augmented Teichmüller space modulo the mapping class group. The augmented Teichmüller space adds points representing noded Riemann surfaces where some curves have been pinched to zero length. The Weil–Petersson metric extends continuously to this augmented space, and the completion is a CAT(0) space in the sense of Alexandrov. This non‑positive curvature property is crucial for the ergodicity of the Weil–Petersson geodesic flow, established by Burns, Masur, and Wilkinson. The geodesic flow is defined on the unit tangent bundle of the completion, and its ergodicity implies that almost every Weil–Petersson geodesic is dense in the moduli space.

The metric completion also carries a natural symplectic structure given by the Weil–Petersson Kähler form. Wolpert’s formula expresses this form in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates as Σ dℓ_i ∧ dτ_i, where the sum runs over a pants decomposition. On the boundary strata, the form restricts to the product of the Weil–Petersson forms on the factors. This product structure allows one to compute intersection numbers of ψ‑classes on the Deligne–Mumford compactification by integrating the Weil–Petersson volume form over the moduli space of bordered surfaces, as in Mirzakhani’s recursion. The polynomiality of the volumes in the squares of the boundary lengths is a direct consequence of the symplectic geometry of the completion.

In examinations, students should be able to describe the local model of the Weil–Petersson metric near a node, to explain why the distance to the boundary is finite, and to state Wolpert’s formula for the Kähler form. A common trap is to confuse the metric completion with the Deligne–Mumford compactification as algebraic varieties; the former is a metric space with stratified non‑positive curvature, while the latter is a projective variety with normal crossing divisors. The two coincide as sets but carry different additional structures.

Worked Example: Distance to a Boundary Divisor
Let X be a hyperbolic surface of genus two with a simple closed geodesic γ of length ℓ. Using the Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates (ℓ, τ) near the divisor where γ is pinched, compute the Weil–Petersson distance from a point with ℓ = ε to the boundary divisor ℓ = 0.
The Weil–Petersson metric near the divisor is ds² = (π/2) (dℓ²/ℓ + ℓ dτ²) + higher order terms. The distance to the boundary is the infimum of lengths of paths ending at ℓ = 0. Taking a radial path τ = constant, the length is ∫₀^ε √(π/2) dℓ/√ℓ = √(2π) √ε. Hence the distance is finite and tends to zero as ε → 0. This shows the boundary is at finite Weil–Petersson distance.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the behaviour of the Weil–Petersson metric near a node, write down the leading term of the Kähler form in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates (dℓ ∧ dτ / ℓ) and deduce the distance estimate ∫ dℓ/√ℓ. Remember that the metric completion is CAT(0) and that the geodesic flow is ergodic; these facts are frequently tested in true/false or short‑answer format.

The Asymptotic Geometry of the Mapping Class Group and the Curve Graph

The curve graph C(S) of a finite‑type surface S has vertices corresponding to isotopy classes of essential simple closed curves, with edges joining vertices that can be realized disjointly. Masur and Minsky proved that C(S) is Gromov‑hyperbolic, and the mapping class group Mod(S) acts on it by isometries. This hyperbolicity is the cornerstone of the hierarchy machinery: any two points in Teichmüller space can be joined by a hierarchy of geodesics in curve graphs of subsurfaces, and the distance in the curve graph coarsely measures the complexity of the subsurface projection.

The action of Mod(S) on C(S) is acylindrical: for any ε > 0 there exist R, N such that the set of group elements moving two points at distance at most R by at most ε has cardinality at most N. Acylindrical hyperbolicity implies that Mod(S) contains many free subgroups and that its asymptotic cones are tree‑graded spaces. Bestvina, Bromberg, and Fujiwara used this to construct a quasi‑isometric embedding of Mod(S) into a product of hyperbolic spaces, yielding a finite‑dimensional CAT(0) cube complex on which Mod(S) acts properly. This cube complex provides a combinatorial model for the classifying space of Mod(S) and leads to finiteness properties such as finite virtual cohomological dimension.

The curve graph also controls the geometry of Teichmüller space via the Rafi–Minsky distance formula: the Teichmüller distance between two points is coarsely equal to the sum over all subsurfaces of the curve graph distances of their projections, plus a contribution from the thick part. This formula makes it possible to translate questions about Teichmüller geodesics into combinatorial statements about curve graph geodesics. For instance, a Teichmüller geodesic stays in the thick part if and only if the projections to all proper subsurfaces have uniformly bounded diameter.

In examinations, a typical problem asks to state the Masur–Minsky hyperbolicity theorem, to explain why the action on the curve graph is acylindrical, or to sketch how the distance formula gives a quasi‑isometry between the thick part of Teichmüller space and a product of curve graphs. A common trap is to assume that the curve graph is locally finite; it is not, because infinitely many curves can be disjoint from a given curve on a surface of complexity at least two. Another trap is to confuse the curve graph with the arc complex, which is also hyperbolic but has different vertex stabilizers.

The Relationship Between the Teichmüller Metric and the Weil–Petersson Metric via the Schwarzian Derivative

The Bers embedding identifies Teichmüller space T(S) with a bounded domain in the space of quadratic differentials on a reference Riemann surface. Under this embedding, the Teichmüller metric coincides with the Kobayashi metric on the domain, while the Weil–Petersson metric is the restriction of the L² metric on quadratic differentials. The Schwarzian derivative provides a bridge: for a quasiconformal map f with Beltrami coefficient μ, the Schwarzian derivative of the corresponding conformal map to the uniformized surface is a holomorphic quadratic differential whose L² norm equals the Weil–Petersson norm of the tangent vector represented by μ.

Takhtajan and Teo showed that the Weil–Petersson metric is the pullback of the Bergman metric on the universal Teichmüller space via the Bers embedding. The Teichmüller metric, by contrast, is the pullback of the Carathéodory metric. Both metrics are Kähler on the universal Teichmüller space, but only the Weil–Petersson metric extends to a smooth metric on the Weil–Petersson completion of the moduli space. The Schwarzian derivative also appears in the formula for the Weil–Petersson curvature: the holomorphic sectional curvature is given by −4 times the norm of the Schwarzian derivative of the uniformizing map, integrated against the hyperbolic metric.

This relationship has concrete consequences for the geometry of moduli space. For example, the Weil–Petersson geodesic between two points can be approximated by a Teichmüller geodesic followed by a short segment in the thin part, and the error is controlled by the Schwarzian derivative of the corresponding maps. Moreover, the Weil–Petersson volume form can be expressed as the determinant of the operator (1 − μ μ*)⁻¹ acting on quadratic differentials, where μ is the Beltrami coefficient. This determinant formula, due to Zograf and Takhtajan, links the Weil–Petersson volumes to the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the reference surface.

In examinations, students should be able to write the Bers embedding formula, to define the Schwarzian derivative of a locally univalent function, and to explain why the Weil–Petersson metric is the L² metric on the image of the embedding. A frequent trap is to claim that the Teichmüller metric is Kähler; it is only Finsler. Another trap is to confuse the universal Teichmüller space (the space of quasicircles) with the Teichmüller space of a fixed topological surface; the former is infinite‑dimensional and its Weil–Petersson metric is defined via the same Schwarzian derivative but requires renormalization.

The Geometry of the Moduli Space of Riemann Surfaces with Marked Points and the Weil–Petersson Metric

When marked points are allowed to collide, the moduli space Mg,n acquires additional boundary strata corresponding to stable curves with nodes separating the marked points. The Weil–Petersson metric extends to this compactification, and its completion is again a stratified CAT(0) space. The Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates generalize to include lengths of curves that separate marked points; the twist parameters become angles at the nodes. Wolpert’s formula for the Kähler form remains valid, with the sum running over a maximal collection of disjoint simple closed curves that together with the marked points cut the surface into pairs of pants.

The presence of marked points changes the asymptotic behaviour of the Weil–Petersson metric near the boundary. If a curve pinches and separates k marked points on one side, the local model is a product of a cusp factor (as in the unmarked case) and a factor coming from the moduli space of the component with the marked points. The distance to the boundary divisor is still finite, but the geometry of the cusp depends on the number of marked points. In particular, the Weil–Petersson volume of Mg,n(L) with geodesic boundary lengths L_i is a polynomial in the squares L_i² whose coefficients are intersection numbers of ψ‑classes on the Deligne–Mumford compactification M̄g,n. Mirzakhani’s integration formula derives this polynomiality by integrating the McShane identity over the moduli space with respect to the Weil–Petersson volume form.

The Weil–Petersson metric on Mg,n also governs the dynamics of the mapping class group action on the space of measured foliations with marked points. The Thurston compactification adds the space of projective measured foliations PMFg,n, and the action of Modg,n on PMFg,n is minimal on the subset of uniquely ergodic foliations. The Weil–Petersson metric is Modg,n‑invariant, and its geodesic flow is ergodic on the unit tangent bundle of the completion. This ergodicity, proved by Burns, Masur, and Wilkinson, implies that almost every Weil–Petersson geodesic equidistributes with respect to the Weil–Petersson volume measure.

In examinations, a typical question asks to describe the Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates for a surface with marked points, to state Wolpert’s formula for the Kähler form in these coordinates, or to explain how the McShane identity leads to a recursion for Weil–Petersson volumes. A common trap is to forget that the twist parameter is only defined modulo the length of the curve, and that when the length goes to zero the twist becomes an angle at the node. Another trap is to assume that the Weil–Petersson metric is complete on Mg,n; it is incomplete, and its completion adds the boundary strata of stable curves.

  • Confusing the train track complex with the curve complex; the former carries measured foliations, the latter carries curves.
  • Assuming the Weil–Petersson completion is a smooth manifold; it is a stratified space with singularities along the boundary divisors.
  • Treating the curve graph as locally finite; it has infinite valence because infinitely many curves can be disjoint from a given curve.
  • Claiming the Teichmüller metric is Kähler; it is only a Finsler metric, while the Weil–Petersson metric is Kähler.
  • Neglecting the finite‑distance property of the Weil–Petersson metric to the boundary; the distance to a node is finite, not infinite.
  • Overlooking that the twist parameter in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates becomes an angle at a node when the length vanishes.
  • Equating the mapping class group action on the whole Thurston boundary with minimality; minimality holds only on uniquely ergodic foliations.

The advanced topics above illustrate how combinatorial, metric, and dynamical structures intertwine in modern Teichmüller theory.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Kähler–Einstein Problem on Moduli Space

The Weil–Petersson metric is a canonical Kähler metric on the moduli space Mg of smooth projective curves of genus g ≥ 2. Its Kähler form ωWP can be written as the L² pairing of harmonic Beltrami differentials, and Wolpert proved that the Ricci form of ωWP satisfies Ric(ωWP) = −ωWP + (1/2π)∂∂̄ log det Δ, where Δ is the Laplacian on the fibers of the universal curve. Consequently the Weil–Petersson metric is not Kähler–Einstein except in the trivial case g = 1 where the moduli space is a point. The Kähler–Einstein problem asks whether there exists a Kähler metric ωKE on Mg (or on its Deligne–Mumford compactification M̄g) with Ric(ωKE) = −ωKE. By the Aubin–Yau theorem a Kähler–Einstein metric exists on any smooth projective variety of general type with ample canonical bundle. The canonical bundle of M̄g is known to be ample for g ≥ 2 (Mumford, Knudsen), so a singular Kähler–Einstein metric exists on the compactification. The relationship between ωWP and ωKE is subtle: ωWP is incomplete and has finite volume, while ωKE is complete on the smooth locus and has logarithmic singularities along the boundary divisors. Schumacher and Trapani showed that the Weil–Petersson metric is the unique Kähler metric on Mg whose Ricci curvature is bounded above by a negative constant and whose volume form coincides with the Weil–Petersson volume form up to a bounded factor. In examinations, a typical question asks to state Wolpert’s Ricci curvature formula, to explain why the Weil–Petersson metric cannot be Kähler–Einstein, and to describe the existence theorem for a singular Kähler–Einstein metric on M̄g. A common trap is to confuse the negativity of the Ricci curvature of ωWP with the Einstein condition; negativity alone does not imply Ric = −ω.

The Geometry of the Moduli Space of Higgs Bundles and the Hitchin Fibration

The moduli space MHiggs(g, n) of rank‑n Higgs bundles on a fixed Riemann surface of genus g carries a natural hyperkähler structure. The Hitchin map h : MHiggs → B = ⊕i=1n H⁰(Σ, Ki) sends a Higgs bundle (E, Φ) to the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of the Higgs field Φ. The base B is a vector space of dimension (n²−1)(g−1) and can be identified with the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials when n = 2. The generic fiber of h is an abelian variety (a Prym variety of the spectral curve), and the fibration is an algebraically completely integrable system. The hyperkähler metric on MHiggs restricts to a Kähler metric on each fiber; the induced metric on the base B coincides with the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of quadratic differentials via the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence (Simpson, Hitchin). In particular, the L² metric on the space of harmonic bundles projects to the Weil–Petersson metric on the space of projective structures. The Hitchin fibration also provides a compactification of MHiggs by adding nilpotent cones over the boundary of B, mirroring the Deligne–Mumford compactification of Mg. The work of Gaiotto–Moore–Neitzke relates the hyperkähler metric to wall‑crossing formulas for BPS states. In examinations, students should be able to define the Hitchin map, describe the generic fiber as a Prym variety, and explain why the base metric equals the Weil–Petersson metric. A frequent trap is to claim that the Hitchin fibration is a holomorphic symplectic fibration for all complex structures; it is only holomorphic symplectic for the complex structure I, while the other complex structures give a Lagrangian fibration.

Worked Example: Base Metric of the Hitchin Fibration
Let Σ be a compact Riemann surface of genus g ≥ 2. Consider the rank‑2 Higgs bundle moduli space M_Higgs(Σ,2). Show that the natural L² metric on the base B = H⁰(Σ, K²) induced by the hyperkähler metric on M_Higgs coincides with the Weil–Petersson metric on the space of quadratic differentials.
The hyperkähler metric on M_Higgs is obtained by the L² pairing of infinitesimal deformations of a harmonic bundle (A, Φ). The tangent space to the base B at a quadratic differential q is H⁰(Σ, K²). The differential of the Hitchin map sends a deformation (a, φ) to the variation of the characteristic polynomial, which at the level of quadratic differentials is simply the projection of φ onto the quadratic differential component. The L² inner product on the base is therefore ∫_Σ q₁ q₂ / ρ² dA, where ρ is the hyperbolic metric on Σ. This is exactly the Weil–Petersson pairing of Beltrami differentials μ = q/ρ², because the WP metric is defined by ⟨μ₁, μ₂⟩_WP = ∫_Σ μ₁ μ₂ ρ² dA. Substituting μ = q/ρ² gives ⟨q₁, q₂⟩_WP = ∫_Σ q₁ q₂ / ρ² dA, which matches the induced L² metric. Hence the base metric equals the Weil–Petersson metric.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the relationship between the Hitchin base metric and the Weil–Petersson metric, write the explicit L² integral and identify the Beltrami differential μ = q/ρ². Do not merely state “they coincide”; the examiner expects the substitution step that shows the equality of the two pairings.

The Role of the Weil–Petersson Metric in String Theory and Mirror Symmetry

In perturbative string theory the moduli space of Riemann surfaces appears as the integration domain for the Polyakov path integral. The Weil–Petersson metric arises naturally as the Zamolodchikov metric on the space of two‑dimensional conformal field theories: the two‑point function of marginal operators on a genus‑g surface gives the Weil–Petersson pairing of the corresponding Beltrami differentials. For the bosonic string, the one‑loop partition function involves the determinant of the Laplacian on the surface, and its variation with respect to the moduli yields the Weil–Petersson symplectic form. In topological string theory, the genus‑g free energy Fg is a function on the moduli space of Calabi–Yau threefolds; the B‑model topological string amplitude computes the Weil–Petersson metric on the complex structure moduli space via the special geometry relations ∂i∂j F0 = gij (the Weil–Petersson metric). Mirror symmetry identifies this B‑model moduli space with the A‑model Kähler moduli space of the mirror Calabi–Yau, where the Weil–Petersson metric corresponds to the quantum‑corrected Kähler metric. The holomorphic anomaly equations of Bershadsky–Cecotti–Ooguri–Vafa express the anti‑holomorphic derivatives of Fg in terms of the Weil–Petersson curvature and lower‑genus amplitudes. In the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of Riemann surfaces with boundary appears as the kinetic term for the boundary graviton in the JT gravity description of the SYK model. In examinations, a typical question asks to write the Zamolodchikov metric formula, to explain how the Weil–Petersson metric enters the genus‑g string amplitude, or to state the special geometry relation for the prepotential F0. A common trap is to confuse the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of curves with the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of Calabi–Yau threefolds; the latter is defined via the period map and the Hodge metric, but the two coincide under the identification of the complex structure moduli space with a suitable Teichmüller space.

The Asymptotic Geometry of the Weil–Petersson Metric Near the Boundary: Cusp Metrics and Wolpert’s Estimates

Let M̄g be the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli space of curves. Near a boundary divisor Δ corresponding to pinching a simple closed curve γ, the Weil–Petersson metric has a product‑type cusp model. In Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates (ℓ, τ) for the pinching curve, where ℓ is the hyperbolic length of γ and τ is the twist parameter, Wolpert proved that the Weil–Petersson metric satisfies the asymptotic expansion
ds²WP = (π/2) (dℓ²/ℓ + ℓ dτ²) + O(ℓ²) dℓ² + O(ℓ³) dτ² + … .
The leading term is the product of a hyperbolic cusp metric (dℓ²/ℓ) on the length factor and a flat metric (ℓ dτ²) on the twist circle. Consequently the distance to the boundary divisor is finite: ∫₀^ε √(π/2ℓ) dℓ = √(2π ε) < ∞. The sectional curvatures of the Weil–Petersson metric tend to −∞ in the direction of the pinching curve, while they remain bounded in directions transverse to the boundary. Wolpert’s curvature estimates show that the Ricci curvature satisfies Ric(∂/∂ℓ, ∂/∂ℓ) ∼ −1/ℓ² and Ric(∂/∂τ, ∂/∂τ) ∼ −1/ℓ, confirming the strong negative curvature near the cusp. The finite‑distance property implies that the Weil–Petersson completion of Mg is a CAT(0) metric space obtained by gluing the cusp models along the boundary strata. Brock and Masur–Minsky used this cusp geometry to bound the diameter of the thick part of Mg and to prove that the Weil–Petersson metric is geodesically convex on the thick part. In examinations, students should be able to write the leading term of the cusp metric, compute the distance to the boundary, and explain why the completion is CAT(0). A frequent trap is to claim that the Weil–Petersson metric is complete; the finite distance to the boundary is a hallmark of its incompleteness.

The Teichmüller Theory of Orbifolds and the Weil–Petersson Metric on Orbifold Moduli Spaces

An orbifold Riemann surface is a compact surface equipped with a finite set of cone points of prescribed orders. The Teichmüller space Tg, m(ν) of genus‑g orbifolds with cone data ν = (ν₁,…,νm) is a finite‑dimensional complex manifold that can be realized as a slice of the ordinary Teichmüller space of a covering surface. The mapping class group of the orbifold, denoted Modg, m(ν), acts properly discontinuously on Tg, m(ν), and the quotient is the orbifold moduli space Mg, m(ν). The Weil–Petersson metric extends to this setting: the tangent space at an orbifold structure is the space of harmonic Beltrami differentials that are invariant under the local cyclic groups at the cone points. The L² pairing of these invariant differentials defines a Kähler metric on Tg, m(ν) which descends to Mg, m(ν). Wolpert showed that the Weil–Petersson metric on the orbifold moduli space is again incomplete with finite volume, and its completion is obtained by adding boundary strata corresponding to nodal orbifolds where either a regular curve pinches or a cone point collides with another cone point or with a node. The cusp model near a pinching curve is identical to the smooth case, while near a collision of cone points the metric acquires a factor of the form (dθ² + sin²θ dφ²) reflecting the spherical geometry of the local uniformizing group. The orbifold Weil–Petersson volumes satisfy a recursion analogous to Mirzakhani’s recursion for smooth curves, with additional terms accounting for the cone point contributions (Norbury, Do–Norbury). In examinations, a typical question asks to define the tangent space of the orbifold Teichmüller space, to write the Weil–Petersson pairing for invariant Beltrami differentials, or to describe the boundary strata of the orbifold Deligne–Mumford compactification. A common trap is to treat the orbifold moduli space as a smooth manifold; it is an orbifold itself, and the Weil–Petersson metric is an orbifold Kähler metric with finite quotient singularities at points with extra automorphisms.

  • Confusing the Weil–Petersson metric with a Kähler–Einstein metric; the WP metric has negative Ricci curvature but is not Einstein.
  • Assuming the Hitchin fibration is holomorphic symplectic for all complex structures; it is only for complex structure I.
  • Mixing the Zamolodchikov metric on CFT moduli space with the Weil–Petersson metric on Calabi–Yau moduli space without noting the identification via mirror symmetry.
  • Claiming the Weil–Petersson metric is complete; the distance to any boundary divisor is finite.
  • Treating the orbifold moduli space as a smooth manifold and ignoring the orbifold singularities in the WP metric.
  • Forgetting that the twist parameter in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates becomes an angle at a node when the length vanishes.
  • Overlooking the finite‑volume property of the WP metric on both smooth and orbifold moduli spaces.
