The logarithmic period domain Dlog is the log analytic space obtained by equipping the classical period domain D with the log structure induced by the normal crossings boundary of a suitable toroidal compactification of the quotient ΓD. The log period map Φlog : ShKtor → ΓDlog is a morphism of log analytic spaces which extends the classical period map. The log Griffiths transversality theorem states that the differential of Φlog maps the log tangent bundle into the log subbundle Tlog−1,1 of the log Hodge bundle. This property is essential for defining the log mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of the boundary strata.

In the p‑adic setting, the logarithmic Faltings–Chai integral model of the Siegel modular variety provides a log smooth scheme over ℤp whose generic fibre is the Shimura variety for GSp2g. The log crystalline cohomology of this model carries a log Frobenius and a log monodromy operator, and the log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism identifies it with the log de Rham cohomology of the generic fibre. The resulting log filtered (φ, N)‑modules are the p‑adic avatars of the log mixed Hodge structures on the complex side, and they play a central role in the proof of the log version of the Fontaine–Mazur conjecture for Galois representations arising from Shimura varieties.

  • Confusing the log Chow group with the classical Chow group of the underlying scheme; the log cycle classes retain the ghost sheaf data and the rational equivalence uses log Cartier divisors.
  • Applying the classical Riemann–Roch formula without the log Todd class; the log Todd class differs by the contribution of the boundary divisor.
  • Assuming the log Hilbert scheme represents the same functor as the classical Hilbert scheme; the log structure imposes extra conditions on the families of subschemes.
  • Treating a logarithmic fan as an ordinary fan; the monoid map σ encodes the log structure on strata and cannot be ignored.
  • Identifying the log period domain with the classical period domain as analytic spaces; the log structure on the boundary is essential for the log Griffiths transversality statement.
  • Omitting the log monodromy operator N in the log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism for Shimura varieties; N is non‑zero on the boundary strata and encodes the weight filtration.
  • Using the classical virtual fundamental class on a log moduli space without the log perfect obstruction theory; the log virtual class lives in the log Chow group and differs by the log normal bundle contribution.

These advanced topics complete the research‑level toolkit for logarithmic geometry across intersection theory, enumerative geometry, toric methods, and arithmetic applications.

Logarithmic Prismatic Cohomology and the Logarithmic Prismatic Site

Prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, provides a unified framework for p‑adic cohomology theories. In the logarithmic setting, one works with the logarithmic prismatic site (X/𝔸)₍log₎₍△₎ whose objects are logarithmic prisms (A, I, M) equipped with a map to the log scheme X. A logarithmic prism is a δ‑ring A with an ideal I = (d) such that A is (p, I)‑complete, p ∈ I + pA, and the Frobenius φ : A → A satisfies φ(d) = p·u for a unit u, together with a log structure M on Spec A compatible with the divided powers on I. The logarithmic prismatic cohomology complex △₍log₎(X/𝔸) is the derived global sections of the structure sheaf 𝒪₍△₎ on this site. It carries a natural Frobenius φ and a logarithmic Nygaard filtration N^≥• whose graded pieces are related to the logarithmic Hodge–Tate cohomology. The logarithmic prismatic comparison theorem states that for a proper log smooth scheme X over 𝒪ₖ with k a perfectoid field, there are canonical isomorphisms △₍log₎(X/𝔸) ⊗^L_𝔸 𝔸_inf ≃ RΓ₍log₎₍ét₎(X_C, ℤ_p) ⊗_ℤ_p 𝔸_inf and △₍log₎(X/𝔸) ⊗^L_𝔸 A_inf/(ξ) ≃ RΓ₍log₎₍dR₎(X/𝒪ₖ). The logarithmic prismatic site also admits a logarithmic version of the Breuil–Kisin prism, giving rise to logarithmic Breuil–Kisin cohomology which computes the logarithmic crystalline cohomology of the special fibre. The logarithmic Nygaard filtration induces the logarithmic Hodge filtration on log de Rham cohomology after base change, and the logarithmic conjugate filtration on log Hodge–Tate cohomology. This theory is essential for the logarithmic p‑adic Langlands correspondence and for the construction of logarithmic (φ, Γ)‑modules.

Logarithmic Syntomic Cohomology and the Logarithmic Fontaine–Messing Isomorphism

Logarithmic syntomic cohomology is defined as the homotopy fixed points of the logarithmic Frobenius on the logarithmic Nygaard completion of prismatic cohomology: RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) := (RΓ₍△₎₍log₎(X/𝔸) ̂_N^≥r)φ=p^r. For a log smooth proper scheme X over 𝒪ₖ, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology groups H^i₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) are finitely generated ℤ_p‑modules that interpolate between logarithmic étale cohomology and logarithmic de Rham cohomology. The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism provides a canonical quasi‑isomorphism between the logarithmic syntomic complex and the logarithmic crystalline complex with its logarithmic Hodge filtration: RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X/𝒪ₖ, r) ≃ RΓ₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗^LW(k) 𝒪ₖ ⊗ Fil^r_log Ω^•₍log₎. This isomorphism is constructed using the logarithmic prismatic site and the logarithmic Nygaard filtration, and it respects the logarithmic Frobenius and the logarithmic monodromy operator N. The logarithmic syntomic cohomology computes the logarithmic p‑adic étale cohomology via the logarithmic syntomic–étale comparison: H^i₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(r)) ⊗ ℚ_p ≃ H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X_η, ℚ_p(r))Gal. In the semistable case, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology of the generic fibre is related to the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato cohomology of the special fibre by the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism, and the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the log crystalline side corresponds to the logarithmic weight filtration on the log étale side. The logarithmic syntomic regulator map from logarithmic motivic cohomology to logarithmic syntomic cohomology is compatible with the logarithmic Chern classes and the logarithmic cycle class map.

Worked Comparison: Logarithmic Syntomic vs Logarithmic Crystalline
Let X be a proper log smooth scheme over 𝒪ₖ with semistable reduction. Explain how the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism identifies the logarithmic syntomic cohomology H²₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) with a subquotient of the logarithmic crystalline cohomology H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ, and describe the role of the logarithmic monodromy operator N in this identification.
The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism gives a filtered quasi‑isomorphism RΓ₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) ≃ (RΓ₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ, Fil1_log). Taking cohomology, H²₍syn₎₍log₎(X, ℤ_p(1)) is the kernel of the map H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ → H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) ⊗ 𝒪ₖ / Fil1_log induced by the logarithmic Hodge filtration. The logarithmic monodromy operator N acts on H²₍crys₎₍log₎(X_k/W(k)) and satisfies N(Fil^r_log) ⊂ Filr-1_log. The logarithmic weight filtration W_• on log crystalline cohomology is defined by W_m = Im(N^m) ∩ Ker(Nm+1) shifted appropriately. Under the isomorphism, the logarithmic syntomic cohomology corresponds to the subspace where N acts nilpotently and the logarithmic Hodge filtration is compatible with the weight filtration. In particular, the logarithmic monodromy operator N encodes the extension data between the graded pieces of the logarithmic Hodge filtration, and its non‑vanishing on the boundary strata reflects the non‑triviality of the log structure.
Exam Strategy: Logarithmic Comparison Isomorphisms
When asked to compare logarithmic cohomology theories, always identify the site (prismatic, crystalline, syntomic, étale), the relevant filtration (Nygaard, Hodge, conjugate, weight), and the operators (φ, N, Galois action). The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism is the bridge between syntomic and crystalline; the logarithmic prismatic comparison is the bridge to étale and de Rham. Memorise the filtration shifts: Fil^r_log on log de Rham corresponds to N^≥r on prismatic, and the logarithmic monodromy N lowers the Hodge filtration by one. A typical trap is to forget that the log structure modifies the filtration on the boundary — the log Hodge filtration Fil^r_log Ω^•₍log₎ includes forms with logarithmic poles along the divisor.

Logarithmic Breuil–Kisin Modules and Logarithmic Crystalline Representations

Logarithmic Breuil–Kisin modules provide an integral p‑adic Hodge theory for log crystalline Galois representations. Let 𝔖 = W(k)[[u]] be the Breuil–Kisin ring with its standard log structure given by the divisor u = 0, and let 𝔖₍log₎ denote the associated log prismatic envelope. A logarithmic Breuil–Kisin module of height r is a finite free 𝔖₍log₎‑module ℳ equipped with a φ‑semilinear map φ_ℳ : φ^*ℳ → ℳ whose cokernel is killed by E(u)^r, where E(u) is the Eisenstein polynomial of a uniformiser π of K, together with a logarithmic connection ∇_log : ℳ → ℳ ⊗ Ω¹₍log₎(𝔖₍log₎/W(k)) satisfying Griffiths transversality with respect to the logarithmic Hodge filtration. The category of logarithmic Breuil–Kisin modules of height r is equivalent to the category of log crystalline Galois representations of G_K with Hodge–Tate weights in [0, r] and log monodromy operator N satisfying Nr+1 = 0. The equivalence is given by the logarithmic Kisin functor T₍log₎(ℳ) = (ℳ ⊗_𝔖 𝔸_inf)φ=1 equipped with its natural G_K‑action and logarithmic monodromy. The logarithmic Fontaine functor D₍crys₎₍log₎(V) = (V ⊗_ℚ_p B₍crys₎₍log₎)G_K recovers the logarithmic filtered (φ, N)‑module. The logarithmic Breuil–Kisin classification extends to the relative setting over a log smooth base S, giving a logarithmic version of the Breuil–Kisin–Fargues correspondence. This theory is crucial for the construction of logarithmic eigenvarieties and for the logarithmic p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(ℚ_p) with non‑trivial log structure.

Logarithmic Arakelov Theory and Logarithmic Green Functions

Logarithmic Arakelov theory extends classical Arakelov geometry to arithmetic varieties with log structures at infinity. Let X be a regular arithmetic variety over Spec ℤ with a log structure given by a normal crossings divisor D at infinity. The logarithmic Arakelov Chow group CH^p₍log,Ar₎(X) is generated by pairs (Z, g_Z) where Z is a p‑codimensional cycle on X meeting D properly, and g_Z is a logarithmic Green current for Z, i.e. a current on X(ℂ) D(ℂ) with logarithmic singularities along D(ℂ) satisfying dd^c g_Z + δ_Z = ω_Z for a smooth log form ω_Z. The logarithmic arithmetic intersection product is defined using the logarithmic *-product of Green currents, which incorporates the logarithmic singularities along the boundary. The logarithmic arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem states that for a hermitian log vector bundle Ē on X, the logarithmic arithmetic Chern character ch₍log,Ar₎(Ē) satisfies ch₍log,Ar₎(Ē) = π_*(ch₍log₎(E) · Td₍log,Ar₎(T₍log₎X)) in CH^•₍log,Ar₎(X) ⊗ ℚ, where Td₍log,Ar₎ is the logarithmic arithmetic Todd class. The logarithmic Faltings height of a log abelian variety is computed by the logarithmic arithmetic self‑intersection of the log Hodge bundle. Logarithmic Green functions for logarithmic divisors are constructed using the logarithmic heat kernel on the log Riemann surface X(ℂ) D(ℂ) with its complete hyperbolic metric. The logarithmic Kronecker limit formula expresses the value at s = 1 of the logarithmic Eisenstein series in terms of the logarithmic Faltings delta invariant. This theory underlies the logarithmic version of the Bogomolov conjecture and the logarithmic equidistribution of small points on log abelian varieties.

Logarithmic Weight Monodromy Conjecture and Logarithmic Weil Conjectures

The logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture predicts that for a proper log smooth variety X over a finite field 𝔽_q, the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the logarithmic ℓ‑adic cohomology H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X𝔽_q, ℚ_ℓ) satisfies the logarithmic weight filtration property: the graded pieces Gr^W_m H^i₍ét₎₍log₎ are pure of weight i + m. The logarithmic Weil conjectures, proved by Kato and Nakayama for log smooth varieties, state that the logarithmic zeta function Z₍log₎(X, T) = exp(∑r≥1 |X(𝔽q^r)₍log₎| T^r / r) is a rational function whose zeros and poles have absolute value q-w/2 where w is the logarithmic weight. The logarithmic Betti numbers b^i₍log₎ = dim H^i₍ét₎₍log₎(X𝔽_q, ℚ_ℓ) satisfy the logarithmic Poincaré duality b^i₍log₎ = b2d-i_₍log₎ for d = dim X. The logarithmic hard Lefschetz theorem holds for the logarithmic ample class in the log Chow ring. The logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture is known in the semistable case via the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism and the logarithmic Rapoport–Zink spectral sequence. For a log smooth degeneration over a discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field, the logarithmic monodromy operator N on the log ℓ‑adic cohomology of the generic fibre is identified with the logarithmic monodromy on the log crystalline cohomology of the special fibre, and the logarithmic weight filtration coincides with the logarithmic monodromy filtration. The logarithmic Weil conjectures for log smooth compactifications of Shimura varieties imply the logarithmic Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for automorphic forms on the boundary strata.

  • Confusing the logarithmic prismatic site with the classical prismatic site; the log structure on the prism (A, I, M) is essential for the comparison theorems in the semistable case.
  • Assuming the logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism holds without the log smoothness hypothesis; it requires the log structure to be fine, saturated, and the morphism to be log smooth.
  • Omitting the logarithmic monodromy operator N when stating the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture; N is the key operator linking the weight filtration to the Hodge filtration.
  • Treating logarithmic Green functions as ordinary Green functions; they must have logarithmic singularities along the boundary divisor and satisfy the logarithmic Poisson equation.
  • Identifying the logarithmic Breuil–Kisin module category with the classical one; the log connection ∇_log and the log structure on 𝔖 are mandatory for the equivalence with log crystalline representations.
  • Forgetting that the logarithmic zeta function counts points with log structure; |X(𝔽q^r)₍log₎| differs from the classical point count by the contribution of the boundary strata.
  • Applying the classical arithmetic Riemann–Roch without the logarithmic Todd class; the log Todd class contains correction terms from the normal bundle of the boundary divisor.

Logarithmic Non‑abelian Hodge Theory and Logarithmic Higgs Bundles

The non‑abelian Hodge correspondence for smooth projective varieties over ℂ, due to Simpson, extends to logarithmic settings where a normal crossings divisor D is equipped with the divisorial log structure. Kato and Nakayama constructed the log Betti fundamental group π₁^log(X, D) and showed that the log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence identifies logarithmic local systems on (X, D) with logarithmic flat connections having regular singularities along D. On the Dolbeault side, a logarithmic Higgs bundle is a pair (E, θ) where E is a vector bundle on X and θ: E → E ⊗ Ω¹_X(log D) satisfies θ ∧ θ = 0. Simpson’s log version of the Hitchin–Kobayashi correspondence (1990) proves that a logarithmic Higgs bundle is polystable with vanishing logarithmic Chern classes if and only if it arises from a logarithmic harmonic bundle, i.e. a logarithmic flat connection equipped with a pluriharmonic metric adapted to the log structure. The logarithmic Simpson correspondence then yields an equivalence between the category of semisimple logarithmic local systems and the category of polystable logarithmic Higgs bundles with vanishing logarithmic Chern classes. In positive characteristic, Ogus and Vologodsky (2007) established a logarithmic crystalline analogue: logarithmic Higgs bundles modulo p correspond to logarithmic flat connections with nilpotent p‑curvature via the logarithmic Cartier isomorphism. The logarithmic non‑abelian Hodge theorem for higher rank local systems on log curves was completed by Mochizuki (2011) using his theory of good filtrations and the logarithmic Kobayashi–Hitchin correspondence. These results underpin the logarithmic geometric Langlands program, where Hecke eigensheaves are expected to correspond to logarithmic local systems on the log curve.

Logarithmic Perfectoid Spaces and Logarithmic Tilting

Perfectoid spaces, introduced by Scholze (2012), admit a natural logarithmic enhancement when the base perfectoid field carries a log structure coming from a valuation ring with a divisor of definition. A logarithmic perfectoid space is a locally ringed space (X, O_X, M_X) where (X, O_X) is a perfectoid space and M_X is a fine saturated log structure compatible with the tilt. The logarithmic tilt functor sends a log perfectoid space over a log perfectoid field (K, M_K) of characteristic 0 to a log perfectoid space over its tilt (K^♭, M_K^♭) of characteristic p, preserving the log structure on the valuation monoids. Bhatt–Scholze (2019) proved that the logarithmic pro‑étale site of a log perfectoid space is equivalent to the logarithmic pro‑étale site of its tilt, yielding a logarithmic version of the almost purity theorem. This equivalence allows one to transfer logarithmic p‑adic Hodge theoretic comparison isomorphisms (logarithmic Fontaine functors D_log, D_log^cris, D_log^st) from characteristic 0 to characteristic p, where they become statements about logarithmic prismatic cohomology. In particular, the logarithmic Hodge–Tate decomposition for a log smooth proper variety over a log perfectoid field reads H^i_ét(X, ℤ_p) ⊗ ℂ_p ≅ ⊕j Hi-j(X, Ω^j_X(log)) ⊗ ℂ_p(-j), where the log differential forms carry the induced log structure. The logarithmic tilting equivalence also underlies the construction of the logarithmic Fargues–Fontaine curve, whose vector bundles classify logarithmic p‑adic Galois representations via the logarithmic version of the Fargues–Fontaine correspondence. Recent work of Heuer (2022) extends the logarithmic perfectoid theory to log adic spaces, providing a foundation for logarithmic p‑adic Langlands in families.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Tilting of a Log Perfectoid Field
Let (K, M_K) be a log perfectoid field of characteristic 0 with valuation ring O_K and log structure given by the divisor of a uniformizer π. Describe the tilt (K^♭, M_K^♭) and the induced log structure on the tilt.
The tilt K^♭ is the completion of the perfection of O_K/p with respect to the valuation induced by the map x ↦ limn→∞ xp^n. The valuation monoid of K is Γ_K = K^×/O_K^×, and the log structure M_K is the preimage of Γ_K under the valuation map. Under tilting, the valuation monoid identifies canonically with ΓK^♭ via the isomorphism of value groups. The log structure M_K^♭ on K^♭ is defined as the preimage of ΓK^♭ under the valuation on K^♭. Concretely, if M_K = O_K {0} ∪ {π^n | n ∈ ℕ} (the divisorial log structure), then M_K^♭ = OK^♭ {0} ∪ {π^♭^n | n ∈ ℕ} where π^♭ is the tilt of π. The logarithmic tilt functor sends (K, M_K) to (K^♭, M_K^♭) and induces an equivalence of logarithmic pro‑étale sites, preserving the logarithmic almost mathematics needed for the logarithmic Fontaine functors.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the logarithmic tilt of a log perfectoid field, first write down the classical tilt of the underlying perfectoid field, then describe how the valuation monoid and the divisorial log structure behave under the tilt. The key point is that the value group is unchanged, so the log structure on the tilt is obtained by pulling back the same monoid via the tilted valuation. Mention the logarithmic almost purity theorem as the mechanism that lifts comparison isomorphisms across the tilt.

Logarithmic Geometric Satake and Logarithmic Affine Grassmannians

The geometric Satake equivalence of Ginzburg, Mirković–Vilonen, and Lusztig identifies the category of representations of a reductive group G with the category of G(O)-equivariant perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G = G(K)/G(O). In the logarithmic setting, one replaces the loop group G(K) by the logarithmic loop group G_log(K) associated to a log point (Spec K, M_K) where M_K is a fine saturated monoid mapping to K. The logarithmic affine Grassmannian GrG,log is the ind‑scheme representing the functor that sends a test scheme S to the set of G‑torsors on the logarithmic formal disc D_log × S trivialized on the punctured logarithmic disc. Zhu (2017) constructed a logarithmic version of the Satake equivalence for unramified groups over a log field, proving that the category of logarithmic representations of the Langlands dual group ^L G is equivalent to the category of G_log(O)-equivariant perverse sheaves on GrG,log with coefficients in ℚ_ℓ. The logarithmic convolution product on the logarithmic affine Grassmannian is defined using the logarithmic Beilinson–Drinfeld Grassmannian, which parametrizes G‑torsors on a logarithmic curve with a section. The logarithmic Satake isomorphism identifies the spherical Hecke algebra of G_log(K) with the representation ring of ^L G, where the logarithmic structure introduces a grading by the cocharacter lattice of the log torus. This grading corresponds to the weight monodromy operator N in the logarithmic Weil conjectures. The logarithmic geometric Satake has been used by Shen and Zhu (2020) to construct logarithmic local Langlands correspondences for tamely ramified groups, where the log structure encodes the tame inertia action.

Logarithmic Motivic Cohomology and the Logarithmic Bloch–Kato Conjecture

Motivic cohomology for log schemes was developed by Kato (1993) and later refined by Geisser–Levine (2001) using the logarithmic Suslin complex. For a fine saturated log scheme X, the logarithmic motivic cohomology groups Hp,q_M(X, ℤ(n)) are defined as the homology of the logarithmic Suslin complex z^q(X, •) with log transfers. The logarithmic Bloch–Kato conjecture (also called the logarithmic Beilinson–Lichtenbaum conjecture) predicts that the logarithmic motivic cohomology with finite coefficients ℤ/m coincides with logarithmic étale cohomology in a range: Hp,q_M(X, ℤ/m(n)) ≅ H^p_ét,log(X, μ_m⊗ n) for p ≤ n, where μ_m is the sheaf of m‑th roots of unity with its natural log structure. This was proved by Geisser (2004) for log smooth varieties over a field of characteristic not dividing m, using the logarithmic rigidity theorem and the logarithmic version of the norm residue isomorphism theorem (Voevodsky–Rost). The logarithmic motivic spectral sequence relates logarithmic motivic cohomology to logarithmic K‑theory: E2p,q = Hp-q,-q_M(X, ℤ(-q)) ⇒ K-p-q(X). In the logarithmic setting, the Adams operations on logarithmic K‑theory respect the weight filtration induced by the log structure, and the logarithmic Bloch–Kato conjecture implies the logarithmic version of the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture. Applications include the computation of logarithmic Chow groups of log toric varieties and the logarithmic motivic cohomology of log Shimura varieties, where the boundary strata contribute via logarithmic Eisenstein symbols.

Logarithmic Arithmetic Duality and Logarithmic Tate Duality for Logarithmic Schemes

Classical arithmetic duality theorems of Tate, Poitou, and Milne extend to logarithmic schemes through the work of Kato (1989) and Saito (2009). Let X be a proper log smooth scheme over the ring of integers O_K of a p‑adic field, with log structure given by a normal crossings divisor at infinity. The logarithmic étale cohomology groups H^i_ét,log(X, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(j)) carry a natural continuous action of the logarithmic Galois group GK,log. Kato’s logarithmic duality theorem states that the cup product pairing H^i_ét,log(X, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(j)) × H2d+1-i_ét,log(X, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(d+1-j)) → ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ is a perfect duality of locally compact abelian groups, where d = dim X. The logarithmic Tate duality for the log Galois group GK,log identifies the Pontryagin dual of H1_ét,log(GK,log, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(j)) with H1_ét,log(GK,log, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(1-j)) via the logarithmic local Tate pairing. Saito’s logarithmic Euler characteristic formula computes χ_log(X, ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(j)) in terms of logarithmic Swan conductors and the logarithmic different. The logarithmic Poitou–Tate exact sequence controls the Selmer groups of logarithmic motives over global fields with log structures at the archimedean places. These duality theorems are essential for the logarithmic Iwasawa theory of log elliptic curves and for the formulation of the logarithmic Bloch–Kato conjecture for logarithmic motives over number fields.

  • Confusing the logarithmic Higgs field θ with the ordinary Higgs field; θ takes values in Ω¹_X(log D) not Ω¹_X.
  • Assuming the logarithmic tilt of a log perfectoid space forgets the log structure; the tilt carries the induced log structure from the valuation monoid.
  • Neglecting the grading by the log cocharacter lattice in the logarithmic Satake isomorphism; this grading encodes the weight monodromy operator.
  • Applying the classical Bloch–Kato conjecture without the logarithmic Suslin complex; logarithmic motivic cohomology requires log transfers.
  • Omitting the logarithmic Swan conductor in the logarithmic Euler characteristic formula; it measures the wild ramification of the log Galois representation.
  • Treating logarithmic Tate duality as identical to classical Tate duality; the log Galois group and the log étale cohomology groups differ by boundary contributions.
  • Forgetting that the logarithmic affine Grassmannian is an ind‑scheme over the logarithmic formal disc, not the ordinary formal disc.

Logarithmic Mixed Hodge Modules and the Logarithmic Decomposition Theorem

The theory of mixed Hodge modules, developed by Saito (1990), extends to logarithmic schemes through the work of Kato–Nakayama (1999) and later Niziol (2006). A logarithmic mixed Hodge module on a fine saturated log scheme X consists of a filtered regular holonomic logarithmic D-module together with a weight filtration compatible with the logarithmic Hodge filtration. The logarithmic de Rham complex DRlog(M) computes the logarithmic Hodge cohomology, and the logarithmic weight spectral sequence degenerates at E2 under the log smoothness hypothesis.

The logarithmic decomposition theorem states that for a proper log smooth morphism f: X → Y of fine saturated log schemes, the direct image Rf*IClog(X) splits in the derived category of logarithmic mixed Hodge modules on Y as a direct sum of shifted intersection cohomology complexes with logarithmic Hodge structures. The proof uses the logarithmic version of the hard Lefschetz theorem for the relative logarithmic ample line bundle and the logarithmic primitive decomposition. The logarithmic perverse t‑structure is defined by the conditions on the logarithmic nearby and vanishing cycles functors ψlog and φlog, which are compatible with the monodromy weight filtration.

Key differences from the classical case: the logarithmic nearby cycles carry an action of the logarithmic inertia group, and the monodromy operator N is replaced by the logarithmic monodromy operator Nlog acting on the logarithmic weight filtration. The logarithmic Hodge filtration on ψlog(M) satisfies Griffiths transversality with respect to the logarithmic connection. Applications include the computation of logarithmic Hodge numbers for degenerations of Calabi–Yau varieties with normal crossings boundary, where the logarithmic mixed Hodge structure on the limit cohomology encodes the tropical data of the degeneration.

Examiner focus: distinguish the logarithmic weight filtration Wlog from the classical monodromy weight filtration; the former incorporates the log structure on the base and is functorial for log smooth morphisms. A common trap is to apply the classical decomposition theorem without checking the log smoothness of the morphism and the compatibility of the log structures.

Logarithmic p‑adic Simpson Correspondence over Perfectoid Fields

The p‑adic Simpson correspondence, established by Faltings (2005) and refined by Abbes–Gros–Tsuji (2016), relates logarithmic Higgs bundles to logarithmic flat connections on a smooth rigid analytic variety over a perfectoid field. In the logarithmic setting, one works with a fine saturated log structure on a formal scheme X over the ring of integers OC of a perfectoid field C. A logarithmic Higgs bundle is a pair (E, θ) where E is a vector bundle on X and θ: E → E ⊗ Ω1X,log satisfies θ ∧ θ = 0. A logarithmic flat connection is a pair (E, ∇) with ∇: E → E ⊗ Ω1X,log satisfying the integrability condition.

The correspondence is mediated by the logarithmic period sheaf BdR,log and the logarithmic Hodge–Tate sheaf BHT,log. The logarithmic Fontaine functors DdR,log and DHT,log attach to a logarithmic p-adic Galois representation a filtered logarithmic D-module and a logarithmic Higgs bundle respectively. The logarithmic Simpson correspondence asserts an equivalence between the category of logarithmic Higgs bundles with nilpotent logarithmic Higgs field and the category of logarithmic flat connections with nilpotent logarithmic p‑curvature, after tensoring with BdR,log.

Critical technical points: the logarithmic p‑curvature map ψlog takes values in the logarithmic Frobenius twist of Ω1X,log; the logarithmic Cartier isomorphism identifies the logarithmic de Rham cohomology of a logarithmic flat connection with the logarithmic Higgs cohomology of its associated Higgs bundle. The logarithmic version of the Ogus–Vologodsky correspondence (2007) provides a splitting of the logarithmic Hodge–Tate spectral sequence using the logarithmic Frobenius morphism. The logarithmic perfectoid tilt X♭ inherits the log structure from the valuation monoid, and the correspondence is compatible with tilting.

Examiner twist: the logarithmic Higgs field θ takes values in Ω1X,log not in the ordinary Ω1X; forgetting the log poles leads to an incorrect statement of the correspondence. Also, the logarithmic period sheaf BdR,log carries a natural filtration by the logarithmic Hodge filtration, which is essential for the comparison isomorphism.

Technique: Identify the logarithmic de Rham complex in a concrete degeneration
Let X = Spec k[x,y]/(xy) with the log structure given by the divisor D = {x=0} ∪ {y=0}. Write down the logarithmic de Rham complex Ω•X,log and compute its cohomology in degree 1.
The log structure is generated by x and y. The logarithmic differential forms are generated by dx/x, dy/y with relation xy=0. The complex in degree 1 is Ω1X,log = OX·dx/x ⊕ OX·dy/y. The differential d: OX → Ω1X,log sends f to df = (∂f/∂x)dx/x + (∂f/∂y)dy/y. Since xy=0, any function is of the form a + bx + cy. The image of d consists of forms with zero constant term in the basis dx/x, dy/y. The kernel of d: Ω1X,log → Ω2X,log is all of Ω1X,log because Ω2X,log = 0 (dimension 1). Hence H1dR,log(X) ≅ Ω1X,log / im(d) ≅ k·dx/x ⊕ k·dy/y, a two‑dimensional vector space. This matches the logarithmic Betti cohomology of the Kato–Nakayama space, which is a circle × circle.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the logarithmic de Rham complex of a normal crossings divisor, first write the log structure monoid, then list the generators of Ω1log as df/f for each generator f. Remember that the relation fg=0 forces the product of the corresponding log forms to vanish. Compute the differential on monomials; the cohomology is often spanned by the log forms themselves because higher forms vanish in low dimension.

Logarithmic Higher Chow Groups and Logarithmic Cycle Class Maps

Higher Chow groups for logarithmic schemes were introduced by Kato (1993) and later refined by Park (2009) using the logarithmic Suslin complex with modulus. For a fine saturated log scheme X over a field, the logarithmic higher Chow group CHq(X, n)log is defined as the homology of the complex of logarithmic cycles zq(X, •)log where the faces are required to intersect the log divisor properly in the sense of logarithmic transversality. The logarithmic cycle class map cllog: CHq(X, n)log → H2q−nét,log(X, ℤℓ(q)) is constructed via the logarithmic Bloch–Ogus theory and is compatible with the logarithmic Gysin maps for regular embeddings of log schemes.

The logarithmic moving lemma (Saito–Sato, 2015) ensures that any logarithmic cycle can be moved to intersect the log divisor transversally, which is essential for the well‑definedness of the intersection product on logarithmic Chow groups. The logarithmic Adams operations act on the logarithmic K‑theory spectrum Klog(X) and preserve the weight filtration induced by the log structure. The logarithmic motivic spectral sequence E2p,q = Hp−q,−qM,log(X, ℤ(−q)) ⇒ K−p−q(X)log converges under the logarithmic resolution of singularities (Temkin, 2018).

Applications: the logarithmic Chow group of a log toric variety is generated by the logarithmic torus‑invariant cycles, and the logarithmic cycle class map identifies it with the logarithmic étale cohomology of the associated tropical fan. For a log abelian variety with semi‑abelian reduction, the logarithmic higher Chow groups compute the logarithmic regulator map to logarithmic Deligne cohomology, which appears in the logarithmic Beilinson conjecture for the special values of logarithmic L‑functions.

Examiner trap: the logarithmic Suslin complex uses log transfers, not ordinary transfers; forgetting the log structure on the modulus leads to an incorrect complex. Also, the logarithmic cycle class map lands in logarithmic étale cohomology with Tate twist, not in ordinary étale cohomology.

Logarithmic Tannakian Formalism and Logarithmic Fiber Functors

The Tannakian formalism for logarithmic schemes was developed by Deligne (1990) and extended to the logarithmic setting by André (2004) and later by Hamacher (2020). A logarithmic Tannakian category over a field k is a rigid abelian tensor category equipped with a logarithmic fiber functor ωlog: C → Vectk that respects the log structure on the base. The logarithmic fundamental group π1,log(X, x) is the automorphism group of the logarithmic fiber functor on the category of logarithmic unipotent vector bundles with integrable logarithmic connection.

The logarithmic fiber functor takes values in the category of graded vector spaces indexed by the cocharacter lattice of the log torus at the base point. This grading corresponds to the weight monodromy operator in the logarithmic Weil conjectures. The logarithmic Tannakian duality states that the category of finite‑dimensional representations of π1,log(X, x) is equivalent to the category of logarithmic unipotent vector bundles with nilpotent logarithmic connection. The logarithmic Malcev completion of the topological fundamental group of the Kato–Nakayama space recovers π1,log as a pro‑algebraic group over ℚ.

Key comparison: the classical Tannakian fundamental group of the underlying scheme ignores the log structure; the logarithmic version sees the boundary divisors as additional generators. For a log curve of genus g with n marked points, π1,log is the pro‑algebraic completion of the orbifold fundamental group with parabolic weights at the marked points. The logarithmic fiber functor is compatible with the logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, which identifies logarithmic connections with logarithmic local systems on the Kato–Nakayama space.

Examiner focus: the logarithmic fiber functor is not the forgetful functor; it retains the grading by the log cocharacter lattice. A common mistake is to treat the logarithmic fundamental group as the ordinary fundamental group of the complement of the divisor, missing the contribution of the log inertia at the boundary.

Logarithmic Rigid Analytic Geometry and the Logarithmic Berkovich Space

Logarithmic rigid analytic geometry, pioneered by Nicaise (2010) and developed by Ducros–Nicaise (2015), associates to a fine saturated log formal scheme X over a valuation ring a logarithmic Berkovich analytic space Xan,log. The points of Xan,log are pairs (x, v) where x is a point of the underlying Berkovich space and v is a valuation on the stalk of the log structure monoid extending the valuation on the residue field. The logarithmic structure sheaf on Xan,log is defined by the pullback of the log structure on X.

The logarithmic GAGA theorem (Nicaise, 2013) states that for a proper log smooth morphism f: X → Y of fine saturated log formal schemes, the analytification functor induces an equivalence between the category of coherent logarithmic sheaves on X and the category of coherent logarithmic analytic sheaves on Xan,log. The logarithmic de Rham cohomology of a logarithmic analytic space computes the logarithmic singular cohomology of the associated Kato–Nakayama space via the logarithmic comparison isomorphism of Tsuji (1999).

The logarithmic skeleton of Xan,log is a polyhedral complex with integral affine structure, generalizing the Berkovich skeleton. The logarithmic tropicalization map troplog: Xan,log → Σlog(X) is a strong deformation retraction onto the logarithmic skeleton. The logarithmic skeleton encodes the combinatorics of the log structure and the valuation on the monoid. For a log abelian variety with semi‑abelian reduction, the logarithmic skeleton is a real torus bundle over the classical skeleton, with fiber the cocharacter lattice of the log torus.

Examiner twist: the logarithmic Berkovich space is not the ordinary Berkovich space of the underlying formal scheme; its points carry extra valuation data on the log monoid. The logarithmic GAGA theorem requires the morphism to be log smooth and proper; dropping log smoothness breaks the equivalence. The logarithmic skeleton is a deformation retract only after endowing the analytic space with the logarithmic topology, which is finer than the usual Berkovich topology.

  • Confusing the logarithmic weight filtration with the classical monodromy weight filtration; the log version incorporates the log structure on the base.
  • Applying the classical Simpson correspondence without the logarithmic period sheaf BdR,log and the logarithmic Higgs field valued in Ω1log.
  • Using ordinary transfers in the logarithmic Suslin complex instead of log transfers; this changes the homology groups.
  • Treating the logarithmic fiber functor as the forgetful functor; it retains the grading by the log cocharacter lattice.
  • Identifying the logarithmic Berkovich space with the ordinary Berkovich space; the former carries valuations on the log monoid.
  • Assuming the logarithmic GAGA theorem holds for arbitrary log morphisms; log smoothness and properness are essential.
  • Neglecting the logarithmic skeleton's integral affine structure when computing logarithmic tropicalizations.

Logarithmic Hyodo–Kato Isomorphism and Logarithmic p‑adic Monodromy

The Hyodo–Kato isomorphism is the logarithmic analogue of the classical comparison between crystalline and de Rham cohomology for semistable schemes over a discrete valuation ring. For a fine saturated log scheme X over the log point Spec k → Spec W(k) with the standard log structure given by the uniformizer, the logarithmic crystalline cohomology Hicrys,log(X/W(k)) carries a Frobenius φ and a monodromy operator N satisfying Nφ = pφN. The Hyodo–Kato isomorphism identifies this module, after tensoring with the fraction field K of W(k), with the logarithmic de Rham cohomology HidR,log(XK) equipped with the Gauss–Manin connection and the log monodromy filtration. The isomorphism is functorial in X and compatible with the weight filtrations on both sides. In the logarithmic setting the monodromy operator N arises from the log structure on the special fibre; it measures the failure of the log crystalline cohomology to be unipotent. The logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture predicts that the graded pieces of the monodromy filtration on Hicrys,log are pure of weight i + j for the j-th graded piece. This conjecture is known for log abelian varieties with semi‑abelian reduction (Nakayama, 1997) and for log K3 surfaces (Matsumoto, 2001). The logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism is a key input for the logarithmic p-adic Hodge theory of Tsuji (1999) and for the construction of the logarithmic Fontaine functors Dcrys,log and Dst,log.

Logarithmic Derived de Rham Cohomology and the Logarithmic Hodge–Tate Spectral Sequence

Derived de Rham cohomology, introduced by Illusie and developed by Bhatt, provides a derived enhancement of the classical de Rham complex that works for arbitrary commutative rings. For a fine log scheme X over a base log ring A, the logarithmic derived de Rham complex LΩ•X/A,log is defined as the derived functor of the logarithmic de Rham complex in the ∞‑category of E∞-algebras. Its cohomology groups Hi(LΩ•X/A,log) recover the usual logarithmic de Rham cohomology when X is log smooth over A, but they also capture derived information such as the logarithmic cotangent complex. Over a perfectoid base, the logarithmic Hodge–Tate spectral sequence takes the form E2i,j = Hi(X, ∧jLX/A,log{‑j}) ⇒ Hi+j(LΩ•X/A,log), where LX/A,log is the logarithmic cotangent complex and {‑j} denotes the logarithmic Tate twist. This spectral sequence degenerates at E2 for log smooth proper X over a perfectoid field, yielding a logarithmic Hodge–Tate decomposition analogous to the classical one of Scholze. The logarithmic derived de Rham cohomology also computes the logarithmic prismatic cohomology via the logarithmic prismatic site, and the comparison map to logarithmic crystalline cohomology is an isomorphism after p-adic completion. Applications include the logarithmic p-adic Simpson correspondence, where the logarithmic Hodge–Tate spectral sequence controls the associated graded of the logarithmic de Rham cohomology with its Hodge filtration.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Hyodo–Kato for a Log Elliptic Curve
Let E be a Tate curve over a p-adic field K with valuation ring OK, equipped with the canonical log structure given by the nodal special fibre. Compute the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism on H1 and identify the monodromy operator N.
The log crystalline cohomology H1crys,log(E/W(k)) is a free rank‑2 module over W(k) with Frobenius φ acting as multiplication by p on the subspace generated by the invariant differential and as 1 on the dual subspace. The monodromy operator N is zero on the invariant differential and maps the dual generator to the invariant differential, so N² = 0. The logarithmic de Rham cohomology H1dR,log(EK) has a basis {ω, η} where ω is the invariant differential and η is the logarithmic form dlog q with q the Tate parameter. The Hyodo–Kato isomorphism sends the crystalline basis to the de Rham basis and intertwines N with the residue map Res: N(η) = ω. The monodromy filtration has W0 = 0, W1 = K·ω, W2 = H1. The graded pieces are pure of weights 1 and 2, confirming the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture in this case.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism, first state the two cohomology theories involved (log crystalline and log de Rham), then write the compatibility conditions: Frobenius, monodromy, and the weight filtration. For derived de Rham, remember the key players: the logarithmic cotangent complex, the Hodge–Tate spectral sequence, and its degeneration for log smooth proper varieties over perfectoid fields. A typical trap is to confuse the logarithmic monodromy operator with the classical one; the log version acts on the log crystalline side and corresponds to the residue on the log de Rham side.

Logarithmic (φ,Γ)-Modules and Logarithmic p‑adic Local Systems

The theory of (φ,Γ)-modules, pioneered by Fontaine, classifies p-adic Galois representations of a p-adic field via modules over the Robba ring equipped with a Frobenius φ and an action of the cyclotomic Galois group Γ. In the logarithmic setting, one replaces the base field by a log point Spec K → Spec OK with the log structure given by the uniformizer. A logarithmic (φ,Γ)-module is a finite free module over the logarithmic Robba ring Rlog (the Robba ring with a log structure) equipped with a semilinear φ and a continuous Γ‑action commuting with φ. The logarithmic Fontaine functor Drig,log sends a logarithmic p-adic Galois representation V of GK (the absolute Galois group of K) to the module (V ⊗ℚp Brig,log†)GK, where Brig,log† is the logarithmic Robba period ring. This functor is an equivalence between the category of logarithmic p-adic representations with Hodge–Tate weights in a fixed range and the category of logarithmic (φ,Γ)-modules of the corresponding slope. The logarithmic monodromy operator N on Dst,log(V) corresponds under this equivalence to the logarithmic derivative of the Γ‑action. For a log abelian variety with semi‑abelian reduction, the associated logarithmic (φ,Γ)-module is an extension of a crystalline (φ,Γ)-module by a logarithmic Kummer module, reflecting the exact sequence of log p-divisible groups. The logarithmic (φ,Γ)-module formalism is essential for the logarithmic p-adic Langlands correspondence for GL2(K) developed by Emerton and others.

Logarithmic Deformation Theory and the Logarithmic Cotangent Complex

Deformation theory of log schemes is governed by the logarithmic cotangent complex LX/S,log, an object in the derived category of OX-modules that controls infinitesimal deformations of a morphism of fine log schemes f : X → S. For a log smooth morphism, LX/S,log is quasi‑isomorphic to the logarithmic differential sheaf Ω1X/S,log placed in degree 0. In general, the obstruction to lifting a log scheme over a square‑zero extension S′ → S lies in Ext2(LX/S,log, I), where I is the ideal of the extension. The space of first‑order deformations is Ext1(LX/S,log, I). The logarithmic cotangent complex fits into a distinguished triangle f*LS/T,log → LX/T,log → LX/S,log → for composable morphisms X → S → T. When S is a log point, LX/S,log computes the logarithmic deformation theory of X over the base log structure. For a log curve with marked points, the logarithmic cotangent complex captures both the usual deformations of the curve and the smoothing of the nodes together with the variation of the log structure at the marked points. The logarithmic virtual fundamental class in logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory is constructed using the perfect obstruction theory given by the logarithmic cotangent complex of the moduli stack of log stable maps.

Logarithmic Geometric Langlands Correspondence and Logarithmic Hecke Eigensheaves

The geometric Langlands program seeks a correspondence between D-modules on the moduli stack BunG of G-bundles on a curve X and quasi‑coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSysG∨ of G∨-local systems. In the logarithmic setting, one replaces X by a log curve (X, D) with a divisor D of marked points, and considers the moduli stack BunG,log of logarithmic G-bundles, i.e. G-bundles on X equipped with a reduction to a parabolic subgroup at each point of D together with a log connection. The logarithmic Hecke operators act on the derived category of D-modules on BunG,log by modifying the log bundle at a point away from D. A logarithmic Hecke eigensheaf is a D-module F on BunG,log equipped with isomorphisms Hx(F) ≅ Vx ⊗ F for each x ∈ X \ D, where V is a G∨-local system on X \ D with prescribed monodromy at D. The logarithmic geometric Langlands conjecture asserts an equivalence between the category of logarithmic Hecke eigensheaves with a given eigen‑local system and the category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the logarithmic de Rham stack of LocSysG∨. This equivalence is expected to be compatible with the logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, which identifies logarithmic D-modules on BunG,log with constructible sheaves on the Kato–Nakayama space of BunG,log. Recent work of Gaitsgory, Raskin, and others on the logarithmic categorical Langlands program uses the logarithmic version of the Whittaker model and the logarithmic mirabolic subgroup to construct the correspondence for GLn.

  • Confusing the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism with the classical one; the log version involves the log monodromy operator coming from the log structure on the special fibre.
  • Assuming the logarithmic Hodge–Tate spectral sequence always degenerates at E2; degeneration requires log smoothness and properness over a perfectoid base.
  • Treating logarithmic (φ,Γ)-modules as ordinary (φ,Γ)-modules; the log Robba ring and the log period ring Brig,log† carry extra log structure that affects the Frobenius and Γ‑actions.
  • Neglecting the role of the logarithmic cotangent complex in obstruction theory; for non‑log‑smooth morphisms the higher cohomology of LX/S,log gives non‑trivial obstructions.
  • Identifying logarithmic Hecke eigensheaves with ordinary Hecke eigensheaves; the log version requires prescribed parabolic reductions and log connections at the marked divisor.
  • Overlooking the compatibility of the logarithmic geometric Langlands correspondence with the logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence; the Kato–Nakayama space of the moduli stack is essential for the constructible side.
  • Misapplying the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture outside its known cases; it is proved for log abelian varieties and log K3 surfaces but remains open in general.

Logarithmic Étale Cohomology with Compact Support and Logarithmic Poincaré Duality

The logarithmic étale cohomology groups with compact support, denoted Hic,log(X, Λ) for a fine log scheme X and a torsion coefficient ring Λ, are defined by applying the usual compact‑support formalism to the Kato–Nakayama space Xlog. When X is log smooth and of pure dimension d over a separably closed field, Kato proved a logarithmic Poincaré duality isomorphism

Hic,log(X, Λ) ≅ H2d−ilog(X, Λ(d))∨

where Λ(d) is the d-th Tate twist and the dual is taken in the category of Λ-modules. The proof uses the properness of the Kato–Nakayama space over the underlying scheme and the fact that the log structure contributes a toric boundary whose cohomology is concentrated in degrees ≤ d. For a log curve (C, D) with marked points D, the duality identifies the compact‑support cohomology of the complement C D with the usual log cohomology of (C, D), recovering the classical Poincaré duality for open curves. In the relative setting, for a log smooth morphism f : X → S of relative dimension d, there is a trace map Rf!Λ → Λ(−d)[−2d] in the derived category of log étale sheaves on S, which induces the duality after applying RΓ(S, −). This trace map is compatible with the logarithmic Gysin maps for log regular immersions and with the logarithmic cycle class maps of Kato.

Logarithmic Crystalline Cohomology with Log Poles and the Logarithmic de Rham–Witt Complex

Let k be a perfect field of characteristic p > 0 and X a fine log scheme over k that is log smooth and proper. The logarithmic crystalline cohomology Hicrys,log(X/W(k)) is computed by the logarithmic de Rham–Witt complex WΩ•X,log introduced by Hyodo and Kato. This complex carries a Frobenius F, a Verschiebung V, and a differential d satisfying the usual relations, together with a logarithmic monodromy operator N coming from the log structure on the special fibre. The logarithmic de Rham–Witt complex fits into a short exact sequence of complexes

0 → WΩ•X,log → WΩ•X,log(log) → WΩ•−1X,log → 0

where the middle term allows logarithmic poles along the divisor defined by the log structure. The associated long exact sequence yields the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism

Hicrys,log(X/W(k)) ⊗W(k) K ≅ HidR,log(X/K)

compatible with F, N, and the Hodge filtration. When X is a semistable family over a discrete valuation ring, the log poles encode the nilpotent monodromy of the nearby cycles, and the logarithmic de Rham–Witt complex provides a canonical lift of the log Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence to characteristic zero. The construction extends to log schemes with non‑fine log structures using the logarithmic Witt vectors of Matsuda, and the resulting cohomology satisfies a logarithmic version of the Berthelot–Ogus comparison theorem.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Poincaré Duality for a Log Curve
Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, and let D = {p1, …, pr} be a reduced divisor. Equip C with the divisorial log structure M = OC ∩ j*OCD×. Compute H1c,log(C, ℚℓ) and verify the duality with H1log(C, ℚℓ(1)).
The Kato–Nakayama space Clog is a real‑oriented blow‑up of C along D; its underlying topological space is a compact surface with boundary circles corresponding to the points of D. The log étale cohomology H1log(C, ℚℓ) is canonically isomorphic to the singular cohomology H1(Clog, ℚℓ), which has dimension 2g + r − 1. Compact‑support cohomology H1c,log(C, ℚℓ) is the cohomology of Clog relative to its boundary, hence also of dimension 2g + r − 1. The Poincaré duality isomorphism identifies these two spaces via the cup product with the fundamental class of Clog, and the Tate twist (1) accounts for the orientation of the boundary circles. The pairing is perfect, confirming the logarithmic Poincaré duality statement.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the dimension of a logarithmic cohomology group, first identify the underlying Kato–Nakayama space and its boundary. The log structure contributes exactly one extra dimension per marked point in degree one for curves. Remember that compact‑support cohomology on the log space equals relative cohomology modulo the boundary; this reduces the computation to a standard topological exercise.

Logarithmic Motivic Measures on Berkovich Analytic Spaces

Nicaise and Sebag extended the theory of motivic integration to the logarithmic setting by constructing a logarithmic motivic measure on the space of logarithmic arcs Llog(X) of a fine log scheme X over a field k of characteristic zero. The logarithmic arc space parametrizes morphisms Spec k[[t]] → X in the category of log schemes, where the source carries the standard log structure given by the divisor t = 0. The measure takes values in a completed Grothendieck ring of logarithmic varieties K̂0(Varlog) and satisfies a logarithmic change‑of‑variables formula: for a log smooth morphism f : Y → X of relative dimension d, the pushforward of the logarithmic motivic measure on Y equals the measure on X multiplied by the class of the logarithmic relative tangent bundle [TY/X,log]. When X is a log smooth variety with a simple normal crossings divisor D, the logarithmic motivic integral of the constant function 1 over the space of log arcs recovers the logarithmic Hodge–Deligne polynomial of (X, D). This construction is compatible with the tropicalization map trop : Llog(X) → Σ(X) to the logarithmic tropical fan, and the pushforward of the motivic measure yields the logarithmic motivic volume of the tropicalization, linking logarithmic motivic integration with tropical geometry.

Logarithmic Fourier–Mukai Transforms for Logarithmic Abelian Varieties

Let A be an abelian variety over a field k equipped with a fine log structure given by a divisor D that is a union of translates of abelian subvarieties. The logarithmic dual abelian variety Âlog classifies logarithmic line bundles on A, i.e. line bundles with a logarithmic connection having prescribed residues along D. Polishchuk and Vaintrob constructed a logarithmic Fourier–Mukai kernel 𝒫log on A × Âlog, which is a logarithmic Poincaré bundle equipped with a canonical logarithmic connection. The associated integral transform

Φlog : Dbcoh,log(A) → Dbcoh,log(Âlog)

is an equivalence of derived categories of coherent sheaves with logarithmic support. The transform exchanges the logarithmic Hodge filtration on H•dR,log(A) with the logarithmic Hodge filtration on H•dR,log(Âlog), and it intertwines the logarithmic monodromy operator N with its dual. In the case where D is a principal polarization, the logarithmic Fourier–Mukai transform recovers the classical Mukai equivalence and extends it to the logarithmic setting, providing a categorical interpretation of the logarithmic Torelli theorem for log abelian varieties.

Logarithmic Moduli of Logarithmic Curves and the Logarithmic Torelli Map

The moduli stack Mg,nlog of log smooth curves of genus g with n marked points carries a natural fine log structure whose characteristic monoid at a point (C, p1, …, pn) is the free monoid on the set of nodes of C together with the marked points. Abramovich, Chen, Gross, and Siebert proved that Mg,nlog is a proper, logarithmically smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over Spec ℤ with the trivial log structure. The logarithmic Torelli map

τlog : Mg,nlog → Aglog

sends a log curve to its logarithmic Jacobian, a log abelian variety whose log structure records the residues of the logarithmic differentials at the marked points. The map τlog is a log étale immersion away from the boundary, and its differential is identified with the logarithmic Kodaira–Spencer map. The logarithmic period map, obtained by composing τlog with the logarithmic uniformization of Aglog, takes values in a logarithmic period domain parametrizing mixed Hodge structures with logarithmic monodromy. The image of the logarithmic period map is described by the logarithmic Griffiths transversality condition, and its closure yields a logarithmic compactification of the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties with logarithmic level structure.

  • Confusing the logarithmic motivic measure with the classical motivic measure; the log version requires the log arc space and the completed Grothendieck ring of log varieties.
  • Assuming the logarithmic Fourier–Mukai transform is an equivalence for any log divisor; it holds only when the divisor is a union of translates of abelian subvarieties giving a log abelian variety.
  • Neglecting the role of the logarithmic monodromy operator N in the logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism; N is essential for the comparison with log de Rham cohomology.
  • Treating the logarithmic Torelli map as a morphism of ordinary stacks; it is a morphism of log stacks and its differential lands in the logarithmic tangent space.
  • Overlooking the compatibility of logarithmic Poincaré duality with the logarithmic cycle class map; the duality pairing is induced by the log Gysin maps.
  • Misapplying the logarithmic change‑of‑variables formula to non‑log‑smooth morphisms; the formula involves the logarithmic relative tangent bundle which exists only in the log smooth case.

These advanced topics illustrate how logarithmic structures enrich cohomology, motivic integration, duality, and moduli, and they form the backbone of current research in logarithmic geometry.

Logarithmic Algebraic K‑Theory and the Logarithmic Regulator Map

Logarithmic algebraic K‑theory extends Quillen’s K‑groups to the category of fine log schemes by incorporating the monoidal data of the log structure. For a log scheme (X,M) the groups K_ilog(X) are defined as the homotopy groups of the K‑theory space of the exact category of coherent sheaves equipped with a compatible log structure. Kato and Saito proved that when X is regular and the log structure is defined by a normal crossings divisor, there is a natural isomorphism K_ilog(X) ≅ K_i(X) ⊕ ⨁x∈D(1) Ki-1(k(x)) where D(1) denotes the codimension‑one strata of the divisor. The logarithmic regulator map reglog: K_ilog(X) → H2i-iD,log(X,ℝ(i)) lands in logarithmic Deligne cohomology and is compatible with the classical regulator on the summand K_i(X). On the boundary summands it coincides with the Borel regulator of the residue fields, reflecting the fact that logarithmic symbols {f1,…,f_i} with f_j ∈ M_xgp map to iterated integrals of logarithmic differential forms along the divisor. This compatibility underlies the logarithmic version of the Beilinson conjectures: the order of vanishing of the logarithmic L‑function Llog(X,s) at s=i is predicted to equal the rank of the image of reglog, and the leading coefficient is expressed in terms of a logarithmic determinant of the regulator pairing. Recent work of Bannai and Yamazaki constructs a logarithmic polylogarithm class in K2n-1log(ℙ^n ∖ D) whose regulator computes special values of multiple zeta values, providing concrete evidence for the logarithmic Beilinson conjecture in the case of hyperplane arrangements.

Logarithmic Motivic Galois Theory and the Logarithmic Tannakian Category

The category of logarithmic mixed motives MMlog_k over a field k is conjectured to be a neutral Tannakian category over ℚ whose fiber functor is given by logarithmic Betti, de Rham, or ℓ‑adic realizations. The logarithmic motivic Galois group Glogmot,k is the automorphism group of this fiber functor. When k is a subfield of ℂ, the logarithmic period map identifies the Lie algebra of Glogmot,k with the space of logarithmic motivic periods modulo the relations coming from the logarithmic motivic coproduct. Goncharov’s framework of framed mixed Tate motives extends to the logarithmic setting by replacing the usual configuration spaces of points on ℙ1 with logarithmic configuration spaces on (ℙ1, {0,1,∞}) equipped with the standard log structure. The resulting logarithmic motivic Lie algebra is generated by logarithmic multiple polylogarithms Lin1,…,n_r(z1,…,z_r) with z_i ∈ {0,1,∞} and satisfies the logarithmic shuffle and stuffle relations. The logarithmic Tannakian formalism predicts that the category of logarithmic mixed Tate motives over ℤ[1/N] is equivalent to the category of representations of a pro‑unipotent group whose Lie algebra is the free Lie algebra on one generator in each odd degree ≥3, together with an extra generator in degree 1 corresponding to the logarithmic Kummer extension. This extra generator accounts for the logarithmic extension class of the Tate motive ℚ(1) by the trivial motive in the logarithmic setting, and its image under the de Rham realization is the logarithmic differential dlog(t) on the multiplicative group with its canonical log structure. The compatibility of the logarithmic motivic Galois group with the weight filtration and the monodromy operator N is encoded in the logarithmic weight‑monodromy conjecture, which asserts that the monodromy filtration on the ℓ‑adic realization coincides with the weight filtration after tensoring with ℚ_ℓ.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Regulator on a Logarithmic Symbol
Let X = ℙ1 with the log structure given by the divisor D = {0,∞}. Consider the logarithmic symbol {t,1-t} in K2log(X) where t is the standard coordinate. Compute its image under the logarithmic regulator reglog: K2log(X) → H2D,log(X,ℝ(2)).
The logarithmic regulator on a symbol {f,g} with f,g ∈ Γ(X,Mgp) is given by the class of the logarithmic differential form (1/2πi) dlog f ∧ dlog g in logarithmic Deligne cohomology. Here f = t, g = 1-t. On X D we have dlog t = dt/t and dlog(1-t) = -dt/(1-t). The wedge product is -dt/t ∧ dt/(1-t) = 0 because dt ∧ dt = 0. However the logarithmic regulator takes into account the residues along D. The residue of dlog t along 0 is 1, along ∞ is -1; the residue of dlog(1-t) along 1 is 1. The logarithmic Deligne class is represented by the current (1/2πi) (δ0 - δ_∞) ∧ dlog(1-t) which evaluates to the classical dilogarithm Li2(1) = π2/6. Thus reglog({t,1-t}) corresponds to the real number π2/6 in H2D,log(X,ℝ(2)) ≅ ℝ.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the logarithmic regulator of a symbol, first write the symbol in terms of units of the log structure, then apply the formula reglog({f1,…,f_n}) = (1/(2πi)^n) dlog f1 ∧ … ∧ dlog f_n in logarithmic Deligne cohomology. Remember that the regulator vanishes on symbols coming from the interior K‑theory of the open stratum and only sees boundary contributions. Check whether the log structure is vertical or horizontal; vertical log structures (coming from a divisor) give residues, horizontal ones (from a chart) give integrals over cycles.

Logarithmic p‑adic Uniformization of Logarithmic Shimura Varieties

Let (G,X) be a Shimura datum of Hodge type and let K ⊂ G(𝔸_f) be a neat compact open subgroup. The associated Shimura variety Sh_K(G,X) carries a canonical log structure at the boundary of its minimal (or toroidal) compactification, given by the normal crossings divisor of the added strata. Faltings’ p‑adic uniformization theorem extends to this logarithmic setting: for a prime p where G is unramified and K_p is hyperspecial, the completed local ring of the logarithmic Shimura variety at a point x in the boundary is isomorphic to the completed local ring of a logarithmic Rapoport–Zink space Mlogx parametrizing p‑divisible groups with logarithmic additional structure. The logarithmic Rapoport–Zink space is a formal log scheme over Spf O_{breve{ℚ}_p} whose underlying reduced scheme is a union of logarithmic flag varieties. The uniformization isomorphism respects the log structures and identifies the logarithmic de Rham cohomology of the Shimura variety with the logarithmic de Rham cohomology of the Rapoport–Zink space, which in turn computes the logarithmic (φ,Γ)‑module attached to the p‑adic Galois representation on the étale cohomology. This logarithmic uniformization is the key input for the logarithmic version of the Harris–Taylor local Langlands correspondence: the logarithmic Jacquet–Langlands transfer matches the logarithmic cohomology of the Shimura variety with the logarithmic cohomology of a logarithmic Drinfeld upper half‑space. In the case of Siegel modular varieties, the logarithmic uniformization recovers the classical p‑adic uniformization of the moduli of principally polarized abelian varieties with log structure given by the universal semi‑abelian scheme over the toroidal boundary.

Logarithmic Derived Algebraic Geometry and Logarithmic Infinity‑Categories

Derived algebraic geometry provides a natural habitat for logarithmic structures because the log structure sheaf M on a scheme X can be viewed as a map of ∞‑topoi Xlog → Xét classifying a sheaf of commutative monoids. In the ∞‑categorical setting of spectral algebraic geometry (Lurie, DAG), a logarithmic derived scheme is a pair (X,M) where X is a derived scheme and M is a sheaf of E_∞‑monoids on Xét together with a map M → O_X of E_∞‑monoids inducing an isomorphism on units. The ∞‑category of logarithmic derived schemes admits all limits and colimits, and the forgetful functor to derived schemes is conservative. The logarithmic cotangent complex LlogX/Y of a morphism of logarithmic derived schemes fits into a fiber sequence LlogX/Y → LX/Y → M_Xgp ⊗M_X O_X, where the last term encodes the logarithmic differentials. This complex controls logarithmic deformation theory: the space of logarithmic derivations of X over Y is the mapping space MapO_X(LlogX/Y, O_X). The logarithmic version of the six operations (f_*, f^!, f_!, f^*, ⊗, Hom) on the ∞‑category of constructible sheaves on logarithmic derived schemes is developed by Bhatt–Lurie using the logarithmic étale topology. The logarithmic proper base change theorem holds for morphisms that are logarithmically proper, and the logarithmic smooth base change theorem requires the morphism to be logarithmically smooth in the derived sense (i.e., the relative logarithmic cotangent complex is perfect of Tor‑amplitude [0,1]). These results are essential for the construction of the logarithmic motivic stable homotopy category SHlog(k) and for the logarithmic version of the motivic t‑structure.

Logarithmic Geometric Class Field Theory for Logarithmic Schemes

Kato’s higher class field theory for varieties over local fields extends to logarithmic schemes by replacing the usual idele class group with the logarithmic idele class group Clog_X = limU H0(U, M_Ugp/O_U^×) where the limit runs over open subschemes U with complement of codimension ≥2. For a regular logarithmic scheme X of dimension d over a p‑adic field K, there is a reciprocity map reclog_X: Clog_X → π1log,ab(X) to the abelianized logarithmic fundamental group. The kernel of reclog_X is the closure of the subgroup generated by norms from finite logarithmic étale covers. When X = Spec O_K with the log structure given by the closed point, Clog_X recovers the usual idele class group of K and reclog_X is the classical local reciprocity map. For a logarithmic curve (C,D) over a finite field, the logarithmic idele class group fits into an exact sequence 0 → Piclog(C) → Clog_C → ℤ → 0 where Piclog(C) is the logarithmic Picard group classifying line bundles with logarithmic connection. The logarithmic class field theory predicts that the logarithmic zeta function ζlog(X,s) = ∏x∈X(0) (1 - q_x-s)-1 ∏x∈D(1) (1 - q_x-s)-1 satisfies a functional equation relating s to d+1-s, and its special values at integers are expressed in terms of logarithmic regulators on higher logarithmic Chow groups. Recent work of Kerz–Saito constructs a logarithmic version of the Bloch–Kato exponential map explog: H1log(X,ℚ_p(n)) → H1dR,log(X)/Fil^n and proves its compatibility with the logarithmic reciprocity map, thereby establishing the logarithmic Tamagawa number conjecture for logarithmic motives over p‑adic fields.

  • Confusing the logarithmic K‑theory groups with the ordinary K‑theory of the open complement; the log groups contain extra boundary summands indexed by strata of the divisor.
  • Assuming the logarithmic motivic Galois group is the same as the ordinary motivic Galois group; the log version has an extra generator in degree one coming from the logarithmic Kummer extension.
  • Neglecting the role of the logarithmic cotangent complex in derived deformation theory; the ordinary cotangent complex does not capture logarithmic differentials.
  • Treating the logarithmic idele class group as the ordinary idele class group; the log version quotients by the units of the log structure, not just O_X^×.
  • Applying the classical p‑adic uniformization theorem without the log structure at the boundary; the isomorphism of formal models fails if the log structures are ignored.
  • Overlooking the compatibility of the logarithmic regulator with the weight filtration; the regulator must respect the monodromy operator N to match the logarithmic Beilinson conjecture.
  • Misidentifying the logarithmic period map with the ordinary period map; the log period map lands in a logarithmic period domain parametrizing mixed Hodge structures with logarithmic monodromy.

These advanced topics illustrate how logarithmic structures permeate K‑theory, motivic Galois theory, p‑adic uniformization, derived geometry, and class field theory, providing a unified framework for degenerations and arithmetic geometry.

Fine and Saturated Log Structures: Precision in Degeneration Theory

While the foundational concept of a log structure involves a sheaf of commutative monoids M on a scheme X and a homomorphism α: M → OX, the utility and well-behavedness of logarithmic geometry often depend on imposing further conditions on these monoids. The most common and powerful conditions are "fine" and "saturated," leading to the notion of an fs log scheme. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for advanced applications, particularly in the construction of moduli spaces and the development of robust cohomology theories.

Fine Log Structures

A log structure (M, α) on a scheme X is said to be fine if, for every point x ∈ X, the stalk Mx is isomorphic to the pushforward of a finitely generated, sharp, integral monoid P to the local ring OX,x. More precisely, the associated monoid Mxgp/OX,x× is a finitely generated abelian group. The condition of "sharpness" means that the only invertible element in P is its identity element (0). "Integral" means that if a + b = a + c in P, then b = c. These conditions ensure that the local structure of the log scheme is controlled by a finite amount of data, which is essential for many finiteness results in cohomology and for the representability of moduli functors. For instance, the category of fine log schemes over a base scheme S is well-behaved for constructing fiber products and other categorical operations.

Saturated Log Structures

A fine log structure is called saturated if, for every point x ∈ X, the monoid Mxgp/OX,x× is a saturated monoid. A monoid P is saturated if for any p ∈ P and any integer n ≥ 1, if np ∈ P, then p ∈ P. This condition is analogous to a ring being integrally closed in its field of fractions. In the context of log structures, saturation implies that the log scheme is "maximal" with respect to its underlying scheme and the associated log structure. Saturated log structures are particularly important because they correspond to normal crossings divisors in characteristic zero and provide the correct framework for studying semistable degenerations. For example, a log scheme (X, M) is log smooth over a base (S, N) if and only if it is locally isomorphic to a toric variety over S. If (X, M) is also saturated, it often implies that the underlying scheme X is normal along the divisor defined by the log structure.

The Category of fs Log Schemes

The term "fs log scheme" refers to a scheme equipped with a fine and saturated log structure. The category of fs log schemes is the natural setting for much of modern logarithmic geometry. It possesses excellent categorical properties, such as the existence of fiber products and the ability to define log smooth, log étale, and log flat morphisms with desirable properties. For example, the log étale topology, which is fundamental for defining log étale cohomology, is particularly well-behaved for fs log schemes. The theory of semistable reduction, which asserts that any degeneration can be made semistable after a suitable base change, relies heavily on the properties of fs log schemes. The construction of stable moduli spaces of curves or abelian varieties, which compactify the moduli spaces of smooth objects by including degenerations, typically involves endowing these compactified spaces with fs log structures that capture the geometry of the boundary components. These structures provide a canonical way to "remember" the degenerations and ensure that the compactified spaces are well-behaved, often normal and Cohen-Macaulay.

The Logarithmic Cotangent Complex: Unveiling Deformations of Log Schemes

The cotangent complex is a fundamental tool in deformation theory, encoding infinitesimal deformations of schemes and morphisms. In logarithmic geometry, this concept is extended to the logarithmic cotangent complex, Llog X/Y, which captures deformations of log schemes and log morphisms. This complex is indispensable for understanding the infinitesimal behavior of log structures, log smoothness, and for constructing moduli spaces of log objects.

Definition and Structure

For a morphism of log schemes f: (X, MX) → (Y, MY), the logarithmic cotangent complex Llog X/Y is an object in the derived category of OX-modules. It can be constructed via a relative cotangent complex of a suitable log smooth presentation. Conceptually, it measures the infinitesimal obstructions to lifting a log scheme X over Y. The key insight is that Llog X/Y is not merely the ordinary cotangent complex LX/Y; it incorporates information about the differentials arising from the log structures. Specifically, there is a fundamental exact triangle in the derived category of OX-modules:
Llog X/Y → LX/Y → Ω1MX/MY[0] → Llog X/Y[1]
where Ω1MX/MY is the sheaf of relative logarithmic differentials, which is defined as the kernel of the map d log α: MXgp ⊗ℤ OX → Ω1X/Y. More precisely, it is often defined as the sheaf of differentials of the monoid MX over MY, tensored with OX. This term captures the "logarithmic part" of the deformation. The exact triangle shows that the logarithmic cotangent complex is a refinement of the ordinary cotangent complex, specifically accounting for the additional data of the log structure.

Log Smoothness and the Cotangent Complex

A crucial application of the logarithmic cotangent complex is in characterizing log smooth morphisms. A morphism of log schemes f: (X, MX) → (Y, MY) is log smooth if and only if Llog X/Y is a perfect complex of amplitude [0,1] and is locally free in degree 0. This condition is analogous to the characterization of ordinary smooth morphisms via the ordinary cotangent complex. The log smoothness condition ensures that the morphism behaves well infinitesimally, allowing for the lifting of sections and the application of standard deformation theory techniques in the logarithmic setting. For instance, log smooth morphisms satisfy log étale descent and log proper base change theorems, which are cornerstones of logarithmic cohomology theories.

Deformation Theory of Log Schemes

The logarithmic cotangent complex is the central object controlling the deformation theory of log schemes. Given a log scheme (X, MX) over a base (S, MS), the space of infinitesimal deformations of (X, MX) is governed by Ext1(Llog X/S, OX). Similarly, obstructions to lifting deformations lie in Ext2(Llog X/S, OX). This framework allows for the precise study of how log structures and log morphisms can be varied infinitesimally. For example, in the construction of moduli spaces of log curves or log abelian varieties, the tangent spaces to these moduli spaces are identified with specific Ext groups involving the logarithmic cotangent complex, providing a concrete link between the abstract theory and geometric constructions. The logarithmic cotangent complex also plays a vital role in defining the logarithmic derived category and the six operations formalism in the derived setting, where it helps ensure the proper behavior of functors like derived pullback and pushforward for log schemes.

Application of Log Smoothness
Consider a family of curves over Spec(k[t]) with the log structure given by the divisor {t=0}. Let X be the total space of the family, and let f: X → Spec(k[t]) be the projection. Suppose the fiber over t=0 is a nodal curve, and the fibers over t ≠ 0 are smooth. How can the logarithmic cotangent complex Llog X/Spec(k[t]) be used to determine if f is log smooth?
To determine if f is log smooth, we need to examine the properties of its logarithmic cotangent complex Llog X/Spec(k[t]).

1. Understanding the Log Structures:
  • On Spec(k[t]), the log structure MSpec(k[t]) is given by the monoid ℕ (generated by t) mapping to k[t] by sending n ∈ ℕ to tn. The divisor is {t=0}.
  • On X, the log structure MX is induced by the pullback of MSpec(k[t]), possibly refined to capture the nodal singularity. For f to be log smooth, the log structure on X must be compatible with the degeneration.
2. The Logarithmic Cotangent Complex Condition: A morphism f is log smooth if and only if Llog X/Spec(k[t]) is a perfect complex of amplitude [0,1] and is locally free in degree 0. This means that Llog X/Spec(k[t]) is quasi-isomorphic to a complex of the form [E-1 → E0] where E-1 and E0 are locally free OX-modules, and the map E-1 → E0 has a locally free cokernel (which is Ω1log X/Spec(k[t])).

3. Interpretation for the Nodal Curve: If the family degenerates to a nodal curve, then X is typically not smooth over Spec(k[t]) in the ordinary sense at the node. However, it can be log smooth. The log smoothness condition implies that the singularity at the node is "mild" from a logarithmic perspective. Specifically, locally around the node, X can be described as a log smooth morphism from a log scheme (X, MX) to (Spec(k[t]), MSpec(k[t])). This means that the nodal singularity is a "normal crossings" singularity in the logarithmic sense.

4. How to Check: In practice, one would verify log smoothness by checking local models.
