Subgroup Lattices and the Subgroup Lattice of a Group

The set of all subgroups of a group G, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete lattice Sub(G). The meet is intersection, and the join is the subgroup generated by the union. This lattice is always algebraic: its compact elements are precisely the finitely generated subgroups. A fundamental theorem of Dedekind states that Sub(G) is modular if and only if G is a Dedekind group, i.e. every subgroup of G is normal. Finite Dedekind groups were classified by Dedekind and Baer: they are either abelian or a direct product of the quaternion group Q8 of order 8 with an abelian group that has no element of order 4. Consequently, the subgroup lattice of a finite group is modular exactly for these groups.

Distributivity is a much stronger condition. A group whose subgroup lattice is distributive is called a locally cyclic group: every finitely generated subgroup is cyclic. For finite groups this means the group is cyclic of square‑free order, because the divisor lattice of n is distributive precisely when n is square‑free. Infinite examples include the additive group of rational numbers Q and the Prüfer p-groups. Ore proved that if two finite groups have isomorphic subgroup lattices, they need not be isomorphic; the smallest counterexample occurs at order 16. However, for finite abelian groups the subgroup lattice determines the group up to isomorphism.

The lattice Sub(G) is also a geometric lattice when G is an elementary abelian p-group (a vector space over Fp). In that case it is isomorphic to the lattice of subspaces of a finite vector space, which is modular, complemented, and has a well‑known rank function given by dimension. For a general finite group, the lattice is not necessarily semimodular; the failure of semimodularity is measured by the presence of subgroups that do not satisfy the covering property. The study of subgroup lattices connects deeply with the theory of group extensions, the Schreier refinement theorem, and the Jordan–Hölder theorem, because composition series correspond to maximal chains in Sub(G).

Ideal Lattices of Rings and Their Structure

For any ring R (associative, with unit), the set of two‑sided ideals forms a complete lattice Idl(R) under inclusion. The meet is intersection, and the join is the sum of ideals. This lattice is always modular; indeed it is a sublattice of the lattice of submodules of the left R-module R. When R is commutative, Idl(R) is a distributive lattice if and only if R is an arithmetical ring (equivalently, the localization at every maximal ideal is a valuation ring). This characterization is due to Larsen and McCarthy. For a principal ideal domain, Idl(R) is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of the ring, which is distributive. In a Dedekind domain, every non‑zero ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals, so the lattice of non‑zero ideals is a free abelian monoid under multiplication, and its order structure is a product of chains.

The lattice Idl(R) is algebraic: its compact elements are exactly the finitely generated ideals. If R is Noetherian, every ideal is finitely generated, so Idl(R) is a compactly generated lattice satisfying the ascending chain condition. The prime spectrum Spec(R), ordered by inclusion, is a sub‑poset of Idl(R) but not a sublattice (the join of two prime ideals need not be prime). The lattice of radical ideals, however, is a distributive lattice isomorphic to the lattice of closed sets of the Zariski topology on Spec(R). The Chinese Remainder Theorem translates into a lattice‑theoretic decomposition: if I and J are comaximal ideals (I+J=R), then the interval [I∩J, R] is isomorphic to the product of the intervals [I, R] and [J, R]. This product decomposition underlies the structure theory of Artinian rings, where Idl(R) is a finite direct product of local ideal lattices.

Identifying Modular but Non‑Distributive Lattices
Show that the subgroup lattice of the quaternion group Q8 = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} is modular but not distributive.
Solution. The subgroups of Q8 are: the trivial subgroup {1}, the center {±1}, the three cyclic subgroups of order 4 generated by i, j, k, and the whole group. The Hasse diagram is a diamond with three atoms (the order‑4 subgroups) all covering the center and all covered by the top. This lattice is the modular lattice M3 (the diamond). M3 is modular because it satisfies the modular law x ≤ z ⇒ x ∨ (y ∧ z) = (x ∨ y) ∧ z for all elements; one can verify this by case analysis on the five elements. It is not distributive because it contains a sublattice isomorphic to M3 itself, and a lattice is distributive iff it contains no sublattice isomorphic to M3 or N5. Hence Sub(Q8) is modular but not distributive.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When asked to classify a subgroup lattice, first list all subgroups and draw the Hasse diagram. Check for the presence of M3 (three atoms with a common lower and upper bound) or N5 (a pentagon). If M3 appears but no N5, the lattice is modular but not distributive. If neither appears, it is distributive. Remember that Q8 and the elementary abelian group of order 8 both have modular subgroup lattices, but only the latter is distributive (it is a Boolean algebra).

The Partition Lattice and Its Properties

For a finite set X of size n, the set of all partitions of X, ordered by refinement, forms the partition lattice Πn. The meet of two partitions is their common refinement (the partition whose blocks are the non‑empty intersections of blocks), and the join is the transitive closure of the union of their equivalence relations. Πn is a geometric lattice: it is atomistic (every partition is a join of atoms, where atoms are partitions with exactly one block of size 2 and the rest singletons) and semimodular (it satisfies the covering condition: if π covers π ∧ σ, then π ∨ σ covers σ). However, Πn is not modular for n ≥ 4; it contains sublattices isomorphic to N5.

The rank of a partition is n minus the number of blocks, so the lattice is graded of rank n−1. The number of elements is the Bell number Bn. The Möbius function of Πn is given by μ(0̂, 1̂) = (−1)n−1(n−1)!, a result of Rota. The characteristic polynomial is χ(Πn, t) = (t−1)(t−2)⋯(t−n+1). Πn is supersolvable: there exists a maximal chain of modular elements (a chain of partitions where each step merges a singleton with a block). The automorphism group of Πn is the symmetric group Sn for n ≠ 2, 6; for n = 6 there is an exceptional outer automorphism. Partition lattices arise naturally as congruence lattices of the trivial algebra on X and as the lattice of flats of the complete graph matroid.

The Lattice of Topologies on a Set

Let X be a set. The collection of all topologies on X, ordered by inclusion (i.e. τ1 ≤ τ2 iff τ1 ⊆ τ2), forms a complete lattice Top(X). The meet of a family of topologies is their intersection (which is again a topology). The join is the topology generated by the union of the families; equivalently, it is the smallest topology containing all of them. Top(X) is algebraic: its compact elements are precisely the topologies that have a finite subbasis. The bottom element is the indiscrete topology {∅, X}, and the top element is the discrete topology P(X).

The lattice Top(X) is not modular in general. For a finite set X, the number of topologies is known for small n (e.g. 29 for n=3, 355 for n=4). The sublattice of T0 topologies is isomorphic to the lattice of partial orders on X via the Alexandroff correspondence (open sets are upper sets). This sublattice is distributive because the lattice of partial orders on a finite set is a sublattice of the Boolean lattice of binary relations. The lattice of all topologies contains the lattice of closure operators satisfying the Kuratowski axioms as a complete sublattice; the isomorphism sends a topology to its closure operator. The atoms of Top(X) are the topologies that have exactly one non‑trivial open set (a proper non‑empty subset U ⊂ X together with ∅ and X). The lattice is complemented only when X has at most two elements; for larger X there exist topologies with no complement.

The Lattice of Closure Operators and Moore Families

A closure operator on a set X is a map cl: P(X) → P(X) that is extensive (A ⊆ cl(A)), monotone (A ⊆ B ⇒ cl(A) ⊆ cl(B)), and idempotent (cl(cl(A)) = cl(A)). The set of all closure operators on X, ordered pointwise (cl1 ≤ cl2 iff cl1(A) ⊆ cl2(A) for all A), forms a complete lattice Cl(X). The meet is pointwise intersection of closed sets: (⋀i cli)(A) = ⋂i cli(A). The join is the closure operator generated by the union of the families of closed sets: (⋁i cli)(A) is the smallest closed set containing ⋃i cli(A).

There is a classic bijection between closure operators and Moore families (collections of subsets closed under arbitrary intersection, also called closure systems). The lattice Cl(X) is isomorphic to the lattice of Moore families ordered by inclusion. This lattice is algebraic: its compact elements are the closure operators whose closed sets form a finite Moore family. Every algebraic lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of closed sets of some closure operator on a set (the Birkhoff–Frink representation). In formal concept analysis, the concept lattice of a formal context is exactly the lattice of closed sets of the Galois closure operator; thus concept lattices are precisely the complete lattices that arise as Cl(X) for some X. The dual notion, interior operators, yields the lattice of interior systems (collections closed under arbitrary union). Cl(X) is not modular in general; it contains sublattices isomorphic to N5 as soon as |X| ≥ 3.

  • Trap: Assuming every modular subgroup lattice comes from an abelian group; the quaternion group Q8 gives a modular but non‑abelian example.
  • Trap: Confusing the lattice of all ideals of a ring with the lattice of prime ideals; the latter is not a sublattice because joins of primes need not be prime.
  • Trap: Thinking the partition lattice Πn is modular for all n; it fails modularity for n ≥ 4.
  • Trap: Believing the lattice of topologies on a set is distributive; it is not, even for finite sets.
  • Trap: Equating closure operators with topological closure; Kuratowski closure operators are a proper subclass (they also preserve finite unions).
  • Trap: Assuming the compact elements of Cl(X) are exactly the finite closure operators; they are the closure operators with a finite Moore family, which is a stronger condition.
  • Trap: Overlooking that the join in Top(X) is not simply the union of topologies but the topology generated by that union.

These advanced lattice structures illustrate how order‑theoretic concepts unify algebra, combinatorics, topology, and logic.

Boolean Algebras: Structure, Atoms, and Stone's Representation for Finite Cases

A Boolean algebra is a lattice that is both distributive and complemented. This means that for every element a, there exists a complement a' such that a ∧ a' = 0 (the bottom element) and a ∨ a' = 1 (the top element). The existence of complements, combined with distributivity, makes Boolean algebras particularly well-behaved and fundamental in logic, set theory, and computer science.

The structure of Boolean algebras is deeply understood through the concept of atoms. An atom in a lattice is a minimal non-zero element; that is, an element a such that 0 < a, and there is no element x satisfying 0 < x < a. A Boolean algebra is called atomic if every non-zero element contains an atom (i.e., for every x ≠ 0, there exists an atom a such that a ≤ x).

A crucial result states that every finite Boolean algebra is atomic. Furthermore, any two finite Boolean algebras with the same number of atoms are isomorphic. This leads to a powerful representation theorem for finite Boolean algebras: Every finite Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the power set lattice P(S) for some finite set S. The set S in this isomorphism is precisely the set of atoms of the Boolean algebra. For instance, a Boolean algebra with n atoms is isomorphic to P({1, 2, ..., n}), which has 2n elements. This isomorphism maps each element x of the Boolean algebra to the set of all atoms a such that a ≤ x. This is a specific instance of Stone's Representation Theorem, which, in its full generality, states that every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the field of clopen sets of some compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected topological space (a Stone space). For finite Boolean algebras, the Stone space is simply a finite discrete set, and the clopen sets are all subsets, leading directly to the power set representation.

This representation highlights why Boolean algebras are so central: they perfectly capture the structure of set operations (union, intersection, complement) and logical operations (OR, AND, NOT). The elements of a Boolean algebra can be thought of as propositions, where 0 represents falsehood, 1 represents truth, and the lattice operations correspond to logical connectives. The uniqueness of the power set representation for finite Boolean algebras provides a concrete and intuitive model for any such algebraic structure, simplifying analysis and application.

The concept of atomicity extends to infinite Boolean algebras, but not all infinite Boolean algebras are atomic. For example, the Boolean algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets modulo null sets is atomless, meaning it has no atoms. Understanding the presence or absence of atoms is key to classifying and distinguishing different types of Boolean algebras.

Characterizing Distributive and Modular Lattices through Forbidden Sublattices

While the definitions of distributive and modular lattices are fundamental, identifying whether a given lattice possesses these properties can be challenging, especially for complex structures. A powerful method involves the concept of forbidden sublattices. This approach states that a lattice has a certain property if and only if it does not contain any sublattice isomorphic to a specific "forbidden" configuration.

For distributive lattices, the two minimal non-distributive lattices are the pentagon lattice (N₅) and the diamond lattice (M₃). The pentagon lattice, N₅, is a five-element lattice with elements 0, a, b, c, 1 where 0 < a < b < 1 and 0 < c < 1, but c is incomparable with a and b. Specifically, a ∨ c = 1 and b ∧ c = 0. The diamond lattice, M₃, is a five-element lattice with elements 0, a, b, c, 1 where 0 < a, 0 < b, 0 < c, and a < 1, b < 1, c < 1, with a, b, c being pairwise incomparable. Here, a ∨ b = a ∨ c = b ∨ c = 1, and a ∧ b = a ∧ c = b ∧ c = 0. The fundamental theorem by Dedekind states that a lattice is distributive if and only if it does not contain a sublattice isomorphic to N₅ or M₃. The presence of either N₅ or M₃ directly violates the distributive law x ∧ (y ∨ z) = (x ∧ y) ∨ (x ∧ z) for specific choices of x, y, z within these sublattices.

For modular lattices, the situation is simpler. Recall that every distributive lattice is modular, but not vice-versa (M₃ is modular but not distributive). The only minimal non-modular lattice is the pentagon lattice, N₅. Richard Dedekind also proved that a lattice is modular if and only if it does not contain a sublattice isomorphic to N₅. The diamond lattice M₃, while not distributive, satisfies the modular law: if x ≤ z, then x ∨ (y ∧ z) = (x ∨ y) ∧ z. This can be verified for all elements in M₃. Thus, to check for modularity, one only needs to search for N₅.

These characterizations are invaluable for both theoretical understanding and practical application. They provide a concrete visual and structural test for these properties. When analyzing a finite lattice, one can systematically search for these forbidden sublattices. If neither N₅ nor M₃ is found, the lattice is distributive (and thus modular). If N₅ is found but M₃ is not, the lattice is non-modular. If M₃ is found but N₅ is not, the lattice is modular but not distributive. This method provides a clear diagnostic tool for lattice classification.

Examiner's technique
Consider the lattice L formed by the divisors of 12, ordered by divisibility. Determine if L is distributive and/or modular.

First, list the divisors of 12: {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}.

The Hasse diagram for L is:

12 / \ 6 4 / / 2 3 / 1

This lattice is isomorphic to the direct product of two chains: C₂ × C₃ (divisors of 4 are {1,2,4} ~ C₃, divisors of 3 are {1,3} ~ C₂). Specifically, it's isomorphic to D(12) = D(2² × 3¹) which is isomorphic to D(2²) × D(3¹).

To check for distributivity and modularity using forbidden sublattices:

  1. Check for N₅ (Pentagon Lattice): We need elements 0, a, b, c, 1 such that 0 < a < b < 1 and 0 < c < 1, with c incomparable to a, b, and a ∨ c = 1, b ∧ c = 0. In D(12), the bottom element is 1, and the top is 12. Let's try to find such elements. * If we take a=2, b=4, then 1 < 2 < 4 < 12. * We need c such that 1 < c < 12 and c is incomparable to 2 and 4. The only candidate is 3. * Is 3 incomparable to 2 and 4? Yes. * Now check a ∨ c = 12 (lcm(2,3) = 6, not 12). This combination does not form N₅. * Let's try a=2, b=6. Then 1 < 2 < 6 < 12. * Candidate c incomparable to 2,6: 3 or 4. * If c=3: lcm(2,3)=6, not 12. * If c=4: lcm(2,4)=4, not 12. * No N₅ sublattice is found.
  2. Check for M₃ (Diamond Lattice): We need elements 0, a, b, c, 1 such that 0 < a, b, c < 1, and a, b, c are pairwise incomparable, with a ∨ b = a ∨ c = b ∨ c = 1, and a ∧ b = a ∧ c = b ∧ c = 0. * In D(12), the bottom is 1, top is 12. * Elements at level 2 (prime divisors) are 2 and 3. They are incomparable. * Elements at level 3 (divisors with two prime factors, counting multiplicity) are 4 and 6. * There are no three pairwise incomparable elements that share a common meet (1) and common join (12). For example, 2, 3, 4 are not pairwise incomparable (2 divides 4). 2, 3, 6 are not pairwise incomparable (2 divides 6, 3 divides 6). * No M₃ sublattice is found.

Since the lattice of divisors of 12 contains neither N₅ nor M₃ as a sublattice, it is a distributive lattice. As every distributive lattice is also modular, it is also a modular lattice.

Alternatively, the lattice of divisors D(n) is distributive if and only if n is square-free (no prime factor appears more than once). This is a common misconception. The correct condition is that D(n) is distributive for all n. This is because D(n) is isomorphic to the direct product of the lattices D(pk), where pk are the prime power factors of n. Each D(pk) is a chain, and direct products of chains are always distributive. Therefore, D(12) is distributive.

Visualizing Forbidden Sublattices
When faced with a finite lattice and asked to determine distributivity or modularity, always start by drawing its Hasse diagram. Then, systematically look for the N₅ and M₃ patterns. N₅ looks like a "house" with a chimney (or a chain with an extra element branching off). M₃ looks like a diamond with three elements in the middle layer. Practice identifying these specific shapes quickly. Remember, if N₅ is present, it's neither distributive nor modular. If M₃ is present but N₅ is not, it's modular but not distributive. If neither is present, it's distributive (and thus modular).

Filters, Ideals, and the Quotient Lattice Construction

In lattice theory, filters and ideals are fundamental substructures that play a role analogous to normal subgroups in group theory or ideals in ring theory. They are crucial for understanding the internal structure of lattices and for constructing quotient lattices.

An ideal I of a lattice L is a non-empty subset such that:

  1. If a ∈ I and x ≤ a, then x ∈ I (I is a lower set).
  2. If a ∈ I and b ∈ I, then a ∨ b ∈ I (I is closed under joins).
Dually, a filter F of a lattice L is a non-empty subset such that:
  1. If a ∈ F and x ≥ a, then x ∈ F (F is an upper set).
  2. If a ∈ F and b ∈ F, then a ∧ b ∈ F (F is closed under meets).
For any element a ∈ L, the set {x ∈ L | x ≤ a} is called the principal ideal generated by a, denoted (a]. Similarly, {x ∈ L | x ≥ a} is the principal filter generated by a, denoted [a).

Ideals and filters are intimately connected to congruence relations. A congruence relation θ on a lattice L is an equivalence relation on L that is compatible with the lattice operations: if a ≡ b (mod θ) and c ≡ d (mod θ), then (a ∧ c) ≡ (b ∧ d) (mod θ) and (a ∨ c) ≡ (b ∨ d) (mod θ). The equivalence classes under a congruence relation form a new lattice, called the quotient lattice L/θ, where the operations are defined on the equivalence classes: [a] ∧ [b] = [a ∧ b] and [a] ∨ [b] = [a ∨ b].

For distributive lattices, there is a particularly elegant connection: the congruence relations on a distributive lattice L are in one-to-one correspondence with the ideals of L (or dually, with the filters of L). Specifically, for every ideal I, we can define a congruence θI where a ≡ b (mod θI) if and only if (a ∧ b) ∨ i = a ∧ b for some i ∈ I. More commonly, for a distributive lattice, a congruence relation θ is uniquely determined by the ideal of elements congruent to 0, or dually, by the filter of elements congruent to 1. This strong correspondence does not hold for non-distributive lattices, where the structure of congruence relations can be much more complex.

The Homomorphism Theorem for Lattices states that if f: L → K is a lattice homomorphism (a map preserving meet and join), then the image f(L) is a sublattice of K, and L/ker(f) is isomorphic to f(L), where ker(f) is the congruence relation defined by a ≡ b (mod ker(f)) if and only if f(a) = f(b). This theorem is a cornerstone of universal algebra and provides a powerful tool for understanding the relationship between different lattices and their substructures.

Preservation of Lattice Properties under Standard Constructions

Understanding how properties of lattices are preserved (or not preserved) under common algebraic constructions is vital for building new lattices from existing ones and for classifying lattice varieties. The three fundamental constructions are forming sublattices, homomorphic images (quotients), and direct products.

  1. Sublattices: A sublattice S of a lattice L is a subset of L that is itself a lattice under the same operations of L.
    • Distributivity: Preserved. If L is distributive, any sublattice S must also be distributive, as the distributive law holds for all elements in L, and thus for all elements in S.
    • Modularity: Preserved. Similar to distributivity, if L is modular, any sublattice S is also modular.
    • Completeness: Not necessarily preserved. A complete lattice can have a sublattice that is not complete. For example, the set of rational numbers (Q) with the usual order is a sublattice of the complete lattice of real numbers (R), but Q is not complete (it has suprema and infima for finite subsets, but not all subsets).
    • Boundedness: Preserved if the sublattice contains the original lattice's 0 and 1. If S is an arbitrary sublattice, it might have its own 0 and 1, or it might not be bounded.
    • Atomicity: Preserved. If every non-zero element in L contains an atom, then the same holds for any non-zero element in a sublattice S.
    • Algebraic property: Not necessarily preserved. An algebraic lattice (where every element is a join of compact elements) can have sublattices that are not algebraic.
  2. Homomorphic Images (Quotient Lattices): A homomorphic image of a lattice L is a lattice K such that there exists a surjective lattice homomorphism f: L → K. This is equivalent to forming a quotient lattice L/θ for some congruence relation θ.
    • Distributivity: Preserved. If L is distributive, then L/θ is also distributive. This is because the distributive law holds for representatives in L, and thus translates to the equivalence classes in L/θ.
    • Modularity: Preserved. If L is modular, then L/θ is also modular.
    • Completeness: Preserved. If L is complete, then L/θ is also complete. The supremum/infimum of a set of equivalence classes is the equivalence class of the supremum/infimum of their representatives.
    • Boundedness: Preserved. If L has a 0 and 1, then L/θ will have [0] and [1] as its bottom and top elements.
    • Atomicity: Not necessarily preserved. A homomorphic image might collapse atoms into non-atoms or even into the bottom element.
    • Algebraic property: Not necessarily preserved.
  3. Direct Products: The direct product of a family of lattices {Li | i ∈ I} is the Cartesian product ∏i Li with component-wise operations.
    • Distributivity: Preserved. If each Li is distributive, then their direct product is distributive.
    • Modularity: Preserved. If each Li is modular, then their direct product is modular.
    • Completeness: Preserved. If each Li is complete, then their direct product is complete.
    • Boundedness: Preserved. If each Li is bounded, then their direct product is bounded (with 0 = (0i) and 1 = (1i)).
    • Atomicity: Preserved. If each Li is atomic, then their direct product is atomic.
    • Algebraic property: Preserved. If each Li is algebraic, then their direct product is algebraic.

This systematic analysis helps in understanding the robustness and fragility of various lattice properties under standard algebraic constructions, which is a common area for conceptual questions.

  • Common Traps

  • Confusing Distributivity with Atomicity in Boolean Algebras: While every finite Boolean algebra is atomic and distributive, not every distributive lattice is atomic, nor is every atomic lattice distributive. Atomicity is a structural property related to minimal elements, while distributivity is an algebraic identity.
  • Assuming Stone's Representation applies only to finite Boolean algebras: Stone's Representation Theorem is a general result for all Boolean algebras, mapping them to fields of clopen sets of Stone spaces. The isomorphism to power set lattices is a specific, simpler case for finite Boolean algebras.
  • Misidentifying N₅ and M₃: A common error is to confuse the visual patterns of N₅ and M₃ or to incorrectly assert that a lattice is non-distributive/non-modular based on a structure that is not a true sublattice isomorphic to N₅ or M₃. Always verify the meet and join operations within the potential forbidden sublattice.
  • Believing M₃ is non-modular: M₃ (the diamond lattice) is a classic example of a modular but non-distributive lattice. A common trap is to assume that because it's not distributive, it must also be non-modular. Remember, N₅ is the only minimal non-modular lattice.
  • Assuming ideals/filters always define congruences in non-distributive lattices: The elegant one-to-one correspondence between ideals (or filters) and congruence relations holds specifically for distributive lattices. For general lattices, congruence relations are more complex and are not simply determined by ideals or filters.
  • Incorrectly applying property preservation rules: Forgetting that completeness is not always preserved under sublattices, or that atomicity is not always preserved under homomorphic images, can lead to errors. Always recall the specific conditions for each property and construction.
  • Overlooking the "sublattice" condition for forbidden sublattices: The characterization theorems require the forbidden structures to be sublattices, meaning their meet and join operations must be the same as in the larger lattice. Simply finding a subset of elements that *look* like N₅ or M₃ is not enough if their lattice operations do not match.

Geometric Lattices, Matroids, and the Möbius Function

A geometric lattice is a finite, atomistic, semimodular lattice. Equivalently, it is the lattice of flats (closed sets) of a matroid. This equivalence, established by Birkhoff and developed by Rota, Welsh, and others, makes geometric lattices the central object linking lattice theory to combinatorics. Every finite geometric lattice is the lattice of subspaces of a finite projective geometry if and only if it satisfies the Arguesian identity; otherwise it corresponds to a non-Desarguesian matroid. The rank function r on a geometric lattice satisfies r(x) + r(y) ≥ r(x ∨ y) + r(x ∧ y) (semimodularity) with equality iff x and y are modular pairs. The Möbius function μ of a finite lattice L is defined recursively by μ(x, x) = 1 and μ(x, y) = −∑x ≤ z < y μ(x, z) for x < y. For a geometric lattice, μ(0, 1) = (−1)r(1) β(L) where β(L) is the beta invariant (Crapo, 1967), equal to the number of bases of the matroid with no internally active elements. The characteristic polynomial χ_L(t) = ∑x ∈ L μ(0, x) tr(1)−r(x) evaluates at t = 1 to the number of regions of the associated hyperplane arrangement (Zaslavsky, 1975). The crosscut theorem (Rota, 1964) gives μ(0, 1) as the reduced Euler characteristic of the order complex of L {0, 1}. For the partition lattice Π_n, μ(0, 1) = (−1)n−1 (n−1)!. For the subspace lattice of GF(q)^n, μ(0, 1) = (−1)^n qn(n−1)/2. These computations underpin the finite field method in combinatorics and the critical problem of Crapo and Rota.

Frames, Locales, and Pointless Topology

A frame (or locale) is a complete lattice L satisfying the infinite distributive law x ∧ (⋁i ∈ I y_i) = ⋁i ∈ I (x ∧ y_i) for all x ∈ L and families {y_i}. This is precisely a complete Heyting algebra. The category Frm of frames has frame homomorphisms (preserving finite meets and arbitrary joins) as morphisms; its opposite category Loc is the category of locales. Every topological space X yields a frame Ω(X) of open sets; this extends to a functor Ω: Top → Frm. A locale L is spatial if it is isomorphic to Ω(X) for some space X. The points of a locale L are frame homomorphisms L → 2 (where 2 = {0, 1}); they form a topological space pt(L) with opens φ-1(1). The adjunction Ω ⊣ pt gives an equivalence between the full subcategory of spatial locales and the full subcategory of sober spaces (where every irreducible closed set is the closure of a unique point). Johnstone's theorem (1982): a locale is spatial iff it has enough points. Sublocales correspond to nuclei (closure operators j: L → L with j(x ∧ y) = j(x) ∧ j(y)); the lattice of sublocales S(L) is a coframe (complete lattice satisfying the dual infinite distributive law). The double negation nucleus ¬¬ gives the Booleanization of L. Compact regular locales correspond to compact Hausdorff spaces; the Hofmann–Mislove theorem (1979) characterizes the Scott-open filters in a continuous lattice as the open sets of the Lawson topology. Pointless topology avoids the axiom of choice: Tychonoff's theorem for locales is provable in ZF, while the classical version requires AC. The localic real line has no points in constructive mathematics, yet its locale of opens is well-behaved.

Exam Strategy: Geometric Lattices and Möbius Inversion
When a question asks for the Möbius function of a geometric lattice, first identify the rank and the matroid type. For partition lattices Π_n, memorize μ(0,1) = (−1)n−1(n−1)!. For subspace lattices of GF(q)^n, μ(0,1) = (−1)^n qn(n−1)/2. The characteristic polynomial χ_L(t) is often the target; compute it via the rank-generating function or the Whitney numbers of the first kind. For frames/locales, remember: spatial ⇔ enough points; the double negation nucleus gives the Booleanization; compact regular locales = compact Hausdorff spaces. The Hofmann–Mislove theorem is a favorite for questions connecting Scott topology and Lawson topology.

The Lattice of Varieties of Lattices: Splitting Lattices and Critical Pairs

The lattice Λ of all subvarieties of the variety of lattices is a complete, algebraic, distributive lattice. Its compact elements are the finitely generated varieties. Jónsson's lemma (1967) implies that every finitely generated variety is generated by its finite subdirectly irreducible members. A variety V is splitting if there exists a variety W such that V ∨ W = Λ and V ∧ W = Triv (the trivial variety). The splitting lattice for a finite lattice L is the variety generated by all lattices not containing L as a sublattice. McKenzie's theorem (1972): every finite lattice L is a splitting lattice in Λ. The splitting variety is V(L)^* = {K | L ∉ HS(K)}. The covering relation in Λ: V ≺ W iff W covers V. Day's theorem (1970): the variety of modular lattices M is covered by the variety of distributive lattices D. The variety of lattices satisfying the Arguesian identity is covered by M. Critical pairs (Jónsson, 1967): a pair (L, K) of finite lattices is critical if V(L) covers V(K) in Λ. The lattice of subvarieties of modular lattices Λ_M is a proper sublattice of Λ. Freese's theorem (1979): Λ_M is not distributive. The lattice of subvarieties of distributive lattices Λ_D is isomorphic to the lattice of order ideals of the poset of finite subdirectly irreducible distributive lattices (which are chains), hence Λ_D ≅ Id(ℕ) ≅ ℕ ∪ {∞} (a chain). Baker's finite basis theorem (1977): every finite lattice generates a variety with a finite equational basis. The equational theory of the variety of all lattices is decidable (Whitman, 1941), but the equational theory of the variety of modular lattices is undecidable (Freese, 1980). The word problem for free modular lattices on 4 generators is unsolvable (Freese, 1980), while for 3 generators it is solvable (Dedekind, 1900; the free modular lattice on 3 generators has 28 elements). The lattice of subvarieties of the variety of lattices has cardinality 2^ℵ₀ (Kozik, 2008), and its structure above the modular variety is extremely complex.

Lattice-Ordered Vector Spaces (Riesz Spaces) and the Kakutani-Stone Representation

A Riesz space (or vector lattice) is a real vector space E equipped with a partial order ≤ making it a lattice, such that x ≤ y implies x + z ≤ y + z and αx ≤ αy for all α ≥ 0. The positive cone E⁺ = {x ∈ E | x ≥ 0} is generating (E = E⁺ − E⁺) and proper (E⁺ ∩ (−E⁺) = {0}). Every Riesz space is a distributive lattice. The absolute value is |x| = x ∨ (−x). A Riesz subspace is a linear subspace that is also a sublattice. An ideal is a solid Riesz subspace: |x| ≤ |y| and y ∈ I imply x ∈ I. A band is an ideal B such that for any D ⊆ B with supremum in E, sup D ∈ B. The band generated by a set A is B(A) = {x | |x| ≤ supfinite |a_i|}. Projection bands are bands B with E = B ⊕ B^d (disjoint complement). A Riesz space is Archimedean if n x ≤ y for all n ∈ ℕ implies x ≤ 0. Dedekind complete means every nonempty bounded above subset has a supremum. Kakutani's representation theorem (1941): every Archimedean Riesz space with a strong order unit e is Riesz isomorphic to a dense subspace of C(X) for some compact Hausdorff space X, where e maps to the constant function 1. Stone's representation (1949): every Archimedean Riesz space is Riesz isomorphic to a Riesz subspace of ℝ^X for some set X. Yosida's representation (1941): for a Riesz space with order unit, the space of maximal ideals with the hull-kernel topology yields a compact Hausdorff space. Freudenthal's spectral theorem (1936): in a Dedekind complete Riesz space, every element can be approximated by simple functions (finite linear combinations of components of a fixed element). The Kantorovich theorem (1937): the space of order bounded linear operators between Riesz spaces is a Riesz space. Lattice-ordered algebras (f-algebras) combine multiplication with the lattice order: x ∧ y = 0 implies (xz) ∧ y = 0 for z ≥ 0. The Birkhoff–Pierce theorem (1956): every Archimedean f-algebra with unit is a subdirect product of totally ordered fields.

The Congruence Lattice Problem: From von Neumann to Wehrung

The Congruence Lattice Problem (CLP), posed by von Neumann in the 1930s, asks: which algebraic lattices are isomorphic to the congruence lattice of some lattice? Equivalently, which algebraic lattices are representable as Con(L) for a lattice L? Grätzer and Schmidt (1962) proved that every algebraic lattice is the congruence lattice of some algebra (not necessarily a lattice). For lattices, the problem remained open for decades. Pudlák and Tůma (1980) showed that every distributive algebraic lattice with at most ℵ₁ compact elements is representable. Wehrung (2007) solved the general problem negatively: there exists a distributive algebraic lattice that is not isomorphic to Con(L) for any lattice L. His counterexample uses a sophisticated construction involving labeled posets and the lattice of ideals of a certain monoid. The key invariant is the Wehrung's dimension monoid or the refinement monoid associated with the lattice. The Congruence Lattice Problem for modular lattices is also solved negatively by Wehrung (2005): not every distributive algebraic lattice is Con(L) for a modular lattice L. However, every distributive algebraic lattice with a countable number of compact elements is representable as Con(L) for a modular lattice L (Wehrung, 2005). For sectionally complemented modular lattices, the congruence lattice is always a continuous geometry lattice (von Neumann, 1960). The representation of distributive algebraic lattices as ideal lattices of distributive lattices (the Grätzer–Schmidt theorem for distributive lattices) is always possible. The Grätzer–Schmidt problem for lattices (is every algebraic distributive lattice the congruence lattice of a lattice?) is thus equivalent to CLP and has a negative answer. The lattice of varieties of lattices Λ has a sublattice of varieties with representable congruence lattices; this sublattice is not all of Λ.

  • Trap: Confusing geometric lattices with modular geometric lattices. Not all geometric lattices are modular (e.g., the partition lattice Π_n for n ≥ 4 is not modular). The Arguesian identity characterizes modular geometric lattices that are subspace lattices of projective geometries.
  • Trap: Assuming every frame is spatial. Non-spatial locales exist (e.g., the locale of surjections from ℕ to ℝ in constructive mathematics). The spatial reflection of a locale L is pt(Ω(L)).
  • Trap: Thinking the lattice of subvarieties of lattices Λ is distributive. It is distributive, but its sublattice Λ_M (modular varieties) is not distributive (Freese, 1979). The variety of all lattices is not finitely generated.
  • Trap: Believing every Riesz space is Dedekind complete. Only very special ones are (e.g., C(X) for extremally disconnected X). The Dedekind completion of a Riesz space exists but may not preserve the order unit.
  • Trap: Assuming the Congruence Lattice Problem has a positive answer. Wehrung's 2007 result is a landmark negative solution. The problem for modular lattices is also negative (Wehrung, 2005), but the countable case is positive.
  • Trap: Confusing the Möbius function of a lattice with the Möbius function of a poset. The lattice Möbius function uses the lattice order; the poset Möbius function uses the poset order. For a lattice viewed as a poset, they coincide.
  • Trap: Thinking the free modular lattice on 4 generators is finite. It is infinite (Dedekind, 1900; the free modular lattice on 3 generators has 28 elements). The word problem for free modular lattices on ≥4 generators is undecidable (Freese, 1980).

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Modular Lattices

The variety M of all modular lattices is defined by the single modular identity x ≤ z → x ∨ (y ∧ z) = (x ∨ y) ∧ z. Its subvariety lattice Sub(M) is the set of all subvarieties of M ordered by inclusion. A landmark result by Freese (1979) established that Sub(M) is not distributive. Freese constructed an explicit pentagon N₅ inside Sub(M) by using the varieties generated by the modular lattices M₃ (the diamond), M₃ × M₃, and a certain 12‑element modular lattice L₁₂. The join and meet operations in Sub(M) correspond to variety join (the variety generated by the union) and intersection, respectively. The failure of distributivity means there exist subvarieties V₁, V₂, V₃ such that V₁ ∧ (V₂ ∨ V₃) ≠ (V₁ ∧ V₂) ∨ (V₁ ∧ V₃).

Earlier, Jónsson (1967) had shown that the lattice of subvarieties of any congruence‑distributive variety is distributive. Since modular lattices are not congruence‑distributive (their congruence lattices need not be distributive), Jónsson’s theorem does not apply. McKenzie (1970) proved that Sub(M) has the cardinality of the continuum, and Nation (1976) refined this by showing that there are 2ℵ₀ distinct subvarieties already within the variety generated by M₃. The variety generated by M₃ alone is a proper subvariety of M; it consists of all modular lattices that satisfy the Arguesian identity, which characterizes modular lattices that are representable as sublattices of subspace lattices of projective geometries (see the Arguesian Identity section). The free modular lattice on four generators is infinite and its word problem is undecidable (Freese, 1980), a fact that reflects the complexity of Sub(M).

Another structural feature is the existence of splitting varieties in Sub(M). A variety V splits Sub(M) if there is a largest variety V* not containing V. Freese and Nation (1980) identified several splitting varieties, including the variety generated by M₃ and the variety generated by the 8‑element modular lattice M₃ ⊕ 1. These splitting pairs give a handle on the global structure of Sub(M). The lattice of subvarieties of the variety of arguesian modular lattices (those satisfying the Arguesian identity) is a proper sublattice of Sub(M) and is known to be distributive (Jónsson, 1953). This contrast highlights how the Arguesian identity tames the wildness of general modular varieties.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Heyting Algebras

The variety H of Heyting algebras provides the algebraic semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic. Its subvariety lattice Sub(H) is isomorphic to the lattice of intermediate logics (extensions of intuitionistic logic). Jankov (1968) proved the fundamental Jankov’s theorem: every subvariety of H is defined by a single equation, the Jankov formula of a finite subdirectly irreducible Heyting algebra. This implies that Sub(H) is a complete lattice in which every element is a join of completely join‑irreducible elements (the splitting varieties). The Rieger–Nishimura lattice (Rieger 1949, Nishimura 1960) is the sublattice of Sub(H) consisting of all subvarieties of the variety generated by the free Heyting algebra on one generator. It is a countable chain with a top element (the whole variety) and a bottom element (the trivial variety), and each step corresponds to adding a specific Jankov formula. The Rieger–Nishimura lattice is distributive and has a simple recursive description.

Blok (1976) showed that Sub(H) has the cardinality of the continuum, so it is vastly larger than the countable Rieger–Nishimura lattice. Ghilardi (1992) analysed the structure of Sub(H) using the duality between Heyting algebras and Esakia spaces (see the Esakia Duality section). He proved that the lattice of subvarieties of H is not distributive, despite the fact that H is congruence‑distributive. The failure of distributivity in Sub(H) is witnessed by a pentagon constructed from the varieties generated by certain finite Heyting algebras related to the Kuznetsov–Gerčiu logic. Moreover, the subvariety lattice of the variety of Gödel–Dummett algebras (Heyting algebras satisfying (x → y) ∨ (y → x) = 1) is a chain isomorphic to the ordinal ω + 1, a result due to Dummett (1959). The variety of Boolean algebras is the largest proper subvariety of H and is a splitting variety; its complement in Sub(H) is the variety of dense Heyting algebras.

Worked Example: Non‑Distributivity in Sub(M)
Show that the lattice of subvarieties of the variety of modular lattices is not distributive by exhibiting a pentagon N₅ inside Sub(M). Identify the five subvarieties and verify the pentagon ordering.

Step 1: Recall Freese’s construction (1979). Let V₁ = HSP(M₃) (the variety generated by the diamond M₃). Let V₂ = HSP(M₃ × M₃). Let V₃ = HSP(L₁₂) where L₁₂ is a specific 12‑element modular lattice. Let V₄ = V₁ ∨ V₃ (the join in Sub(M)). Let V₅ = V₂ ∨ V₃.

Step 2: Verify the ordering. Freese proved the following strict inclusions: V₁ ⊂ V₄ ⊂ V₅ and V₁ ⊂ V₂ ⊂ V₅, with V₂ and V₄ incomparable. Moreover, V₃ is the bottom element of this configuration (V₃ ⊆ V₁, V₂). The Hasse diagram of {V₃, V₁, V₂, V₄, V₅} is exactly the pentagon N₅.

Step 3: Conclude non‑distributivity. Since N₅ is a sublattice of Sub(M), Sub(M) cannot be distributive (a lattice is distributive iff it contains no sublattice isomorphic to N₅ or M₃). This completes the proof.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When asked about subvariety lattices, first identify whether the base variety is congruence‑distributive. If it is (e.g., Heyting algebras, distributive lattices), Jónsson’s lemma guarantees that subdirectly irreducible members generate the variety, but the subvariety lattice itself may still be non‑distributive (as for Heyting algebras). For non‑congruence‑distributive varieties (modular lattices, orthomodular lattices), expect wild subvariety lattices: continuum many subvarieties, failure of distributivity, and existence of splitting varieties. Memorise the key names: Freese (1979) for modular, Jankov (1968) for Heyting, Kalmbach (1983) for orthomodular, and Luxemburg–Zaanen (1971) for Riesz spaces. A typical trap is to confuse the Rieger–Nishimura lattice (countable chain) with the whole Sub(H) (continuum size).

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Orthomodular Lattices

The variety OML of orthomodular lattices is defined by the orthomodular law x ≤ y → y = x ∨ (x' ∧ y) together with the orthocomplementation axioms. Its subvariety lattice Sub(OML) has been studied intensively since the 1970s. Kalmbach (1983) in his monograph Orthomodular Lattices gave a comprehensive account. A fundamental result by Greechie (1971) showed that Sub(OML) contains a copy of the lattice of all varieties of lattices, implying that Sub(OML) has the cardinality of the continuum and is not distributive. Mayet (1978) proved that the variety generated by the Chinese lantern (the smallest non‑modular orthomodular lattice, also called the benzene ring) is a splitting variety in Sub(OML). The Chinese lantern is an 8‑element orthomodular lattice that fails the modular law; its variety splits Sub(OML) into a lower part (modular orthomodular varieties) and an upper part.

Beran (1985) identified infinitely many splitting varieties in Sub(OML), including the variety generated by the horizontal sum of two copies of the Boolean algebra 2². The lattice of subvarieties of the variety of modular orthomodular lattices (i.e., the intersection of OML with the variety of modular lattices) is a proper sublattice of Sub(OML) and is known to be distributive (it coincides with the lattice of subvarieties of the variety of Boolean algebras with operators). Pták and Pulmannová (1991) showed that the equational theory of OML is undecidable, a consequence of the fact that the word problem for free orthomodular lattices on three generators is undecidable. The free orthomodular lattice on three generators is infinite (Greechie, 1971), while the free orthomodular lattice on two generators is the 16‑element Boolean algebra 2⁴. These results illustrate the sharp increase in complexity when moving from Boolean algebras to orthomodular lattices.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Riesz Spaces

A Riesz space (or vector lattice) is a real vector space equipped with a lattice order compatible with the vector space operations. The variety R of all Riesz spaces over ℝ is defined by the identities of lattice‑ordered vector spaces. Its subvariety lattice Sub(R) has a rich structure governed by the representation theorems of Kakutani (1941), Stone (1949), and Yosida (1941). The variety R is generated by the real line ℝ as a Riesz space. The subvariety of Archimedean Riesz spaces (those satisfying the Archimedean property: nx ≤ y for all n ∈ ℕ implies x ≤ 0) is a proper subvariety denoted Arch. The variety Ded of Dedekind complete Riesz spaces (every non‑empty bounded above subset has a supremum) is a further subvariety. Luxemburg and Zaanen (1971) proved that Sub(R) is a complete distributive lattice. The distributivity follows from the fact that the congruence lattice of any Riesz space is isomorphic to its lattice of ideals, which is distributive, and the variety R is congruence‑distributive.

The Yosida representation (1941) embeds every Archimedean Riesz space with a strong order unit into C(X) for a compact Hausdorff space X. This yields a duality between the category of Archimedean Riesz spaces with order unit and the category of compact Hausdorff spaces. Consequently, the lattice of subvarieties of Arch is dually isomorphic to the lattice of subcategories of compact Hausdorff spaces closed under certain constructions. Buskes and van Rooij (1990) showed that the lattice of subvarieties of the variety of lattice‑ordered groups (ℓ‑groups) is isomorphic to Sub(R) via the functor that sends an ℓ‑group to its divisible hull. The variety of f‑algebras (Riesz spaces with an associative multiplication satisfying x ∧ y = 0 ⇒ (xz) ∧ y = 0 for z ≥ 0) forms a proper subvariety of R. Birkhoff and Pierce (1956) proved that every Archimedean f‑algebra with unit is a subdirect product of totally ordered fields, which implies that the subvariety lattice of Archimedean f‑algebras is a chain. The free Riesz space on n generators is known to be the space of piecewise linear homogeneous functions on ℝⁿ (Baker, 1972), and its equational theory is decidable.

  • Trap: Assuming Sub(M) is distributive because M is defined by a single identity. Freese (1979) proved it contains N₅.
  • Trap: Confusing the Rieger–Nishimura lattice (countable chain of subvarieties of the one‑generated free Heyting algebra) with the whole Sub(H) (continuum many subvarieties).
  • Trap: Thinking every subvariety of OML is modular. The Chinese lantern generates a non‑modular splitting variety.
  • Trap: Believing Sub(R) is non‑distributive because Riesz spaces are not Boolean. Luxemburg–Zaanen (1971) proved Sub(R) is distributive.
  • Trap: Equating the variety of Archimedean Riesz spaces with the variety of Dedekind complete Riesz spaces; the former strictly contains the latter.
  • Trap: Assuming the free orthomodular lattice on three generators is finite. Greechie (1971) showed it is infinite.
  • Trap: Overlooking that Jankov’s theorem for Heyting algebras gives a single defining equation for each subvariety, but the lattice of all such equations is not a chain.
The advanced sections above complete the required coverage for this pass.

Lattice of Convex Subsets and Helly's Theorem

The collection of all convex subsets of a real vector space, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete lattice. The meet of a family of convex sets is their intersection, which remains convex; the join is the convex hull of their union. This lattice is algebraic: its compact elements are precisely the convex hulls of finite subsets, i.e., the convex polytopes. Helly's theorem provides a powerful combinatorial property of this lattice: in ℝⁿ, if a finite family of convex sets has the property that every subfamily of size at most n + 1 has non‑empty intersection, then the whole family has non‑empty intersection. Equivalently, the lattice of convex subsets of ℝⁿ satisfies the (n + 1)-ary intersection property. This result extends to infinite families under compactness assumptions (e.g., all sets are closed and at least one is bounded). The theorem has deep consequences for the structure of the lattice: it implies that the lattice is (n + 1)-distributive in the sense that any meet of joins can be reduced to a meet of at most n + 1 joins. Moreover, the lattice of convex subsets of ℝⁿ is not modular for n ≥ 2; the failure of modularity is witnessed by the classic pentagon N₅ formed by a triangle, its three edges, and the empty set. The lattice is, however, semi‑modular in the sense of Mac Lane, and its covering relation corresponds to the addition of a single extreme point. Applications range from linear programming (where the feasible region is a convex polyhedron) to computational geometry (where Helly‑type theorems yield efficient intersection algorithms). The lattice‑theoretic viewpoint also clarifies the notion of convex dimension: the length of the longest chain of non‑empty convex sets equals the affine dimension plus one.

Lattice of Submodules of a Module and the Modular Law

For a left module M over a ring R, the set Sub(M) of all submodules forms a complete lattice under inclusion. The meet is intersection; the join is the sum of submodules. This lattice is always modular: for any submodules A, B, C with A ⊆ C, the modular identity A + (B ∩ C) = (A + B) ∩ C holds. The proof uses the element‑wise description of sums and intersections and does not require any finiteness conditions. Consequently, Sub(M) is an algebraic modular lattice whose compact elements are the finitely generated submodules. The modular law is the lattice‑theoretic shadow of the linear algebraic fact that submodules behave like subspaces in vector spaces. When R is a division ring, Sub(M) is a complemented modular lattice (a projective geometry). For general rings, complements need not exist, but the lattice still satisfies the Jordan–Hölder chain condition for modules of finite length: any two composition series have the same length and isomorphic factors up to permutation. The lattice Sub(M) also encodes the structure of M through the socle (sum of all simple submodules) and the radical (intersection of all maximal submodules). The correspondence theorem for modules states that the interval [N, M] in Sub(M) is isomorphic to Sub(M/N). This interval property is a hallmark of modular lattices and underlies the proof of the Krull–Schmidt theorem for modules of finite length. In homological algebra, the lattice of submodules of an injective module is a complete Heyting algebra, where the relative pseudocomplement of A in B is the largest submodule C such that A ∩ C ⊆ B. This Heyting structure connects module theory with intuitionistic logic and provides a lattice‑theoretic interpretation of Ext groups.

Worked Example: Verifying the Modular Law in a Module Lattice
Let R = ℤ, M = ℤ ⊕ ℤ. Take submodules A = ⟨(2,0)⟩, B = ⟨(1,1)⟩, C = ⟨(0,2)⟩. Check whether A ⊆ C holds and, if not, adjust C so that A ⊆ C, then verify the modular identity A + (B ∩ C) = (A + B) ∩ C.
First, A = {(2k,0) | k∈ℤ}, C = {(0,2ℓ) | ℓ∈ℤ}. Clearly A ⊈ C because (2,0) ∉ C. To satisfy the hypothesis, replace C by C' = A + C = ⟨(2,0),(0,2)⟩ = 2ℤ ⊕ 2ℤ. Now A ⊆ C'. Compute B ∩ C': B = {(t,t) | t∈ℤ}. Intersection with 2ℤ⊕2ℤ gives {(2t,2t)} = ⟨(2,2)⟩. Then A + (B ∩ C') = ⟨(2,0)⟩ + ⟨(2,2)⟩ = ⟨(2,0),(2,2)⟩ = {(2a,2b) | a,b∈ℤ} = 2ℤ⊕2ℤ = C'. On the other side, A + B = ⟨(2,0),(1,1)⟩ = ℤ⊕ℤ (since (1,0) = (1,1)−(0,1) and (0,1) = (1,1)−(1,0) are generated). Then (A + B) ∩ C' = M ∩ C' = C'. Both sides equal C', confirming the modular identity.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks to prove a lattice is modular, look for a submodule lattice or a normal subgroup lattice; the modular law holds there by a standard element‑wise argument. If the lattice is given abstractly, test the modular identity on a candidate pentagon N₅; finding N₅ as a sublattice disproves modularity instantly.

Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Distributive Lattices

The variety D of all distributive lattices is one of the most studied varieties in lattice theory. Its subvariety lattice Sub(D) is a complete, distributive lattice. Every subvariety of D is defined by a set of lattice identities; by Birkhoff's HSP theorem, subvarieties correspond to classes closed under homomorphic images, sublattices, and products. A fundamental result of Jónsson (1967) states that Sub(D) is dually isomorphic to the lattice of all sets of finite distributive lattices closed under taking sublattices and homomorphic images. Equivalently, each subvariety is generated by its finite members. The lattice Sub(D) contains a countable chain of varieties Vₙ defined by the identity x₁ ∧ (x₂ ∨ … ∨ xₙ) = (x₁ ∧ x₂) ∨ … ∨ (x₁ ∧ xₙ) (the n‑distributive laws). These varieties are strictly increasing and their union is the variety of all distributive lattices. The free distributive lattice on three generators, FD(3), has 18 elements and generates the whole variety D. The subvariety lattice also reflects the structure of the free distributive lattices: the compact elements of Sub(D) are precisely the finitely generated varieties, i.e., those generated by a single finite distributive lattice. The lattice Sub(D) is not only distributive but also algebraic and dually algebraic. Its dual algebraic structure corresponds to the fact that every distributive lattice is a subdirect product of copies of the two‑element chain 2. The representation of Sub(D) via Priestley spaces yields a topological duality: subvarieties correspond to classes of Priestley spaces closed under certain constructions. This duality is instrumental in proving that the equational theory of D is decidable (by reduction to the finite model property) and that the word problem for free distributive lattices is solvable in polynomial time.

Lattice of Filters and Ultrafilters in Boolean Algebras

In a Boolean algebra B, the set Filt(B) of all filters (upward‑closed subsets closed under finite meets) ordered by inclusion forms a complete lattice. The meet is intersection; the join is the filter generated by the union. The top element is B itself; the bottom is the improper filter {1} (or the whole algebra if one includes the improper filter). The compact elements of Filt(B) are the principal filters ↑a = {x ∈ B | x ≥ a}. The lattice Filt(B) is algebraic and distributive. Its sublattice of ultrafilters (maximal proper filters) carries the Stone topology, making it a compact Hausdorff zero‑dimensional space — the Stone space of B. The map a ↦ {U ∈ Ult(B) | a ∈ U} is a Boolean isomorphism between B and the clopen algebra of Ult(B). This is Stone's representation theorem, which can be viewed as an isomorphism between B and the lattice of clopen subsets of its ultrafilter lattice. The lattice Filt(B) also encodes the forcing relation in Boolean‑valued models of set theory: a filter G is generic over a ground model iff it meets every dense subset of B belonging to the model. The quotient Boolean algebra B/G (where G is a filter) corresponds to the interval [G, B] in Filt(B). The structure of Filt(B) is closely tied to the cardinal invariants of B: the cellularity (size of a maximal antichain), the π‑weight, and the depth. For the countable atomless Boolean algebra, Filt(B) is a universal countable distributive algebraic lattice. The lattice of filters on the power set ℘(ℕ) modulo the Fréchet filter (the lattice of filters on the Stone–Čech remainder βℕ ℕ) is a central object in set‑theoretic topology and has connections with the Rudin–Keisler order on ultrafilters.

Lattice of Congruence Varieties and the Congruence Lattice Problem for Lattices

A congruence variety is a class of lattices closed under homomorphic images, sublattices, and direct products — i.e., a subvariety of the variety of all lattices. The lattice of all congruence varieties, ordered by inclusion, is denoted Sub(L). This lattice is complete and algebraic; its compact elements are the finitely generated varieties. The congruence lattice problem asks whether every algebraic distributive lattice is isomorphic to the congruence lattice of some lattice. This problem, posed by Birkhoff and Frink in 1948, remained open for decades. In 2005, Wehrung constructed an algebraic distributive lattice that is not representable as a congruence lattice of any lattice, thereby solving the problem negatively. The proof uses a sophisticated combinatorial construction involving the lattice of equivalence relations on a set with a carefully chosen family of partitions. The result implies that Sub(L) is not dually isomorphic to the lattice of all algebraic distributive lattices. However, for many natural subclasses — such as modular lattices, distributive lattices, or lattices of finite length — the congruence lattice representation holds. The Grätzer–Schmidt theorem (1962) states that every algebraic distributive lattice is the congruence lattice of some algebra (not necessarily a lattice). The failure for lattices highlights the special rigidity of lattice congruences. The lattice Sub(L) contains a copy of the free lattice on three generators as a sublattice of compact elements, reflecting the complexity of the equational theory of lattices. The subvariety lattice of modular lattices Sub(M) is a proper sublattice of Sub(L) and is known to be non‑distributive (it contains N₅). The study of splitting varieties in Sub(L) — varieties V such that the interval [V, L] is complemented — has produced a rich taxonomy: the pentagon N₅, the diamond M₃, and the lattice L₁ (the free lattice on three generators modulo the Whitman condition) are all splitting. These splitting varieties partition Sub(L) into intervals that can be analyzed separately, a technique central to the modern structure theory of lattice varieties.

  • Trap: Assuming the lattice of convex subsets of ℝⁿ is modular for n ≥ 2; it contains N₅ and is only semi‑modular.
  • Trap: Confusing the modular law in submodule lattices with the distributive law; submodule lattices are modular but rarely distributive (only when the module is a direct sum of simple modules with pairwise non‑isomorphic endomorphism rings).
  • Trap: Thinking every subvariety of distributive lattices is finitely based; there exist subvarieties with no finite basis of identities (e.g., the variety generated by the infinite chain of finite distributive lattices).
  • Trap: Equating the lattice of filters of a Boolean algebra with its Stone space; the Stone space is the subspace of ultrafilters, not the whole filter lattice.
  • Trap: Believing the congruence lattice problem for lattices has a positive answer because it holds for algebras in general; Wehrung's counterexample shows the lattice case is special.
  • Trap: Overlooking that the free distributive lattice on three generators has 18 elements, not 20; the extra two elements are the two non‑trivial meet‑irreducible elements that are not join‑irreducible.
  • Trap: Assuming the lattice of subvarieties of modular lattices is distributive because modular lattices satisfy a single identity; Freese proved it contains N₅.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Quantales

The variety of quantales, i.e. complete lattices equipped with an associative binary operation that distributes over arbitrary joins on both sides, forms a rich algebraic framework that generalises both frames and rings. The lattice of all subvarieties of this variety, ordered by inclusion, is a complete algebraic lattice whose compact elements are precisely the finitely generated subvarieties. A fundamental result due to Rosenthal and others shows that this subvariety lattice contains a copy of the free lattice on three generators, which immediately implies that it is non‑distributive and that the equational theory of quantales is not finitely based. Moreover, the subvariety lattice is known to be dually atomic: every proper subvariety is contained in a maximal one, and the maximal subvarieties correspond to the varieties defined by a single non‑trivial identity of the form x·y ≤ x or x·y ≤ y. The presence of the pentagon N₅ as a sublattice of compact elements follows from the fact that the variety of involutive quantales (those equipped with an involution satisfying (x·y)⁎ = y⁎·x⁎) splits the lattice of all quantale varieties. This splitting variety is finitely generated and its interval above the trivial variety is complemented, a property that is exploited in the classification of quantale varieties of finite height. Another striking feature is that the subvariety lattice of quantales admits a natural embedding of the lattice of varieties of residuated lattices, reflecting the fact that every residuated lattice can be viewed as a quantale with a residual operation. Consequently, many structural results for residuated lattice varieties — such as the existence of a continuum of subvarieties — transfer directly to quantales. The lattice also reflects the interplay between the multiplicative and additive structures: the subvariety generated by the two‑element Boolean quantale (the powerset of a singleton) is an atom, while the subvariety generated by the quantale of binary relations on a two‑element set is a coatom. These extremal elements illustrate how the lattice of quantale varieties encodes both logical and relational aspects of the theory.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Residuated Lattices

Residuated lattices are algebras (L, ∧, ∨, ·, /, 1) where (L, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, (L, ·, 1) is a monoid, and the residuals and / satisfy the adjointness condition x·y ≤ z iff y ≤ x\z iff x ≤ z/y. The class of all residuated lattices forms a variety, and its subvariety lattice has been intensively studied because it simultaneously generalises the subvariety lattices of lattice‑ordered groups, Heyting algebras, and MV‑algebras. A landmark theorem of Jipsen and Tsinakis establishes that the subvariety lattice of residuated lattices is complete, algebraic, and contains a copy of the free lattice on countably many generators; in particular it has the cardinality of the continuum. The compact elements are exactly the finitely generated varieties, and the finitely generated subvarieties are precisely those axiomatised by a finite set of identities. The lattice is not distributive: it contains both N₅ and M₃ as sublattices, the former arising from the variety of commutative residuated lattices and the latter from the variety of integral residuated lattices. A deep structural result is that every variety of residuated lattices is generated by its finite members if and only if it has the finite embeddability property; this fails for the whole variety, but holds for many important subvarieties such as the variety of Heyting algebras and the variety of MV‑algebras. The lattice also exhibits a rich interval structure: the interval between the variety of lattice‑ordered groups and the whole variety is dually isomorphic to the lattice of varieties of negative cones of ℓ‑groups, a fact that connects the representation theory of ℓ‑groups with the equational logic of residuated lattices. Splitting varieties in this lattice have been classified up to the level of varieties generated by finite chains; each such splitting variety corresponds to a critical pair of finite residuated lattices, and the associated splitting identity is a single equation of the form t ≤ s where t and s are lattice terms. These splitting varieties partition the subvariety lattice into intervals that can be analysed independently, a technique that has yielded a complete description of the subvariety lattice of commutative integral residuated lattices of finite width.

Worked Example: Identifying a Splitting Variety in Residuated Lattices
Show that the variety V generated by the three‑element chain C₃ = {0 < a < 1} with multiplication defined by x·y = min(x, y) and residuals given by the usual Heyting implication is a splitting variety in the lattice of subvarieties of residuated lattices.
The algebra C₃ is a finite Heyting algebra, hence a finite residuated lattice. By a theorem of Jipsen, any variety generated by a finite residuated lattice that is subdirectly irreducible and has a unique critical pair is a splitting variety. C₃ is subdirectly irreducible (its monolith is the congruence identifying 0 and a). The only proper subvariety of V is the trivial variety, because any non‑trivial subvariety must contain a non‑trivial simple algebra, and the only simple algebra in V is C₃ itself. Therefore the interval [V, RL] (where RL denotes the variety of all residuated lattices) is complemented: the complement of V is the variety defined by the identity x ≤ y ∨ (x·y). This identity holds in all residuated lattices not containing C₃, and fails in C₃. Hence V is a splitting variety with splitting identity x ≤ y ∨ (x·y).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a given finite algebra generates a splitting variety, first check subdirect irreducibility and then determine the critical pairs. If the algebra is finite, simple, and its variety has exactly one proper non‑trivial subvariety, it is almost always a splitting variety. Write down the splitting identity explicitly; examiners award full marks for the correct identity even if the proof sketch is brief.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of MV‑Algebras

MV‑algebras are the algebraic counterpart of Łukasiewicz infinite‑valued logic; they are bounded commutative residuated lattices satisfying the double negation law and the identity (x → y) → y = (y → x) → x. The variety of MV‑algebras is generated by the standard MV‑algebra on the real unit interval [0,1] with operations x ⊕ y = min(1, x+y) and ¬x = 1−x. The subvariety lattice of MV‑algebras is a well‑understood, countable, distributive lattice. A classical result of Komori and later refined by Di Nola and Lettieri shows that every subvariety of MV‑algebras is generated by a single finite chain, and the lattice of subvarieties is isomorphic to the lattice of all sets of natural numbers ordered by inclusion, where each natural number n corresponds to the variety generated by the (n+1)‑element Łukasiewicz chain. Consequently the subvariety lattice is a countable Boolean algebra without atoms (the atom would correspond to the variety generated by the two‑element Boolean algebra, which is the smallest non‑trivial variety). The compact elements are exactly the finitely generated varieties, which correspond to finite sets of natural numbers. The lattice is also known to be dually isomorphic to the lattice of varieties of lattice‑ordered abelian groups with strong unit, via Mundici’s equivalence. This duality transfers many structural results: for instance, the free MV‑algebra on κ generators corresponds to the free ℓ‑group with strong unit on κ generators, and the projective MV‑algebras correspond to the finitely presented ℓ‑groups with strong unit. The subvariety lattice of MV‑algebras therefore serves as a benchmark for the general theory of subvariety lattices of residuated lattices: it is distributive, countable, and every variety is finitely based (each is axiomatised by a single equation of the form n·x ≤ (n−1)·x for some n). These properties fail dramatically for larger classes such as all residuated lattices or all quantales, highlighting the special algebraic tameness of MV‑algebras.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Lattice‑Ordered Groups

The variety of lattice‑ordered groups (ℓ‑groups) consists of groups equipped with a lattice order compatible with the group operation. Its subvariety lattice has been a central object of study since the work of Conrad, Holland, and McCleary. A fundamental theorem of Holland states that the subvariety lattice of ℓ‑groups is complete, algebraic, and contains a copy of the free lattice on three generators; in particular it is non‑distributive and of cardinality continuum. The compact elements are the finitely generated varieties, and every variety is generated by its finitely generated members. A striking structural feature is the existence of a minimal non‑trivial variety: the variety of abelian ℓ‑groups, which is an atom in the subvariety lattice. Above this atom, the lattice splits into two incomparable intervals: the interval of representable ℓ‑groups (those embeddable into a direct product of totally ordered groups) and the interval of non‑representable ℓ‑groups. The variety of representable ℓ‑groups is itself a splitting variety, with splitting identity the so‑called “π‑identity” (x ∧ y)⁻¹ ≤ x⁻¹ ∨ y⁻¹. The complement of this splitting variety is the variety generated by the free ℓ‑group on two generators, which is known to be non‑representable. The lattice also reflects the Conrad program: the subvariety lattice of normal‑valued ℓ‑groups is a proper sublattice that is dually isomorphic to the lattice of varieties of lattice‑ordered rings. Moreover, the subvariety lattice of ℓ‑groups admits a natural embedding of the subvariety lattice of MV‑algebras via Mundici’s equivalence, and an embedding of the subvariety lattice of lattice‑ordered rings via the construction of the positive cone. These embeddings show that the complexity of the ℓ‑group subvariety lattice subsumes the complexities of both MV‑algebras and lattice‑ordered rings. Recent work by Martinez and others has identified a continuum of splitting varieties in the ℓ‑group lattice, each corresponding to a critical pair of finite ℓ‑groups, and has shown that the lattice of subvarieties of the variety of normal‑valued ℓ‑groups is itself a free lattice on countably many generators.

The Lattice of Subvarieties of the Variety of Lattice‑Ordered Rings

Lattice‑ordered rings (ℓ‑rings) are rings equipped with a lattice order that makes them lattice‑ordered groups under addition and such that multiplication distributes over finite joins and meets. The variety of ℓ‑rings is a proper subvariety of the variety of lattice‑ordered groups (via the additive reduct) and its subvariety lattice inherits many of the complexities of the ℓ‑group lattice while adding new phenomena coming from the multiplicative structure. A theorem of Birkhoff and Pierce shows that the subvariety lattice of ℓ‑rings is complete, algebraic, and contains a copy of the free lattice on three generators; hence it is non‑distributive and of continuum cardinality. The compact elements are the finitely generated varieties. An important atom is the variety of totally ordered rings (the so‑called “o‑rings”), which is generated by the ring of integers with the usual order. Above this atom, the lattice splits into the interval of commutative ℓ‑rings and the interval of non‑commutative ℓ‑rings. The variety of commutative ℓ‑rings is a splitting variety, with splitting identity the commutativity law xy = yx; its complement is the variety generated by the free ℓ‑ring on two non‑commuting generators. The subvariety lattice of commutative ℓ‑rings is known to be dually isomorphic to the lattice of varieties of f‑rings (ℓ‑rings where multiplication by positive elements preserves finite meets), a result due to Bigard, Keimel, and Wolfenstein. This duality transfers the rich structure of f‑ring varieties — including the existence of a continuum of splitting varieties — to commutative ℓ‑rings. On the non‑commutative side, the variety of ℓ‑rings that are also lattice‑ordered algebras over a fixed totally ordered field forms a proper sublattice that is isomorphic to the subvariety lattice of the corresponding variety of lattice‑ordered vector spaces (Riesz spaces). The interplay between the additive ℓ‑group structure and the multiplicative ring structure is captured by the “π‑identity” (x ∧ y)z = xz ∧ yz for positive z, which defines the variety of d‑rings (distributive ℓ‑rings). The subvariety lattice of d‑rings is a proper sublattice that is distributive and countable, in stark contrast to the full ℓ‑ring lattice. This dichotomy illustrates how imposing a single multiplicative identity can collapse the complexity of the subvariety lattice from continuum to countable.

  • Assuming the subvariety lattice of quantales is distributive because quantales generalise frames; it contains N₅ and is non‑distributive.
  • Confusing the splitting identity for the variety of representable ℓ‑groups with the commutativity identity; the former is (x ∧ y)⁻¹ ≤ x⁻¹ ∨ y⁻¹, the latter is xy = yx.
  • Believing every subvariety of MV‑algebras is generated by a single finite chain but forgetting that the generating chain must be a Łukasiewicz chain, not an arbitrary finite chain.
  • Thinking the lattice of subvarieties of residuated lattices is countable; it has the cardinality of the continuum.
  • Overlooking that the variety of abelian ℓ‑groups is an atom in the ℓ‑group subvariety lattice, not the whole variety of ℓ‑groups.
  • Equating the subvariety lattice of commutative ℓ‑rings with that of all ℓ‑rings; the former is a proper sublattice and is dually isomorphic to f‑ring varieties.
  • Assuming the free lattice on three generators embeds in every subvariety lattice of a non‑trivial variety; it fails for the variety of MV‑algebras, whose subvariety lattice is distributive.
