hand/geometric-langlands.html:
The Affine Grassmannian and the Geometric Satake Equivalence

The affine Grassmannian GrG = G((t))/G[[t]] is an ind‑scheme whose points parametrize G‑bundles on the formal disc together with a trivialization on the punctured disc. Its geometry encodes the representation theory of the Langlands dual group LG through the geometric Satake equivalence, which identifies the category of G[[t]]‑equivariant perverse sheaves on GrG with the category of finite‑dimensional representations of LG. The convolution product on perverse sheaves corresponds to the tensor product of representations, and the fiber functor given by taking stalks at the base point recovers the forgetful functor to vector spaces.

Mirković–Vilonen cycles provide a combinatorial basis for the intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties in GrG, giving a geometric realization of the crystal basis of quantum groups. The affine Grassmannian also carries a natural action of the loop rotation torus, whose fixed points are indexed by dominant coweights; the resulting equivariant cohomology ring is isomorphic to the representation ring of LG. This construction is functorial with respect to homomorphisms of reductive groups and underlies the compatibility of the geometric Satake equivalence with the Langlands duality functor.

In the geometric Langlands program, the Hecke functors acting on D‑modules on BunG are defined by convolution with the standard sheaves on the affine Grassmannian. The geometric Satake equivalence translates the Hecke eigen‑condition into the statement that the corresponding object on the Galois side is a local system whose monodromy representation factors through LG. Thus the affine Grassmannian serves as the bridge between the automorphic Hecke operators and the spectral data of LG‑local systems.

Recent work of Bezrukavnikov–Finkelberg–Mirković extends the equivalence to the derived setting, replacing perverse sheaves by constructible complexes and incorporating the monoidal structure of the derived category. This derived geometric Satake equivalence is a key input for the categorical geometric Langlands conjecture of Gaitsgory–Lurie, where the category of D‑modules on BunG is expected to be equivalent to the category of ind‑coherent sheaves on LocLG(X).

The affine Grassmannian also admits a symplectic structure coming from the loop group, and its quantization leads to the spherical Hecke algebra at a generic level. At the critical level the center of the completed universal enveloping algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra is identified with the algebra of functions on the space of LG‑opers, a result of Feigin–Frenkel that underlies the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence.

Critical Level Quantum Geometric Langlands and the Feigin–Frenkel Center

The quantum geometric Langlands correspondence depends on a complex parameter k (the level). When k equals the negative dual Coxeter number −h∨, the theory reaches the critical level. At this value the quantum Hitchin connection becomes flat on the whole moduli space, and the center of the affine vertex algebra V−h∨(g) is isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of LG‑opers on the curve X. This isomorphism, proved by Feigin and Frenkel, identifies the quantum Hamiltonians of the Gaudin model with the classical Hitchin Hamiltonians evaluated on opers.

Opers are special LG‑connections with a prescribed reduction to a Borel subgroup and a transversality condition. The space of LG‑opers, denoted OpLG(X), is a finite‑dimensional affine space modeled on the Hitchin base. The Feigin–Frenkel center acts on any module of the affine vertex algebra at the critical level by scalars, and these scalars are precisely the values of the oper parameters. Consequently, a critical‑level representation of the affine Kac–Moody algebra determines a point in OpLG(X), i.e. a LG‑oper.

On the automorphic side, critical‑level D‑modules on BunG are modules over the sheaf of chiral differential operators twisted by the critical line bundle. The Hecke eigensheaf condition at the critical level translates into the requirement that the corresponding D‑module be an eigensheaf for the action of the Feigin–Frenkel center, with eigenvalues given by a LG‑oper. This yields a bijection between irreducible critical‑level representations of the affine Kac–Moody algebra and LG‑opers, which is the local (or “quantum”) geometric Langlands correspondence at the critical level.

The critical level is also the point where the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence becomes symmetric under the exchange of k and k∨ = −h∨ − k. The S‑duality of N=4 SYM maps the parameter τ = k + h∨ to −1/τ, and at the critical level τ = 0 the duality exchanges the theory with its “mirror” at infinite coupling. This symmetry is reflected in the isomorphism between the categories of D‑modules on BunG and ind‑coherent sheaves on LocLG(X) after appropriate completion.

Recent advances by Gaitsgory, Raskin, and others have constructed the categorical equivalence at the critical level using the theory of factorization algebras and the Ran space. The resulting equivalence identifies the category of D‑modules on BunG with the category of ind‑coherent sheaves on the derived stack of LG‑local systems, with the Feigin–Frenkel center acting as the algebra of functions on the oper locus. This provides a rigorous mathematical framework for the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence at the critical level.

Worked Example: Critical Level Oper Eigenvalues
Let G = SL2 and X = ℙ1. The critical level is k = −2. The Feigin–Frenkel center is generated by the quadratic Segal–Sugawara field. Show that the eigenvalue of this generator on a critical‑level vacuum module is given by the projective connection of an SL2‑oper on ℙ1.
At the critical level the affine vertex algebra V−2(sl2) has a central element S(z) = :Ja(z)Ja(z): (the Sugawara field). Its zero mode acts on any module by a scalar. By the Feigin–Frenkel theorem, the center is isomorphic to the algebra of functions on OpPGL2(ℙ1). An SL2‑oper on ℙ1 is a connection ∇ = d + (0 1; q(z) 0)dz with q(z) a quadratic differential. The eigenvalue of S(z) is precisely q(z). For the vacuum module, the corresponding oper is the trivial oper q(z)=0, so the eigenvalue vanishes. For a non‑trivial oper with q(z) = ∑ ci/(z−zi)2 + …, the eigenvalue is that projective connection. Thus the central charge of the vacuum module matches the oper data.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the critical level, immediately write k = −h∨. Recall that the Feigin–Frenkel center is the algebra of functions on the oper space. For classical groups, the oper space is an affine space modeled on the Hitchin base; its dimension equals the rank of the group times (g−1) plus the number of marked points. Use this dimension count to check consistency of any proposed eigenvalue formula.

Ramified Geometric Langlands and Parabolic Bundles

The classical geometric Langlands correspondence assumes that the G‑bundles and local systems are unramified, i.e. they are defined on the whole smooth curve X. In many arithmetic and geometric applications one must allow prescribed singularities at a finite set of points D ⊂ X. This leads to the ramified geometric Langlands correspondence, where on the automorphic side one considers parabolic G‑bundles (or G‑bundles with a reduction to a parabolic subgroup at each point of D) and on the spectral side one considers LG‑local systems with prescribed monodromy (or irregular singularities) at D.

Parabolic bundles are equipped with a weight (or “parabolic structure”) given by a dominant coweight of G at each marked point. The moduli stack BunG,par of parabolic bundles is an algebraic stack of finite type, and its category of D‑modules carries an action of the ramified Hecke functors. These functors are defined by modifying the parabolic structure at a point away from D, and by allowing a change of the parabolic weight at points of D according to the Satake correspondence for the affine Grassmannian with a fixed level structure.

On the Galois side, the moduli stack LocLG,ram(X) parametrizes LG‑local systems with a fixed conjugacy class of monodromy (or a fixed irregular type) at each point of D. The ramified geometric Langlands conjecture predicts an equivalence between the derived category of D‑modules on BunG,par and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocLG,ram(X), compatible with the Hecke functors and the spectral decomposition.

When the ramification is tame (regular singularities with semi‑simple monodromy), the correspondence can be approached via the parabolic Hitchin system. The parabolic Hitchin fibration maps the moduli space of parabolic Higgs bundles to a base that includes the residues at the marked points. The fibers are again abelian varieties (generalized Prym varieties), and mirror symmetry exchanges the parabolic Hitchin systems for G and LG. The work of Donagi–Pantev and others extends the SYZ picture to the parabolic setting.

For wild ramification (irregular singularities), the situation is more subtle. The moduli of irregular local systems carries a Stokes filtration, and the corresponding automorphic objects are D‑modules on the moduli of bundles with a “wild” parabolic structure. The quantum geometric Langlands correspondence at a generic level provides a framework for wild ramification via the theory of opers with irregular singularities, as developed by Frenkel–Gross and others. The categorical equivalence in the wild case is an active area of research, with recent progress by Gaitsgory–Raskin using the theory of factorization algebras on the Ran space with prescribed singularities.

Derived Categories, Ind‑Coherent Sheaves, and the Categorical Equivalence

The categorical geometric Langlands conjecture, formulated by Gaitsgory and Lurie, asserts an equivalence of ∞‑categories between the derived category of D‑modules on BunG and the derived category of ind‑coherent sheaves on the derived stack LocLG(X) of LG‑local systems. This is a far‑reaching generalization of the original sheaf‑theoretic correspondence, which only dealt with the abelian categories of perverse sheaves or holonomic D‑modules.

Ind‑coherent sheaves, introduced by Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum, are a generalization of quasi‑coherent sheaves that behave well on singular and derived stacks. On a smooth scheme they coincide with quasi‑coherent sheaves, but on the derived stack LocLG(X) they capture the correct homotopical information, including the derived structure coming from the deformation theory of local systems. The category IndCoh(LocLG(X)) carries a natural t‑structure whose heart is the category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the classical truncation.

On the automorphic side, the derived category D‑mod(BunG) is the category of modules over the sheaf of differential operators on the stack BunG. Because BunG is a smooth algebraic stack, D‑modules can be described via crystals or via the theory of D‑modules on Artin stacks developed by Gaitsgory. The Hecke functors act on D‑mod(BunG) by convolution with the standard sheaves on the affine Grassmannian, and they generate a monoidal category equivalent to Rep(LG) via the geometric Satake equivalence.

The proof strategy for the categorical equivalence proceeds by constructing a functor from D‑mod(BunG) to IndCoh(LocLG(X)) using the theory of factorization algebras on the Ran space of X. The Ran space parametrizes finite non‑empty subsets of X, and factorization algebras encode the local‑to‑global principle for chiral algebras. The Feigin–Frenkel center appears as the factorization algebra of observables in the critical‑level chiral algebra, and its action on D‑modules gives the spectral decomposition.

Recent breakthroughs (Gaitsgory–Raskin, 2020s) have established the equivalence for G = GLn and for all reductive groups at the critical level, assuming certain conjectures on the geometry of the affine Grassmannian and the behavior of the Whittaker category. The proof uses the “spectral gluing” technique, which reduces the global equivalence to a collection of local equivalences at each point of the Ran space, together with a descent argument. This categorical framework also incorporates the quantum parameter ℏ = 1/(k + h∨) and provides a unified treatment of the classical, quantum, and critical‑level correspondences.

Non‑Abelian Hodge Theory and the Real Geometric Langlands

Non‑abelian Hodge theory, due to Hitchin, Simpson, Corlette, and Donaldson, provides a homeomorphism between the moduli space MH(G) of semistable Higgs bundles and the character variety MB(G) of representations of the fundamental group π1(X) into G. This correspondence is a diffeomorphism but not holomorphic; it intertwines the complex structure of MH(G) with the symplectic structure of MB(G) and vice versa. The Hitchin fibration on MH(G) corresponds under this homeomorphism to the “Betti” integrable system on MB(G) given by the traces of monodromy.

The real geometric Langlands program, initiated by Kapustin–Witten and developed by Ben‑Zvi–Nadler, replaces the complex curve X by a real surface Σ and considers the topological twist of N=4 SYM on Σ × C where C is a complex curve. The resulting two‑dimensional theory on Σ has a category of boundary conditions given by the Fukaya category of MH(G) (or its mirror MH(LG)). S‑duality then predicts an equivalence between the Fukaya category of MH(G) and the category of B‑branes on MH(LG), which is precisely the derived category of coherent sheaves on the Hitchin moduli space of the dual group.

In the real setting, the geometric Langlands correspondence becomes a statement about the equivalence of the Fukaya category of the Hitchin moduli space (with its natural hyperkähler structure) and the category of D‑modules on the moduli of real G‑bundles. The Hecke eigensheaf condition translates into the condition that a Lagrangian brane in MH(G) be invariant under the action of the Hitchin Hamiltonians. This perspective connects the geometric Langlands program with homological mirror symmetry and the theory of topological strings.

The P=W conjecture, proved by de Cataldo–Hausel–Migliorini and later by Maulik–Shen, relates the perverse filtration on the cohomology of MH(G) coming from the Hitchin fibration to the weight filtration on the cohomology of the character variety MB(G). This equality of filtrations is a topological shadow of the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence and provides a concrete test of the geometric Langlands predictions at the level of cohomology.

Recent work by Gaiotto–Moore–Neitzke on wall‑crossing and the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula has given a physical interpretation of the Stokes phenomena for irregular Hitchin systems. The resulting “spectral networks” provide a combinatorial description of the Fukaya category of MH(G) and its mirror, linking the real geometric Langlands to the theory of cluster varieties and the Fock–Goncharov coordinates on the moduli of local systems. This circle of ideas continues to drive progress in both the mathematical and physical aspects of the Langlands program.

  • Confusing the affine Grassmannian with the affine flag variety; the former parametrizes G‑bundles with trivialization on the punctured disc, the latter includes a Borel reduction.
  • Assuming the Feigin–Frenkel center is the whole center of the affine vertex algebra at all levels; it is only at the critical level that the center is large enough to be identified with functions on opers.
  • Treating ramified and unramified geometric Langlands as identical; parabolic structures and prescribed monodromy change both the moduli stacks and the Hecke functors.
  • Equating ind‑coherent sheaves with quasi‑coherent sheaves on singular stacks; ind‑coherent sheaves are designed to have the correct homotopical behavior on derived stacks.
  • Overlooking the role of the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence in translating between the Hitchin moduli space and the character variety; the P=W conjecture is a precise cohomological formulation of this translation.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the categorical equivalence at generic level and at the critical level; the critical level equivalence uses the Feigin–Frenkel center and opers, while the generic level involves a deformation parameter ℏ.
  • Misidentifying the S‑duality group as SL(2,ℤ) acting only on the coupling τ; it also acts on the choice of boundary conditions, exchanging electric and magnetic branes.

biology/genetics-evolution.html:
Epigenetic Regulation and Inheritance

Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve alterations in the DNA sequence itself. The three principal mechanisms are DNA methylation, histone post‑translational modifications, and non‑coding RNA‑mediated silencing. In mammals, DNA methylation occurs predominantly at CpG dinucleotides; methylation of promoter CpG islands recruits methyl‑CpG‑binding proteins and histone deacetylases, leading to a compact chromatin state that blocks transcription factor access. Histone modifications — acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination — create a combinatorial “histone code” that is read by effector proteins to either activate or repress transcription. For example, H3K4me3 marks active promoters, whereas H3K27me3, deposited by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, marks facultative heterochromatin. Long non‑coding RNAs such as XIST recruit chromatin‑modifying complexes to silence one X chromosome in female mammals, illustrating RNA‑directed epigenetic regulation.

During early embryogenesis, the genome undergoes two waves of global demethylation and remethylation, erasing most parental epigenetic marks. However, a subset of loci — imprinted genes and certain transposable elements — escape this reprogramming, allowing transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. Environmental factors such as diet, stress, and toxins can alter epigenetic marks in somatic cells and, in some model organisms, in the germline, providing a mechanistic basis for the developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) hypothesis. In humans, epidemiological studies of the Dutch Hunger Winter cohort show persistent hypomethylation of the IGF2 differentially methylated region in individuals exposed to famine periconceptionally, linking early‑life nutrition to adult metabolic phenotypes.

Epigenetic dysregulation underlies numerous diseases. Aberrant promoter hypermethylation silences tumour‑suppressor genes (e.g., MLH1 in colorectal cancer, BRCA1 in breast cancer), while global hypomethylation promotes chromosomal instability. Histone‑modifier mutations are recurrent in haematological malignancies (e.g., EZH2 gain‑of‑function in lymphoma, KMT2A rearrangements in acute leukaemia). Therapeutically, DNA‑methyltransferase inhibitors (azacitidine, decitabine) and histone deacetylase inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin) are approved for myelodysplastic syndromes and cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, respectively, demonstrating that epigenetic modifications are reversible targets.

Key Points for Examination

  • DNA methylation at CpG islands = transcriptional repression; maintained by DNMT1 during replication.
  • Histone acetylation = open chromatin (euchromatin); deacetylation = closed chromatin (heterochromatin).
  • XIST RNA mediates X‑chromosome inactivation via recruitment of PRC2 and H3K27me3.
  • Epigenetic reprogramming occurs in primordial germ cells and pre‑implantation embryo; imprinted loci resist erasure.
  • Environmental exposures can modify epigenetic marks, providing a molecular link for DOHaD.
  • Epigenetic drugs target writers (DNMTs), erasers (HDACs), and readers (bromodomain proteins).

Genomic Imprinting and Associated Disorders

Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon whereby a subset of genes is expressed in a parent‑of‑origin‑specific manner. In mammals, approximately 100–200 genes are imprinted, many of which regulate fetal growth, placental development, and postnatal metabolism. Imprinting is established during gametogenesis: differentially methylated regions (DMRs) acquire methylation in either the male or female germline and retain this mark after fertilisation. The classic example is the Igf2/H19 locus on mouse chromosome 7 (human 11p15.5). The paternal allele expresses the growth‑promoting IGF2 protein, while the maternal allele expresses the non‑coding H19 RNA that acts as a tumour suppressor. An imprinting control region (ICR) upstream of H19 is methylated on the paternal allele, blocking CTCF binding and allowing enhancers to activate IGF2; on the maternal allele, the unmethylated ICR binds CTCF, insulating IGF2 from the enhancers and directing them to H19.

Disruption of imprinting causes well‑characterised syndromes. Prader‑Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS) both map to chromosome 15q11‑q13 but arise from loss of paternal or maternal contribution, respectively. PWS results from deletion of the paternal 15q11‑q13 region, maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 15, or an imprinting defect that silences the paternal allele. Clinical features include neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulties, hyperphagia leading to obesity, hypogonadism, and intellectual disability. AS is caused by maternal deletion, paternal UPD, or mutation in the maternally expressed UBE3A gene; patients exhibit severe developmental delay, ataxia, inappropriate laughter, and seizures. Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) involves dysregulation of the 11p15.5 imprinted domain, leading to overgrowth, macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, and increased embryonal tumour risk (Wilms tumour, hepatoblastoma). Silver‑Russell syndrome (SRS) is the growth‑restriction counterpart, often due to hypomethylation of the H19 ICR on the paternal allele or maternal UPD7.

Diagnosis relies on methylation‑specific PCR or microarray analysis of DMRs. Uniparental disomy detection requires polymorphic markers to confirm the absence of one parental allele. Management is multidisciplinary: growth hormone for PWS, anti‑epileptics for AS, tumour surveillance for BWS. Emerging epigenetic therapies aim to reactivate the silenced allele — for example, antisense oligonucleotides targeting the UBE3A antisense transcript in AS mouse models have shown phenotypic rescue, illustrating the therapeutic potential of modulating imprinting.

Key Points for Examination

  • Imprinting = parent‑of‑origin‑specific expression established by germline DMR methylation.
  • Igf2/H19 locus: paternal methylation of ICR → IGF2 on; maternal unmethylated ICR → CTCF binds → H19 on.
  • PWS = loss of paternal 15q11‑q13; AS = loss of maternal 15q11‑q13 (or UBE3A mutation).
  • BWS = gain of methylation at H19 ICR or loss of methylation at KCNQ1OT1 ICR; SRS = opposite methylation changes.
  • UPD detection requires microsatellite or SNP analysis; methylation‑specific PCR is first‑line test.
  • Epigenetic editing (CRISPR‑dCas9‑TET1/DNMT3A) is experimental for imprinting disorders.
Technique: Methylation‑Specific PCR (MS‑PCR)
A neonate presents with severe hypotonia, poor suck, and failure to thrive. Chromosomal microarray reveals a 5 Mb deletion at 15q11.2‑q13.1. The parents are phenotypically normal. Which parental allele is deleted in this child, and which syndrome is most likely?
The deletion encompasses the imprinted 15q11‑q13 region. Prader‑Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternally expressed genes (e.g., SNRPN, NDN) in this interval, whereas Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternally expressed UBE3A. The clinical picture of neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulty is classic for Prader‑Willi syndrome. Therefore, the deleted allele is the paternal one, and the diagnosis is Prader‑Willi syndrome. Confirmation is obtained by MS‑PCR showing absence of the paternal methylation pattern at the SNRPN DMR.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question describes a 15q11‑q13 deletion, first note the clinical features: hypotonia + hyperphagia/obesity = Prader‑Willi (paternal loss); severe developmental delay + ataxia + happy demeanour = Angelman (maternal loss). Memorise the parent‑of‑origin for each syndrome and the key genes (SNRPN for PWS, UBE3A for AS). Methylation‑specific PCR is the standard diagnostic test; know that it distinguishes parental alleles by methylation status, not by sequence change.

Mitochondrial Genetics and Maternal Inheritance

Mitochondria possess their own circular double‑stranded DNA (mtDNA) of 16.5 kb in humans, encoding 13 protein‑coding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes, 22 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs. Unlike nuclear DNA, mtDNA is present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell and is inherited almost exclusively through the oocyte; sperm mitochondria are selectively degraded after fertilisation. This strict maternal inheritance means that mtDNA mutations are transmitted from mother to all offspring, but not from father. However, the proportion of mutant mtDNA molecules can vary among tissues and individuals — a phenomenon termed heteroplasmy. The phenotypic expression of a pathogenic mtDNA mutation typically requires the mutant load to exceed a tissue‑specific threshold (often 60–90 %), explaining variable penetrance and severity within families.

Classic mitochondrial disorders illustrate these principles. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is caused primarily by three point mutations (m.3460G>A, m.11778G>A, m.14484T>C) in complex I subunit genes; it shows incomplete penetrance and male predominance, likely due to nuclear modifier genes and hormonal influences. Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke‑like episodes (MELAS) is most often due to the m.3243A>G mutation in the tRNALeu(UUR) gene; heteroplasmy level correlates with age of onset and severity. Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged‑red fibres (MERRF) is associated with m.8344A>G in tRNALys. Kearns‑Sayre syndrome (KSS) and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) are frequently caused by large‑scale mtDNA deletions that arise somatically and are not transmitted through the germline because they are lost during the mitochondrial bottleneck in oogenesis.

The mitochondrial bottleneck — a drastic reduction in mtDNA copy number during primordial germ cell development followed by random amplification — shapes the heteroplasmy level in the next generation. This stochastic process can shift mutant load dramatically between mother and child, making genetic counselling probabilistic. Prenatal diagnosis via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis can estimate fetal heteroplasmy, but the predictive value is limited by tissue‑specific segregation. Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT), including pronuclear transfer and maternal spindle transfer, has been developed to prevent transmission of pathogenic mtDNA by transferring the nuclear genome into an enucleated donor oocyte with healthy mitochondria. The first live births using MRT were reported in 2016, and the technique is now regulated in several jurisdictions.

Key Points for Examination

  • mtDNA = 16.5 kb circular, maternal inheritance, high copy number, no introns, overlapping genes.
  • Heteroplasmy = coexistence of mutant and wild‑type mtDNA; threshold effect determines phenotype.
  • LHON: complex I point mutations, incomplete penetrance, male bias.
  • MELAS: m.3243A>G tRNALeu(UUR), stroke‑like episodes, lactic acidosis.
  • MERRF: m.8344A>G tRNALys, myoclonus, ragged‑red fibres.
  • Large deletions (KSS, CPEO) usually sporadic, not maternally transmitted.
  • Mitochondrial bottleneck causes random heteroplasmy shifts; MRT prevents transmission.

Quantitative Genetics: Heritability and QTL Mapping

Quantitative genetics deals with traits that show continuous variation (e.g., height, blood pressure, yield) and are influenced by multiple loci (polygenic) and environment. The phenotypic variance (VP) is partitioned into genetic variance (VG) and environmental variance (VE), with VG further divided into additive (VA), dominance (VD), and epistatic (VI) components. Narrow‑sense heritability (h²) = VA / VP predicts the response to selection (R = h²S, where S is the selection differential). Broad‑sense heritability (H²) = VG / VP includes all genetic effects. In human studies, heritability is estimated from twin designs (comparing monozygotic vs dizygotic concordance) or from genome‑wide relatedness matrices (GREML) using SNP data.

Mapping quantitative trait loci (QTL) identifies genomic regions contributing to trait variation. Traditional linkage analysis in pedigrees or experimental crosses uses recombination fractions to locate QTL intervals (typically 10–20 cM). Association mapping (genome‑wide association studies, GWAS) exploits linkage disequilibrium in populations to achieve finer resolution (often <100 kb). GWAS have identified thousands of common variants (minor allele frequency >5 %) with small effect sizes (odds ratios 1.05–1.2) for complex diseases and traits. However, these variants collectively explain only a fraction of the heritability estimated from family studies — the “missing heritability” problem. Proposed explanations include rare variants of larger effect not captured by SNP arrays, structural variants, gene‑gene and gene‑environment interactions, and overestimation of heritability due to shared environment.

Polygenic scores (PGS) aggregate the effects of many GWAS‑significant SNPs to predict individual genetic risk. PGS are increasingly used for risk stratification (e.g., coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes) and in embryo selection debates. Their predictive accuracy depends on the trait’s heritability, sample size of the discovery GWAS, and ancestry match between discovery and target populations. Fine‑mapping and functional annotation (eQTL colocalisation, chromatin interaction data) aim to pinpoint causal variants and mechanisms. Emerging methods such as Mendelian randomisation use genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between exposures and outcomes, leveraging the random assortment of alleles at meiosis.

Key Points for Examination

  • VP = VA + VD + VI + VE; h² = VA/VP, H² = VG/VP.
  • Response to selection R = h²S (breeder’s equation).
  • Twin studies: h² ≈ 2(rMZ – rDZ).
  • Linkage mapping = low resolution, family‑based; GWAS = high resolution, population‑based.
  • Missing heritability: rare variants, structural variants, epistasis, G×E, overestimation.
  • Polygenic scores sum SNP effects; limited by ancestry mismatch and winner’s curse.
  • Mendelian randomisation uses genetic instruments for causal inference.

Molecular Phylogenetics and Molecular Clocks

Molecular phylogenetics reconstructs evolutionary relationships by comparing DNA, RNA, or protein sequences. The fundamental steps are sequence acquisition, multiple sequence alignment (MSA), model selection, and tree inference. Alignment algorithms such as ClustalW, MAFFT, or MUSCLE handle insertions/deletions; poorly aligned regions are often trimmed (e.g., with Gblocks) to avoid phylogenetic artefacts. Substitution models describe the probability of nucleotide or amino‑acid changes over time. For DNA, the general time‑reversible (GTR) model with gamma‑distributed rate heterogeneity (GTR+Γ) is standard; for proteins, models like LG+Γ or WAG+Γ are used. Model selection employs information criteria (AIC, BIC) or hierarchical likelihood ratio tests.

Tree inference methods fall into three categories: distance‑based (Neighbour‑Joining, UPGMA), maximum parsimony (minimising total character changes), and maximum likelihood (ML) / Bayesian inference (BI). ML finds the tree topology and branch lengths that maximise the likelihood of the observed data under the chosen model; software includes RAxML, IQ‑TREE, and PhyML. BI uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior distribution of trees, providing clade credibility values (e.g., MrBayes, BEAST). Bootstrap resampling (typically 1000 replicates) assesses branch support in ML; posterior probabilities serve the same role in BI. Concordance between bootstrap values ≥70 % and posterior probabilities ≥0.95 is considered strong support.

The molecular clock hypothesis posits that genetic divergence accumulates at a roughly constant rate over time, allowing divergence dating. A strict clock assumes a single rate across all lineages; relaxed clocks (uncorrelated lognormal, autocorrelated) allow rate variation among branches. Calibration points — fossil constraints, biogeographic events, or known substitution rates — anchor the clock. BEAST implements Bayesian relaxed‑clock dating, jointly estimating topology, rates, and node ages with credible intervals. Molecular clocks have dated the human‑chimpanzee split to ~6–7 Ma, the origin of placental mammals to ~90–100 Ma, and the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) to >3.5 Ga. However, rate heterogeneity, saturation at deep timescales, and calibration uncertainty limit precision. Phylogenomics — using hundreds to thousands of loci — mitigates stochastic error and improves resolution of contentious nodes (e.g., the root of the eukaryotic tree, relationships among major animal phyla).

Key Points for Examination

  • MSA quality critical; trim ambiguous regions before analysis.
  • Substitution models: GTR+Γ for DNA, LG+Γ for proteins; select via AIC/BIC.
  • ML and Bayesian methods are statistically consistent; distance/parsimony less so.
  • Bootstrap ≥70 % and posterior probability ≥0.95 = strong clade support.
  • Strict clock = single rate; relaxed clocks (uncorrelated lognormal) accommodate rate variation.
  • Calibration: fossils (minimum ages), biogeography, known rates; use soft bounds.
  • Phylogenomics reduces stochastic error; concatenation vs coalescent (ASTRAL) approaches.
  • Confusing narrow‑sense and broad‑sense heritability; only h² predicts selection response.
  • Assuming GWAS hits are causal; most are tag SNPs in LD with the true variant.
  • Treating mitochondrial heteroplasmy level as fixed; it shifts due to bottleneck and mitotic segregation.
  • Misidentifying parental origin in imprinting disorders; remember PWS = paternal loss, AS = maternal loss.
  • Overinterpreting molecular clock dates without considering calibration uncertainty and rate variation.
  • Neglecting that epigenetic marks are largely erased in early embryogenesis except at imprinted loci and some transposons.
  • Assuming polygenic scores transfer across ancestries without loss of accuracy.

hand/diff-geometry.html:
Second Fundamental Form and Shape Operator

The first fundamental form captures intrinsic metric properties of a surface, but extrinsic geometry — how the surface sits in ambient space — is encoded in the second fundamental form. For an immersed surface S in ℝ³ with unit normal field N, the second fundamental form II is the symmetric bilinear form defined by II(X,Y) = ⟨−dN(X), Y⟩ = ⟨X, dN(Y)⟩ for tangent vectors X,Y. The linear map S = −dN : TpS → TpS is the shape operator (Weingarten map). Its eigenvalues are the principal curvatures κ₁, κ₂; the mean curvature is H = (κ₁+κ₂)/2 and the Gaussian curvature is K = κ₁κ₂ = det(S). The coefficients of II in a parametrisation r(u,v) are e = ⟨ruu, N⟩, f = ⟨ruv, N⟩, g = ⟨rvv, N⟩. The matrix of S relative to the basis {ru, rv} is the product of the inverse first fundamental form matrix and the second fundamental form matrix. The Gauss equation relates the Riemann curvature tensor of the induced metric to the second fundamental form: R(X,Y)Z = II(Y,Z)S(X) − II(X,Z)S(Y). The Codazzi–Mainardi equations express the symmetry of the covariant derivative of II. Together, Gauss and Codazzi–Mainardi are the integrability conditions for the existence of an immersion with given first and second fundamental forms (Bonnet's theorem). In higher codimension, the second fundamental form takes values in the normal bundle, and the shape operator becomes a family of operators indexed by normal directions. The mean curvature vector is the trace of the second fundamental form; a submanifold is minimal iff its mean curvature vector vanishes identically.

Parallel Transport, Holonomy, and the Ambrose–Singer Theorem

Parallel transport along a curve γ in a Riemannian manifold (M,g) moves a tangent vector while keeping it covariantly constant: ∇γ̇V = 0. The result depends on the path; for a closed loop the initial and final vectors differ by a linear isometry of the tangent space at the base point. The set of all such linear maps obtained from piecewise‑smooth loops based at p forms the holonomy group Holp(M). For a connected manifold, holonomy groups at different points are conjugate, so one speaks of the holonomy group Hol(M). The Ambrose–Singer theorem (1953) characterises the Lie algebra of Hol(M) as the span of curvature endomorphisms R(X,Y) evaluated at points reachable by horizontal curves in the frame bundle. In particular, if the curvature tensor vanishes identically, the holonomy group is trivial and the manifold is locally isometric to Euclidean space. On a surface, parallel transport around a simple closed curve rotates a vector by the integral of Gaussian curvature over the enclosed region (the angle defect). This is a direct consequence of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for geodesic triangles. For a sphere of radius R, the holonomy of a spherical triangle with angles α, β, γ equals the spherical excess α+β+γ−π. In higher dimensions, the restricted holonomy group (loops homotopic to zero) is a connected Lie subgroup of O(n). Berger's classification (1955) lists the possible irreducible holonomy groups of non‑symmetric Riemannian manifolds: SO(n), U(n/2), SU(n/2), Sp(n/4), Sp(n/4)·Sp(1), G₂ (n=7), Spin(7) (n=8). Each corresponds to a special geometric structure: Kähler, Calabi–Yau, hyper‑Kähler, quaternion‑Kähler, etc. The holonomy group controls the existence of parallel tensor fields; for instance, a parallel spinor exists iff the holonomy is contained in G₂ or Spin(7). This link underlies many constructions in string theory and M‑theory.

Technique: Computing Holonomy on the 2‑Sphere
Show that parallel transport of a tangent vector around a spherical triangle of angles α, β, γ rotates the vector by the spherical excess α+β+γ−π.
Let the sphere have radius R. The Gaussian curvature is K = 1/R². The area of a spherical triangle with interior angles α, β, γ is A = R²(α+β+γ−π) (Girard's theorem). By the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for a geodesic triangle, the total turning of the tangent vector along the boundary equals the integral of geodesic curvature plus the integral of K over the interior. Since the sides are geodesics, geodesic curvature vanishes. The parallel transport angle equals the negative of the total turning of the tangent vector, which is exactly the integral of K over the triangle: ∫Δ K dA = (1/R²)·R²(α+β+γ−π) = α+β+γ−π. Thus the vector is rotated by the spherical excess.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for holonomy, first identify the curvature form; on a surface the holonomy equals the integral of Gaussian curvature over the enclosed region. Use the Gauss–Bonnet theorem to convert area integrals to angle sums. For higher dimensions, recall Berger's list: if the manifold is Kähler, holonomy is contained in U(n); if Ricci‑flat Kähler, it reduces to SU(n). Recognising these special holonomies often yields immediate topological constraints (e.g., existence of parallel forms).

Cartan's Method of Moving Frames

Élie Cartan's method of moving frames (repère mobile) provides a powerful computational framework for submanifold geometry and equivalence problems. Instead of working with coordinate‑dependent Christoffel symbols, one chooses a local orthonormal frame {e₁,…,eₙ} on the manifold and its dual coframe {ω¹,…,ωⁿ}. The Levi‑Civita connection is encoded in the connection 1‑forms ωⁱⱼ defined by ∇eᵢ = ωⁱⱼ ⊗ eⱼ, satisfying ωⁱⱼ = −ωʲⁱ (metric compatibility) and the first structure equation dωⁱ + ωⁱⱼ ∧ ωʲ = 0 (torsion‑free). The curvature 2‑forms Ωⁱⱼ = dωⁱⱼ + ωⁱₖ ∧ ωᵏⱼ give the Riemann tensor components via Ωⁱⱼ = ½ Rⁱⱼₖₗ ωᵏ ∧ ωˡ. For a surface in ℝ³, one adapts the frame so that e₁, e₂ are tangent and e₃ is the unit normal. The second fundamental form appears as the normal component of the connection forms: ω¹₃ = h¹₁ ω¹ + h¹₂ ω², ω²₃ = h²₁ ω¹ + h²₂ ω², where hⁱⱼ are the coefficients of the shape operator. The Gauss equation becomes Ω¹₂ = −ω¹₃ ∧ ω³₂ = −K ω¹ ∧ ω², directly yielding K = det(hⁱⱼ). Cartan's method excels at solving the equivalence problem: given two geometric structures, one constructs invariants by normalising the frame bundle and computing the structure functions. The process terminates with a complete set of invariants (the Cartan invariants) that classify the structure up to local diffeomorphism. This approach underlies the classification of homogeneous spaces, the study of G‑structures, and modern treatments of exterior differential systems. In practice, moving frames simplify computations on symmetric spaces and principal bundles, and they are the foundation of the Cartan–Kähler theorem for analytic solutions of PDE systems.

Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry

Comparison theorems relate the geometry of a Riemannian manifold to that of a model space of constant curvature. The Rauch comparison theorem (1951) compares the differential of the exponential map on a manifold with sectional curvature bounded above by K to that on the space form of constant curvature K. If sec ≤ K, then Jacobi fields grow at least as fast as in the model; if sec ≥ K, they grow at most as fast. This yields the Toponogov triangle comparison theorem: in a manifold with sec ≥ K, geodesic triangles are "fatter" than corresponding triangles in the model space of curvature K. The Bishop–Gromov volume comparison theorem states that if Ric ≥ (n−1)K, then the volume of geodesic balls divided by the volume of balls in the model space is a non‑increasing function of the radius. Consequently, the volume of a complete manifold with Ric ≥ 0 is at most the Euclidean volume growth, and equality forces the manifold to be isometric to ℝⁿ. The Myers theorem (1941) uses Ric ≥ (n−1)K > 0 to bound the diameter by π/√K, implying compactness and finite fundamental group. The Cheeger–Gromoll splitting theorem (1971) shows that a complete manifold with Ric ≥ 0 containing a line splits isometrically as a product ℝ × N. These results are proved by analysing the index form of geodesics and applying the second variation formula. Modern extensions include the Lott–Villani–Sturm theory of metric measure spaces with Ricci curvature bounded below in the sense of optimal transport, which generalises comparison geometry to non‑smooth spaces. In exam questions, typical tasks are: apply Rauch to estimate the norm of a Jacobi field, use Toponogov to bound angles in a triangle, or invoke Bishop–Gromov to deduce volume growth constraints.

Minimal Surfaces and the Plateau Problem

A minimal surface is an immersed surface with zero mean curvature H = 0 at every point. Equivalently, it is a critical point of the area functional under compactly supported variations. The classical Plateau problem asks: given a Jordan curve Γ in ℝ³, does there exist a disk‑type minimal surface spanning Γ? Jesse Douglas and Tibor Radó independently solved this in 1930–31 using the direct method of the calculus of variations: minimise the Dirichlet energy ∫|∇u|² among maps from the unit disk to ℝ³ with boundary values parametrising Γ. The solution is a conformal harmonic immersion, hence a minimal surface. Regularity theory (Morrey, De Giorgi, Nash) shows that the minimiser is smooth up to the boundary if Γ is smooth. For higher genus or non‑disk topologies, the problem becomes more subtle; Almgren's work on varifolds and geometric measure theory provided existence for arbitrary boundary curves and prescribed topological type. The Weierstrass representation gives a local parametrisation of minimal surfaces in terms of holomorphic data: if f is meromorphic and g is holomorphic on a Riemann surface, then X(z) = Re ∫ (½(1−g²), i/2(1+g²), g) f dz defines a minimal surface. Classical examples include the catenoid, helicoid, Scherk's surface, and the Enneper surface. The Gauss map of a minimal surface is conformal, and its image omits at most four points (Osserman's theorem). The total curvature of a complete minimal surface of finite topology is an integer multiple of 2π (Jorge–Meeks formula). In recent decades, minimal surface theory has merged with mean curvature flow, where surfaces evolve by their mean curvature vector; singularities are modelled by self‑shrinking minimal surfaces. The solution of the Willmore conjecture by Marques and Neves (2012) used minimal surfaces in the 3‑sphere to bound the Willmore energy of tori.

  • Confusing the second fundamental form with the shape operator; they are related by the metric but have different index positions.
  • Assuming holonomy is always the full orthogonal group; special holonomy imposes strong topological restrictions.
  • Neglecting the torsion‑free condition when writing Cartan's first structure equation; it is essential for the Levi‑Civita connection.
  • Applying Rauch comparison without checking the curvature bound direction (upper vs lower bound).
  • Thinking every minimal surface is area‑minimising; minimal means critical, not necessarily global minimum.
  • Overlooking the conformality of the Gauss map for minimal surfaces, which is key to the Weierstrass representation.
  • Misstating the Bishop–Gromov monotonicity as applying to sectional curvature instead of Ricci curvature.

These advanced topics form the backbone of modern differential geometry and appear frequently in rigorous examinations.

hand/geometry.html:
Euler Line and Triangle Centers

The centroid, orthocenter, circumcenter, and nine‑point center of any non‑equilateral triangle are collinear. This line is called the Euler line. The centroid divides the segment joining the orthocenter and circumcenter in the ratio 2:1, with the centroid twice as close to the circumcenter as to the orthocenter. The nine‑point center lies exactly midway between the orthocenter and circumcenter. In an equilateral triangle all four centers coincide, so the Euler line degenerates to a point.

Proof sketch: Let O be the circumcenter, H the orthocenter, and G the centroid. The vector relation OH = 3OG holds for any triangle. The nine‑point center N is the midpoint of OH, giving ON = ½OH. Consequently G lies on ON and divides it in the ratio 2:1. These relations are derived from the fact that the medial triangle is homothetic to the original triangle with center G and factor –½.

Applications in competitive problems: (1) Given coordinates of two centers, the third can be found instantly using the 2:1 ratio. (2) The distance OH satisfies Euler’s formula OH² = R² – 8R²cos Acos Bcos C, where R is the circumradius. (3) The nine‑point circle radius is R/2, and its center N is the midpoint of OH.

Key Ratios on the Euler Line

  • OG : GH = 1 : 2
  • ON = NH = ½ OH
  • Nine‑point radius = R/2

When a problem asks for the distance between the circumcenter and orthocenter, compute R from the side lengths (using R = abc / 4Δ) and then apply Euler’s formula or the 2:1 centroid relation if the centroid is known.

Power of a Point and Radical Axis

The power of a point P with respect to a circle of radius r and center O is defined as Pow(P) = OP² – r². If P lies outside the circle, the power equals the square of the tangent length from P to the circle. If P lies inside, the power is negative and its absolute value equals the product of the segments of any chord through P. For a secant intersecting the circle at A and B, PA·PB = Pow(P).

The radical axis of two non‑concentric circles is the locus of points having equal power with respect to both circles. It is a straight line perpendicular to the line of centers. If the circles intersect, the radical axis is their common chord. If they are tangent, the radical axis is the common tangent at the point of tangency. For three circles taken pairwise, the three radical axes are concurrent at the radical center (provided the centers are not collinear).

Practical uses: (1) Finding the length of a common external tangent between two circles: draw the radical axis, locate the homothety centers, and apply similar triangles. (2) Solving problems where a variable circle passes through two fixed points — its center moves along the perpendicular bisector, and its power with respect to a given circle is constant along the radical axis. (3) Determining the equation of a circle orthogonal to two given circles: the center must lie on their radical axis and satisfy the orthogonality condition d² = r₁² + r₂².

Radical Axis Equation

For circles x² + y² + 2g₁x + 2f₁y + c₁ = 0 and x² + y² + 2g₂x + 2f₂y + c₂ = 0, subtracting gives the radical axis: 2(g₁–g₂)x + 2(f₁–f₂)y + (c₁–c₂) = 0.

Worked Example: Radical Axis and Tangent Length
Two circles have equations x² + y² – 6x – 8y + 9 = 0 and x² + y² – 2x – 4y – 11 = 0. Find the length of the common external tangent.
First rewrite each in center‑radius form. Circle 1: (x–3)² + (y–4)² = 16 → center C₁(3,4), r₁ = 4. Circle 2: (x–1)² + (y–2)² = 16 → center C₂(1,2), r₂ = 4. Distance between centers d = √[(3–1)² + (4–2)²] = √8 = 2√2. Since r₁ = r₂, the external tangent length L = √(d² – (r₁–r₂)²) = √(8 – 0) = 2√2. Alternatively, the radical axis is the perpendicular bisector of C₁C₂; the homothety center lies on the line of centers at infinity, confirming the tangents are parallel and equal to the distance between the parallel lines through the centers offset by the radius. Answer: 2√2 units.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem gives two circles in general form, immediately subtract the equations to obtain the radical axis. This single line often replaces several steps of coordinate geometry and directly yields the chord of contact, common tangent direction, or the locus of centers of circles orthogonal to both.

Coordinate Geometry of Circles and Conics

The general second‑degree equation Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 represents a circle iff A = C ≠ 0 and B = 0. Completing the square yields center (–D/2A, –E/2A) and radius √[(D²+E²–4AF)/(4A²)]. The condition for a real circle is D²+E²–4AF > 0.

Tangents: For a point (x₁,y₁) on the circle, the tangent line is xx₁ + yy₁ + g(x+x₁) + f(y+y₁) + c = 0 (using the form x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0). For an external point, the chord of contact has the same equation with (x₁,y₁) replaced by the external point. The polar of a point with respect to a circle is defined identically; if the point lies on the circle the polar coincides with the tangent.

Conics: The discriminant Δ = B² – 4AC classifies the conic: Δ < 0 → ellipse (circle if A=C, B=0); Δ = 0 → parabola; Δ > 0 → hyperbola. The center of a central conic (ellipse or hyperbola) solves the linear system ∂/∂x = 0, ∂/∂y = 0. Rotating axes to eliminate the xy term uses the angle θ satisfying tan 2θ = B/(A–C). After rotation, the standard forms reveal axes lengths, eccentricity, and foci.

Useful Shortcuts

  • Length of tangent from (x₁,y₁) to circle x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0 is √(x₁²+y₁²+2gx₁+2fy₁+c).
  • Equation of pair of tangents from (x₁,y₁): SS₁ = T², where S is the circle equation, S₁ = S(x₁,y₁), and T is the tangent form.
  • Director circle of an ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is x²+y² = a²+b²; for a hyperbola it is x²+y² = a²–b² (if a > b).

Solid Geometry: Cross Sections, Nets, and Volume by Dissection

A cross section of a solid is the intersection of the solid with a plane. The shape of the cross section depends on the orientation of the cutting plane. For a right circular cone, sections parallel to the base are circles; sections through the apex are triangles; oblique sections produce ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas (the conic sections). For a sphere, every cross section is a circle whose radius varies with the distance of the plane from the center.

Cavalieri’s principle states that if two solids have equal heights and every parallel cross‑sectional area at the same level is equal, then the volumes are equal. This principle underlies the derivation of the volume of a sphere (by comparing with a cylinder minus a cone) and the volume of a pyramid (by comparing with a prism of the same base and height). It also justifies the formula V = ⅓ Base Area × Height for any pyramid or cone, regardless of base shape.

Nets are two‑dimensional unfoldings of a polyhedron’s faces. A valid net must satisfy Euler’s formula V – E + F = 2 and the sum of face angles around each vertex in the net must be less than 360°. For a cube there are 11 distinct nets. Recognizing nets quickly helps in surface‑area problems where the solid is “opened” and the total area is the sum of the planar faces.

Volume by Dissection Examples

  • Sphere volume: inscribe the sphere in a cylinder of radius r and height 2r. Remove a double cone of same base and height. The remaining solid has cross‑sectional area π(r²–x²) at distance x from the center, matching the sphere’s cross‑section. Hence Vsphere = Vcylinder – Vdouble cone = 2πr³ – ⅔πr³ = ⁴⁄₃πr³.
  • Frustum of a cone: treat as difference of two similar cones. If heights are h₁, h₂ and radii r₁, r₂, then V = ⅓πh(r₁²+r₂²+r₁r₂) where h = h₂–h₁.

Geometric Transformations: Isometries, Homothety, and Inversion

An isometry preserves distances and angles. The four plane isometries are translation, rotation, reflection, and glide reflection. Any composition of isometries is again an isometry. The group generated by reflections in two intersecting lines is a rotation about their intersection by twice the angle between the lines; the group generated by reflections in two parallel lines is a translation by twice the distance between the lines.

Homothety (central similarity) with center O and ratio k maps any point P to P′ such that O, P, P′ are collinear and OP′ = |k|·OP. It preserves angles and maps lines to parallel lines (or the same line if they pass through O). The composition of two homotheties with different centers is either a homothety (if the product of ratios ≠ 1) or a translation (if the product = 1). This fact solves many “spiral similarity” problems where a segment is rotated and scaled simultaneously.

Inversion in a circle of radius R centered at O sends a point P ≠ O to P′ on ray OP with OP·OP′ = R². Inversion maps circles not passing through O to circles, circles through O to lines not through O, and lines not through O to circles through O. Angles are preserved (inversion is conformal). The power of a point with respect to the inversion circle is exactly the product OP·OP′. Inversion is a powerful tool for converting difficult circle‑tangent configurations into simpler line‑tangent ones.

Typical Inversion Tricks

  • Two intersecting circles become two lines after inversion centered at one intersection point.
  • A circle orthogonal to the inversion circle maps to itself.
  • The image of a line not through the center is a circle through the center; its radius is R²/(2d) where d is the distance from the center to the line.
  • Confusing the Euler line ratio: the centroid is 2/3 of the way from the orthocenter to the circumcenter, not the reverse.
  • Assuming the radical axis always passes through the intersection points of two circles — it does only when the circles intersect.
  • Forgetting that the chord of contact equation uses the external point’s coordinates in the tangent form, not the point of tangency.
  • Applying Cavalieri’s principle without verifying that cross‑sectional areas are equal at every height.
  • Treating a homothety with negative ratio as a pure dilation; it includes a half‑turn about the center.
  • Using inversion without checking whether the inversion circle passes through the center of a given circle, which changes the image type.
  • Review these traps before the exam.

hand/arithmetic.html:
Modular Arithmetic and Cyclicity of Unit Digits

Modular arithmetic provides a systematic way to handle remainders, which appear repeatedly in competitive‑exam questions on divisibility, powers, and calendar problems. The notation a ≡ b (mod m) means that a and b leave the same remainder when divided by m. Basic properties — addition, subtraction, multiplication, and exponentiation — hold under congruence, allowing large numbers to be reduced step by step.

The most common exam application is finding the unit digit of a large power. Because only the unit digit of the base matters, we study the cyclicity of each digit 0‑9. For example, powers of 2 cycle through 2, 4, 8, 6 (length 4); powers of 3 cycle through 3, 9, 7, 1 (length 4); powers of 4 cycle through 4, 6 (length 2); powers of 5 and 6 are constant; powers of 7 cycle through 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4); powers of 8 cycle through 8, 4, 2, 6 (length 4); powers of 9 cycle through 9, 1 (length 2). To find the unit digit of an, compute n mod cycle length (using the remainder, with 0 treated as the cycle length) and pick the corresponding element.

When the exponent itself is a power, such as 777, apply Euler’s theorem or Carmichael function for modulus 10. Since φ(10)=4, any odd base coprime to 10 satisfies a4 ≡ 1 (mod 10). Reduce the exponent modulo 4: 77 mod 4 = (−1)7 mod 4 = 3. Hence the unit digit equals that of 7³ = 343 → 3.

Modular arithmetic also solves “find the remainder when N is divided by m” for large N expressed as sums or products. Break N into parts, reduce each part modulo m, then combine. For instance, remainder of (1234 × 5678) ÷ 9: 1234 ≡ 1 (mod 9), 5678 ≡ 8 (mod 9), product ≡ 8 (mod 9). This technique extends to factorial remainders, where Wilson’s theorem (p prime ⇒ (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p)) and its corollaries give quick answers for prime moduli.

Examiners often combine cyclicity with negative remainders. Remember that a remainder can be expressed as a negative number: 7 ≡ −3 (mod 10). Using negative remainders sometimes shortens calculations, e.g., 9odd ≡ −1 (mod 10) gives unit digit 9 directly.

Advanced LCM–HCF Applications: Remainder Problems and Synchronization

The relationship LCM × HCF = Product of two numbers holds only for two numbers; for three or more numbers the product of LCM and HCF is not equal to the product of the numbers. This distinction is a frequent trap. Advanced problems use LCM and HCF to model real‑world synchronization: bells tolling together, runners meeting at a starting point, or traffic lights turning green simultaneously.

Remainder‑based LCM problems ask for the smallest number that leaves specific remainders when divided by given divisors. If a number N leaves remainder ri when divided by di, and the differences di − ri are equal (say k), then N = LCM(d1, d2, …) − k. Example: find the least number which when divided by 6, 7, 8 leaves remainders 4, 5, 6 respectively. Differences are 2, 2, 2 → k = 2. LCM(6,7,8)=168. Answer = 168 − 2 = 166.

If the differences are not equal, use the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) for pairwise coprime moduli, or solve stepwise by constructing a number satisfying the first two conditions, then adjusting by the LCM of those two moduli to meet the third, and so on. For non‑coprime moduli, a solution exists only if the remainders are congruent modulo the HCF of the respective moduli.

HCF in grouping problems: The maximum number of identical groups that can be formed from quantities a, b, c is HCF(a, b, c). Conversely, the minimum number of groups when each group must contain the same number of items from each type is also governed by HCF. Example: 360 pens, 480 pencils, 600 erasers to be packed in boxes with equal numbers of each item per box. Maximum items per box = HCF(360,480,600)=60. Number of boxes = (360+480+600)/60 = 24.

Synchronization of periodic events: Three bells toll at intervals of 12, 15, 18 seconds. They toll together at t=0. Next simultaneous toll = LCM(12,15,18)=180 seconds. If the first toll is not simultaneous, find the first time they align after a given offset by solving a system of congruences.

Examiners also test LCM of fractions: LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators ÷ HCF of denominators. HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators. This appears in problems where rates are given as fractions and a common cycle is needed.

Worked Example — Remainder Synchronization
Find the smallest positive integer which when divided by 5, 6, 7 leaves remainders 3, 4, 5 respectively.
Observe the differences: 5−3 = 2, 6−4 = 2, 7−5 = 2. The common difference k = 2. Compute LCM(5,6,7) = 210. Required number = LCM − k = 210 − 2 = 208. Verification: 208 ÷ 5 = 41 rem 3; 208 ÷ 6 = 34 rem 4; 208 ÷ 7 = 29 rem 5. Answer: 208.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a remainder problem shows a constant difference between divisor and remainder, immediately apply the LCM‑minus‑k shortcut. It saves 30‑40 seconds versus stepwise CRT. If differences vary, check pairwise coprimality first; if moduli are coprime, CRT gives a unique solution modulo the product. For non‑coprime sets, verify the consistency condition (remainders congruent modulo HCF) before attempting construction.

Componendo–Dividendo and Proportion Manipulations

The componendo–dividendo rule states that if a/b = c/d, then (a+b)/(a−b) = (c+d)/(c−d), provided denominators are non‑zero. This transformation converts a simple proportion into a form where the unknown often appears linearly, making it a powerful algebraic shortcut in competitive arithmetic.

Derivation: From a/b = c/d = k, we have a = bk, c = dk. Then (a+b)/(a−b) = (bk+b)/(bk−b) = (k+1)/(k−1). Similarly (c+d)/(c−d) = (dk+d)/(dk−d) = (k+1)/(k−1). Hence the equality holds. The rule also works in reverse: if (a+b)/(a−b) = (c+d)/(c−d), then a/b = c/d, provided a≠b and c≠d.

Typical exam pattern: “If (x+3)/(x−3) = 5/3, find x.” Apply componendo–dividendo on the right side: (5+3)/(5−3) = 8/2 = 4. So (x+3)/(x−3) = 4 ⇒ x+3 = 4x−12 ⇒ 3x = 15 ⇒ x = 5. The same result is obtained by cross‑multiplication, but componendo–dividendo avoids expanding brackets when the proportion is nested.

Extended forms: Componendo alone gives (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d. Dividendo alone gives (a−b)/b = (c−d)/d. Combining both yields the full rule. These partial forms are useful when only sum or difference appears in the question.

Application in mixture problems: If two mixtures have milk‑to‑water ratios a:b and c:d, and they are mixed in equal quantities, the resultant ratio can be found by converting each to fractions of milk, averaging, then converting back. Componendo–dividendo can shortcut the algebra when the final ratio is given and the mixing proportion is asked.

Another advanced manipulation is alternendo: a/b = c/d ⇒ a/c = b/d. And invertendo: a/b = c/d ⇒ b/a = d/c. These are often combined with componendo–dividendo to solve systems of proportions quickly.

Examiners also test the property of equal ratios: If a/b = c/d = e/f = k, then each ratio equals (a+c+e)/(b+d+f) = k. This extends to any number of equal ratios and is the basis for solving problems where several quantities are in proportion and their sum or difference is known.

Alligation with Replacement and Multi‑Stage Mixtures

Standard alligation finds the ratio in which two ingredients at given prices (or concentrations) must be mixed to obtain a target mean. Replacement problems add a dynamic layer: a portion of a mixture is removed and replaced by another substance, repeated several times. The quantity of the original component after n replacements follows a geometric progression.

If a vessel contains V litres of pure liquid A, and each operation removes r litres of the mixture and replaces it with liquid B, then after one operation the amount of A left = V − r = V(1 − r/V). After n operations, amount of A = V(1 − r/V)n. The concentration of A = (1 − r/V)n. This formula assumes thorough mixing each time.

Example: 40 litres of milk. 4 litres removed and replaced by water, repeated 3 times. Milk left = 40(1 − 4/40)3 = 40(0.9)3 = 40 × 0.729 = 29.16 litres. Water = 40 − 29.16 = 10.84 litres. Ratio milk:water = 29.16:10.84 = 729:271 (multiply by 100 to clear decimals).

Multi‑stage mixtures involve more than two components or successive mixing steps. For three components, alligation can be applied pairwise. Suppose we have three varieties of tea at ₹100, ₹150, ₹200 per kg, and we want a blend at ₹140. First mix the cheapest and dearest to get ₹140: alligation gives (200−140):(140−100) = 60:40 = 3:2. So 3 parts of ₹100 tea with 2 parts of ₹200 tea yields ₹140. The ₹150 tea is not needed. If the target lies between the middle and one extreme, use the two relevant extremes.

When the target price lies outside the range of given prices, the problem has no solution with positive quantities — a common trap. Also, if the mixture is not homogeneous (e.g., layered liquids), the simple replacement formula fails; the problem will explicitly state “thoroughly mixed”.

Another variant: evaporation or addition without removal. If only water evaporates from a salt solution, the amount of salt stays constant while total volume decreases. Concentration increases inversely with remaining volume. If pure water is added, salt amount constant, volume increases, concentration decreases proportionally.

Examiners combine replacement with profit‑loss: a milkman replaces milk with water, sells the mixture at cost price of pure milk, and the profit percentage equals the percentage of water in the final mixture. This links alligation directly to the profit‑loss framework.

Compound Interest with Varying Rates, Installments, and Compounding Periods

The standard formula A = P(1 + R/100)T assumes a constant annual rate and annual compounding. Competitive exams frequently vary these assumptions.

Varying annual rates: If rates are R₁%, R₂%, …, RT% for successive years, the amount after T years is A = P(1 + R₁/100)(1 + R₂/100)…(1 + RT/100). No single “average rate” works unless the rates are equal. Example: ₹10,000 at 10% first year, 12% second year. Amount = 10000 × 1.10 × 1.12 = ₹12,320. CI = ₹2,320.

Half‑yearly and quarterly compounding: When interest is compounded m times a year at nominal annual rate R%, the effective rate per period = R/m %. Number of periods = mT. Amount = P(1 + R/(100m))mT. The effective annual rate (EAR) = (1 + R/(100m))m − 1. For R=12%, half‑yearly: EAR = (1.06)² − 1 = 12.36%. Quarterly: EAR = (1.03)⁴ − 1 ≈ 12.55%. Examiners ask “find the effective rate” or “compare CI under different compounding frequencies”.

Installments (loan repayment): A loan of P at rate R% per annum compounded annually is repaid in n equal annual installments of X. The present value of installments equals P: X/(1+r) + X/(1+r)² + … + X/(1+r)n = P, where r = R/100. This is a geometric series: X × [1 − (1+r)−n]/r = P ⇒ X = P r / [1 − (1+r)−n]. For half‑yearly installments, adjust r and n accordingly.

Growing installments: If each installment increases by a fixed percentage g%, the present value formula becomes X/(1+r) + X(1+g)/(1+r)² + … . This sums to X/(r−g) × [1 − ((1+g)/(1+r))n] provided r ≠ g.

Difference between CI and SI for fractional years: For non‑integer T, SI = P × R × T / 100 (simple proportion). CI uses the formula with fractional exponent: A = P(1+r)T. Some exams approximate CI for half‑year by taking half the annual rate for half a year, but the exact method is the fractional exponent.

Population growth and depreciation are modeled identically: growth rate = r, depreciation rate = −r. The same formulas apply, with “amount” replaced by “population” or “value”.

  • Assuming LCM × HCF = product for more than two numbers — this holds only for a pair.
  • Using the LCM‑minus‑k shortcut when divisor‑remainder differences are not equal — leads to wrong answer.
  • Applying componendo–dividendo without checking that denominators (a−b) and (c−d) are non‑zero — division by zero invalidates the step.
  • Treating replacement problems as simple subtraction of volumes instead of geometric decay — ignores the mixing effect.
  • Using a single average rate for varying‑rate compound interest — the product of growth factors is required.
  • Confusing nominal rate with effective rate when compounding frequency changes — always convert to per‑period rate before applying the formula.
  • Forgetting that the present‑value installment formula assumes payments at the end of each period; beginning‑of‑period payments require multiplication by (1+r).

hand/astroparticle-physics.html:
Ultra-High-Energy Cosmic Ray Composition and the Muon Puzzle

The energy spectrum of cosmic rays extends beyond 1020 eV, but the chemical composition at the highest energies remains uncertain. The Pierre Auger Observatory measures the depth of shower maximum (Xmax) and its fluctuations to infer the mass of the primary particle. Data show a gradual shift from a light, proton‑dominated composition around the “ankle” (≈5×1018 eV) to a heavier, iron‑like composition above ≈2×1019 eV. However, the number of muons observed in air showers exceeds predictions from hadronic interaction models (EPOS‑LHC, QGSJet‑II‑04) by 30–60 % for the same Xmax. This “muon puzzle” suggests either an incomplete description of forward particle production in proton–air collisions or a heavier primary composition than Xmax alone indicates. The Auger upgrade (AugerPrime) adds scintillator detectors and radio antennas to separate the electromagnetic and muonic components event‑by‑event, aiming to resolve the tension. A simultaneous fit of Xmax and muon content currently favours a mixed composition (proton, helium, nitrogen, iron) with a growing iron fraction above 1019.5 eV, but the exact fractions depend on the hadronic model used. The Telescope Array, operating in the northern hemisphere, reports a lighter composition at comparable energies, hinting at possible anisotropy or systematic differences in energy calibration. Understanding the composition is essential for testing the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff interpretation and for identifying the sources of ultra‑high‑energy cosmic rays (UHECRs).

Dark Matter Direct Detection: Recoil Spectra and Annual Modulation

Direct detection experiments search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) scattering off target nuclei. The differential recoil rate dR/dER depends on the WIMP–nucleon cross section, the local dark matter density (≈0.3 GeV cm−3), the WIMP velocity distribution (usually a truncated Maxwellian with v0≈220 km s−1), and the nuclear form factor (Helm or dipole). For spin‑independent interactions the rate scales as A2, favouring heavy targets such as xenon (XENONnT, LUX‑ZEPLIN) or argon (DarkSide). Spin‑dependent couplings are probed with fluorine (PICO) or iodine (COSINE‑100). The expected recoil spectrum falls exponentially with energy, typically peaking below 10 keVnr for WIMP masses of 10–100 GeV. An annual modulation arises because the Earth’s orbital velocity adds vectorially to the Sun’s motion through the halo, producing a ≈2–5 % sinusoidal variation in the rate with a phase peaking around 2 June. The DAMA/LIBRA experiment has reported a persistent modulation at 12.9 σ over two decades, but the signal is incompatible with standard WIMP interpretations when confronted with null results from XENONnT, LUX‑ZEPLZ, and CDMSlite, unless one invokes non‑standard velocity streams, inelastic scattering, or isospin‑violating couplings. Modern analyses employ profile likelihood methods to combine multiple targets and energy windows, setting upper limits on the spin‑independent cross section down to ≈4×10−48 cm2 at 30 GeV. Future low‑threshold detectors (SuperCDMS SNOLAB, CRESST‑III) aim to explore the “neutrino floor” where coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering becomes an irreducible background.

Worked Calculation
A WIMP of mass 50 GeV scatters spin‑independently off a xenon‑131 nucleus (A=131). Assuming a local density 0.3 GeV cm−3, a Maxwellian velocity distribution with v0=220 km s−1, and a cross section σSI=1×10−46 cm2, estimate the total event rate per tonne‑year for recoil energies above 5 keVnr. Use the Helm form factor approximation F2(q)≈exp(−q2s2) with s=0.9 fm.
The differential rate is dR/dER = (ρ0 σSI A2 F2(q))/(2 mχ μχN2) η(vmin), where μχN is the reduced mass, q=√(2 mN ER), and η(vmin) = ∫vminvesc (f(v)/v) dv. For mχ=50 GeV, mN≈122 GeV, μ≈35 GeV. At ER=5 keV, q≈50 MeV, q s≈0.23, F2≈0.95. η(vmin)≈1.2×105 s km−1. Plugging numbers gives dR/dER≈0.8 events keV−1 tonne−1 yr−1. Integrating from 5 keV to 50 keV (exponential fall‑off) yields ≈4 events tonne−1 yr−1. This order‑of‑magnitude matches published XENON1T sensitivity curves.
Exam Day Strategy
When a question asks for the scaling of the direct‑detection rate with target mass number A, remember the A2 coherence factor for spin‑independent interactions and the absence of such enhancement for spin‑dependent couplings. For annual modulation, the phase (early June) and the fractional amplitude (few per cent) are standard textbook numbers; do not confuse them with the diurnal modulation from Earth’s rotation, which is negligible for WIMPs.

Neutrino Oscillation Physics in Matter: MSW Effect and Non‑Standard Interactions

The Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein (MSW) effect modifies neutrino flavour conversion when neutrinos propagate through matter. In the Sun, electron neutrinos experience a charged‑current potential VCC=√2 GF ne that adds to the Hamiltonian in the flavour basis. For solar neutrinos (E≈1–10 MeV) the resonance condition Δm2 cos2θ = 2 E VCC is satisfied inside the solar core, leading to an adiabatic conversion νe→νμ,τ and the observed survival probability Pee≈0.3 at high energy, rising to ≈0.55 at low energy. The same formalism applies to supernova neutrinos, where the dense envelope creates multiple resonances (H‑resonance for Δm312, L‑resonance for Δm212) and collective effects from neutrino‑neutrino refraction. Non‑standard interactions (NSI) introduce additional flavour‑changing or flavour‑conserving potentials εαβ VCC. Current global fits constrain |εeτ|, |εeμ| ≲ 0.1–0.3, while εee−εμμ can shift the effective solar mixing angle. Long‑baseline accelerator experiments (T2K, NOvA, DUNE) are sensitive to NSI through matter effects in the Earth’s crust; a non‑zero εeτ can mimic CP violation or alter the mass‑ordering sensitivity. Future atmospheric neutrino measurements with IceCube‑Upgrade and ORCA will probe NSI in the multi‑GeV to TeV range, where the matter potential grows linearly with energy.

Gamma‑Ray Burst Central Engines: Magnetar versus Black Hole Models

The nature of the compact object powering a GRB jet distinguishes two leading central‑engine scenarios. In the collapsar model, a rapidly rotating massive star collapses to a Kerr black hole of mass 3–10 M⊙ surrounded by a massive accretion torus (≈0.1–1 M⊙). The Blandford–Znajek mechanism extracts rotational energy via magnetic fields threading the horizon, yielding jet powers LBZ≈1050–1052 erg s−1 for dimensionless spin a≈0.5–0.9 and poloidal field B≈1015 G. The accretion rate required is Ṁ≈0.1–1 M⊙ s−1, sustained for tens of seconds, consistent with long GRB durations. In the magnetar model, a newly born, millisecond‑period, highly magnetised neutron star (B≈1015–1016 G) loses rotational energy via magnetic dipole radiation and a relativistic wind. The spin‑down luminosity Lsd≈1049(P/1 ms)−2(B/1015 G)2 erg s−1 can power the prompt emission and the X‑ray plateau observed in many Swift afterglows. The plateau’s abrupt end is interpreted as the magnetar’s collapse to a black hole once differential rotation is lost or the mass exceeds the supramassive limit. Observational discriminants include the plateau luminosity–duration correlation (La∝Ta−1), the presence of a high‑energy cut‑off in the prompt spectrum (expected for magnetar photospheres), and the detection of gravitational waves from a post‑merger remnant in short GRBs. Current multimessenger data favour a black‑hole central engine for the majority of long GRBs, while a subset of low‑luminosity GRBs and some short GRB plateaus are compatible with a stable or supramassive magnetar.

Multimessenger Astrophysics: Joint Gravitational Wave, Gamma‑Ray Burst, and Neutrino Observations

The era of multimessenger astronomy began with GW170817/GRB 170817A, a binary neutron star merger detected in gravitational waves by LIGO–Virgo and in gamma rays by Fermi‑GBM and INTEGRAL. The 1.7 s delay between the GW merger time and the GRB onset constrains the jet launch mechanism and the Lorentz factor (Γ≳100). The kilonova AT2017gfo confirmed r‑process nucleosynthesis in the ejecta. No high‑energy neutrinos were detected by IceCube or ANTARES, consistent with an off‑axis jet or a low baryon loading. For binary black hole mergers, no electromagnetic counterpart is expected unless the environment supplies gas (e.g., active galactic nucleus disks). Core‑collapse supernovae produce MeV neutrino bursts (as seen from SN 1987A) and, if the progenitor is rapidly rotating, a long GRB; the joint detection of a Galactic supernova neutrino burst and a GW signal would probe the explosion mechanism and the equation of state. Future detectors (Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, Hyper‑Kamiokande, IceCube‑Gen2) will increase the horizon for joint GW–neutrino–EM observations to several hundred megaparsecs. The key analysis technique is a time‑coincident, sky‑localisation overlap: GW sky maps (tens to hundreds of deg2) are cross‑matched with GRB error boxes (arcminutes for Swift, degrees for Fermi) and neutrino point‑spread functions (≈1° for track‑like events). A statistically significant triplet would provide a direct measurement of the Hubble constant independent of the cosmic distance ladder, test Lorentz invariance via arrival‑time differences, and constrain the neutron‑star equation of state through the tidal deformability imprinted on the GW waveform.

  • Assuming the muon puzzle is solved solely by a heavier composition without checking hadronic model dependence.
  • Confusing the annual modulation phase (early June) with the diurnal modulation phase (local midnight).
  • Treating the MSW resonance condition as energy‑independent; it scales linearly with neutrino energy.
  • Equating the Blandford–Znajek power with the total accretion power; the former extracts only black‑hole spin energy.
  • Expecting a neutrino counterpart for every binary neutron star merger; off‑axis jets and low baryon loading can suppress the neutrino flux below detectability.
  • Using the A2 scaling for spin‑dependent WIMP–nucleon cross sections, which instead depend on the nuclear spin content.
  • Neglecting the extragalactic background light attenuation when interpreting TeV gamma‑ray spectra from distant blazars.

These advanced topics illustrate how composition measurements, recoil spectroscopy, matter‑enhanced oscillations, central‑engine physics, and multimessenger coincidences together shape modern astroparticle physics.
