Level‑k networks, where each biconnected component contains at most k reticulations, form a hierarchy that captures many biologically relevant classes; for fixed k, many hard problems become polynomial‑time solvable.

In genome assembly, de Bruijn graphs built from k‑mers of sequencing reads are the standard model. Vertices correspond to (k − 1)‑mers, directed edges to k‑mers, and an Eulerian path in the graph spells a candidate genome. Real data introduce errors, repeats, and coverage variation, turning the ideal Eulerian graph into a tangled structure with bubbles, tips, and chimeric connections. The classic algorithm of Pevzner, Tang, and Waterman (2001) simplifies the graph by removing tips (low‑coverage dead ends) and collapsing bubbles (parallel paths caused by heterozygosity or errors). More recent assemblers such as SPAdes (Bankevich et al., 2012) employ multi‑size de Bruijn graphs and iterative repeat resolution using paired‑end read information, which can be modeled as constraints on the distance between two vertices in the graph. The problem of finding a Hamiltonian path that respects mate‑pair distances is NP‑hard, but practical heuristics based on graph contraction, flow‑based repeat resolution, and integer linear programming achieve high contiguity on real datasets. The interplay between graph topology (branching factor, cycle structure) and sequencing parameters (read length, insert size, error rate) determines the theoretical limits of assembly, formalized by the notion of the assembly graph’s “reconstructibility” (Medvedev, Brudno, 2009).

Graph Theory in Social Network Analysis: Community Detection, Centrality, and Influence Maximization

Community detection seeks a partition of vertices into dense subgraphs with sparse inter‑connections. The modularity function Q = (1 / 2m) ∑ij (Aij − k_i k_j / 2m) δ(c_i, c_j) (Newman‑Girvan, 2004) measures the excess of internal edges over a configuration‑model null model. Maximizing Q is NP‑hard, but the Louvain method (Blondel et al., 2008) provides a fast greedy heuristic that iteratively moves vertices to neighboring communities and then aggregates communities into super‑vertices, achieving near‑linear runtime on graphs with millions of edges. Statistical significance of detected communities can be assessed via the map equation (Rosvall, Bergstrom, 2008), which minimizes the description length of a random walk on the graph. Overlapping community detection extends the framework by allowing vertices to belong to multiple groups; the Clique Percolation Method (Palla et al., 2005) defines communities as unions of k‑cliques that share (k − 1) vertices, while the BigCLAM algorithm (Yang, Leskovec, 2013) uses non‑negative matrix factorization on the adjacency matrix to infer soft memberships.

Centrality measures quantify vertex importance. Betweenness centrality σ(v) = ∑s≠t≠v σst(v) / σst counts the fraction of shortest paths passing through v; Brandes’ algorithm computes all betweenness scores in O(n m) time for unweighted graphs. PageRank (Page et al., 1999) defines a stationary distribution of a random walk with teleportation, solvable by power iteration in O(m / ε) time for ε‑accuracy. Influence maximization asks for a seed set S of size k that maximizes the expected number of activated vertices under the Independent Cascade or Linear Threshold diffusion models. Kempe, Kleinberg, and Tardos (2003) proved the objective is monotone submodular, so the greedy algorithm yields a (1 − 1/e)‑approximation. Scalable implementations such as CELF (Leskovec et al., 2007) exploit submodularity to avoid redundant marginal gain evaluations, and recent work on reverse reachable sets (Borgs et al., 2014) achieves near‑optimal (1 − 1/e − ε) approximation in O((n + m) log n / ε²) time. These algorithmic tools, grounded in graph structure and probabilistic analysis, form the backbone of modern large‑scale social network analytics.

  • Assuming that a sparse Tanner graph automatically guarantees good LDPC performance; expansion and girth are both required, and irregular degree distributions need density‑evolution analysis.
  • Confusing the semi‑streaming space bound O(n polylog n) with the stricter O(log n) space of the standard streaming model; many lower bounds only hold in the latter.
  • Believing that any phylogenetic network with reticulation number r can be reconstructed in polynomial time; tree‑containment and hybridization number are NP‑hard, only FPT in r.
  • Treating de Bruijn graph assembly as a pure Eulerian path problem without accounting for repeat‑induced branching; practical assemblers must resolve repeats using paired‑end constraints, which is NP‑hard.
  • Equating modularity maximization with the true community structure; modularity has a resolution limit and can merge small communities, so statistical validation (e.g., map equation) is essential.
  • Using betweenness centrality on massive graphs without approximation; exact Brandes algorithm is O(n m) and infeasible for n > 10⁶, while sampling‑based estimators give provable guarantees.
  • Assuming the greedy influence maximization algorithm always runs in O(k n m) time; the CELF optimization and reverse‑reachable‑set methods reduce the complexity dramatically and are expected in exam answers.

Graph Neural Networks: Spectral Convolutions and Message Passing

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) translate classical graph‑theoretic operations into differentiable layers that can be trained end‑to‑end. The two foundational families are spectral convolutions and spatial message‑passing. Spectral methods originate from the graph Fourier transform: given a graph Laplacian L = D − A, its eigendecomposition L = U Λ Uᵀ defines a basis in which a filter gθ(Λ) can be applied as U gθ(Λ) Uᵀ x. Bruna et al. (2014) proposed learning diagonal filter matrices gθ directly, but the O(n²) cost of the eigenbasis limited scalability. Defferrard, Bresson, and Vandergheynst (2016) approximated gθ with a truncated Chebyshev polynomial of order K, yielding a K‑localized convolution that runs in O(K|E|) time and avoids eigen‑decomposition. Kipf and Welling (2017) further simplified to a first‑order polynomial with a renormalization trick, producing the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) layer H⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = σ( D̃⁻¹ᐟ² Ã D̃⁻¹ᐟ² H⁽ˡ⁾ W⁽ˡ⁾ ), where Ã = A + I and D̃ is its degree matrix. Spatial message‑passing, formalized by Gilmer et al. (2017) as the Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) framework, updates each vertex representation by aggregating messages from neighbours: hᵥ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾ = γ( hᵥ⁽ᵗ⁾, □u∈N(v) φ( hᵥ⁽ᵗ⁾, hᵤ⁽ᵗ⁾, eᵥᵤ ) ). Here φ is a message function, □ a permutation‑invariant aggregation (sum, mean, max), and γ a vertex update. GraphSAGE (Hamilton, Ying, Leskovec, 2017) introduced sampling‑based aggregation to scale to billions of edges, while Graph Attention Networks (Veličković et al., 2018) replace uniform aggregation with learned attention coefficients αᵥᵤ = softmax( aᵀ [Whᵥ || Whᵤ] ). Theoretical work by Xu et al. (2019) showed that the expressive power of GNNs is bounded by the 1‑dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman (WL) test; architectures that inject higher‑order subgraph counts or use k‑GNNs can surpass this barrier. Training objectives range from semi‑supervised node classification (GCN on citation networks) to unsupervised graph‑level representation learning (InfoGraph, GraphCL). Practical deployments include molecular property prediction (MoleculeNet benchmarks), traffic forecasting (ST‑GCN), and recommendation systems (PinSage). The field continues to address over‑smoothing in deep GNNs, heterophily, and the design of scalable mini‑batch samplers such as Cluster‑GCN and GraphSAINT.

Distributed Graph Algorithms: The CONGEST Model and Locality Lower Bounds

The CONGEST model captures synchronous message‑passing on a network where each node initially knows only its incident edges and can send O(log n) bits per edge per round. The central question is how many rounds are required to solve classic graph problems. For global problems such as Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), the seminal lower bound of Ω(√n + D) rounds (Peleg & Rubinovich, 2000) matches the upper bound of O(√n log* n + D) by Kutten & Peleg (1998), where D is the network diameter. The proof constructs a “two‑party” communication reduction across a cut of size Θ(√n), showing that any algorithm must transmit Ω(n) bits across the cut, which in CONGEST forces Ω(√n) rounds. For local problems like Maximal Independent Set (MIS) and (Δ+1)‑coloring, Linial’s Ω(log* n) lower bound (1992) holds even in the LOCAL model (unbounded bandwidth), and the classic Luby (1986) and Alon‑Babai‑Itai (1986) randomized algorithms achieve O(log n) rounds in CONGEST. Barenboim, Elkin, and Kuhn (2014) gave a deterministic (Δ+1)‑coloring in O(Δ³/² log Δ + log* n) rounds, later improved to O(Δ log Δ + log* n) by Fraigniaud, Heinrich, and Kosowski (2016). The recent “shattering” technique (Ghaffari, 2016) reduces MIS to O(log Δ + 2O(√log log n)) rounds, and the deterministic derandomization of Chang & Pettie (2017) yields O(log² Δ log n) rounds. For approximate optimization, the (1+ε)‑approximate MST can be computed in O(√n / ε + D) rounds (Khan et al., 2015), while a (1+ε)‑approximate minimum cut requires Ω(√n) rounds (Ghaffari & Kuhn, 2013). The CONGESTED CLIQUE variant, where every pair of nodes can communicate, admits MST in O(log log n) rounds (Jurdziński & Nowicki, 2018) and triangle detection in O(n1/3) rounds (Dolev, Lenzen, Peled, 2012). Lower bounds in CONGESTED CLIQUE often rely on reductions from two‑party set‑disjointness, yielding Ω(n1/3) for exact triangle counting. Understanding these round complexities is essential for designing algorithms in wireless sensor networks, data‑center topologies, and blockchain peer‑to‑peer overlays.

Worked Example: Round Complexity of MST in CONGEST
Prove that any deterministic CONGEST algorithm that computes a Minimum Spanning Tree on an n‑node graph with diameter D requires Ω(√n + D) rounds.
Construct a family of graphs consisting of two dense expanders of size Θ(n) connected by a single “bridge” path of length Θ(√n). The two expanders each contain a hidden edge of weight 1; all other edges have weight 2. The MST must include exactly one of the two hidden edges, which can be determined only by learning the weight of the hidden edge on the opposite side. Any CONGEST algorithm must transmit Ω(n) bits across the bridge cut of size Θ(√n). Since each round carries at most O(√n log n) bits across the cut, at least Ω(√n / log n) = Ω(√n) rounds are needed. Additionally, information must travel the length of the bridge, contributing an additive D term. Hence any algorithm needs Ω(√n + D) rounds.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a round‑complexity lower bound in CONGEST, first identify whether the problem is global (requires information from the whole graph) or local (depends only on a constant‑radius neighbourhood). For global problems, recall the √n‑cut construction; for local problems, cite Linial’s log* n bound. Always state the model (CONGEST vs LOCAL) and whether the algorithm is deterministic or randomized, as the bounds differ.

Expander Graphs in Cryptography: Pseudorandomness and Hardness Amplification

Expander graphs are sparse graphs with strong connectivity properties quantified by the spectral gap λ = λ₂(L) of the normalized Laplacian or the second‑largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix. A d‑regular graph is a (n, d, λ)‑expander if λ ≤ 1 − ε for constant ε > 0. Margulis (1973) and Gabber–Galil (1981) gave explicit constant‑degree expanders; Lubotzky‑Phillips‑Sarnak (1988) constructed Ramanujan graphs achieving the optimal spectral bound λ ≤ 2√(d−1)/d. In cryptography, expanders underpin three major primitives. First, they serve as the backbone of pseudorandom generators (PRGs) via the “expander walk” construction: a short random seed selects a start vertex, and a walk of length ℓ on the expander outputs the visited vertices. The resulting distribution is ε‑close to uniform for ℓ = O(log n / ε²) (Impagliazzo & Zuckerman, 1989). Second, hardness amplification uses the “direct product” theorem: if a function f is mildly hard on average, the function F(x₁,…,x_k) = (f(x₁),…,f(x_k)) evaluated on vertices of an expander walk becomes exponentially harder (Impagliazzo, Jaiswal, Kabanets, 2006). Third, expander‑based codes (Tanner codes, 1981) yield Low‑Density Parity‑Check (LDPC) codes with linear distance and constant rate; the Sipser‑Spielman decoder runs in linear time thanks to the expansion property. Recent work by Dinur (2007) on the PCP theorem uses expander‑based assignment testers to achieve constant‑query PCPs with sub‑constant soundness error. In lattice‑based cryptography, the “expander‑graph” construction of Ajtai (1996) gives worst‑case to average‑case reductions for the Shortest Vector Problem. The Zig‑Zag product (Reingold, Vadhan, Wigderson, 2002) provides a combinatorial method to build larger expanders from smaller ones, preserving the spectral gap and enabling log‑space undirected connectivity (Reingold, 2008). For exam purposes, remember the three parameters (n, d, λ), the Alon‑Boppana bound λ ≥ 2√(d−1)/d − o(1), and the fact that Ramanujan graphs meet this bound. Typical questions ask to derive the mixing time of a random walk (O(log n / (1−λ))) or to explain how the Zig‑Zag product preserves expansion.

Dynamic Graph Algorithms: Maintaining Connectivity Under Edge Updates

Dynamic graph algorithms maintain a graph property while edges are inserted or deleted. The fully dynamic connectivity problem asks to answer whether two vertices are connected after each update. Frederickson (1985) gave an O(√m) worst‑case update time using topology trees. Eppstein, Galil, Italiano, and Nissenzweig (1997) improved to O(log² n) amortized via Euler‑tour trees and a hierarchy of spanning forests (the “dynamic trees” of Sleator & Tarjan, 1983). Holm, de Lichtenberg, and Thorup (2001) achieved O(log² n) worst‑case update and O(log n / log log n) query by maintaining a logarithmic number of spanning forest levels and using a clever “edge‑sampling” technique to promote/demote edges. The current best deterministic bound is O(log² n) (Kapron, King, Mountjoy, 2013) using a randomized Monte‑Carlo algorithm with O(log⁴ n) update that can be derandomized. For incremental (insertion‑only) connectivity, Union‑Find with path compression and union by rank gives α(n) amortized time per operation (Tarjan, 1975). Decremental connectivity (deletions only) on undirected graphs admits O(m log n) total time (Even & Shiloach, 1981) and near‑linear total time O(m log² n) for exact distances (Bernstein & Chechik, 2016). In the partially dynamic setting where only edge insertions occur, dynamic transitive closure can be maintained in O(n²) total time (Italiano, 1988). Lower bounds: Patrascu & Demaine (2004) proved an Ω(log n) cell‑probe lower bound for dynamic connectivity in the worst case, matching the polylogarithmic upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. Recent breakthroughs by Chen, Khanna, and Nagda (2022) gave a fully dynamic algorithm with O(log n (log log n)²) amortized update using a combination of hierarchical sparsifiers and the “cut‑sparsifier” framework of Karger (1999). For exam questions, be prepared to describe the Euler‑tour tree representation of a forest, the role of “tree edges” vs “non‑tree edges” in the Holm‑de Lichtenberg‑Thorup hierarchy, and the amortized analysis that charges each edge promotion to a previous deletion.

Parameterized Approximation: Kernelization and Approximation Schemes for Graph Problems

Parameterized approximation blends parameterized complexity with approximation algorithms to obtain guarantees that are both fixed‑parameter tractable (FPT) and close to optimal. A kernelization algorithm reduces an instance (G, k) to an equivalent instance (G′, k′) with |G′| ≤ f(k) in polynomial time. For Vertex Cover, the classic 2k kernel (Buss & Goldsmith, 1993) follows from the crown rule and the fact that any vertex of degree > k must be in the cover. For Feedback Vertex Set, a 4k² kernel exists (Thomassé, 2010) using the “iterative compression” technique. On the approximation side, the (1+ε)‑approximation scheme for Planar Vertex Cover runs in 2O(1/ε) nO(1) time (Baker, 1994) via layering and dynamic programming on bounded‑treewidth graphs. For general graphs, the best known parameterized approximation for Vertex Cover is a (2−ε)‑approximation in 2O(k) time (Bourgeois et al., 2011). The “parameterized approximation” framework of Marx (2008) defines a (ρ, f(k))‑approximation: an algorithm that runs in f(k)·nO(1) time and returns a solution within factor ρ of optimum. For Dominating Set on graphs of degeneracy d, a (1+ε)‑approximation in (d/ε)O(k) nO(1) time is known (Fomin, Grandoni, Kratsch, 2009). The “lossy kernelization” concept (Lokshtanov et al., 2017) allows a kernel that preserves an α‑approximation: a polynomial‑size kernel for Vertex Cover that yields a (1+ε)‑approximation exists for any ε > 0. For the Steiner Tree problem, a (1+ε)‑approximation in 2O(k/ε) nO(1) time is achievable via the “Dreyfus‑Wagner” DP on a tree‑decomposition of the terminal set (Feldmann & Marx, 2016). Recent work by Feldmann, Karthik, and others (2020) introduced “parameterized approximation schemes” (PAS) for problems on graphs excluding a fixed minor, running in f(k, ε)·nO(1) time. In exams, typical tasks include: (i) designing a kernel for a given problem and proving its size bound, (ii) explaining how Baker’s layering technique yields a PTAS on planar graphs, and (iii) distinguishing between “parameterized approximation” and “FPT‑approximation” (the latter requires the approximation factor to be a function of k only).

  • Confusing the CONGEST bandwidth O(log n) with the LOCAL model’s unbounded bandwidth; lower bounds that hold in LOCAL do not automatically transfer.
  • Assuming every expander is Ramanujan; the Alon‑Boppana bound only gives a limit, explicit Ramanujan constructions are a strict subset.
  • Treating dynamic connectivity amortized bounds as worst‑case guarantees; many textbook algorithms (e.g., Euler‑tour trees) are amortized only.
  • Mixing up kernelization size bounds (e.g., 2k for Vertex Cover) with approximation ratios; a kernel does not imply an approximation guarantee.
  • Believing that a (1+ε)‑approximation scheme for planar graphs works on all graphs; Baker’s technique crucially uses bounded treewidth after layer removal.
  • Overlooking the distinction between deterministic and randomized round complexities in CONGEST; randomized algorithms can break deterministic lower bounds.
  • Forgetting that the Zig‑Zag product preserves expansion only when the second graph is a good expander itself; the product of two poor expanders need not be an expander.

Clique‑Width and Its Algorithmic Applications

Clique‑width is a graph parameter that measures how well a graph can be constructed using four operations: creating a new vertex with a label, taking the disjoint union of two labelled graphs, adding all edges between vertices of label i and label j (i ≠ j), and renaming a label. A graph has clique‑width at most k if it can be built using at most k distinct labels. Unlike treewidth, clique‑width remains bounded on dense graphs such as cliques (clique‑width 2) and complete bipartite graphs (clique‑width 2), while treewidth grows with the size of the clique. Every graph of treewidth t has clique‑width at most 3·2t‑1, but the converse fails: graphs of bounded clique‑width can have arbitrarily large treewidth.

The algorithmic significance of clique‑width stems from Courcelle‑type meta‑theorems. Courcelle, Makowsky and Rotics (2000) proved that for every monadic second‑order sentence φ that quantifies only over vertex sets (MSO₁), there is an algorithm deciding whether a graph G satisfies φ in time f(|φ|, cw(G))·|V(G)|, provided a k‑expression (a construction sequence using at most k labels) is given. Consequently, many NP‑hard problems — Hamiltonian cycle, graph coloring, dominating set, Steiner tree — become fixed‑parameter tractable when parameterized by clique‑width, assuming the expression is part of the input. If the expression is not given, recognizing whether cw(G) ≤ k is NP‑complete for k ≥ 4, but for each fixed k there is a polynomial‑time algorithm (O(n³) for k = 3, O(nO(1)) for any constant k). Approximation algorithms achieve an O(log n) factor for the optimal clique‑width.

Rank‑width, introduced by Oum and Seymour (2006), approximates clique‑width within a factor of two: rw(G) ≤ cw(G) ≤ 2rw(G)+1‑1. Rank‑width admits a cubic‑time exact algorithm for fixed width and a polynomial‑time 3‑approximation, making it a more tractable proxy for algorithm design. Many dynamic‑programming routines on k‑expressions can be transferred to rank‑decompositions with only a constant factor loss in the exponent.

Typical exam questions ask to (i) construct a k‑expression for a given graph, (ii) explain why a problem expressible in MSO₁ becomes FPT on bounded clique‑width, or (iii) contrast the expressive power of MSO₁ versus MSO₂ on graphs of bounded clique‑width (MSO₂ model checking remains hard). A common pitfall is assuming that bounded clique‑width implies bounded treewidth; the complete graph K_n is a counterexample.

Graph Classes of Bounded Expansion and Nowhere Dense Graphs

Bounded expansion and nowhere dense classes form a hierarchy of sparse graph families that generalize planar graphs, graphs excluding a fixed minor, and graphs of bounded degree. A class 𝒞 has bounded expansion if for every integer r ≥ 0 there exists a constant ∇_r such that every r‑shallow minor of any graph in 𝒞 has average degree at most ∇_r. An r‑shallow minor is obtained by contracting vertex‑disjoint subgraphs of radius at most r and then deleting vertices and edges. If the condition holds only for the existence of a graph H_r that is not an r‑shallow minor of any member of 𝒞, the class is called nowhere dense. Every bounded expansion class is nowhere dense, but the converse is false: the class of graphs that are subdivisions of all graphs (each edge subdivided once) is nowhere dense but has unbounded expansion.

These notions were introduced by Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez (2008). They admit several equivalent characterizations: low treedepth colorings, low treewidth colorings, and uniform quasi‑wideness. For bounded expansion classes, there exist vertex colorings with a bounded number of colors such that the union of any i color classes induces a graph of treedepth at most i. This structural property yields linear‑time algorithms for first‑order (FO) model checking (Dvořák, Král', Thomas 2010). On nowhere dense classes, FO model checking is fixed‑parameter tractable with parameter the formula size (Grohe, Kreutzer, Siebertz 2014). Moreover, many classical problems — subgraph isomorphism, dominating set, independent set — become FPT when parameterized by the solution size on nowhere dense graphs.

Examples of bounded expansion classes include planar graphs (∇_r ≤ 3·(2r+1)), graphs excluding a fixed minor H (∇_r depends only on |H| and r), and graphs of bounded degree (∇_r ≤ Δ). Classes of bounded genus are also of bounded expansion because they exclude a fixed minor. Nowhere dense classes that are not of bounded expansion include graphs of bounded average degree but unbounded shallow‑minor density, such as the class of all graphs that are 1‑subdivisions of arbitrary graphs.

Exam tasks often require (i) verifying that a given class has bounded expansion by bounding the average degree of its r‑shallow minors, (ii) explaining why FO model checking is linear on bounded expansion but only FPT on nowhere dense classes, or (iii) distinguishing bounded expansion from bounded treewidth (bounded treewidth implies bounded expansion, but not vice versa). A frequent trap is confusing the definition of shallow minor with that of ordinary minor; the radius bound on contracted pieces is essential.

Worked Example
Show that the class of graphs with maximum degree at most Δ has bounded expansion. Give an explicit bound for ∇_r in terms of Δ and r.
Take any graph G with Δ(G) ≤ Δ and any r‑shallow minor H of G. Each vertex of H corresponds to a connected subgraph of G of radius ≤ r. The maximum degree of such a subgraph in G is at most Δ, and the number of vertices in a radius‑r ball in a Δ‑regular tree is at most 1 + Δ + Δ(Δ‑1) + … + Δ(Δ‑1)r‑1 ≤ Δr+1. Contracting each piece can only increase the average degree by a factor equal to the maximum size of a piece. Therefore the average degree of H is at most Δ·Δr+1 = Δr+2. Hence we can set ∇_r = Δr+2, which depends only on Δ and r, proving bounded expansion.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a class has bounded expansion, first check if the class is minor‑closed or degree‑bounded; both guarantee bounded expansion. If the class is defined by forbidding a topological minor, it is nowhere dense but may lack bounded expansion. Write down the definition of r‑shallow minor and bound the size of the contracted pieces using the given sparsity parameter (degree, genus, excluded minor). A clean bound on ∇_r earns full marks even if the constant is not optimal.

The Directed Grid Theorem and Directed Graph Minors

The directed grid theorem, proved by Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer (2015), is the directed analogue of the Robertson–Seymour grid minor theorem. It states that for every integer k there exists an integer N(k) such that every directed graph with directed treewidth at least N(k) contains a directed grid of size k as a butterfly minor. A directed grid of size k consists of k² vertices arranged in a k×k grid with all horizontal edges oriented consistently (say left‑to‑right) and all vertical edges oriented consistently (top‑to‑bottom), together with the two diagonal directions to make the grid strongly connected. A butterfly minor is obtained by a sequence of vertex deletions, edge deletions, and butterfly contractions — contracting an edge (u,v) only when u has out‑degree 1 or v has in‑degree 1, preserving the direction of the remaining edges.

Directed treewidth, introduced by Johnson, Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (2001), is a width parameter for digraphs based on arboreal decompositions. It is minor‑monotone under butterfly minors and satisfies a duality theorem: a digraph has directed treewidth < k iff it admits a haven of order k, a directed analogue of the bramble‑treewidth duality. The directed grid theorem implies that large directed treewidth forces a highly structured directed grid minor, just as large undirected treewidth forces a large undirected grid minor.

Algorithmic consequences are profound. Many problems that are W[1]‑hard on general digraphs become fixed‑parameter tractable when parameterized by directed treewidth, including directed Hamiltonian cycle, directed disjoint paths, and directed Steiner tree. The theorem also yields an approximation algorithm for directed treewidth: one can either find a directed grid of size k (certifying large width) or produce a decomposition of width f(k). The function N(k) in the original proof is non‑elementary; subsequent work has not substantially improved the bound, so the theorem is primarily a structural tool rather than a practical algorithm.

Exam questions may ask to (i) define butterfly contraction and explain why it preserves directed treewidth, (ii) sketch how the directed grid theorem leads to an FPT algorithm for directed Hamiltonian cycle parameterized by directed treewidth, or (iii) contrast directed treewidth with undirected treewidth (e.g., a directed cycle has directed treewidth 1 but undirected treewidth 2). A common mistake is to apply the undirected grid theorem to a digraph by ignoring edge directions; the resulting undirected grid does not guarantee a directed grid minor.

Graph Minors on Surfaces: The Genus‑Bounded Minor Theorem

For any fixed surface Σ (orientable of genus g or non‑orientable of cross‑cap number c), the class of graphs embeddable on Σ is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation. This is an immediate corollary of the Robertson–Seymour theorem, but a stronger statement holds: there exists a finite set of forbidden minors Obs(Σ) such that a graph embeds on Σ iff it contains none of the graphs in Obs(Σ) as a minor. The set Obs(Σ) is known explicitly for the sphere (Kuratowski’s theorem: K₅ and K3,3), the projective plane (35 graphs, Glover, Huneke, Wang 1979), the torus (over 16 000 graphs, computed by computer), and the Klein bottle. For higher genus the exact sets are unknown, but finiteness is guaranteed by the general graph minor theorem.

The genus‑bounded minor theorem has direct algorithmic implications. Mohar (1999) gave a linear‑time algorithm to test whether a graph can be embedded on a fixed surface Σ, using the excluded‑minor characterization together with the Robertson–Seymour minor‑testing algorithm. Once an embedding is found, many NP‑hard problems become polynomial on graphs of bounded genus via dynamic programming on branch decompositions of width O(√{g·n}). For example, graph coloring, Hamiltonian cycle, and maximum independent set can be solved in time 2^{O(√{g·n})}·nO(1). The theorem also implies that the class of graphs of genus at most g has bounded local treewidth, which yields PTASes for many optimization problems via Baker’s layering technique.

It is important to distinguish genus from crossing number. A graph may have crossing number 1 but arbitrarily large genus (e.g., a large planar graph plus one crossing edge). Conversely, bounded genus implies bounded crossing number, but the converse fails. The excluded‑minor sets for bounded crossing number are not known to be finite for crossing number ≥ 2; this is a major open problem.

Typical exam tasks: (i) list the forbidden minors for the projective plane, (ii) explain why the existence of a finite forbidden‑minor set for each surface follows from the Robertson–Seymour theorem, (iii) describe how an embedding on a fixed surface can be used to obtain a branch decomposition of width O(√{g·n}). A frequent trap is to claim that the set of forbidden minors for the torus is known to be exactly the 16 000+ graphs found by computer; the proof of completeness relies on the graph minor theorem, not on exhaustive enumeration alone.

The Graph Minor Theorem for Graphs of Bounded Pathwidth

Pathwidth is a graph parameter defined via path decompositions: a sequence of bags (vertex subsets) such that each vertex appears in a contiguous subsequence, each edge has both ends in some bag, and the width is the maximum bag size minus one. Pathwidth is minor‑monotone (taking a minor never increases pathwidth) and satisfies pw(G) ≤ tw(G) ≤ pw(G)·log₂|V(G)| for general graphs, while for trees pw = tw. The class of graphs with pathwidth at most k is minor‑closed, so by the Robertson–Seymour theorem it is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors Forb(k). For k = 1 the forbidden minors are exactly the cycles (graphs of pathwidth 1 are forests). For k = 2 the set Forb(2) is known and contains 110 graphs (Kinnersley 1992). For k ≥ 3 the exact forbidden sets are unknown, but finiteness is guaranteed.

Algorithmic applications of bounded pathwidth are often sharper than those for treewidth. Many dynamic‑programming algorithms on path decompositions run in time 2O(pw)·n, whereas the treewidth analogue may have a factor nO(tw). For instance, Hamiltonian path can be solved in 2pw·nO(1) time, and the graph searching number (node search) equals pw + 1. The vertex separation number, which is the minimum over all linear layouts of the maximum number of vertices to the left of a cut that have neighbours to the right, equals pathwidth. This equivalence yields a simple linear‑time algorithm to compute pathwidth on interval graphs.

The excluded‑minor characterization for bounded pathwidth also implies that the class of graphs with pathwidth ≤ k is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation, and that any property expressible in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₂) can be decided in linear time on this class (by Courcelle’s theorem, since bounded pathwidth implies bounded treewidth). However, the dependence on k in the MSO₂ algorithm is non‑elementary because the forbidden‑minor set is not explicitly known.

Exam questions may ask to (i) construct a path decomposition of width 2 for a given graph, (ii) prove that pathwidth is minor‑monotone, (iii) explain why the node search number equals pw + 1, or (iv) contrast the known forbidden minors for pathwidth 1 and 2 with the unknown situation for higher k. A common error is to state that pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct inequality is treewidth ≤ pathwidth. Another trap is to assume that the forbidden‑minor set for pathwidth k is the same as for treewidth k; they are different because the classes are not identical.

  • Confusing clique‑width with treewidth; remember that cliques have clique‑width 2 but unbounded treewidth.
  • Assuming bounded expansion implies bounded treewidth; planar graphs have bounded expansion but unbounded treewidth.
  • Applying the undirected grid theorem to directed graphs without respecting edge directions.
  • Mixing up genus and crossing number; a graph of crossing number 1 can have arbitrarily large genus.
  • Stating that pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct relation is treewidth ≤ pathwidth.
  • Believing the forbidden‑minor set for bounded pathwidth is known for all k; it is known only for k = 1,2.
  • Thinking that the directed grid theorem gives a polynomial bound N(k); the bound is non‑elementary.

Pathwidth, Vertex Separation, and Linear Layouts

Pathwidth is a graph parameter defined via a path decomposition: a sequence of bags (vertex subsets) such that each vertex appears in a contiguous subsequence, each edge has both ends in some bag, and the width is the maximum bag size minus one. The vertex separation number of a linear layout (an ordering of the vertices) is the maximum, over all cuts between a prefix and its suffix, of the number of vertices in the prefix that have neighbours in the suffix. A fundamental theorem states that the pathwidth of a graph equals its vertex separation number. Consequently, computing pathwidth is equivalent to finding an optimal linear layout.

Pathwidth is minor‑monotone: taking a minor never increases pathwidth. By the Robertson–Seymour theorem, for every fixed k the class of graphs with pathwidth at most k is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. For k = 1 the forbidden minors are exactly the cycles (graphs of pathwidth 1 are forests). For k = 2 the forbidden set is known and contains 110 graphs (Kinnersley 1992). For k ≥ 3 the exact forbidden sets are unknown, but finiteness is guaranteed.

Relation to treewidth: for any graph G, tw(G) ≤ pw(G) ≤ tw(G)·log₂|V(G)|. For trees the two parameters coincide. Many dynamic‑programming algorithms on path decompositions run in time 2O(pw)·n, which is often sharper than the nO(tw) dependence for treewidth. For example, Hamiltonian path can be solved in 2pw·nO(1) time, and the node‑search number (graph searching with node searchers) equals pw + 1.

Algorithmic applications: bounded pathwidth yields fixed‑parameter tractable algorithms for a host of NP‑hard problems (Independent Set, Dominating Set, Chromatic Number, etc.) with running time 2O(pw)·nO(1). Courcelle’s theorem also applies because bounded pathwidth implies bounded treewidth, but the dependence on k is non‑elementary when the forbidden‑minor set is not explicitly known.

Common exam tasks: (i) construct a path decomposition of width 2 for a given graph, (ii) prove that pathwidth is minor‑monotone, (iii) explain why the node‑search number equals pw + 1, (iv) contrast the known forbidden minors for pathwidth 1 and 2 with the unknown situation for higher k.

Boolean‑Width: Definition, Properties, and Algorithmic Uses

Boolean‑width is a graph parameter defined via branch decompositions. For a partition (A, B) of the vertex set, consider the bipartite graph between A and B. Over the field GF(2), each vertex a ∈ A defines a characteristic vector of its neighbours in B. The boolean dimension of the cut is the dimension of the subspace spanned by these vectors. The boolean‑width of a branch decomposition is the maximum boolean dimension over all its cuts; the boolean‑width of the graph is the minimum over all branch decompositions.

Key inequalities: for every graph G, mim‑width(G) ≤ boolw(G) ≤ rw(G) ≤ cw(G), where mim‑width is maximum induced matching width, rw is rank‑width, and cw is clique‑width. Boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone, but it is monotone under taking induced subgraphs. Graph classes of bounded boolean‑width include interval graphs, permutation graphs, trapezoid graphs, and more generally all graphs of bounded rank‑width.

Algorithmic meta‑theorem: any problem expressible in monadic second‑order logic with quantification over vertex sets only (MSO₁) can be solved in time nO(boolw) on graphs of boolean‑width at most boolw. This yields polynomial‑time algorithms for Independent Set, Dominating Set, and many other problems on graph classes where boolean‑width is bounded by a constant. Computing the exact boolean‑width is NP‑hard, but there exist approximation algorithms that produce a branch decomposition of width at most 2boolw in polynomial time.

Typical exam questions: (i) define boolean‑width formally, (ii) prove boolw(G) ≤ rw(G), (iii) explain why MSO₁ model‑checking is fixed‑parameter tractable parameterized by boolean‑width, (iv) give an example of a graph class with bounded boolean‑width but unbounded treewidth.

Worked Example
Let G be a graph with boolean‑width 2. Show that the Independent Set problem can be solved in polynomial time on G.
Since boolw(G) = 2, there exists a branch decomposition of G where every cut has boolean dimension at most 2. Independent Set is expressible in MSO₁ (∃S ⊆ V: ∀u,v ∈ S, ¬E(u,v)). By the algorithmic meta‑theorem for boolean‑width, MSO₁ model‑checking runs in time nO(boolw) = nO(1). Therefore Independent Set is solvable in polynomial time on G.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a width parameter that guarantees polynomial‑time MSO₁ model‑checking, recall the hierarchy mim‑width ≤ boolw ≤ rw ≤ cw. Boolean‑width is the weakest parameter among them that still yields an nO(k) algorithm for MSO₁. If the problem is MSO₂ (edge‑set quantification), you need treewidth or rank‑width, not boolean‑width.

Mim‑Width: A Unified Width Parameter for Graph Classes

Maximum induced matching width (mim‑width) is defined via branch decompositions. For a cut (A, B) of a branch decomposition, consider the bipartite graph H with parts A and B and edges those of G crossing the cut. The mim‑width of the cut is the size of a maximum induced matching in H. The mim‑width of the decomposition is the maximum over its cuts; the mim‑width of G is the minimum over all branch decompositions.

Mim‑width generalizes several classical parameters: interval graphs and permutation graphs have mim‑width 1; more generally, any graph class with a linear ordering where the neighbourhoods of vertices in one part form a chain has mim‑width 1. Bounded mim‑width also holds for H‑graphs, circular‑arc graphs, and many others. Importantly, mim‑width is not minor‑monotone and not closed under taking minors.

Algorithmic consequences: a large family of problems (Independent Set, Dominating Set, r‑Dominating Set, Induced Matching, etc.) can be solved in time nO(mimw) on graphs of mim‑width at most mimw. This is achieved by dynamic programming on a branch decomposition, where the state space at each cut is bounded by the number of induced matchings. Computing mim‑width exactly is NP‑hard, but for many graph classes a decomposition of constant mim‑width can be found in polynomial time.

Relation to other widths: mim‑width ≤ boolw ≤ rw ≤ cw. There are graph classes with bounded mim‑width but unbounded treewidth (e.g., interval graphs have treewidth equal to the size of the maximum clique minus one, which can be arbitrarily large while mim‑width stays 1). Conversely, bounded treewidth does not imply bounded mim‑width.

Exam focus: (i) define mim‑width and give an example of a graph with mim‑width 1, (ii) explain why mim‑width is not minor‑monotone, (iii) describe the dynamic‑programming paradigm that yields nO(mimw) algorithms, (iv) contrast mim‑width with pathwidth and treewidth.

Excluded Minor Characterizations for Graphs of Bounded Boolean‑Width

Unlike treewidth, pathwidth, or rank‑width, boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone. Therefore the Robertson–Seymour theorem does not apply, and the class of graphs with boolean‑width at most k is not characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. In fact, for any fixed k ≥ 1 there exist graphs of boolean‑width greater than k that contain arbitrarily large minors of boolean‑width at most k, showing that the class is not minor‑closed.

However, boolean‑width is monotone under taking induced subgraphs, and it is characterized by a finite set of forbidden vertex‑minors for each fixed k? This is an open problem. For rank‑width, Oum (2005) proved that graphs of rank‑width at most k are characterized by a finite set of forbidden vertex‑minors. For boolean‑width, no such characterization is known, and it is conjectured that the class of graphs of bounded boolean‑width may not admit a finite forbidden vertex‑minor characterization.

What is known: if a graph class has bounded boolean‑width, then it also has bounded rank‑width, and therefore it is characterized by forbidden vertex‑minors for rank‑width. But the converse fails: there are graph classes of bounded rank‑width (hence characterized by forbidden vertex‑minors) that have unbounded boolean‑width. This separation shows that boolean‑width captures a strictly smaller family of graph classes than rank‑width.

Typical exam traps: assuming that bounded boolean‑width implies a finite forbidden‑minor set (it does not), confusing vertex‑minor and minor characterizations, and believing that the algorithmic meta‑theorem for boolean‑width extends to MSO₂ (it does not; MSO₂ requires treewidth or rank‑width).

The Directed Grid Theorem and Parameterized Algorithms on Directed Graphs

The directed grid theorem (Kawarabayashi & Kreutzer 2015) states that for every integer k there exists a number N(k) such that every directed graph with directed treewidth at least N(k) contains a directed grid of order k as a butterfly minor. The directed grid of order k is a directed graph on a k × k grid where each horizontal edge points right and each vertical edge points down, together with all edges of the form (i, j) → (i+1, j+1). The function N(k) is known to be non‑elementary (a tower of exponentials of height proportional to k).

Directed treewidth is a parameter for directed graphs that generalizes undirected treewidth. Many problems that are fixed‑parameter tractable parameterized by undirected treewidth become W[1]‑hard when parameterized by directed treewidth (e.g., Directed Hamiltonian Cycle). However, on classes of directed graphs that exclude a fixed directed grid as a butterfly minor, several problems admit subexponential or even polynomial‑time parameterized algorithms. This mirrors the bidimensionality theory for undirected graphs.

Algorithmic applications: the directed grid theorem is used to prove that problems such as Directed Disjoint Paths, Directed Feedback Vertex Set, and Directed Cycle Packing are fixed‑parameter tractable on directed graphs of bounded directed treewidth, but the dependence on the parameter is typically non‑elementary due to the bound N(k). Recent work has developed approximation algorithms for directed treewidth and fixed‑parameter algorithms for specific problems on graphs excluding a directed grid.

Exam focus: (i) state the directed grid theorem precisely, (ii) explain why the bound N(k) is non‑elementary, (iii) contrast directed treewidth with undirected treewidth, (iv) give an example of a problem that is FPT on undirected graphs of bounded treewidth but W[1]‑hard on directed graphs of bounded directed treewidth.

  • Confusing pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct inequality is treewidth ≤ pathwidth.
  • Assuming the forbidden‑minor set for bounded pathwidth is known for all k; it is known only for k = 1,2.
  • Treating boolean‑width as minor‑monotone; it is not, so Robertson–Seymour does not give a finite forbidden‑minor characterization.
  • Believing that bounded boolean‑width implies bounded treewidth; interval graphs have boolean‑width 1 but unbounded treewidth.
  • Thinking mim‑width is minor‑monotone; it is not, and bounded mim‑width does not imply bounded treewidth.
  • Assuming the directed grid theorem gives a polynomial bound N(k); the bound is non‑elementary.
  • Applying the undirected grid theorem to directed graphs without respecting edge directions.
