For bounded domains with Lipschitz boundary the same embeddings hold by extension operators.

Capacity provides a fine measure of the size of exceptional sets where Sobolev functions may be irregular. The p‑capacity of a compact set K ⊂ ℝⁿ is capp(K) = inf{‖φ‖W1,pp : φ ∈ Cc∞(ℝⁿ), φ ≥ 1 on K}. A property holds quasi‑everywhere (q.e.) if it holds outside a set of zero p‑capacity. Every function in W1,p has a quasi‑continuous representative, and two representatives coincide q.e. The capacity is the correct gauge for removable singularities: a compact set K is removable for W1,p (i.e. every W1,p function on Ω\\K extends to Ω) iff capp(K) = 0. This is the analytic counterpart of the fact that sets of zero Lebesgue measure are removable for Lp.

The Trudinger–Moser inequality sharpens the critical embedding W1,n(ℝⁿ) BMO: for any α ≤ αn = nωn−11/(n−1) the exponential integral ∫ exp(α|u|n/(n−1)) dx is uniformly bounded on the unit ball of W1,n. This borderline case appears in geometric analysis (prescribed curvature equations) and in the study of the Jacobian determinant of W1,n maps. Examiners may ask to prove the embedding W1,p Lp* via the representation u(x) = ∫ ∇u(y)·(x−y)/|x−y|n dy and the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality, or to show that a function in W1,p can be modified on a set of arbitrarily small capacity to become continuous.

Gaussian Measures on Separable Banach Spaces and the Cameron–Martin Theorem

A centered Gaussian measure γ on a separable Banach space B is a Borel probability measure such that every continuous linear functional ℓ ∈ B* induces a centered Gaussian random variable ℓ#γ on ℝ. The covariance operator Q : B* → B** is defined by ⟨Qℓ₁, ℓ₂⟩ = ∫ ℓ₁(x)ℓ₂(x) dγ(x). The Cameron–Martin space H ⊂ B is the completion of Q(B*) under the inner product ⟨Qℓ₁, Qℓ₂⟩H = ⟨ℓ₁, Qℓ₂⟩. It is a separable Hilbert space densely and continuously embedded in B. The Cameron–Martin theorem states that for any h ∈ H, the translated measure γh(A) = γ(A−h) is absolutely continuous with respect to γ, with Radon–Nikodym derivative dγh/dγ(x) = exp(⟨x, h⟩H − ½‖h‖H²), where ⟨x, h⟩H denotes the Paley–Wiener integral. If h ∉ H, then γh and γ are mutually singular.

This result underpins the Malliavin calculus: the derivative operator D acts on smooth cylinder functions F(x) = f(ℓ₁(x),…,ℓm(x)) by DF(x) = ∑ ∂if(ℓ(x)) Qℓi, taking values in H. The integration‑by‑parts formula ∫ ⟨DF, h⟩H dγ = ∫ F ⟨x, h⟩H dγ follows directly from the Cameron–Martin density. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup Pt = e−tL with generator L = −δD (where δ is the divergence) is symmetric in L²(γ) and satisfies the hypercontractivity estimate ‖Pt‖L²→Lq ≤ 1 for q = 1+e2t. This is the infinite‑dimensional analogue of Nelson’s hypercontractivity for the Gaussian measure on ℝⁿ.

On an abstract Wiener space (i.e. a Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space with Cameron–Martin space H), the Gross–Malliavin–Sobolev spaces Dk,p are defined as the closures of smooth cylinder functions under the norm (‖F‖Lᵖᵖ + ∑j=1k ‖DjF‖Lᵖ(H⊗j)ᵖ)1/p. The Meyer inequalities give equivalence of norms defined via the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator. Examiners often test the absolute continuity criterion: given a shift h in a concrete Wiener space (e.g. B = C[0,1] with Wiener measure), decide whether h belongs to the Cameron–Martin space (it does iff h is absolutely continuous with square‑integrable derivative). Another common question asks to derive the integration‑by‑parts formula for the Malliavin derivative from the Cameron–Martin density.

  • Confusing the weak‑type (1,1) constant for the centered maximal function with that for the uncentered version; the constants differ by a factor of 3ⁿ versus 5ⁿ.
  • Applying Marcinkiewicz interpolation without verifying sublinearity of the operator; the theorem fails for merely linear operators that are not sublinear.
  • Assuming that BMO functions are bounded; log|x| is the standard counterexample.
  • Using the duality (H¹)* = BMO without the atomic decomposition or a truncation argument to justify the pairing ∫ f g.
  • Forgetting that the Sobolev embedding W1,n BMO is sharp and does not improve to L∞; the Trudinger–Moser exponential integrability is the correct replacement.
  • Treating capacity zero sets as Lebesgue null sets; there are compact sets of positive Lebesgue measure but zero p‑capacity for p > n.
  • Assuming that every shift of a Gaussian measure on a Banach space is absolutely continuous; the Cameron–Martin theorem restricts absolute continuity to shifts in the Cameron–Martin Hilbert space.

Kolmogorov Extension Theorem and Construction of Stochastic Processes

The Kolmogorov extension theorem provides the measure‑theoretic foundation for building stochastic processes with prescribed finite‑dimensional distributions. Let (Ω, ℱ, ℙ) be a probability space and let {X_t}t∈T be a family of random variables indexed by a set T (often ℝ₊ or ℕ). The finite‑dimensional distributions are the push‑forward measures μt₁,…,t_k = ℙ ∘ (Xt₁,…,Xt_k)⁻¹ on ℝ^k. Kolmogorov’s theorem states that if a consistent family of probability measures {μt₁,…,t_k} on ℝ^k satisfies the compatibility conditions (marginalisation and permutation invariance), then there exists a probability space and a process with exactly those finite‑dimensional distributions. The proof constructs the product space ℝ^T equipped with the cylinder σ‑algebra and defines a pre‑measure on cylinder sets; Carathéodory’s extension theorem then yields a unique probability measure on the product σ‑algebra. This result underpins the existence of Brownian motion, Poisson processes, and Lévy processes. A crucial refinement is the Kolmogorov continuity criterion: if there exist constants α, β, C > 0 such that 𝔼[|X_t − X_s|^α] ≤ C |t − s|1+β for all s, t, then the process admits a modification with Hölder‑continuous sample paths of any order γ < β/α. This criterion is the standard tool for proving that Brownian motion has continuous paths.

Key Steps in the Construction

  1. Specify the index set T and the state space E (usually ℝ^d).
  2. Define a consistent family of finite‑dimensional distributions on E^k.
  3. Verify the Kolmogorov consistency conditions (projective limits).
  4. Apply Carathéodory’s extension to obtain a measure on the cylinder σ‑algebra of E^T.
  5. If path regularity is needed, check the continuity criterion to get a continuous modification.

Examiners often ask to verify consistency for a given covariance function (e.g., the Brownian covariance min(s,t)) or to derive the continuity exponent from a moment bound. The theorem also extends to processes taking values in Polish spaces, where Prokhorov’s theorem replaces the finite‑dimensional argument.

Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities and Hypercontractivity

Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (LSI) quantify the rate at which a probability measure smooths functions under a diffusion semigroup. For the standard Gaussian measure γ on ℝ^n, Gross’s LSI states that for every smooth f with ∫ f² dγ = 1,

∫ f² log f² dγ ≤ 2 ∫ |∇f|² dγ.

The constant 2 is sharp and is attained by linear functions. This inequality is equivalent to the hypercontractivity of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup P_t = e−tL where L = −Δ + x·∇ is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator. Hypercontractivity means that for 1 < p < q < ∞ and t ≥ ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)), the operator norm satisfies ‖P_t‖L^p(γ)→L^q(γ) ≤ 1. The equivalence is proved via the entropy method: differentiate the map t ↦ ‖P_t f‖Lp(t) with a suitably chosen p(t) and use the LSI to show the derivative is non‑positive. LSI also implies a Poincaré inequality (spectral gap) with constant 1 for the Gaussian measure, and it tensorises: if μ_i satisfy LSI with constants C_i, then the product measure satisfies LSI with constant max C_i. This tensorisation is crucial for high‑dimensional concentration phenomena. In the context of Markov chains, a modified LSI (with Dirichlet form ℰ(f,f) = ½ ∑x,y (f(x)−f(y))² π(x)P(x,y)) yields exponential convergence in relative entropy: Ent_π(P_t f) ≤ e−2ρ t Ent_π(f) where ρ is the LSI constant. Examiners may ask to derive the Gaussian LSI from the heat kernel representation, to prove hypercontractivity for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup, or to show that the LSI constant for the uniform measure on the discrete cube {−1,1}^n is 1/2 (Bobkov–Götze).

Worked Example: Hypercontractivity Exponent
Let P_t be the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup on ℝ with invariant Gaussian measure γ. For p=2 and q=4, find the minimal t such that ‖P_t f‖L4(γ) ≤ ‖f‖L2(γ) for all f ∈ L2(γ).
The hypercontractivity condition requires t ≥ ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)). Here p=2, q=4, so (q−1)/(p−1) = 3/1 = 3. Hence t ≥ ½ log 3. The minimal time is t = ½ log 3. At this time the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup maps L2(γ) contractively into L4(γ).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the hypercontractivity time, always write the formula t = ½ log((q−1)/(p−1)) and substitute the given p,q. Do not confuse the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup with the heat semigroup; the latter satisfies ‖etΔ‖L^p→L^q ≤ 1 for t ≥ (1/4) log((q−1)/(p−1)) on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure. The constants differ because the invariant measure is Gaussian versus Lebesgue.

Fractional Sobolev Spaces and the Gagliardo Seminorm

For s ∈ (0,1) and p ∈ [1,∞), the fractional Sobolev space Ws,p(ℝ^n) consists of functions f ∈ L^p(ℝ^n) for which the Gagliardo seminorm

[f]Ws,p = (∫ℝ^n∫ℝ^n |f(x)−f(y)|^p / |x−y|n+sp dx dy)1/p

is finite. The full norm is ‖f‖Ws,p = (‖f‖L^p^p + [f]Ws,p^p)1/p. These spaces interpolate between L^p (s=0) and W1,p (s=1) and are the natural domain of the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s/2. The embedding theorems mirror the integer‑order case: if sp < n, then Ws,p(ℝ^n) Lp* with p* = np/(n−sp) (Sobolev exponent); if sp = n, the critical embedding is into BMO or exponential Orlicz spaces (Trudinger–Moser type); if sp > n, functions are Hölder continuous of order s−n/p. The Gagliardo seminorm is also the quadratic form of the fractional Laplacian: for p=2, [f]Ws,22 = Cn,s ∫ |ξ|2s |ℱf(ξ)|2 dξ. This Fourier representation shows that Ws,2 = H^s (Bessel potential spaces) with equivalent norms. On bounded domains, extension operators exist for Lipschitz boundaries, allowing the same seminorm definition via restriction. Examiners frequently test the scaling argument: under f_λ(x) = f(λx), the seminorm scales as [f_λ]Ws,p = λs−n/p [f]Ws,p, which immediately yields the critical exponent p* = np/(n−sp). Another common question asks to prove the compact embedding Ws,p(Ω) L^p(Ω) for bounded Ω using the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem and the fact that the seminorm controls translations.

Besov and Triebel–Lizorkin Spaces via Real Interpolation

Besov spaces B^sp,q and Triebel–Lizorkin spaces F^sp,q refine the Sobolev scale by measuring smoothness with two indices p (integrability) and q (fine‑tuning of the dyadic decomposition). Let φ be a smooth radial function supported in an annulus such that ∑j∈ℤ φ(2−jξ) = 1 for ξ ≠ 0. The Littlewood–Paley blocks are Δ_j f = ℱ⁻¹[φ(2−j·) ℱf]. Then

‖f‖B^sp,q = (‖Δ−1f‖L^p^q + ∑j≥0 2jsq ‖Δ_j f‖L^p^q)1/q (with the usual modification for q=∞),

‖f‖F^sp,q = ‖(∑j≥−1 2jsq |Δ_j f|^q)1/q‖L^p.

These spaces coincide with classical ones for special parameters: B^s2,2 = F^s2,2 = H^s, B^sp,2 = F^sp,2 for 1

, and B^sp,∞ captures borderline regularity (e.g., B0∞,∞ = BMO). Real interpolation gives (L^p, W1,p)θ,q = B^θp,q for 0<θ<1, while complex interpolation yields [L^p, W1,p]_θ = F^θp,2. The embedding B^sp,q₁ B^sp,q₂ holds for q₁ ≤ q₂, and F^sp,q₁ F^sp,q₂ for q₁ ≥ q₂. The duality (B^sp,q)' = B−sp',q' (with 1/p+1/p'=1, 1/q+1/q'=1) is valid for 1

. Examiners may ask to identify the Besov space corresponding to the trace of a Sobolev function on a hyperplane (answer: Bs−1/pp,p) or to prove that the solution of the heat equation with initial data in B^sp,q stays in the same space with norm controlled by the initial norm. The atomic decomposition of Besov spaces (using smooth atoms with moment conditions) is a powerful tool for nonlinear PDEs.

Concentration of Measure on the Sphere and Gaussian Isoperimetry

Concentration of measure describes the phenomenon that Lipschitz functions on high‑dimensional metric probability spaces are sharply concentrated around their median. On the Euclidean sphere Sn−1 with uniform probability measure σ_n, Lévy’s lemma states that for any 1‑Lipschitz function f : Sn−1 → ℝ and any t > 0,

σ_n({|f − M_f| ≥ t}) ≤ 2 exp(−(n−1)t²/2),

where M_f is a median of f. The Gaussian analogue (Tsirelson–Ibragimov–Sudakov) says that for the standard Gaussian measure γ_n on ℝ^n and any 1‑Lipschitz f,

γ_n({|f − M_f| ≥ t}) ≤ 2 exp(−t²/2).

Both inequalities are consequences of the isoperimetric profile: among sets of given measure, half‑spaces (for Gaussian) or spherical caps (for the sphere) minimise the boundary measure. The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality states that for any Borel set A ⊂ ℝ^n with γ_n(A) = Φ(a) (where Φ is the standard normal CDF), the Minkowski content satisfies γ_n+(A) ≥ φ(a) where φ is the Gaussian density. This yields the concentration bound via the Herbst argument: the log‑Sobolev inequality for γ_n implies Entγ_n(eλf) ≤ λ²/2 ∫ eλf dγ_n for 1‑Lipschitz f, which after optimisation gives the sub‑Gaussian tail. On the sphere, the same argument uses the Bakry–Émery curvature‑dimension condition CD(n−1, n−1). Concentration of measure underpins many results in high‑dimensional probability: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, Dvoretzky’s theorem, and the existence of almost Euclidean sections of convex bodies. Examiners often ask to derive the Gaussian concentration inequality from the log‑Sobolev inequality, or to compute the median of the norm ‖X‖ for X ∼ γ_n (it is √n + O(1/√n)) and then bound the deviation ℙ(|‖X‖ − √n| ≥ t).

  • Confusing the Gagliardo seminorm scaling exponent; the correct homogeneity is s − n/p, not s − n.
  • Applying the Kolmogorov continuity criterion without checking that the moment bound holds uniformly in the index set; the constants must be independent of s,t.
  • Assuming that hypercontractivity holds for the heat semigroup on ℝ^n with the same time exponent as the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup; the Gaussian invariant measure changes the constant.
  • Using the Besov norm B^sp,q with q=∞ as if it were a Hilbert space; duality fails at the endpoints q=1,∞.
  • Forgetting that the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality gives the optimal constant 1/2 in the exponent of the concentration bound; any larger constant would contradict the half‑space extremals.
  • Treating the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s/2 as a local operator; its non‑local nature is essential for the Gagliardo seminorm representation.
  • Overlooking that the Kolmogorov extension theorem only guarantees existence on the product σ‑algebra; path regularity requires a separate modification argument.

Fourier Analysis on Locally Compact Abelian Groups and the Plancherel Theorem

Let G be a locally compact abelian (LCA) group with Haar measure μ. The dual group Ĝ consists of all continuous characters χ: G → 𝕋 equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. The Fourier transform of f ∈ L¹(G) is defined by ̂f(χ) = ∫_G f(x) χ(x)⁻¹ dμ(x). This map extends uniquely to a unitary isomorphism ℱ: L²(G) → L²(Ĝ) — the Plancherel theorem — satisfying ‖f‖₂ = ‖̂f‖₂ and the inversion formula f(x) = ∫_Ĝ ̂f(χ) χ(x) dν(χ) for f ∈ L¹(G) ∩ L²(G), where ν is the dual Haar measure normalised so that Plancherel holds. The convolution theorem ̂(f * g) = ̂f · ̂g and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma ̂f ∈ C₀(Ĝ) for f ∈ L¹(G) are immediate consequences. When G = ℝⁿ the dual is again ℝⁿ and the transform reduces to the classical Euclidean Fourier transform; when G = 𝕋ⁿ the dual is ℤⁿ and the transform becomes the Fourier series. Examiners frequently test the normalisation of Haar measures: the product of the measures on G and Ĝ must equal (2π)ⁿ in the Euclidean case, and the inversion formula carries a factor (2π)⁻ⁿ. A common trap is to forget that the Plancherel theorem requires f ∈ L² and does not hold pointwise for arbitrary L¹ functions.

Spectral Theorem for Unbounded Self‑Adjoint Operators and Spectral Measures

Let H be a separable Hilbert space and A a densely defined self‑adjoint operator. The spectral theorem asserts the existence of a unique projection‑valued measure E on the Borel σ‑algebra of ℝ such that A = ∫_ℝ λ dE(λ) and the domain of A consists of those ψ ∈ H for which ∫_ℝ λ² d⟨E(λ)ψ, ψ⟩ < ∞. For any Borel function f: ℝ → ℂ one defines f(A) = ∫_ℝ f(λ) dE(λ) on its natural domain. The functional calculus yields the unitary group U(t) = eitA solving the Schrödinger equation, and the resolvent R(z) = (A − z)⁻¹ = ∫_ℝ (λ − z)⁻¹ dE(λ) for z ∉ ℝ. The spectrum σ(A) coincides with the support of E. The spectral measure μ_ψ(·) = ⟨E(·)ψ, ψ⟩ encodes the cyclic subspace generated by ψ; the operator is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by λ on a direct integral of L² spaces. In exams, a typical question asks to prove that if A has compact resolvent then its spectrum consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity accumulating only at infinity. Another frequent twist: given a symmetric operator with deficiency indices (n,n), describe all self‑adjoint extensions via von Neumann’s formula and the associated boundary conditions.

Worked Example: Spectral Measure of the Position Operator
Let H = L²(ℝ) and (Xψ)(x) = x ψ(x) with domain {ψ ∈ L² : xψ ∈ L²}. Determine the spectral measure E of X and verify the functional calculus for f(λ) = ei t λ.
For any Borel set B ⊂ ℝ define (E(B)ψ)(x) = 1_B(x) ψ(x). Then E is a projection‑valued measure: E(B) is an orthogonal projection, E(∅)=0, E(ℝ)=I, and countable additivity holds in the strong operator topology. For ψ ∈ Dom(X), ∫_ℝ λ d⟨E(λ)ψ, ψ⟩ = ∫_ℝ x |ψ(x)|² dx = ⟨Xψ, ψ⟩, confirming X = ∫ λ dE(λ). For f(λ)=ei t λ, f(X) = ∫ ei t λ dE(λ) acts as multiplication by ei t x, i.e. (f(X)ψ)(x) = ei t x ψ(x), which is exactly the unitary translation group U(t) on L²(ℝ). The spectral measure of a vector ψ is μ_ψ(B) = ∫_B |ψ(x)|² dx, the probability density of the position observable in quantum mechanics.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for the spectral measure of a multiplication operator, write down the projection‑valued measure immediately as multiplication by indicator functions. For functional calculus, remember that f(A) is defined on the set of vectors where ∫ |f(λ)|² dμ_ψ(λ) < ∞. If the question involves deficiency indices, compute the kernels of A* ± i explicitly; the dimension of these kernels gives the indices.

Malliavin Calculus: Integration by Parts on Wiener Space

Let (Ω, ℱ, ℙ) be the classical Wiener space of continuous paths ω: [0,1] → ℝ with ω(0)=0 under Wiener measure. The Cameron–Martin space H consists of absolutely continuous paths h with square‑integrable derivative, equipped with the inner product ⟨h₁, h₂⟩_H = ∫₀¹ h₁'(t) h₂'(t) dt. For a smooth cylindrical functional F = f(W(h₁),…,W(h_n)) where W(h) = ∫₀¹ h'(t) dW_t is the Wiener integral, the Malliavin derivative DF is the H-valued random variable DF = ∑i=1^n ∂_i f(W(h₁),…,W(h_n)) h_i. The operator D is closable from L^p(Ω) into L^p(Ω; H) for p ≥ 1; its domain is the Sobolev space 𝔻1,p. The divergence operator δ (Skorokhod integral) is the adjoint of D: for u ∈ Dom(δ) ⊂ L²(Ω; H), 𝔼[⟨DF, u⟩_H] = 𝔼[F δ(u)]. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator L = −δD satisfies L F = −∑i=1^n λ_i ∂_i f on the Wiener chaos expansion, and its inverse L⁻¹ on the orthogonal complement of constants yields the integration‑by‑parts formula 𝔼[F δ(u)] = 𝔼[⟨DF, u⟩_H]. A cornerstone application is the proof of Hörmander’s theorem on hypoellipticity: if the Malliavin covariance matrix σ_F = ⟨DF, DF⟩_H is almost surely invertible, then F has a smooth density. Examiners often ask to compute D and δ for simple functionals such as F = ∫₀¹ W_t² dt or to verify the chain rule D(φ(F)) = φ'(F) DF for φ ∈ C_b¹(ℝ).

Metric Measure Spaces, Ricci Curvature Lower Bounds, and the CD(K,N) Condition

A metric measure space (X, d, m) consists of a complete separable metric space (X, d) and a locally finite Borel measure m with full support. The L²-Wasserstein space 𝒫₂(X) of probability measures with finite second moment is geodesic when (X, d) is geodesic. The curvature‑dimension condition CD(K, N) (with K ∈ ℝ, N ∈ [1, ∞]) is defined via displacement convexity of the Rényi entropy Ent_m(μ) = ∫ ρ log ρ dm for μ = ρ m: for any two measures μ₀, μ₁ ∈ 𝒫₂(X) there exists a geodesic (μ_t) such that Ent_m(μ_t) ≤ (1−t) Ent_m(μ₀) + t Ent_m(μ₁) − (K/2) t(1−t) W₂²(μ₀, μ₁) − (1/N) ∫₀¹ … (the precise distortion coefficients involve sin or sinh depending on the sign of K). When N = ∞ the condition reduces to CD(K, ∞), equivalent to the Bakry–Émery Γ₂ ≥ K Γ inequality on a suitable Dirichlet form. Fundamental consequences: the Bishop–Gromov volume comparison, the Bonnet–Myers diameter bound for K > 0, the Lichnerowicz spectral gap λ₁ ≥ K N/(N−1), and the Gaussian concentration inequality m({f ≥ M_f + r}) ≤ exp(−K r²/2) for 1-Lipschitz f. The stability of CD(K, N) under measured Gromov–Hausdorff convergence (Lott–Villani, Sturm) enables compactness arguments. In exams, a typical question asks to verify CD(0, N) for the Euclidean space ℝⁿ with Lebesgue measure, or to deduce the Brunn–Minkowski inequality from CD(0, N).

Transport‑Entropy Inequalities: Talagrand’s T₂, HWI, and Concentration

Let μ be a probability measure on a Polish space X. The quadratic transportation cost inequality T₂(C) states that for all ν ≪ μ, W₂²(ν, μ) ≤ 2 C Ent_μ(ν), where Ent_μ(ν) = ∫ log(dν/dμ) dν is the relative entropy. Talagrand proved that the standard Gaussian measure γ on ℝⁿ satisfies T₂(1) with optimal constant C = 1. The HWI inequality (Otto–Villani) interpolates between entropy, Wasserstein distance, and Fisher information: Ent_μ(ν) ≤ W₂(ν, μ) √I_μ(ν) − (K/2) W₂²(ν, μ) for measures satisfying a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant K. Here I_μ(ν) = ∫ |∇ log(dν/dμ)|² dν is the Fisher information. From T₂(C) one obtains sub‑Gaussian concentration: for any 1-Lipschitz f, μ({f ≥ ∫ f dμ + r}) ≤ exp(−r²/(4C)). Conversely, Gaussian concentration implies T₂ (Bobkov–Götze). The equivalence between T₂, logarithmic Sobolev, and Poincaré inequalities is a central theme. Examiners often ask to derive the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality from T₂(1) via the Herbst argument, or to prove that a product measure μ⊗ n satisfies T₂(C) with the same constant C as μ (tensorisation). A common trap is to confuse the constant in T₂ with the constant in the logarithmic Sobolev inequality; they differ by a factor of 2 in the Gaussian case.

Common Traps

  • Forgetting the normalisation of Haar measures when applying the Plancherel theorem on ℝⁿ; the inversion formula carries a factor (2π)⁻ⁿ.
  • Assuming the spectral theorem holds for symmetric operators without checking self‑adjointness; deficiency indices must be zero.
  • Confusing the Malliavin derivative D with the Fréchet derivative on Wiener space; D takes values in the Cameron–Martin space H, not in L²([0,1]).
  • Applying the CD(K,N) condition without verifying that the space is a geodesic metric measure space; the definition requires existence of W₂-geodesics.
  • Mixing the constants in Talagrand’s T₂ inequality and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality; for the Gaussian measure T₂(1) corresponds to log‑Sobolev constant 2.
  • Neglecting the tensorisation property of transport‑entropy inequalities; the constant does not increase under products.
  • Review these traps before the exam.

Maharam's Theorem and the Classification of Measure Algebras

Maharam's theorem gives a complete structural description of complete Boolean algebras equipped with a strictly positive finite measure. Every such measure algebra is isomorphic to a countable direct sum of homogeneous measure algebras, each of which is determined up to isomorphism by its Maharam type — the minimal cardinality of a dense subset. The homogeneous components are precisely the measure algebras of the product spaces {0,1}κ with the usual product measure, where κ is an infinite cardinal. The theorem implies that any separable measure algebra (Maharam type ℵ₀) is isomorphic to the Lebesgue measure algebra on [0,1]; non‑separable algebras decompose into a sum of such homogeneous pieces. The proof proceeds by constructing a maximal family of pairwise disjoint elements of equal measure, then using the Maharam–Carathéodory extension to identify each block with a product measure. Applications include the classification of von Neumann algebras of type I and the representation of stochastic processes via measure‑algebra homomorphisms. In examinations, a typical question asks to show that the measure algebra of a Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space is separable, hence isomorphic to the Lebesgue algebra, or to compute the Maharam type of the measure algebra of a product of uncountably many copies of {0,1}.

Nonstandard Measure Theory: Loeb Measures and Ultraproducts

Loeb measure construction turns an internal finitely additive measure on a hyperfinite set into a standard countably additive measure on the associated Loeb σ‑algebra. Start with a nonstandard extension *X of a standard set X, an internal algebra 𝒜 of subsets of *X, and an internal finitely additive probability measure μ on 𝒜. The Loeb σ‑algebra L(𝒜) is the σ‑algebra generated by 𝒜, and the Loeb measure L(μ) is the unique countably additive extension of the standard part map st∘μ. The resulting measure space ( *X, L(𝒜), L(μ) ) is complete and saturated. Ultraproducts of measure spaces provide a systematic way to produce such hyperfinite approximations: given a sequence (Xn, Σn, μn) and a free ultrafilter 𝒰 on ℕ, the ultraproduct ∏𝒰 Xn carries an internal measure defined by μ([An]) = lim𝒰 μn(An). The Loeb measure of this ultraproduct recovers the weak limit of the original sequence. This framework yields elegant proofs of the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, and the existence of Brownian motion as a Loeb‑measure‑induced process on a hyperfinite time line. Examiners often ask to construct the Loeb measure of the hyperfinite counting measure on {1,…,N} (N unlimited) and to verify that the resulting space is isomorphic to the Lebesgue unit interval, or to prove that the ultraproduct of a sequence of probability spaces satisfies the countable saturation property needed for the Loeb construction.

Worked Example: Loeb Measure of a Hyperfinite Counting Space
Let N be an unlimited hyperinteger and let Ω = {1,2,…,N}. Define the internal algebra 𝒜 = *𝒫(Ω) and the internal measure μ(A) = |A|/N for A ∈ 𝒜. Show that the Loeb measure space (Ω, L(𝒜), L(μ)) is measure‑theoretically isomorphic to ([0,1], ℒ, λ) where ℒ is the Lebesgue σ‑algebra and λ is Lebesgue measure.
Define the internal map φ: Ω → *[0,1] by φ(k) = k/N. This map is internal and injective. For any internal set A ⊆ Ω, μ(A) = |A|/N = *λ(φ(A)) where *λ is the internal Lebesgue measure on *[0,1]. The Loeb σ‑algebra L(𝒜) is generated by the internal sets, and the Loeb measure L(μ) satisfies L(μ)(A) = st(μ(A)) = st(*λ(φ(A))) = λ(st(φ(A))). The standard part map st∘φ sends Ω onto [0,1] and pushes L(μ) forward to λ. Since φ is a bijection modulo null sets, the two measure spaces are isomorphic.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a Loeb measure construction, first identify the hyperfinite approximation (often a hyperfinite set with counting measure). Write down the internal measure explicitly, then apply the standard part map. Remember that the Loeb σ‑algebra is the completion of the σ‑algebra generated by internal sets; any set that differs from an internal set by a Loeb‑null set belongs to it. Use the transfer principle to move standard measure‑theoretic facts to the internal universe, then take standard parts.

Stochastic Integration in Banach Spaces: UMD Spaces and Martingale Type

The theory of stochastic integration for Banach‑space‑valued processes requires geometric conditions on the target space. A Banach space B is said to have the UMD (unconditional martingale differences) property if for every B‑valued martingale difference sequence (dn) and every choice of signs εn ∈ {−1,1}, the series ∑ εn dn converges in Lp(Ω;B) whenever ∑ dn does, for some (equivalently all) p ∈ (1,∞). This property is equivalent to the boundedness of the Hilbert transform on Lp(ℝ;B) and to the existence of a bounded H∞ functional calculus for the associated sectorial operators. UMD spaces include all Hilbert spaces, Lp spaces for 1

k,p with the same range of p. They exclude L1, L∞, C(K), and c0. Martingale type and cotype provide quantitative refinements: B has martingale type p ∈ (1,2] if there exists C such that for every B‑valued martingale (Mn), 𝔼‖Mn‖p ≤ C ∑ 𝔼‖dk‖p; cotype q ∈ [2,∞) is defined dually. The Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequalities extend to UMD spaces with constants depending only on the UMD constant. Stochastic integrals ∫ Φ dW for cylindrical Brownian motion W are well defined for predictable Φ taking values in the space of γ‑radonifying operators from the Cameron–Martin space into B, precisely when B is UMD. This framework underpins the well‑posedness theory for stochastic evolution equations in Banach spaces. In examinations, a common task is to prove that Lp(μ) is UMD for 1

p and the vector‑valued extrapolation theorem, or to show that the stochastic integral of a simple process satisfies the Itô isometry in a UMD space.

Free Probability: Noncommutative Measure Theory and Free Independence

Free probability replaces classical independence with free independence, defined in a noncommutative probability space (𝒜, φ) where 𝒜 is a unital algebra and φ a linear functional with φ(1)=1. Subalgebras 𝒜1,…,𝒜n are freely independent if φ(a1⋯ak)=0 whenever each aj ∈ 𝒜i(j) with φ(aj)=0 and adjacent indices differ. The joint distribution of freely independent variables is determined by their individual distributions via the free convolution operation ⊞. The R‑transform linearises free convolution: RX+Y(z)=RX(z)+RY(z) for freely independent X,Y. The semicircle law plays the role of the Gaussian; its R‑transform is R(z)=z. The free central limit theorem states that the normalized sum of freely independent, identically distributed variables with zero mean and unit variance converges in distribution to the semicircle law. The S‑transform linearises free multiplicative convolution ⊠ for positive variables. Voiculescu's free entropy χ and free Fisher information Φ provide analogues of classical entropy and Fisher information, satisfying a free logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Free probability connects to random matrix theory: the empirical eigenvalue distribution of independent GUE matrices converges almost surely to the free convolution of their limiting spectra. In examinations, typical questions ask to compute the R‑transform of a Bernoulli variable, to derive the free additive convolution of two semicircle laws, or to prove that the Cauchy transform G(z)=φ((z−X)−1) satisfies the functional equation G(z)=1/(z−R(G(z))).

Large Deviations for Empirical Measures: Sanov's Theorem and the Level‑2 Principle

Sanov's theorem gives the large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical measure Ln = (1/n)∑i=1n δXi of i.i.d. random variables Xi with law μ on a Polish space 𝒳. The rate function is the relative entropy H(ν|μ) = ∫ log(dν/dμ) dν if ν≪μ, and +∞ otherwise. The LDP holds in the weak topology on the space of probability measures 𝒫(𝒳) with speed n: for any Borel set Γ, −infν∈Γ° H(ν|μ) ≤ liminf (1/n) log ℙ(Ln∈Γ) ≤ limsup (1/n) log ℙ(Ln∈Γ) ≤ −infν∈Γ̄ H(ν|μ). The proof uses the exponential tightness of the sequence and the variational formula for relative entropy. The level‑2 LDP for empirical measures of Markov chains (Donsker–Varadhan) replaces the i.i.d. assumption with a stationary ergodic Markov process; the rate function is the Donsker–Varadhan functional I(ν) = supf>0 ∫ (L f)/f dν where L is the generator. For empirical processes indexed by a function class, the level‑3 LDP concerns the empirical measure on the path space. Applications include the Gibbs conditioning principle: conditioning on a rare event forces the empirical measure to concentrate on the minimiser of the rate function over the conditioning set. In examinations, a standard problem is to derive the LDP for the empirical measure of a finite‑state Markov chain using the Gärtner–Ellis theorem, or to compute the rate function for the empirical measure of a Poisson point process and identify the most likely profile under a large deviation constraint.

  • Confusing the Maharam type of a measure algebra with the cardinality of the underlying space; the type is the minimal cardinality of a dense subset in the measure algebra, not the cardinality of the sample space.
  • Assuming every internal finitely additive measure yields a Loeb measure without checking that the internal algebra is closed under the relevant operations; the Loeb construction requires an internal algebra, not just an arbitrary internal collection.
  • Applying the UMD property to spaces that lack it, such as L1 or C(K); stochastic integrals in these spaces require different techniques (e.g., nuclear operators or the theory of integration in non‑UMD spaces).
  • Treating free independence as classical independence; free independence is defined by vanishing of mixed moments with centred variables, which leads to different convolution rules (R‑transform vs. characteristic functions).
  • Using the relative entropy rate function in Sanov's theorem without verifying that the underlying space is Polish; the LDP in the weak topology requires a Polish space to ensure the rate function is lower semicontinuous and the level sets are compact.
  • Neglecting the distinction between level‑1, level‑2, and level‑3 large deviation principles; each level concerns a different random object (sample mean, empirical measure, empirical process) and has its own rate function.
  • Forgetting that the Loeb measure of a hyperfinite counting space is isomorphic to Lebesgue measure only after taking the standard part map; the internal map itself is not measure‑preserving in the standard sense.

Orlicz Spaces and the Luxemburg Norm

Orlicz spaces generalize the classical Lp scale by replacing the power function t ↦ tp with a Young function Φ: [0,∞) → [0,∞) that is convex, increasing, and satisfies Φ(0)=0, Φ(t)/t → 0 as t→0, and Φ(t)/t → ∞ as t→∞. The Luxemburg norm of a measurable function f on a measure space (X,𝒜,μ) is defined by ‖f‖Φ = inf{ λ>0 : ∫ Φ(|f|/λ) dμ ≤ 1 }. This norm makes the space LΦ(μ) a Banach space. When Φ(t)=tp/p the Luxemburg norm coincides with the usual Lp norm up to the constant p1/p. The complementary Young function Ψ is defined by Ψ(s)=supt≥0(st−Φ(t)); the pair (Φ,Ψ) satisfies the Young inequality st ≤ Φ(t)+Ψ(s). Hölder's inequality holds in the form ∫ |fg| dμ ≤ 2‖f‖Φ‖g‖Ψ. The Δ2 condition (Φ(2t) ≤ KΦ(t) for large t) characterizes separability and reflexivity of LΦ. If Φ satisfies Δ2 globally, simple functions are dense and the dual space is isometrically isomorphic to LΨ. Orlicz spaces appear naturally in the study of exponential integrability (Trudinger–Moser inequalities), in the theory of Hardy–Littlewood maximal operators on endpoint spaces, and in the analysis of nonlinear PDEs with nonstandard growth. The modular functional ρΦ(f)=∫ Φ(|f|) dμ provides an alternative topology; convergence in norm is equivalent to modular convergence when Φ satisfies Δ2. The Luxemburg norm is not uniformly convex in general, but the Orlicz space can be renormed to be uniformly convex if both Φ and Ψ satisfy Δ2. In examinations, typical tasks include proving the equivalence of the Luxemburg and Orlicz norms, verifying the Δ2 condition for Φ(t)=et2−1, and showing that the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator is bounded from LΦ to weak‑LΦ when Φ(t)=t log+ t.

Weighted Norm Inequalities and Muckenhoupt Ap Weights

A weight w is a locally integrable, almost everywhere positive function on ℝn. For 1
