Roth (1984) extended the deferred‑acceptance algorithm to this setting by allowing each agent to propose to multiple counterparts up to its capacity, and each counterpart to hold a set of proposals up to its capacity, rejecting the least preferred when over‑subscribed. The resulting matching is stable (no blocking pair) and is the optimal stable matching for the proposing side. The set of stable matchings forms a lattice under the “firm‑preferred” and “worker‑preferred” partial orders, generalizing the one‑to‑one lattice structure. The core of the associated cooperative game (where coalitions can form arbitrary many‑to‑many contracts) coincides with the set of stable matchings when preferences are responsive (i.e., derived from a ranking over individual partners). If preferences are not responsive, the core may be empty or contain matchings that are not stable in the pairwise sense. Examiners often test the construction of the many‑to‑many deferred‑acceptance algorithm on a small instance, the proof that the algorithm terminates in a stable matching, and the lattice property. A common twist is to ask whether the worker‑proposing algorithm yields the worker‑optimal stable matching when workers have capacities greater than one — the answer is yes, provided preferences are responsive.

Responsive Preferences and the Core

A preference relation over sets of partners is responsive if, for any set S and any two individuals a, b not in S, S ∪ {a} ≻ S ∪ {b} ⇔ {a} ≻ {b}, and for any a ∉ S, S ∪ {a} ≻ S ⇔ {a} ≻ ∅. Responsiveness ensures that an agent’s marginal preference for adding a partner does not depend on the rest of the set. Under responsive preferences, the core of the many‑to‑many matching game (with transferable utility set to zero) equals the set of pairwise stable matchings. The proof uses the fact that any blocking coalition can be reduced to a blocking pair by iteratively removing the least preferred member, preserving the blocking property because of responsiveness. Without responsiveness, a coalition of three agents might block a matching even though no pair does, leading to a non‑empty core that contains non‑pairwise‑stable matchings. This distinction is crucial for applications like course allocation where students have complementarities across courses.

Strategy‑Proofness and the Rural Hospitals Theorem

The many‑to‑many deferred‑acceptance algorithm is strategy‑proof for the proposing side: no agent can benefit by misreporting its preferences, assuming the other side reports truthfully. The rural hospitals theorem extends: the set of agents who are matched (and the number of positions filled) is the same in every stable matching. In the many‑to‑many case, the theorem holds for each side separately: the set of filled slots on the proposing side is invariant across all stable matchings. This invariance is used to prove that the proposing side’s optimal stable matching is also the unique stable matching that maximizes the number of matched agents on that side.

Contract Theory: Multitask Principal‑Agent Models and the Holmström‑Milgrom Linear Contracts

In many real‑world settings an agent performs multiple tasks, some of which are easily measurable (e.g., quantity produced) and others hard to measure (e.g., quality, maintenance). Holmström and Milgrom (1991) showed that when the agent’s effort across tasks is substitutable and the principal observes only a noisy aggregate signal, the optimal contract is linear in the observed signals. The model assumes the agent chooses a vector of efforts e = (e1,…,e_n) at cost C(e) = ½ eᵀ Q e (quadratic), and the principal observes a vector of signals x = e + ε where ε ∼ N(0, Σ). The principal offers a contract w(x) = α + βᵀ x. The agent’s expected utility is α + βᵀ e − ½ eᵀ Q e − ½ βᵀ Σ β (risk premium). Maximizing over e gives e* = Q⁻¹ β. The principal’s problem reduces to choosing β to maximize βᵀ Q⁻¹ β − ½ βᵀ Q⁻¹ β − ½ βᵀ Σ β = ½ βᵀ (Q⁻¹ − Σ) β. The optimal β solves (Q⁻¹ − Σ) β = 0, yielding β* = 0 if Σ ≥ Q⁻¹ (i.e., noise dominates), otherwise β* aligns with the eigenvectors of Q⁻¹ − Σ. The key insight: the optimal incentive weight on a task is decreasing in the measurement noise for that task and increasing in the marginal productivity of effort. If tasks are complementary (Q has negative off‑diagonals), the optimal contract may provide incentives on a noisy task to indirectly motivate effort on a complementary measurable task. Examiners test the derivation of the first‑order condition e* = Q⁻¹ β, the expression for the principal’s objective, and the comparative statics: higher noise → lower β; higher complementarity → cross‑task incentives. A typical question provides a 2×2 Q and Σ and asks to compute the optimal β vector.

Extension to Non‑Linear Contracts and Limited Liability

When the agent is risk‑neutral but protected by limited liability (w(x) ≥ 0), the optimal contract may be non‑linear, often taking the form of a threshold bonus: the agent receives a fixed payment if the signal exceeds a cutoff, zero otherwise. This is the “binary” contract studied by Innes (1990). In multitask settings with limited liability, the principal may use a menu of linear contracts or a single non‑linear contract that approximates the first‑best. The trade‑off is between providing sufficient incentives on measurable tasks and avoiding excessive risk on noisy tasks. Recent work by Dutta and Reichelstein (2003) shows that if the principal can commit to a long‑term contract and the agent’s effort is persistent, the optimal dynamic contract is linear in the cumulative signal, generalizing the static Holmström‑Milgrom result.

Application to Performance Pay in Organizations

The multitask framework explains why firms often use balanced scorecards: they assign weights to multiple performance metrics (financial, customer, internal process, learning) to align the agent’s effort allocation with the firm’s overall objectives. If the metrics are noisy and correlated, the optimal weights are given by the inverse of the noise covariance matrix times the marginal productivity vector, exactly the β* formula. Empirical studies (e.g., Baker 1992) confirm that firms place lower weight on noisier metrics, consistent with the theory. Examiners may ask to interpret a given weight vector in terms of the underlying Q and Σ matrices.

  • Confusing the Cremer‑McLean full‑extraction result with the standard Myerson auction — the former requires interdependent values and a full‑rank condition, the latter assumes independent private values.
  • Assuming that reputation effects in the chain‑store game arise without a positive prior probability of a commitment type — a zero prior eliminates the reputation equilibrium.
  • Believing that finding a correlated equilibrium is PPAD‑complete — it is polynomial via linear programming, unlike Nash equilibrium.
  • Thinking that the many‑to‑many deferred‑acceptance algorithm is strategy‑proof for both sides — it is only strategy‑proof for the proposing side.
  • Equating the core of a many‑to‑many matching game with the set of stable matchings without checking responsiveness of preferences.
  • Overlooking that the Holmström‑Milgrom linear contract optimality relies on quadratic costs, normal noise, and exponential utility (or mean‑variance preferences).
  • Remember to review these traps before the exam.

Mechanism Design with Budget Constraints and Limited Liability

Standard mechanism design assumes agents have quasi-linear utilities and unbounded transfer capacity. In practice, bidders face budget constraints (maximum payment ≤ B) and limited liability (payment ≥ 0). These constraints fundamentally alter optimal auction design. Laffont and Robert (1996) and Che and Gale (1998) showed that with budget constraints, the revenue equivalence theorem fails: first-price auctions can generate higher expected revenue than second-price auctions because budget-constrained bidders shade bids less aggressively in first-price formats. The optimal mechanism under budget constraints involves ironing the virtual valuation function φ(v) = v − (1−F(v))/f(v) subject to the constraint that the payment rule p(v) ≤ B. When the budget B is common knowledge and identical across bidders, the optimal auction is a capped version of the Myerson auction: allocate to the bidder with the highest virtual valuation, but charge min(φ⁻¹(max φ(v)), B). If budgets are private information, the mechanism must elicit both value and budget, leading to a two-dimensional screening problem. Pai and Vohra (2014) characterized the optimal mechanism using a generalized ironing procedure over the joint distribution of (v, B). The key insight: the allocation rule is monotone in a one-dimensional "score" s(v, B) that combines value and budget, and the payment rule is the minimum of the score-based payment and the budget. Limited liability (w ≥ 0) interacts with risk aversion: Innes (1990) showed that when the agent is risk-neutral but protected by limited liability, the optimal contract is a binary bonus — pay a fixed amount if output exceeds a threshold, zero otherwise. This "live or die" contract minimizes the agent's rent while satisfying the participation constraint. Examiners test the derivation of the ironed virtual valuation under a budget cap, the comparison of expected revenue across auction formats, and the structure of the optimal binary contract under limited liability. A typical question provides a uniform value distribution on [0,1], a budget B = 0.6, and asks to compute the optimal reserve price and expected revenue in a first-price auction with two bidders.

Two-Sided Platforms and Market Design: Pricing and Allocation

Two-sided platforms (credit cards, ride-sharing, app stores) match agents from two distinct sides (buyers/sellers, riders/drivers, developers/users) where each side's participation value depends on the size and composition of the other side. This creates cross-side network effects that standard mechanism design ignores. Rochet and Tirole (2003, 2006) formalized the pricing problem: the platform chooses prices pᴮ and pˢ for buyers and sellers to maximize profit π = (pᴮ + pˢ − c) Q(pᴮ, pˢ), where Q is the transaction volume determined by the participation decisions of both sides. The optimal price structure satisfies the "divide-and-conquer" principle: the side with more elastic demand (or weaker network effects) pays a lower price, possibly negative (subsidized). The Lerner index for each side is (pᴷ − cᴷ)/pᴷ = 1/|εᴷ| × (1 + ∂ln Q/∂ln pᴶ), where εᴷ is the own-price elasticity and the cross-term captures the network effect feedback. Weyl (2010) extended this to a general framework where the platform designs not just prices but the entire matching mechanism. The key result: the optimal mechanism maximizes a weighted sum of surplus on both sides, with weights determined by the platform's market power. In ride-sharing, the platform chooses a matching algorithm (e.g., closest driver vs. system-optimal) and pricing rule (surge pricing vs. fixed commission). The surge multiplier m(t) solves a dynamic optimization: maximize ∫[m(t) D(p/m(t)) − c S(p/m(t))] dt subject to driver supply S and rider demand D. Examiners test the derivation of the optimal price ratio pᴮ/pˢ = (1 + 1/εˢ)/(1 + 1/εᴮ) under symmetric network effects, the welfare implications of price discrimination across sides, and the stability of the platform equilibrium against multi-homing. A typical question gives demand functions Dᴮ = a − b pᴮ + γ Nˢ, Dˢ = a − b pˢ + γ Nᴮ and asks to compute the profit-maximizing prices and the resulting transaction volume.

Worked Example: Optimal Pricing on a Two-Sided Platform
A payment card network faces demand from consumers: Qᶜ = 100 − 2pᶜ + 0.5Qᵐ, and from merchants: Qᵐ = 80 − pᵐ + 0.4Qᶜ. The marginal cost per transaction is c = 10. The network sets prices pᶜ and pᵐ to maximize profit π = (pᶜ + pᵐ − 10) × min(Qᶜ, Qᵐ). Assume the market clears (Qᶜ = Qᵐ = Q). Find the optimal prices and transaction volume.
Step 1: Substitute Qᶜ = Qᵐ = Q into the demand equations. Q = 100 − 2pᶜ + 0.5Q ⇒ 0.5Q = 100 − 2pᶜ ⇒ Q = 200 − 4pᶜ. Q = 80 − pᵐ + 0.4Q ⇒ 0.6Q = 80 − pᵐ ⇒ Q = (80 − pᵐ)/0.6 = 133.33 − 1.667pᵐ. Step 2: Equate the two expressions for Q: 200 − 4pᶜ = 133.33 − 1.667pᵐ ⇒ 4pᶜ = 66.67 + 1.667pᵐ ⇒ pᶜ = 16.67 + 0.417pᵐ. Step 3: Express profit in terms of pᵐ. Q = 133.33 − 1.667pᵐ. pᶜ = 16.67 + 0.417pᵐ. π = (pᶜ + pᵐ − 10)Q = (6.67 + 1.417pᵐ)(133.33 − 1.667pᵐ). Step 4: Maximize π w.r.t. pᵐ. dπ/dpᵐ = 1.417(133.33 − 1.667pᵐ) − 1.667(6.67 + 1.417pᵐ) = 0. 188.93 − 2.362pᵐ − 11.12 − 2.362pᵐ = 0 ⇒ 177.81 = 4.724pᵐ ⇒ pᵐ* ≈ 37.64. Step 5: Compute pᶜ* = 16.67 + 0.417(37.64) ≈ 32.36. Q* = 133.33 − 1.667(37.64) ≈ 70.58. Profit π* = (32.36 + 37.64 − 10) × 70.58 ≈ 60 × 70.58 ≈ 4235. The network subsidizes consumers (lower price) because their demand is more elastic (coefficient 2 vs 1) and they generate stronger cross-side effects (0.5 vs 0.4).
Exam Strategy: Two-Sided Market Questions
When a question gives cross-side network effects, first write the system of equations for quantities on both sides. Impose market clearing (Qᴮ = Qˢ = Q) unless the question explicitly allows rationing. Solve for Q as a function of each price, then substitute into the profit function. The first-order conditions will yield a linear system in the prices. Remember: the side with higher demand elasticity and stronger cross-side effect gets the lower price (possibly a subsidy). Check whether the platform is a monopoly or faces competition — competitive platforms drive prices to marginal cost on both sides, eliminating the divide-and-conquer distortion.

Moral Hazard in Teams: The Holmström Model and Budget Breaking

When multiple agents contribute to a joint output but individual efforts are unobservable, the principal faces a team moral hazard problem. Holmström (1982) showed that if the principal can observe only the total output x = Σ eᵢ + ε (where ε is noise), and agents are risk-averse with utility u(w) − c(e), the first-best effort profile cannot be implemented by any budget-balanced sharing rule. The reason: any sharing rule sᵢ(x) that satisfies Σ sᵢ(x) = x for all x creates a free-rider problem — each agent's marginal benefit from effort is ∂sᵢ/∂x < 1, while the social marginal benefit is 1. Holmström's solution: introduce a "budget breaker" — a third party (or the principal) who absorbs the residual Σ sᵢ(x) − x. The optimal contract makes each agent's share depend on a sufficient statistic for their effort. If output is x = Σ eᵢ + ε with ε ∼ N(0, σ²), and agents have CARA utility with risk aversion r, the optimal linear sharing rule is sᵢ(x) = αᵢ + βᵢ x, where βᵢ = (1/rσ²) / (1/rσ² + c''(eᵢ)). The budget breaker receives the residual R(x) = x − Σ sᵢ(x). The principal's problem is to choose βᵢ to maximize Σ eᵢ − Σ (αᵢ + ½ r βᵢ² σ²) subject to the incentive compatibility eᵢ = argmax βᵢ e − c(e). The first-order condition gives c'(eᵢ) = βᵢ. The optimal βᵢ balances incentive provision against risk sharing: βᵢ = 1 / (1 + r σ² c''(eᵢ)). If the principal cannot commit to a budget breaker (e.g., in a partnership), the second-best involves selling the firm to the agents (making them residual claimants) or using a tournament. Examiners test the derivation of the optimal βᵢ, the role of the budget breaker in restoring efficiency, and the comparison between team production and independent moral hazard problems. A typical question provides a team of n agents with quadratic costs c(e) = ½ e², CARA utility with r = 2, σ² = 4, and asks to compute the optimal sharing rule and the efficiency loss relative to first-best.

Mechanism Design with Costly Verification and Partial Evidence

Standard mechanism design assumes the principal cannot verify the agent's type. In many settings (tax audits, insurance claims, procurement), the principal can acquire costly evidence about the agent's report. Townsend (1979) and Border and Sobel (1987) introduced the costly state verification model: the agent reports a type θ, the principal chooses a verification probability p(θ) at cost c(p), and if verification reveals a lie, the agent pays a penalty M. The optimal mechanism uses a "random audit" schedule: verify with probability p(θ) when the reported type is in a certain range. The agent's incentive constraint is u(θ) ≥ u(θ') + p(θ')[u(θ) − u(θ') − M] for all θ' ≠ θ. The optimal p(θ) is monotone decreasing in the reported type (audit low reports more often). Ben-Porath, Dekel, and Lipman (2014) extended this to "partial evidence": the agent can present hard evidence (e.g., receipts) that partially reveals their type. The mechanism designer can use the evidence structure to reduce verification costs. The key concept is "evidence monotonicity": if type θ can produce evidence E, and θ' > θ can also produce E, then the mechanism should not give θ' a strictly better allocation than θ when both present E. The optimal mechanism with evidence is a "direct revelation mechanism with evidence" where the agent reports (θ, E) and the mechanism specifies allocation x(θ, E) and payment t(θ, E). The revelation principle holds if the evidence structure satisfies "normality" (the set of evidence available to θ is nested). Examiners test the derivation of the optimal audit probability p(θ) = (u(θ) − u(θ'))/M in the two-type case, the role of evidence monotonicity in implementing efficient allocations, and the comparison between costly verification and standard screening. A typical question gives a two-type model (θₕ = 10, θₗ = 5) with prior 0.5, verification cost c = 1, penalty M = 20, and asks to compute the optimal audit probability for the low type and the resulting expected social surplus.

Algorithmic Game Theory: The Smoothness Framework and Price of Anarchy Bounds

The Price of Anarchy (PoA) measures the efficiency loss due to selfish behavior in games. Roughgarden (2009, 2015) developed the smoothness framework to bound PoA for broad classes of games without computing equilibria explicitly. A game is (λ, μ)-smooth if for any two strategy profiles s and s*, Σᵢ uᵢ(sᵢ*, s₋ᵢ) ≥ λ Σᵢ uᵢ(s*) − μ Σᵢ uᵢ(s). If a game is (λ, μ)-smooth with λ > 0 and μ < 1, then the PoA for coarse correlated equilibria (and hence for mixed, correlated, and pure Nash equilibria) is at most μ/(1−λ) for maximization games, or (1+μ)/λ for minimization games. The framework applies to congestion games, auctions, and scheduling. For atomic congestion games with affine latency functions ℓₑ(x) = aₑ x + bₑ, the game is (1, 3/4)-smooth, giving PoA ≤ 5/2 for pure Nash equilibria. For first-price auctions with submodular valuations, the game is (1−1/e, 1)-smooth, giving PoA ≤ e/(e−1) ≈ 1.58. The smoothness proof for congestion games uses the inequality x(a x + b) ≤ x*(a x* + b) + (3/4) x*(a x + b) for all x, x* ≥ 0. For auctions, the key inequality is vᵢ(Sᵢ*) ≤ vᵢ(Sᵢ) + vᵢ(Sᵢ* Sᵢ) for submodular vᵢ. Examiners test the verification of (λ, μ)-smoothness for a given game, the derivation of PoA bounds from smoothness parameters, and the extension to coarse correlated equilibria. A typical question provides a congestion game with latency functions ℓₑ(x) = x² and asks to find the smallest μ such that the game is (1, μ)-smooth, then compute the PoA bound.

  • Confusing the budget breaker in Holmström's team model with the principal — the budget breaker is a distinct entity that absorbs residual risk; if the principal acts as budget breaker, the model reduces to standard moral hazard with a single agent.
  • Assuming that two-sided platform pricing always subsidizes the "demand side" — the side that gets subsidized is the one with higher elasticity and stronger cross-side network effects, which may be the supply side (e.g., drivers in ride-sharing).
  • Forgetting that the smoothness bound for coarse correlated equilibria applies to all equilibrium concepts (pure, mixed, correlated) — a common trap is to compute PoA only for pure Nash and claim it is the worst case.
  • In costly verification models, assuming the penalty M can be arbitrarily large — limited liability or legal constraints often cap M, which changes the optimal audit schedule from deterministic to randomized.
  • Believing that evidence monotonicity is always satisfied — many real-world evidence structures (e.g., a high-type agent can fake low-type evidence but not vice versa) violate normality, requiring more complex mechanisms.
  • Overlooking that the Myerson-Satterthwaite impossibility assumes independent private values and no budget constraints — with budget constraints, efficient trade may be possible even with bilateral monopoly.
  • Confusing the Price of Anarchy (worst-case equilibrium) with the Price of Stability (best-case equilibrium) — examiners often ask for both and the smoothness framework gives bounds only for PoA, not PoS.

Combinatorial Auctions and the VCG Mechanism with Complementarities

Standard auction theory assumes goods are substitutes or independent. In spectrum auctions, airport slot allocation, and procurement, bidders value bundles of items — a license for region A is worth more when combined with region B. A combinatorial auction allows bids on arbitrary subsets of items. The allocation problem is a winner determination problem (WDP): maximize ΣS⊆M bi(S) xi,S subject to Σi,S: j∈S xi,S ≤ 1 for all items j, xi,S ∈ {0,1}. This is NP-hard (reducible to weighted set packing). The VCG mechanism extends to combinatorial settings: allocate to maximize reported welfare, charge each bidder the externality they impose. VCG is dominant-strategy incentive compatible (DSIC) and efficient if the WDP is solved exactly. In practice, exact WDP is intractable for large instances; approximations break DSIC. The core-selecting auctions (Day & Milgrom 2008) choose core outcomes (no blocking coalition) and charge minimum core payments. They are not DSIC but have good incentive properties in large markets. The combinatorial clock auction (CCA) used in UK 4G/5G spectrum auctions combines a clock phase (ascending prices on individual items) with a supplementary round for package bids. Activity rules enforce consistent bidding. Examiners test the WDP formulation, the VCG payment formula pi = maxx∈X Σj≠i vj(x) − Σj≠i vj(x*), the core constraints Σi∈C pi ≥ V(C) for all coalitions C, and the trade-off between computational tractability and incentive compatibility.

Career Concerns and Implicit Incentives in Contract Theory

Holmström (1999) introduced career concerns: an agent exerts effort not only for explicit wages but to signal ability to the labor market. The model: agent ability η ∼ N(0, ση2), effort e ∈ ℝ+, output y = η + e + ε, ε ∼ N(0, σε2). The market observes y and forms posterior E[η | y]. The agent's payoff is w(y) + δ E[η | y] − c(e), where δ is the weight on future wages. In the unique linear equilibrium, effort e* = δ / c''(e*) (assuming quadratic cost). The market's inference creates an implicit incentive that substitutes for explicit incentives. Key results: (1) Effort is decreasing in career length — young agents work harder. (2) Explicit incentives (w(y) = α + βy) crowd out implicit incentives if β > 0; the optimal contract may set β = 0 early in career. (3) Multiple tasks: if only some outputs are observable, career concerns distort effort toward observable tasks (multitask distortion). (4) Team production: career concerns can mitigate free-riding if individual contributions are partially observable. The Gibbons & Murphy (1992) extension adds explicit contracts: optimal β balances risk-sharing against the crowding-out of career concerns. Examiners test the derivation of e* = δ / c''(e*), the comparative statics of ση and σε on effort, the crowding-out condition β = 0 when δ is large, and the application to CEO compensation, academic tenure tracks, and public sector motivation.

Worked Problem: Career Concerns with Two Periods
An agent lives for two periods. Ability η ∼ N(0, 1). Period-1 effort e₁, output y₁ = η + e₁ + ε₁, ε₁ ∼ N(0, 1). Period-2 effort e₂, output y₂ = η + e₂ + ε₂, ε₂ ∼ N(0, 1). Cost c(e) = e²/2. The market observes y₁ and pays w₂ = E[η | y₁] in period 2. The agent maximizes E[w₂ − c(e₁) − c(e₂)]. Find the equilibrium effort e₁*.
The market's posterior: E[η | y₁] = Cov(η, y₁)/Var(y₁) · y₁ = 1/(1+1) · y₁ = y₁/2. The agent chooses e₁ to maximize E[y₁/2] − e₁²/2 = (η + e₁)/2 − e₁²/2. Taking expectation over η (E[η]=0): maxe₁ e₁/2 − e₁²/2. FOC: 1/2 − e₁ = 0 ⇒ e₁* = 1/2. In period 2, no career concerns remain, so e₂* = 0. The implicit incentive from period-2 wages generates effort 1/2 in period 1.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a career concerns question appears, first identify the information structure: what does the market observe, and when? Write the posterior expectation E[η | observed signals] using normal updating formulas. The agent's objective always includes the discounted future wage based on this posterior. Differentiate to get the effort FOC. Remember: career concerns vanish in the final period (no future market), creating a natural experiment for testing the theory. If explicit incentives β are present, the total marginal incentive is β + δ · ∂E[η|y]/∂e; set β = 0 if the implicit incentive is strong enough to achieve first-best effort.

Mechanism Design with Externalities: The Jehiel–Moldovanu Framework

Standard mechanism design assumes private values: agent i's payoff depends only on their own allocation and type. With externalities, payoffs depend on others' allocations: ui(x, θ) where x = (x1, ..., xn). Examples: mergers (rival's acquisition affects my profit), spectrum licenses (competitor's bandwidth affects my coverage), pollution permits. Jehiel & Moldovanu (2001) show that with externalities, the revelation principle fails for dominant-strategy implementation: a direct mechanism where agents report types may not exist even if an indirect mechanism implements the social choice function. The reason: in an indirect mechanism, an agent's strategy can depend on others' messages, creating "information linkage" that cannot be replicated in a direct mechanism where the agent reports only their own type. For Bayesian implementation, the revelation principle holds if externalities are "separable": ui(x, θ) = vi(xi, θi) + Σj≠i wij(xj, θi). The optimal auction with externalities maximizes virtual welfare Σi [vi(xi, θi) − (1−Fi(θi))/fi(θi) · ∂vi/∂θi] + Σi Σj≠i wij(xj, θi). The externality term wij enters without information rent adjustment because it does not depend on agent i's private information. Jehiel, Moldovanu, & Stacchetti (1996) analyze multilateral bargaining with externalities: the core may be empty, and efficient outcomes may not be implementable. Examiners test the failure of the revelation principle (construct a 3-agent example where indirect mechanism works but direct does not), the separable externalities condition, the modified virtual welfare formula, and the application to merger regulation (should the authority allow a merger that creates negative externalities on rivals?).

Dynamic Contracting with Persistent Private Information

In long-term principal-agent relationships, the agent's type (e.g., productivity) evolves persistently. The Pavan, Segal, & Toikka (2014) framework: agent type θt follows a Markov process θt+1 = ρ θt + εt+1, ρ ∈ [0,1]. The principal offers a long-term contract specifying allocations xt(θt) and payments pt(θt) as functions of the history of reports θt = (θ1, ..., θt). The agent's payoff is Σ βt-1 [θt xt − pt − c(xt)]. The key friction: dynamic incentive compatibility requires that truth-telling at each history is optimal given future truth-telling. The envelope condition gives the information rent: Ut(θt) = Ut(θtmin) + Σs=1t βs-1 xs(θs) ∂θs/∂θt. With persistence (ρ > 0), today's report affects the distribution of future types, creating intertemporal linkage. The optimal contract exhibits distortion at the top: even the highest type gets distorted allocation to reduce information rents. The distortion is larger when ρ is high (types are more persistent) because a high report today signals high future types. The stochastic Euler equation for the principal's problem: the marginal cost of increasing xt equals the marginal benefit plus the shadow cost of tightening future incentive constraints. Examiners test the derivation of the dynamic envelope formula, the role of ρ in determining the severity of distortions, the comparison with the static Myerson solution (ρ=0), and the implementation via "bank accounts" or "promised utility" state variables.

Game Theory in Cryptoeconomics: MEV and Incentive Compatibility in Blockchain Protocols

Blockchain consensus protocols are mechanism design problems where validators (miners/stakers) have incentives to deviate from honest behavior. Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) refers to the profit a block proposer can extract by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions within a block. In Ethereum, MEV arises from DEX arbitrage, liquidations, and sandwich attacks. The proposer-builder separation (PBS) mitigates MEV by separating block building (specialized builders bid for the right to propose a block) from block proposing (validators). This is a first-price auction for block space: builders submit bids, the proposer selects the highest bid. The auction is not incentive compatible; builders shade bids. MEV-Boost implements PBS via a trusted relay. Incentive compatibility of consensus: Nakamoto consensus is not strictly incentive compatible — selfish mining (Eyal & Sirer 2014) shows a coalition with >33% hash power can gain by withholding blocks. Proof-of-Stake (PoS) protocols like Gasper (Ethereum 2.0) use slashing conditions to penalize equivocation (signing two blocks at the same height) and surround votes. The weak subjectivity assumption (Buterin & Griffith 2017) requires new nodes to trust a recent checkpoint. Staking derivatives and liquid staking introduce principal-agent problems: the staker (principal) delegates to a validator (agent) who may misbehave; slashing risk is shared. Examiners test the selfish mining revenue calculation: Rselfish = (α(1−α)²(4α+γ(1−2α)) − α³) / (1−α(1+α(2−α))) where α is attacker hash power, γ is fraction of honest miners building on attacker's block. They also test the slashing condition design: a validator is slashed if they sign two distinct blocks at the same slot (equivocation) or sign a vote that surrounds another vote (surround vote). The price of anarchy in transaction fee mechanisms (EIP-1559) analyzes the base fee adjustment rule: basefeet+1 = basefeet × (1 + (gast − target)/target/8). This is a feedback control system; stability requires the adjustment parameter (1/8) to be small enough.

  • Confusing the VCG payment formula in combinatorial auctions with the single-item case — the externality is computed over bundles, not individual items, and the WDP must be solved for the counterfactual allocation without bidder i.
  • Assuming career concerns always increase effort — if the market observes a noisy signal of effort, high noise (large σε) weakens the inference and reduces effort; also, explicit incentives can crowd out implicit ones.
  • Believing the revelation principle holds universally with externalities — it fails for dominant-strategy implementation; the Jehiel-Moldovanu counterexample with 3 agents and negative externalities is a standard exam trap.
  • Overlooking the role of persistence ρ in dynamic contracting — when ρ = 0, the problem reduces to a sequence of static problems; when ρ > 0, the dynamic envelope formula has cross-period terms ∂θs/∂θt = ρs-t that create intertemporal distortions.
  • Treating MEV as a simple front-running problem — MEV includes arbitrage, liquidations, sandwich attacks, and time-bandit attacks (reorgs); the proposer's payoff is not just transaction fees but the full MEV extracted.
  • Assuming EIP-1559's base fee mechanism is incentive compatible — it is not; users still bid tips, and the base fee adjustment rule can be gamed by miners/stakers who control gas usage in their blocks.
  • Confusing the core-selecting auction payment rule with VCG — core payments are the minimum payments in the core, which are generally higher than VCG payments; the bidder-optimal core outcome coincides with VCG only when the VCG outcome is in the core.

Mechanism Design with Risk‑Averse Participants and Non‑Quasilinear Utilities

Standard mechanism design assumes quasilinear preferences: each agent’s utility equals valuation minus payment. When agents are risk‑averse, utility becomes a concave function u(v − p) with u″ < 0. The revelation principle still holds, but the envelope theorem must incorporate the curvature of u. The incentive‑compatibility (IC) condition for a direct mechanism M = (x, p) reads u(v − p(v)) + u′(v − p(v))·x(v) ≥ u(v − p(v′)) + u′(v − p(v′))·x(v′) for all v, v′. Differentiating the binding IC at v′ = v yields the modified envelope formula U′(v) = u′(v − p(v))·x(v). The principal’s expected revenue becomes ∫[v − U(v) − c(x(v))] dF(v) where c is the cost of allocation. Because u′ < 1, the marginal information rent is reduced relative to the risk‑neutral case, allowing the principal to extract more surplus. However, the allocation rule is distorted downward: the virtual valuation becomes φ(v) = v − (1 − F(v))/f(v)·u′(v − p(v))/u′(v − p(v)). When u is CARA (u(w) = −e−ρw/ρ), the optimal mechanism can be implemented by a menu of lotteries that trade off risk exposure against expected payment. Examiners often ask for the derivation of the modified virtual valuation and for a comparison of the optimal deterministic allocation versus a lottery‑based allocation when ρ > 0.

Dynamic Mechanism Design under Limited Commitment and Renegotiation

In many long‑run relationships the principal cannot commit to a full‑horizon contract; after each period the parties may renegotiate. The model consists of a sequence of periods t = 1,…,T with private type θt drawn from a Markov process. The principal offers a mechanism Mt at the start of each period, but after observing the agent’s report the principal may propose a new continuation contract. The equilibrium concept is **Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium with Renegotiation‑Proofness**: no continuation contract can be Pareto‑improved upon by both parties after any history. The key technical tool is the **recursive formulation** using the agent’s promised utility W as a state variable. The principal’s Bellman equation is V(W) = maxx,p,W′ { θ·x − p + δ 𝔼[V(W′)] } subject to (i) **Promise‑keeping**: u(θ·x − p) + δ 𝔼[W′] = W, (ii) **IC**: u(θ·x − p) + δ 𝔼[W′] ≥ u(θ·x(θ′) − p(θ′)) + δ 𝔼[W′(θ′)], (iii) **Renegotiation‑proofness**: V(W′) ≥ V(W″) for any W″ that the agent could propose. The solution exhibits **front‑loading** of distortions: early periods are more distorted because the principal anticipates future renegotiation that will erode information rents. When the discount factor δ → 1, the optimal contract converges to the **full‑commitment** solution; when δ is low, the contract resembles a sequence of static mechanisms. Examiners test the construction of the recursive program, the role of the promised‑utility state, and the comparative statics of δ on the distortion profile.

Worked Example: Renegotiation‑Proof Dynamic Contract
A principal interacts with an agent for two periods (T = 2). The agent’s type θ ∈ {L, H} with probabilities 0.5 each, i.i.d. across periods. Utility is quasilinear: u(θ·x − p) = θ·x − p. The principal’s discount factor δ = 0.9. The principal cannot commit to a second‑period contract; after the first‑period report the principal may offer a new contract. Find the renegotiation‑proof equilibrium allocation and payments.
Step 1 – Second period (no further renegotiation). With full commitment in the last period, the optimal static mechanism is the Myerson auction. Virtual valuations: φ(L) = L − (1 − 0.5)/0.5 = L − 1, φ(H) = H − 0.5/0.5 = H − 1. Since φ(L) < 0, the low type receives x = 0, payment p = 0. The high type receives x = 1, payment p = H − 1. Expected second‑period surplus for the principal: 0.5·0 + 0.5·(H − 1) = 0.5(H − 1). Step 2 – First period with renegotiation. Let the first‑period allocation be x₁(θ) and payment p₁(θ). After the report, the principal can propose a new second‑period contract. Renegotiation‑proofness requires that the continuation value V(W) for the promised utility W after period 1 cannot be improved by a new contract. Because the second‑period problem is static, the continuation value is exactly the Myerson surplus computed above, independent of the first‑period report. Hence the principal’s first‑period problem reduces to a static mechanism with the agent’s outside option equal to the expected second‑period rent 0.5(H − 1). The IC constraints are θ·x₁(θ) − p₁(θ) ≥ θ·x₁(θ′) − p₁(θ′). The envelope gives U′(θ) = x₁(θ). With binary types, the optimal allocation is x₁(H) = 1, x₁(L) = 0. Payments: p₁(H) = H − U(H), p₁(L) = 0. The participation constraint for the low type: U(L) ≥ 0. The high type’s rent U(H) = U(L) + ∫LH x₁(θ)dθ = H − L. Thus p₁(H) = L. The principal’s total expected payoff: first period 0.5·L + second period 0.5(H − 1) = 0.5(L + H − 1). This is the renegotiation‑proof equilibrium.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a dynamic mechanism design question mentions limited commitment, immediately write down the recursive Bellman equation with promised utility as the state variable. Identify whether the horizon is finite or infinite; for finite horizons solve by backward induction, noting that the last period is a standard static mechanism. Renegotiation‑proofness simply means the continuation value must be on the Pareto frontier of the continuation game — often it coincides with the static optimum. Use this shortcut to avoid re‑deriving the full dynamic program in the exam.

Information Design with Multiple Senders and Competing Persuasion

The classic Bayesian persuasion model (Kamenica & Gentzkow 2011) features a single sender who commits to a signal structure. With **multiple senders**, each chooses a signal πi : Θ → Δ(Si) and the receiver observes the joint signal (s₁,…,sn) before acting. The equilibrium concept is **Bayes‑Nash equilibrium in signaling strategies**: each sender’s signal maximizes his expected payoff given the others’ signals and the receiver’s best response. A key result (Gentzkow & Kamenica 2017) shows that when senders have **aligned preferences** (identical state‑dependent utilities), the equilibrium outcome coincides with the single‑sender optimum — they can effectively pool their information. With **conflicting preferences**, the equilibrium is generally inefficient: each sender over‑provides information to sway the receiver, leading to **information overload** and a lower joint payoff. The **concavification** technique extends: the receiver’s posterior belief after observing all signals is a martingale; each sender’s problem is to choose a distribution of posteriors that maximizes his payoff subject to the martingale constraint induced by the others’ signals. In the **binary‑state, binary‑action** case, the equilibrium can be characterized by a system of **first‑order conditions** that equate the marginal benefit of shifting probability mass toward the sender’s preferred action to the marginal cost of reducing the receiver’s responsiveness. When senders move **sequentially**, the first mover gains a commitment advantage and can induce a more favorable posterior distribution; the second mover’s best response is a **best‑reply correspondence** that can be computed by a linear program. Examiners frequently ask for the construction of the equilibrium signal structures in a two‑sender, two‑state example, and for a comparison of the receiver’s welfare under simultaneous versus sequential moves.

Network Games with Incomplete Information and Bayesian Nash Equilibrium

Consider a finite network G = (N, E) where each node i chooses an action ai ∈ {0, 1}. Payoffs exhibit **strategic complements**: ui(ai, a−i; θi) = θi·ai + β·ai·∑j∈N(i) aj − c·ai, with β > 0, c > 0. Each player’s type θi is drawn independently from a distribution F on [θ̲, θ̅]. Players observe their own type but not others’. A **Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)** is a mapping σi : [θ̲, θ̅] → {0, 1} such that for each i and θi, σi(θi) maximizes expected payoff given the distribution of neighbors’ actions induced by σ−i. Because actions are binary, the best response is a threshold rule: there exists a cutoff θi* such that σi(θi) = 1 iff θi ≥ θi*. The cutoff satisfies θi* = c − β·∑j∈N(i) Pr(θj ≥ θj*). This system of equations can be solved by **fixed‑point iteration** on the vector of cutoffs. When the network is **regular** (all degrees equal d) and types are i.i.d., symmetry implies a common cutoff θ* satisfying θ* = c − β·d·(1 − F(θ*)). The function on the right is decreasing in θ*; a unique BNE exists if β·d·f(θ) < 1 for all θ (the **contraction condition**). If the condition fails, multiple BNEs may arise, corresponding to **high‑participation** and **low‑participation** equilibria. The **price of anarchy** in this setting compares the total expected welfare under the worst BNE to the socially optimal action profile (which internalizes the network externalities). Examiners test the derivation of the threshold equation, the contraction condition for uniqueness, and the welfare comparison between the highest and lowest equilibria.

Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Approximate Envy‑Freeness and the MNW Allocation

When goods are indivisible, an exact envy‑free allocation may not exist. The **Maximum Nash Welfare (MNW)** allocation maximizes the product of agents’ utilities ∏i ui(Ai) over all partitions (A₁,…,An) of the item set. For additive utilities, MNW satisfies **EF1** (envy‑free up to one good): for any i, j there exists an item g ∈ Aj such that ui(Ai) ≥ ui(Aj \ {g}). The proof uses the **Fisher market** interpretation: MNW corresponds to the competitive equilibrium from equal incomes (CEEI) in a market where each agent has unit budget and prices are the Lagrange multipliers of the MNW program. The **EF1** guarantee is tight; there are instances where no allocation satisfies EF (exact envy‑freeness). A stronger notion, **EFX** (envy‑free up to any good), is not always attainable; existence is open for general additive valuations but holds for **binary** or **identical ordering** valuations. The **approximate envy‑freeness** parameter ε‑EF requires ui(Ai) ≥ (1 − ε)·ui(Aj) for all i, j. For additive utilities, MNW achieves ε = 1 / (n + 1) in the worst case. Computing MNW is **NP‑hard** (reduction from partition), but a **polynomial‑time approximation scheme (PTAS)** exists via the **ellipsoid method** on the convex program log ∑ ui(Ai). In practice, the **round‑robin** algorithm with **envy‑cycle elimination** yields an EF1 allocation in O(n·m) time. Examiners often ask to prove EF1 for MNW, to construct a counterexample where EFX fails, and to describe the PTAS outline.

  • Confusing the modified virtual valuation under risk aversion with the standard Myerson formula — the curvature of u enters both the numerator and denominator of the information‑rent term.
  • Assuming full commitment in a dynamic mechanism when the problem explicitly states limited commitment — the recursive promised‑utility formulation is essential.
  • Treating multiple senders in information design as a simple concatenation of single‑sender problems — strategic interaction changes the concavification constraints.
  • Neglecting the contraction condition β·d·f(θ) < 1 when analyzing uniqueness of Bayesian Nash equilibrium in network games — multiple equilibria arise precisely when this fails.
  • Believing MNW always yields an exact envy‑free allocation for indivisible goods — it guarantees only EF1, and EFX may be impossible.
  • Overlooking the NP‑hardness of exact MNW computation and presenting a polynomial‑time algorithm without approximation guarantees.
  • Misapplying the envelope theorem in dynamic contracts with renegotiation — the promise‑keeping constraint replaces the standard envelope condition.
The advanced sections above equip you with the precise derivations, equilibrium concepts, and examiner‑focused traps needed for top‑level game‑theory questions.

Revenue Equivalence Theorem and Its Extensions

The Revenue Equivalence Theorem (RET) states that any two standard auction formats that allocate the object to the bidder with the highest value and give a bidder with the lowest possible value an expected payoff of zero yield the same expected revenue for the seller, provided four key assumptions hold: (1) bidders are risk‑neutral, (2) private values are drawn independently from a common distribution, (3) bidders are symmetric, and (4) the payment rule depends only on the reported values. Under these conditions the first‑price sealed‑bid auction, the second‑price sealed‑bid auction, the English auction, and the Dutch auction are revenue‑equivalent. The theorem was proved independently by Myerson (1981) and Riley & Samuelson (1981). The expected revenue equals the expected virtual valuation of the winner, where the virtual valuation for a value v drawn from distribution F with density f is φ(v)=v−(1−F(v))/f(v).

When any assumption fails, revenue equivalence breaks down and a revenue ranking emerges. With risk‑averse bidders, the first‑price auction generates higher expected revenue than the second‑price auction because bidders shade their bids less aggressively to reduce variance. With interdependent values, the linkage principle (Milgrom & Weber, 1982) shows that revealing more information (as in the English auction) increases revenue relative to sealed‑bid formats. Asymmetric bidders (different distributions) destroy symmetry; the optimal auction then uses ironed virtual valuations and may treat bidders differently (Myerson, 1981). Budget constraints introduce a kink in the virtual valuation function, and the revenue‑maximising mechanism may involve lotteries or partial allocation (Che & Gale, 1998). Correlated values allow the Cremer‑McLean (1985) full surplus extraction mechanism, which can exceed the revenue of any standard auction.

Examiners frequently test the direction of revenue ranking when a single assumption is relaxed. A typical trap is to claim that the English auction always raises more revenue than the first‑price auction, ignoring that this holds only under interdependent values or risk aversion, not under the baseline independent private‑values model. Another common error is to apply the standard virtual valuation formula φ(v)=v−(1−F(v))/f(v) when the distribution is not regular (i.e., φ is not monotone); the correct approach is to iron the virtual valuation as in Myerson’s optimal auction.

The Revelation Principle and Its Limitations

The Revelation Principle (Myerson, 1979; Gibbard, 1973) asserts that for any Bayesian game induced by a mechanism, there exists a direct revelation mechanism in which truthful reporting of types constitutes a Bayesian Nash equilibrium and yields the same allocation and payoff profiles. The principle relies on three pillars: (i) quasi‑linear utilities, (ii) the mechanism designer’s full commitment to the announced rule, and (iii) independent private values (or at least a known common prior). Under these conditions any indirect mechanism can be “simulated” by a direct one where each agent simply announces a type.

Limitations arise when any pillar is violated. With multi‑dimensional types, a single‑dimensional direct mechanism may not exist; Rochet (1985) showed that the revelation principle can fail because incentive constraints couple across dimensions. Limited commitment (e.g., the designer cannot credibly promise not to renegotiate after seeing reports) invalidates the static reduction; dynamic mechanisms require a recursive formulation of promised utilities (Pavan, Segal & Toikka, 2014). Non‑quasi‑linear preferences (risk aversion, budget constraints) break the transferable‑utility structure that underpins the standard proof. Externalities among agents (e.g., network effects) mean that an agent’s payoff depends on others’ reported types in ways that cannot be captured by a simple direct mechanism without expanding the message space. Finally, costly verification or partial evidence (Ben‑Porath, Dekel & Lipman, 2014) introduces a verification stage that cannot be collapsed into a pure direct revelation mechanism without loss of generality.

Examiner traps include applying the revelation principle to a setting with after‑market resale (where commitment fails), to a multi‑attribute procurement auction (multi‑dimensional types), or to a mechanism with costly state verification. In each case the correct answer is to identify which assumption is violated and to describe the appropriate extension (e.g., dynamic mechanism design, multi‑dimensional screening, or verification‑augmented mechanisms).

Revenue Equivalence Application
Two risk‑neutral bidders have values drawn independently from the uniform distribution on [0,1]. They participate in a first‑price sealed‑bid auction. Derive the symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium bidding function and compute the expected revenue. Compare this with the expected revenue of a second‑price sealed‑bid auction.
In a symmetric first‑price auction with two bidders, the equilibrium bidding function solves b(v)=v−∫₀ᵛ (F(t)/F(v)) dt. For uniform [0,1], F(v)=v, so b(v)=v−∫₀ᵛ (t/v) dt = v−v/2 = v/2. The expected payment of a bidder with value v is b(v)·Pr(win|v)= (v/2)·v = v²/2. Integrating over v∈[0,1] gives expected revenue = ∫₀¹ v²/2 dv = 1/6 per bidder, total 1/3. In a second‑price auction the expected payment of the winner is the expected second‑highest value, which for two uniform draws is also 1/3. Hence the two auctions are revenue‑equivalent, confirming the theorem under the baseline assumptions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to compare auction formats, first list the four RET assumptions. If the problem statement violates any of them (risk aversion, correlation, asymmetry, budget limits), immediately state which extension applies and the direction of the revenue ranking. Do not simply assert “revenue equivalence holds” without checking the assumptions.

Dynamic Games with Private Monitoring and the Folk Theorem

In repeated games with private monitoring each player observes a private signal that is correlated with the action profile chosen by all players. Unlike public monitoring, there is no common history; players must form beliefs about others’ beliefs. The private‑monitoring folk theorem (Fudenberg, Levine & Maskin, 1994) states that for any feasible, strictly individually rational payoff vector there exists a sequential equilibrium that approximates it arbitrarily closely, provided the discount factor δ is sufficiently close to 1 and the monitoring structure satisfies a “pairwise identifiability” or “full support” condition. The construction uses belief‑free review strategies: play is divided into blocks; after each block players review the private signals and, if the empirical distribution deviates from the target, they switch to a punishment phase that is itself a belief‑free equilibrium of the stage game.

Key technical requirements: (1) the signal distribution must have full support so that every action profile can generate every signal with positive probability; (2) the monitoring must be “almost public” in the sense that the correlation of signals across players is high enough to allow statistical tests; (3) the equilibrium is only approximate — exact efficiency is generally unattainable because of the inherent noise. The result contrasts sharply with the public‑monitoring folk theorem, where exact payoffs can be sustained for any δ above a threshold. Examiners often test the distinction by asking whether the standard folk theorem applies when monitoring is private; the correct answer is “only an approximate folk theorem holds, and it requires stronger conditions on the signal structure.”

A common mistake is to cite the public‑monitoring folk theorem (Abreu, Pearce & Stacchetti, 1990) in a private‑monitoring setting, ignoring the need for belief‑free strategies and the approximate nature of the result. Another trap is to assume that any discount factor δ<1 works; the theorem requires δ→1 as the approximation error ε→0.

Fair Division of Divisible Goods: Adjusted Winner and Cut‑and‑Choose

When goods are perfectly divisible (e.g., a cake, land, time), classic procedures guarantee envy‑free allocations for two parties. The Cut‑and‑Choose protocol: one party cuts the cake into two pieces they value equally; the other party chooses the piece they prefer. This yields an envy‑free and proportional allocation for two agents. The Adjusted Winner (AW) procedure (Brams & Taylor, 1996) handles multiple divisible items. Each party distributes 100 points across items reflecting their valuations. Items are initially awarded to the party with the higher point total for that item. If the total points differ, items (or fractions thereof) are transferred from the higher‑scoring party to the lower‑scoring party in increasing order of the ratio of the two parties’ valuations until point totals equalise. AW guarantees an allocation that is (i) envy‑free, (ii) Pareto efficient, and (iii) equitable (both parties receive the same total points).

For n>2 agents, moving‑knife procedures such as the Dubins‑Spanier “continuous” protocol or the discrete “last diminisher” algorithm achieve proportionality but not necessarily envy‑freeness. The existence of an envy‑free division for any number of agents with additive valuations was proved by Stromquist (1980) using a continuous moving‑knife method, but the procedure is not finite. Examiner traps include applying AW to three or more parties without modification (AW is defined only for two parties), confusing proportionality (each gets at least 1/n of their value) with envy‑freeness (no one prefers another’s bundle), and assuming that AW works when items are indivisible (it requires divisibility to transfer fractions).

Network Games with Strategic Substitutes and Complementarities

Consider a network G=(N,E) where each player i chooses a continuous action a_i≥0. Payoffs are u_i(a_i,a−i)=a_i−½a_i²+β a_i Σj∈N(i) a_j. The parameter β captures strategic interaction: β>0 implies strategic complements (best response increases with neighbours’ actions), β<0 implies strategic substitutes (best response decreases). For complements, the game is supermodular; by Topkis’s theorem a pure‑strategy Nash equilibrium exists and the set of equilibria forms a complete lattice. The equilibrium can be found by solving the linear system (I−βG)a=1, where G is the adjacency matrix. A unique equilibrium exists if the spectral radius ρ(βG)<1, which guarantees (I−βG) is invertible and the best‑response mapping is a contraction.

For substitutes (β<0), the game is a potential game (Monderer & Shapley, 1996) with potential function Φ(a)=Σ_i (a_i−½a_i²)+½β Σ(i,j)∈E a_i a_j. Any maximiser of Φ is a pure Nash equilibrium, but multiple equilibria can arise because the potential may have several local maxima. The best‑response dynamics converge to a pure equilibrium under asynchronous updates, but the limit depends on initial conditions. Examiner traps: assuming uniqueness for substitutes (the potential game structure only guarantees existence), ignoring the spectral radius condition for complements (if ρ(βG)≥1 the linear system has no solution and equilibria may not exist or may be unbounded), and confusing the direction of best‑response monotonicity when β changes sign.

  • Assuming revenue equivalence holds under risk aversion or correlated values.
  • Applying the revelation principle to mechanisms with limited commitment or multi‑dimensional types without checking conditions.
  • Confusing the public‑monitoring folk theorem with the private‑monitoring version; forgetting the need for approximate efficiency and belief‑free strategies.
  • Using Adjusted Winner for three or more parties without a generalization; overlooking the requirement of additive, divisible valuations.
  • Treating strategic substitutes as guaranteeing a unique pure Nash equilibrium; neglecting potential game structure and possible multiple equilibria.
  • Overlooking the spectral radius condition for equilibrium existence in network games with complements.
  • Remember: these traps are the most frequent sources of lost marks.

Algorithmic Game Theory: Complexity of Computing Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games

Anonymous games are a subclass of normal‑form games in which each player’s payoff depends only on her own action and the empirical distribution of actions taken by the other players. Formally, for a game with n players and action set A, the payoff to player i when she plays ai and the remaining players’ action profile induces a histogram h ∈ ℕ|A| is ui(ai, h). This symmetry reduces the description size from exponential in n to polynomial, making anonymous games a natural model for large populations such as congestion games, voting, and mean‑field limits.

The computational complexity of finding a Nash equilibrium in anonymous games contrasts sharply with that of general games. For general games, computing an exact Nash equilibrium is PPAD‑complete even for two‑player games (Daskalakis, Goldberg, Papadimitriou 2009). In anonymous games the problem remains PPAD‑complete when the number of actions is part of the input (Daskalakis, Papadimitriou 2009). However, if the number of actions k is treated as a constant, the landscape changes: there exists a polynomial‑time approximation scheme (PTAS) for ε‑Nash equilibria (Daskalakis, Papadimitriou 2015). The algorithm discretises the space of mixed‑strategy profiles and uses dynamic programming over the histogram of actions, achieving running time polynomial in n and 1/ε but exponential in k. For the special case of two actions (k=2), an exact equilibrium can be found in polynomial time via a reduction to a one‑dimensional fixed‑point problem (Papadimitriou, Roughgarden 2008).

These results have direct implications for algorithmic mechanism design. When a mechanism’s outcome rule induces an anonymous game among participants (e.g., a uniform price auction with many bidders), the PTAS guarantees that an approximately incentive‑compatible outcome can be computed efficiently for any fixed number of bid types. Examiners often test the boundary: “Is computing an exact Nash equilibrium in anonymous games with three actions PPAD‑complete?” The answer is yes, because the PPAD‑hardness reduction uses three actions. A common mistake is to assume that the PTAS extends to exact computation; the PTAS only yields ε‑equilibria, and the exponent in k prevents a fully polynomial‑time exact algorithm unless PPAD ⊆ P.

Mechanism Design for Kidney Exchange: Priority Mechanisms and Strategy‑Proofness

Kidney exchange programs match incompatible patient‑donor pairs through cycles and altruistic‑donor‑initiated chains. The market can be modelled as a directed compatibility graph where vertices are patient‑donor pairs (and altruistic donors) and edges indicate medical compatibility. A mechanism selects a collection of vertex‑disjoint cycles and chains to maximise a social objective, typically the number of transplants.

The priority mechanism (Roth, Sönmez, Ünver 2004) assigns a strict priority ordering to all patients (e.g., by waiting time or medical urgency). It then processes patients in that order, giving each the best available compatible kidney from the remaining pool, possibly forming cycles of bounded length k. This mechanism is Pareto efficient with respect to the reported preferences and respects the priority order, but it is not strategy‑proof. A patient can misreport her acceptable kidneys to manipulate the set of cycles formed later in the process, thereby obtaining a more preferred kidney. The manipulation exploits the fact that the mechanism’s greedy construction does not satisfy the “no‑envy” condition required for strategy‑proofness in matching with cycles.

In contrast, the top‑trading‑cycles (TTC) mechanism adapted to kidney exchange (Ashlagi, Roth 2014) achieves strategy‑proofness when each patient’s preferences are over kidneys and a fixed priority order is used to break ties. The algorithm repeatedly lets the highest‑priority patient point to her most preferred available kidney; the owner of that kidney points to her most preferred available kidney, and so on, until a cycle forms. The cycle is executed and removed. Because each step is a standard TTC round on a reduced graph, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy for every patient. The mechanism remains Pareto efficient and respects the priority order. However, TTC requires that cycles be of unrestricted length; imposing a maximum cycle length k destroys strategy‑proofness.

Altruistic donors introduce chains that are not cycles. The chain‑based priority mechanism processes altruistic donors first, then applies the priority mechanism to the remaining pairs. This hybrid is also not strategy‑proof. Recent work (Anderson et al. 2015) shows that a “priority‑augmented TTC” that treats altruistic donors as a special top‑priority vertex restores strategy‑proofness while allowing long chains. Examiners frequently ask: “Which kidney‑exchange mechanism is both strategy‑proof and Pareto efficient for any cycle length?” The correct answer is the unrestricted TTC mechanism with a fixed priority order; any bound on cycle length or any greedy priority rule fails strategy‑proofness.

Worked Example: Strategy‑Proofness in Kidney Exchange
Consider a kidney‑exchange pool with three patient‑donor pairs (P1, P2, P3) and one altruistic donor A. Compatibility edges: A→P1, P1→P2, P2→P3, P3→P1. Priorities: A > P1 > P2 > P3. Under the priority mechanism with maximum cycle length 2, P1 reports truthfully that she accepts kidneys from P3 only. Show how P1 can benefit by misreporting that she also accepts a kidney from P2.
Step 1: Truthful reports. A donates to P1 (chain). Remaining pairs: P1 (now satisfied), P2, P3. Priority order processes P2 then P3. P2’s only compatible donor is P1 (already used), so P2 gets nothing. P3’s compatible donor is P2 (unused), but cycle length limit 2 prevents a 2‑cycle P3→P2→P3 because P2 has no donor left. Outcome: only P1 receives a transplant. Step 2: P1 misreports, adding P2 as acceptable. A still donates to P1. Now P2 is processed; P2’s compatible donor is P1 (used), so P2 gets nothing. P3 is processed; P3’s compatible donor is P2 (unused). Since P1 now “accepts” P2, a 2‑cycle P3→P2→P3 is not formed because P2 has no donor. However, the mechanism may allow a 2‑cycle P1→P2→P1 if P1’s donor (A) is considered available? Actually A already used. The key is that by misreporting, P1 can induce the mechanism to form a 2‑cycle P1P2 when A’s kidney is allocated to P2 instead of P1, giving P1 a kidney from P2 which she prefers. The exact allocation depends on tie‑breaking, but the existence of a profitable misreport demonstrates the mechanism is not strategy‑proof.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to compare kidney‑exchange mechanisms, first identify whether the mechanism imposes a cycle‑length bound. Any bound ⇒ not strategy‑proof. If the mechanism is described as “top‑trading‑cycles with a fixed priority order and no cycle‑length limit”, it is strategy‑proof and Pareto efficient. Memorise the pair (TTC, unrestricted cycles) as the unique strategy‑proof efficient mechanism in this setting.

Evolutionary Game Theory: Stochastic Stability and the Role of Mutation

Classical evolutionary game theory studies the replicator dynamics in infinite populations, where only the fittest strategies survive. In finite populations, however, random mutations (or experimentation) prevent the system from getting trapped in strict Nash equilibria that are not globally optimal. The framework of stochastic stability (Kandori, Mailath, Rob 1993; Young 1993) analyses the long‑run behaviour of a Markov chain on the state space of population profiles when mutations occur with small probability ε > 0.

Consider a symmetric 2×2 coordination game with two strict Nash equilibria, A and B. Let the payoff matrix be such that (A,A) yields payoff 4, (B,B) yields 3, and miscoordination yields 0. Under the replicator dynamics without mutation, both equilibria are asymptotically stable. With mutation, the process becomes an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on the finite set of population states. Its unique stationary distribution με converges, as ε → 0, to a distribution supported on the stochastically stable states. The resistance of a transition from state x to y is the minimum number of simultaneous mutations required; the stochastic potential of a state is the minimum total resistance of a spanning tree rooted at that state. The states with minimum stochastic potential are stochastically stable.

For the coordination game above, the risk‑dominant equilibrium (the one with the larger basin of attraction under best‑response dynamics) is B, because a player expects the opponent to play B with probability > ½ when uncertain. The stochastic stability calculation shows that B has lower stochastic potential than A, so the long‑run distribution places all weight on B as ε → 0. This result generalises: in any 2×2 coordination game, the risk‑dominant equilibrium is uniquely stochastically stable. In potential games, the set of stochastically stable states coincides with the set of maximisers of the potential function (Young 1998). Thus stochastic stability provides a refinement that selects among multiple Nash equilibria based on the “ease” of escaping their basins via mutations.

Examiners often test the distinction between risk dominance and payoff dominance. A common trap: “In a coordination game where (A,A) yields higher payoffs than (B,B), which equilibrium is stochastically stable?” The answer is the risk‑dominant one, not the payoff‑dominant one, unless the two coincide. Another trap is to assume that stochastic stability always selects a unique equilibrium; in games with multiple potential maximisers, several states can be stochastically stable simultaneously.

Game Theory in Machine Learning: Adversarial Robustness and Minimax Optimization

Adversarial robustness of a classifier can be cast as a two‑player zero‑sum game between a learner (choosing model parameters θ ∈ Θ) and an adversary (choosing a perturbation δ ∈ Δ(x) for each input x). The learner’s loss on a data distribution D is L(θ, δ) = 𝔼(x,y)∼D[ℓ(fθ(x+δ(x)), y)], where ℓ is a classification loss and Δ(x) is a norm‑bounded perturbation set (e.g., ℓ∞ ball of radius ε). The learner wishes to minimise the worst‑case loss, leading to the minimax problem minθ∈Θ maxδ∈Δ L(θ, δ).

When Θ is convex and L(θ, δ) is convex in θ and concave in δ, von Neumann’s minimax theorem guarantees the existence of a saddle point (θ*, δ*) such that maxδ L(θ*, δ) = minθ maxδ L(θ, δ) = maxδ minθ L(θ, δ). In deep learning, however, the loss is highly non‑convex in θ, so a global saddle point need not exist. Practical adversarial training (Goodfellow et al. 2015; Madry et al. 2018) approximates the inner maximisation by projected gradient descent (PGD) on δ and then performs a gradient step on θ. This procedure can be viewed as seeking a local Nash equilibrium of the non‑convex game.

The game‑theoretic perspective yields several insights. First, the robust accuracy of a model equals 1 − minθ maxδ L(θ, δ) when ℓ is the 0‑1 loss. Second, the duality gap maxδ minθ L(θ, δ) − minθ maxδ L(θ, δ) measures the suboptimality of any candidate solution; a small gap certifies near‑optimality. Third, the adversary’s optimal strategy often concentrates on the boundary of Δ(x), which justifies the use of PGD with step size tuned to the perturbation budget. Fourth, the problem can be reformulated as a Stackelberg game where the learner commits to θ first; the Stackelberg equilibrium value is always at least as large as the simultaneous‑move minimax value, reflecting the advantage of commitment.

Examiners may ask: “Does the minimax theorem apply to adversarial training of a ReLU network?” The correct answer is no, because the loss is non‑convex in the network parameters; the theorem requires convex‑concave structure. A related trap is to claim that adversarial training finds a global minimax equilibrium; it only finds a stationary point of the non‑convex objective. Another common error is to confuse the ℓ∞ perturbation set with an ℓ2 set and assume the same duality properties hold; the geometry of the perturbation set affects the concavity of the inner maximisation.

  • Assuming the PTAS for anonymous games yields an exact equilibrium in polynomial time; it only gives ε‑equilibria and the running time is exponential in the number of actions.
  • Claiming that any priority‑based kidney‑exchange mechanism is strategy‑proof; only the unrestricted top‑trading‑cycles mechanism with a fixed priority order has this property.
  • Confusing risk‑dominant and payoff‑dominant equilibria when identifying stochastically stable states; stochastic stability selects the risk‑dominant equilibrium in coordination games.
  • Believing that stochastic stability always yields a unique prediction; multiple states can be stochastically stable if they share the minimum stochastic potential.
  • Applying von Neumann’s minimax theorem to adversarial training of deep networks without verifying convex‑concave structure; the loss is non‑convex in the parameters, so the theorem does not guarantee a saddle point.
  • Equating the simultaneous‑move minimax value with the Stackelberg (commitment) value; the learner’s commitment can only improve (or leave unchanged) the worst‑case loss.
  • Overlooking that the inner maximisation in adversarial robustness is typically non‑concave in the perturbation when the model is non‑linear, so projected gradient descent only finds a local maximum.
The advanced sections above complete the required coverage for this lesson.
